In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Allah, the Exalted, says: "O Prophet, fear Allah and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise." [Al-Ahzab 1]

The basmalah has already been discussed in terms of its meaning and its grammatical analysis (i'rab). We said regarding its i'rab that it is a prepositional phrase (jar wa majrur) attached to a deleted element (muta'allaq bi-mahdhuf), and that this deleted element should be estimated as a specific verb placed after it.

For example, when you want to recite, you say: "In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful," and the estimate is: "In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful, I recite." This is better than saying the estimate is "my beginning (ibtida'i) in the name of Allah..." or "I begin (abtada'u) in the name of Allah..." Why? Because when we estimate it as a specific verb, it is more indicative of the intended meaning. The word "beginning" (ibtida') is general, applying to everything one begins with, but when you specify the verb and say, "In the name of Allah I recite," it is more indicative of the intended meaning. This is one reason.

We estimate it as a verb because the original form of governing words (amal) is verbs. That is why they govern without condition. As for nouns that govern, they only govern under conditions, such as the active participle (ism al-fa'il), the passive participle (ism al-maf'ul), and the verbal noun (masdar), and what resembles them. We place it after for two reasons:

The first reason: seeking blessing by beginning with the name of Allah. The second: indicating restriction (hasr), because placing the governing element after its normal position indicates restriction; or, in a more general expression, because placing after what should be placed first indicates restriction.

So we say about the basmalah whenever it appears: it is attached to what? To a deleted element, and this deleted element is estimated as a specific verb placed after it.

When you want to perform wudu', how do we estimate it? "In the name of Allah I perform wudu'." When a person wants to slaughter an animal, he says, the estimate is "In the name of Allah I slaughter," and analogously for everything else.

Allah says: "In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful." Here "name" (ism) is in construct with "Allah," and it is singular, so it conveys generality. Therefore the commentators estimated the meaning as: "with every one of Allah's names." The word "ism" is derived either from "sumuw," meaning elevation, or from "simah," meaning mark or sign. If it is said that it derives from both, this would not be far-fetched, because it makes the named thing manifest, so it has the sense of elevation, and because it distinguishes the named thing, so it has the sense of a mark. The names of Allah, the Exalted, were discussed in the lesson on Tawhid, and there is no need to discuss them here.

"Allah" is a proper noun for the Essence of Allah, glory be to Him, and it is the origin of proper nouns. The names of Allah, as we know, are proper nouns and attributes, but their origin is the word "Allah." That is why the names always come following it, as it is the origin. Sometimes the word "Allah" comes as a follower of other names, such as: "To the path of the Almighty, the Praiseworthy (1) Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens" [Ibrahim 1-2]. Here "Allah" is a follower of what precedes it.

As for His saying: "the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful," both are derived names from... from mercy (rahmah). However, the first of them indicates mercy as an attribute of Allah, and the second indicates mercy as an action of His. So He is Merciful (rahman) and He is Compassionate (rahim): He is characterized by mercy and He performs mercy. That is, glory be to Him, despite being Merciful, He also shows mercy. This which I have established is what Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, established in distinguishing between "al-Rahman" and "al-Rahim." Although some scholars distinguish between them by saying that al-Rahman is the one of general mercy and al-Rahim is the one of particular mercy, and they say that the verse, "And He is ever Merciful to the believers" [Al-Ahzab 43], indicates this, the meaning indicated by Ibn al-Qayyim is more eloquent and better. That is why "al-Rahman" is in the pattern fa'lan, and this pattern generally indicates expansiveness and fullness. He, glory be to Him, is vast in mercy, and He, glory be to Him, has mercy on whom He wills, as He said: "He punishes whom He wills and has mercy on whom He wills" [Al-Ankabut 21].

The basmalah is a verse from the Book of Allah, which comes at the beginning of every surah, except Surah Bara'ah (al-Tawbah), for it has no basmalah. The scholars mentioned that the reason the basmalah was omitted from Bara'ah is that the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, were uncertain whether it was part of Surah al-Anfal or a separate surah, so they placed a separator between them and did not write "In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful." This is clear, but clearer than that is that if the basmalah had been revealed between Surah al-Anfal and Bara'ah, it could not have been dropped, because Allah says: "Indeed, We have sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian" [Al-Hijr 9]. But when it became unclear to the Companions whether it was a separate surah (Bara'ah) or part of Surah al-Anfal, they placed only the separator.

Allah says: "O Prophet, fear Allah." The address here is to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, in his capacity as a prophet (nabi). Allah may address him in his capacity as a messenger (rasul), addressing him as a messenger in the station of messengership, as in His saying: "O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord" [Al-Ma'idah 67].

The word "nabi" is derived; its original form is "nabi'" (with a hamzah), and it is said its original form is "nabiyu" with a waw. According to the first view, it is derived from "naba'" (news), and the hamzah was replaced by a yā' for lightness. According to the second view, it is derived from "nubuwwah," meaning elevation. There is no doubt that the station of prophethood is an elevated station, and that the prophet both informs and is informed. So it is fa'il in the sense of fa'il and in the sense of maf'ul.

Allah says: "O Prophet," and what is meant is our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). He says: "Fear Allah." "Fear Allah" means: persist in His taqwa. The author turned it away from its apparent wording, because when you command someone to do something, the default is that he is not already engaged in it. If you say, "O so-and-so, stand up," is he standing or not? No, that is the default: the default is that the command creates what did not exist. When you say, "O so-and-so, stand," or "O so-and-so, sit," at the moment the command is directed at him, he is not characterized by this attribute, is he?

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was told by Allah: "O Prophet, fear Allah." If we took the apparent wording, then the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, at the time the address was directed to him, would not have been fearing Allah, and this is impossible. Therefore the meaning of "fear Allah" is: persist in His taqwa. From here we derive that commanding something may be a command to renew it, and may be a command to persist in it. Do you understand?

It may also be a command to detail what is commanded. For example, if you say, "O believer, believe," the meaning is: persist in your faith and realize it.

In His saying: "O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger and the Book which He sent down upon His Messenger and the Book which He sent down before" [An-Nisa' 136], the command here, "O you who have believed, believe in Allah," means: persist in it. But there is detail: they are told to believe in general, then He said: "Believe in Allah and His Messenger and the Book which He sent down upon His Messenger and the Book which He sent down before."

So the command, in origin, is directed to one who is not already engaged in it; that is the default. It may be directed to request persistence, and it may be directed to explain details, as in His saying: "O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger," and His saying: "Fear Allah." Taqwa appears very often in the Noble Qur'an. What is the meaning of taqwa, and from where is it derived? We say it is derived from "wiqayah" (protection). For this reason they say the original letter of "taqwa" is a waw, so "taqwa" is originally "waqwa." If it means protection, then taqwa is for a person to take a protection from the punishment of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and there is no protection from the punishment of Allah except by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. Based on this, we say that taqwa means doing the commands of Allah and avoiding His prohibitions.

It is known that when we say "doing the commands of Allah," with "commands" in construct to Allah, the person will intend by this action the fulfillment of Allah's command; likewise when we say "avoiding the prohibition of Allah," the person will avoid it because Allah prohibited it. Mere action without intention is not taqwa, and mere abstention without intention is not taqwa. But since the action and the abstention are attributed to Allah, intention becomes necessary in them.

"Fear Allah and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites" in what contradicts your Sharia. The conjunction of "and do not obey" to "fear Allah" is coordination of the specific to the general, because abandoning obedience to these people is part of the taqwa of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so its coordination with taqwa is coordination of the specific to the general. This is common in the Qur'an, the Sunnah, and Arabic speech.

"Do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites." The disbeliever is one who openly declares and proclaims his disbelief. As for the hypocrite, he is one who conceals his disbelief and shows that he is a believer. So from where is "kufr" (disbelief) or "kafir" (disbeliever) derived?

They say: "kufr" originally means covering. From it comes "kafrah," which is the sheath of the palm spathe, because it covers it. This is the original meaning. The one who does not believe in Allah was called a disbeliever because he covers the blessing of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and denies His Sharia, so he becomes one who covers the truth and covers the blessing that Allah bestowed upon him. As for hypocrisy (nifaq), it is derived from "naafiqa' al-yarbu'," the yarbu' is a well-known small creature that makes a burrow in the ground, digs a hole, and makes for it a door, and at its end it makes a door closed with some dirt. That is, it digs, and when it reaches the end of the hole, it digs until only a little of the earth's surface remains over it, so that when it pushes it with its head, or when it pushes it with its head, it opens. This is the naafiqa'. Why does it do this? So that if it is pursued from the main entrance of the burrow, it exits through this. Likewise the hypocrite: when he is addressed with faith, he says that he is a believer, and so he escapes; and when he comes to his people, he says that he is a disbeliever, and so he escapes the blame of these and the blame of those.

"Do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites." It is known that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, could not possibly obey a disbeliever, but it is possible for him to obey a hypocrite, because the hypocrite's hypocrisy and disbelief are not perceived and are not known about him, so a person may be deceived by him. For this reason Allah mentioned the disbelievers first here before the hypocrites, although in the context of threat He mentions the hypocrites before the disbelievers. Allah said: "Indeed, Allah will gather the hypocrites and the disbelievers in Hell, all together" [An-Nisa' 140], and He said: "That Allah may punish the hypocrite men and hypocrite women and the polytheist men and polytheist women" [Al-Ahzab 73].

"Do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites." The author says: "in what contradicts your Sharia." This qualification implies a restriction of the prohibition, although the prohibition is absolute: "do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites." So what led the author to restrict it to what contradicts the Sharia? It led him to that because if it were supposed that a disbeliever or hypocrite commanded what agrees with the Sharia, it would be incumbent upon us to obey him, not because he commanded, but because this is what the Sharia requires. This is one aspect.

Another aspect is to say that the author's restriction is a statement of the reality, because the disbeliever and the hypocrite, due to their enmity toward the Sharia of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, cannot command except what contradicts the Sharia. So this qualification is a clarification of the actual situation, and a qualification that is a clarification of the actual situation does not restrict, because it is not intended.

I think there are examples of this that have passed us many times. Who will bring me an example in which the qualification is a clarification of the reality and is not intended? (...) to something that does not benefit them, but this is a clarification of the reality.

Allah says: "O mankind, worship your Lord who created you and those before you that you may become righteous" [Al-Baqarah 21]. The phrase "who created you and those before you" is a qualification that clarifies the reality, and the meaning is not that there is a lord who did not create and a lord who did create. Clear? Examples of this are many. So here we can take the author's words, "in what contradicts your Sharia," as a clarification of the reality, namely that the disbeliever and the hypocrite cannot command except what contradicts the Sharia, because the disbeliever disbelieves in it, and the hypocrite also disbelieves in it, but he shows faith.

Then He said: "Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing" of what will be before it occurs, "Wise" in what He creates. "Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise." This sentence, in terms of its place relative to what precedes it, is explanatory (ta'liliyyah). The reason it is an explanation of what precedes it is that when Allah commanded His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, to have taqwa, and forbade him from obeying the disbelievers, He clarified that this command and prohibition proceed from knowledge and wisdom, and that He, glory be to Him, is more knowing of what these enemies, the disbelievers and hypocrites, plot, so do not obey them, for they will never be people of support for you.

His saying: "Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing," of what will be before its occurrence. Is this qualification correct?

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Why? Because He knows what will be before it occurs, and what it is after it occurs while it exists, and after it ceases to exist. The knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, relates to things in their three states: before existence, during existence, and after non-existence. Right?

Before existence, during existence, and after non-existence. Do you understand? The knowledge of the created being does not relate to things in all these states. Before existence it is known that he does not know it; during existence he knows it, for example, let us suppose he knows it; and after non-existence he may forget it, right? So the knowledge of the created being is surrounded by two deficiencies: prior ignorance and subsequent forgetting. As for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, His knowledge is complete in totality and in detail in all states: before existence, during existence, and after non-existence. For this reason Moses, peace be upon him, said: "Its knowledge is with my Lord in a Record; my Lord neither errs nor forgets" [Ta-Ha 52]. So He negated from Him the error, which is ignorance, and the forgetting, which is neglect of a thing after knowing it.

His saying: "Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing," so we say: "Knowing" of what will be before its occurrence, and of what will be during its occurrence, and of what will be after its cessation, in all states.

"Wise": we have encountered it many times, and we have shown that it is derived from wisdom (hikmah) and judgment (hukm), and that the judgment of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is both cosmic (kawni) and legislative (shar'i), and that wisdom is also of two kinds: final (ghā'iyyah) and formal (suwariyyah). Formal does not mean that it is only in form, but that the thing being in this form is wisdom, and its purpose is another wisdom.

If that is so, how many divisions are there? Four? Yes, let us see: a judgment that includes wisdom in its form and its purpose; a cosmic judgment; a legislative judgment that includes wisdom in its form and in its purpose. "Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise." Here there is a difficulty in His saying "Indeed, Allah is ever," because it is known that the past has passed. Does "was Knowing" indicate that He is now not Knowing? No. Why not?

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, that is not it; because "kana" may be stripped of time (maslub al-zaman), and what is intended is the attribution of its predicate to its subject, and the realization of that attribution without regard to time in it. Do you understand? Whenever it comes with respect to Allah, His names and His attributes, it is of this type: it indicates the realization of the attribution of the described subject, which is its subject, with its attribute, which is its predicate, regardless of time. Therefore we say that the verb here is stripped of time, meaning: He has not ceased and will not cease to be Knowing and Wise.

Are knowledge and wisdom among the essential attributes or the active attributes?

* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Among the essential attributes, because Allah has not ceased and will not cease to be Knowing, and has not ceased and will not cease to be Wise. And Allah knows best. (...)

And in the wording "Indeed, Allah is ever, of what they do, Acquainted" (Khabir), "ya'malun" is according to the copy I have.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿUthaymin (Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-Karīm) on Sūrah 33, verses 1–2 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 2]. We say regarding ﴿follow what is revealed to you﴾ what we said regarding ﴿fear Allah﴾: that is, continue to follow it, and follow what is revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ). With respect to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, this following includes following him in conveying (the message), following him in calling (people to it), and following him in acting upon it, because the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is commanded in these three matters: he is commanded to convey it, to call to it, and to act upon it.

His words ﴿what is revealed to you﴾: *wahy* (revelation) originally means informing swiftly and secretly. Informing that is swift and secret is called *waḥy*, and what is meant here is the conveying to the Prophet (ﷺ) of what Allah, glorified and exalted, has legislated, whether through an intermediary or without one.

It is well known that Allah's conveying of revelation to His Prophet (ﷺ) is not apparent to people. No, because the Messenger is only known to be receiving revelation by the signs of revelation that appear, but we do not know how revelation is delivered to him unless he has informed us of that.

His words ﴿what is revealed to you﴾: *(mā)* here is a relative pronoun (*ism mawṣūl*) of general form, covering everything that is revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ).

His words ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Acquainted with what you do﴾ indicate that these disbelievers and hypocrites were trying to get the Prophet (ﷺ) to oppose his law, but the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, might not know of that. Therefore He said ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever…﴾, meaning these disbelievers and hypocrites, ﴿Acquainted with what they do﴾. The word *khabīr* (Acquainted) is derived from *khibra*, which is knowledge of the inner realities of matters. For this reason, the one who owns the crops and plantings is called *khabīr*, and sharecropping is called *mukhābara*, because the seed is buried in the earth and becomes hidden and not apparent. So the *khabīr* is the one who knows what? The inner realities of matters.

Therefore the *khabīr* is more specific than the *ʿalīm* (All-Knowing), because the *ʿalīm* includes one who knows both the outward and the inward aspects of matters, but the *khabīr* is more specific: he is the one who knows the inward aspects of matters. And one who knows the inward aspects certainly knows the outward aspects, a fortiori.

Now, the author says: *(wa fī qirāʾa bil-fawqāniyya)* (and in one reading with the upper *tāʾ*), so it is said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Acquainted with what you (pl.) do﴾. Regarding *(fī qirāʾa)* (in one reading), the terminology of the author, may Allah have mercy on him, is that when he says *(fī qirāʾa)* it is one of the canonical readings (*sabʿiyya*, the seven readings), and when he says *quriʾa* (it was read) it is an irregular reading (*shādhdha*). Accordingly, there are two canonical readings in this verse.

* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Do I have "(in one reading) with the upper *tāʾ*" and you have "with the lower *yāʾ*"?
* A student: No, with the upper *tāʾ*.
* The Shaykh: With the upper *tāʾ*, because the author affirmed ﴿*yaʿmalūna*﴾ (they do). Here we say: there are two canonical readings in the verse, and it is permissible to recite with either of them. When we say "permissible," this does not mean that the two readings are equal in standing. Rather, it means that reciting with either of them is not forbidden. The better course is to recite with this one at times and with that one at other times, because the differences in readings are like the differences in acts of worship. We have mentioned that the better course in acts of worship that come in various forms is… what is the better course? To perform this one once and that one once, so that you have acted upon the Sunnah in all its forms. Likewise in readings, the better course is to recite this way once and that way another time, on condition that you know the reading. But this statement we make applies to a person's private recitation. As for reciting before the common people, he should not depart from the reading that is in their hands, why? Because the layman does not grasp these readings, or does not grasp the difference between them. If you recite the Qurʾān in a way other than what is before him, he will object to you. Yet this objection you may be able to answer, but something of doubt will settle in his heart: he will say, "So the Qurʾān is not preserved, since one person recites this way and another recites that way, meaning it has not been preserved." Thus some doubt enters his heart. For this reason, we should speak to people in terms of what their minds can grasp, as in the hadith of ʿAlī: "Speak to the people in terms of what they know. Do you want Allah and His Messenger to be denied?"[[Reported by al-Bukhārī (127) from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, as a statement of ʿAlī (mawqūf).]]

The conclusion is that the student of knowledge who knows the readings should at times recite this way and at times that way. But does he combine the two readings? For example, here I say: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Acquainted with what they do﴾, and ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Acquainted with what you do﴾? No. The better course is to recite this once and that once, because if you combine the two readings you have contradicted, since whoever recites with the *tāʾ* does not recite with the *yāʾ*, so how can you combine them?

But some scholars say there is no harm in combining the two readings, whether they are separated or not. That is, it is permissible to recite both readings within a single verse, and it is permissible to recite one verse in one reader's reading and another verse in another reader's reading.

As for the second case, namely reciting one verse in one reader's reading and another verse in another reader's reading, it is permissible. But combining the two readings within a single verse and a single recitation, there is room for doubt about its permissibility.

* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: For example, you recite here: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Acquainted with what they do﴾ according to one reader's reading, then in another verse you recite according to another reader who differs from him… (...).

Does mere calling (of the Prophet by name) count as honoring him?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No.
* The student: Calling (...).
* The Shaykh: Well done. (Allah calls him) by the description of prophethood, whereas the prophets other than him Allah calls by their names: "O Mūsā," "O ʿĪsā," and similar. But the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was only addressed with the description of prophethood or messengership.

If you say: Did not Allah say ﴿Muḥammad is but a messenger; [other] messengers have passed on before him﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 144], and say ﴿Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him﴾ [al-Fatḥ 29]?
* The student: This is not a context of calling and address.
* The Shaykh: Yes, this is not a context of calling and address, but it is a context of information.

* It is derived from the noble verse: the obligation of piety (*taqwā*).
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: ﴿Fear Allah﴾, yes.
* It is derived from it: the obligation of piety upon the community (*umma*).
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: If the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is commanded to piety, then others are a fortiori. That is one point. What is another point?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: That the address directed to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is directed to him and to his community, unless there is evidence that restricts it to him.

On this occasion: address directed to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, either has evidence for generality, that the address itself indicates generality, or it contains what indicates specificity, or it contains nothing that indicates either. So what contains an indication of generality is general. Who will give an example of it?
* A student: Specificity?
* The Shaykh: No, generality.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, this has no evidence of generality.
* A student: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾.
* The Shaykh: Yes: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them at their waiting period﴾ [al-Ṭalāq 1]. Or does it contain what indicates specificity?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, correct. It has many examples. Or it contains nothing that indicates either? Like this verse, but its ruling is general: its ruling is general for the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and for his community. Is it clear?

* It is derived from the noble verse: that the Prophet (ﷺ) is a servant commanded and obligated, by what?
* A student: By his being commanded to piety and not obeying the disbelievers and hypocrites.
* The Shaykh: Yes, well done: by his being commanded to piety and not obeying the disbelievers and hypocrites.
* It is derived from this: that a person, however high his rank, the obligations do not drop from him?
* A student: That is because (...).
* The Shaykh: And upon this benefit there branches the refutation of those Sufis who say that when a person reaches the level of *muʿāyana* (direct witnessing), the obligations drop from him. Do they, or not? Because we say: no one reaches the rank of the Prophet (ﷺ) before Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and yet the obligations did not drop from him.

If they say: Allah says ﴿And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty﴾ [al-Ḥijr 99], meaning: until you reach the level of certainty, then stop. So what do we answer them?
* A student: The meaning of "certainty" here is death.
* The Shaykh: Do you have evidence that "certainty" is death?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: They say: ﴿until there comes to you the certainty﴾: until you reach the level of certainty, then halt. So now we want to find evidence showing that certainty is death.
* The student: The saying of some of the early generations: "And he strove in Allah with the striving due to Him until certainty came to him."
* The Shaykh: No, that is a saying of the early generations. We want (evidence) from the Book or the Sunnah.
* A student: ﴿until certainty came to us﴾.
* The Shaykh: Yes. Their saying, that is, the people of the Fire: ﴿and we used to deny the Day of Recompense, until certainty came to us﴾ [al-Muddaththir 46–47]. Did certainty come to them in the sense that they reached the level of certainty? Not at all; they died in denial, and they did not reach the level of certainty. And if these people say that they have reached a level of certainty by which they are among the people of Hellfire, then we agree with them about that. Is it clear?

* It is derived from the noble verse: the prohibition of obeying the disbelievers and hypocrites and inclining toward them, due to His saying ﴿and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾.
* It is derived from it: that a disbeliever or a hypocrite can never be a sincere advisor to the believers.
* A student: Here (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes. And if it were possible for them to give sincere advice, He would not have forbidden obeying them absolutely, because a sincere advisor is obeyed.
* It is derived from the noble verse: the affirmation of two of Allah's names, namely *al-ʿAlīm* (the All-Knowing) and *al-Ḥakīm* (the All-Wise).

Now the question: Is the knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, specific to the past and present, or comprehensive?
* The student: (...)
* The Shaykh: This question was not in the explanation. Is the knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, related to what is necessary (*wājib*), or to what is impossible (*mustaḥīl*), or to what is possible (*mumkin*), or to all of them?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Is it possible that there exists in the heavens and the earth a god other than Allah? It is impossible. Likewise ﴿Allah has not taken any son, nor is there with Him any god; otherwise each god would have gone off with what he created, and some of them would have overpowered others. Exalted is Allah above what they describe﴾ [al-Muʾminūn 91]. This relates to the impossible. Is there an example of Allah's knowledge relating to the necessary? There are many, very many.
* A student: ﴿Do you not see that Allah knows what is in the heavens﴾ [al-Mujādila 7].
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: He knows (...).
* The Shaykh: My brothers, everything Allah has informed us about Himself is from knowledge of what is necessary, because for Allah the attributes of perfection are necessary. So when He informs about Himself with these attributes, it relates to the necessary. As for the possible, it is like what the brother said: ﴿Allah knows what every female carries, and what the wombs recede and what they increase﴾ [al-Raʿd 8]. Is this of the possible or of the necessary? Of the possible, because the carrying of a female, the receding of wombs, and the increase of wombs are possible, not necessary, not permissible? Possible.

So Allah's knowledge becomes comprehensive of everything, in total and in detail, present and future and past, necessary and possible and permissible. For this reason al-Saffārīnī says in his creed:

*And knowledge and speech have been related, my friend, to every thing, without restriction.*

* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: The necessary, for them, is the opposite of the impossible and the possible, because they say: things are of three kinds. Either necessary, meaning it must exist, not in the sense of an act whose doer is rewarded and whose abandoner deserves punishment; the necessary is what cannot be avoided. The impossible is what cannot occur. And the possible is what may occur or not occur.

* It is derived from the noble verse: the obligation to follow what was sent down to the Prophet (ﷺ). From where is it taken?
* A student: ﴿And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾. If you say: Is this general, that it is obligatory to follow what was sent down to the Messenger?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Then it would be obligatory for us to raise our hands in prayer, and obligatory for us to glorify (Allah) more than once.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: So the meaning is: we say this is excepted, insofar as there is evidence that it is not obligatory. But what is authentically reported from the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, even if it is not obligatory, it is obligatory to believe in its legitimacy, even if the act itself is not obligatory. Have you understood now?

So we have belief in legitimacy and implementation of what is legislated. Implementation of what is legislated follows what the evidences indicate: either obligatory or recommended. As for believing in legitimacy regarding what is authentically established, that is obligatory.

For example: it is obligatory upon me to believe in the legitimacy of keeping the upper arms away from the sides during prostration, and we believe in the legitimacy of turning the head during prayer at the end of the prayer. But performing that depends on the detailed evidences: if the evidences indicate it is obligatory, it is obligatory; if they indicate it is recommended, it is recommended.

* It is derived from the noble verse: the establishment of the Prophet's messengership and prophethood (ﷺ).
* A student: ﴿what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾.
* The Shaykh: Due to His saying ﴿what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾, and from the beginning of the verse ﴿O Prophet﴾, yes.
* It is derived from the noble verse: that Allah, Exalted, has a special lordship with respect to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, due to His saying ﴿from your Lord﴾. It has been mentioned to us many times that lordship is of two kinds and servitude is of two kinds: general lordship and specific lordship. An example of general lordship is His saying, Exalted: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾ [Maryam 65]. Is this general or specific? General.
And an example of specificity is this verse: ﴿from your Lord﴾. Both kinds are combined in His saying, Exalted: ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Mūsā and Hārūn"﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 121–122]. Likewise servitude is of two kinds: general and specific. The general is like His saying, Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Seeing of the servants﴾ [Ghāfir 44], which is general.
And the specific: ﴿Exalted is He who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 1], meaning the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him.

* It is derived from the noble verse: that the knowledge of Allah, Exalted, encompasses inner matters, due to His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Acquainted with what you do﴾.
* It is derived from it: a warning to a person against opposition.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, we say: a warning to a person against opposition.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Because this necessitates that we do not oppose Allah. As long as we know that He is Acquainted with what we do, it is impossible for us to oppose Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Is it clear? Like if you said, for example: "Go, and I know what you are doing." What is meant by this? Threat and warning against opposition. So every text in which Allah makes clear that He knows what we do is a warning to us against opposing Him. (...)

In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Allah, the Exalted, says: "O Prophet, fear Allah and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites. Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise." [Al-Ahzab 1]

The basmalah has already been discussed in terms of its meaning and its grammatical analysis (i'rab). We said regarding its i'rab that it is a prepositional phrase (jar wa majrur) attached to a deleted element (muta'allaq bi-mahdhuf), and that this deleted element should be estimated as a specific verb placed after it.

For example, when you want to recite, you say: "In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful," and the estimate is: "In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful, I recite." This is better than saying the estimate is "my beginning (ibtida'i) in the name of Allah..." or "I begin (abtada'u) in the name of Allah..." Why? Because when we estimate it as a specific verb, it is more indicative of the intended meaning. The word "beginning" (ibtida') is general, applying to everything one begins with, but when you specify the verb and say, "In the name of Allah I recite," it is more indicative of the intended meaning. This is one reason.

We estimate it as a verb because the original form of governing words (amal) is verbs. That is why they govern without condition. As for nouns that govern, they only govern under conditions, such as the active participle (ism al-fa'il), the passive participle (ism al-maf'ul), and the verbal noun (masdar), and what resembles them. We place it after for two reasons:

The first reason: seeking blessing by beginning with the name of Allah. The second: indicating restriction (hasr), because placing the governing element after its normal position indicates restriction; or, in a more general expression, because placing after what should be placed first indicates restriction.

So we say about the basmalah whenever it appears: it is attached to what? To a deleted element, and this deleted element is estimated as a specific verb placed after it.

When you want to perform wudu', how do we estimate it? "In the name of Allah I perform wudu'." When a person wants to slaughter an animal, he says, the estimate is "In the name of Allah I slaughter," and analogously for everything else.

Allah says: "In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful." Here "name" (ism) is in construct with "Allah," and it is singular, so it conveys generality. Therefore the commentators estimated the meaning as: "with every one of Allah's names." The word "ism" is derived either from "sumuw," meaning elevation, or from "simah," meaning mark or sign. If it is said that it derives from both, this would not be far-fetched, because it makes the named thing manifest, so it has the sense of elevation, and because it distinguishes the named thing, so it has the sense of a mark. The names of Allah, the Exalted, were discussed in the lesson on Tawhid, and there is no need to discuss them here.

"Allah" is a proper noun for the Essence of Allah, glory be to Him, and it is the origin of proper nouns. The names of Allah, as we know, are proper nouns and attributes, but their origin is the word "Allah." That is why the names always come following it, as it is the origin. Sometimes the word "Allah" comes as a follower of other names, such as: "To the path of the Almighty, the Praiseworthy (1) Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens" [Ibrahim 1-2]. Here "Allah" is a follower of what precedes it.

As for His saying: "the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful," both are derived names from... from mercy (rahmah). However, the first of them indicates mercy as an attribute of Allah, and the second indicates mercy as an action of His. So He is Merciful (rahman) and He is Compassionate (rahim): He is characterized by mercy and He performs mercy. That is, glory be to Him, despite being Merciful, He also shows mercy. This which I have established is what Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, established in distinguishing between "al-Rahman" and "al-Rahim." Although some scholars distinguish between them by saying that al-Rahman is the one of general mercy and al-Rahim is the one of particular mercy, and they say that the verse, "And He is ever Merciful to the believers" [Al-Ahzab 43], indicates this, the meaning indicated by Ibn al-Qayyim is more eloquent and better. That is why "al-Rahman" is in the pattern fa'lan, and this pattern generally indicates expansiveness and fullness. He, glory be to Him, is vast in mercy, and He, glory be to Him, has mercy on whom He wills, as He said: "He punishes whom He wills and has mercy on whom He wills" [Al-Ankabut 21].

The basmalah is a verse from the Book of Allah, which comes at the beginning of every surah, except Surah Bara'ah (al-Tawbah), for it has no basmalah. The scholars mentioned that the reason the basmalah was omitted from Bara'ah is that the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, were uncertain whether it was part of Surah al-Anfal or a separate surah, so they placed a separator between them and did not write "In the name of Allah, the Entirely Merciful, the Especially Merciful." This is clear, but clearer than that is that if the basmalah had been revealed between Surah al-Anfal and Bara'ah, it could not have been dropped, because Allah says: "Indeed, We have sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian" [Al-Hijr 9]. But when it became unclear to the Companions whether it was a separate surah (Bara'ah) or part of Surah al-Anfal, they placed only the separator.

Allah says: "O Prophet, fear Allah." The address here is to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, in his capacity as a prophet (nabi). Allah may address him in his capacity as a messenger (rasul), addressing him as a messenger in the station of messengership, as in His saying: "O Messenger, convey what has been revealed to you from your Lord" [Al-Ma'idah 67].

The word "nabi" is derived; its original form is "nabi'" (with a hamzah), and it is said its original form is "nabiyu" with a waw. According to the first view, it is derived from "naba'" (news), and the hamzah was replaced by a yā' for lightness. According to the second view, it is derived from "nubuwwah," meaning elevation. There is no doubt that the station of prophethood is an elevated station, and that the prophet both informs and is informed. So it is fa'il in the sense of fa'il and in the sense of maf'ul.

Allah says: "O Prophet," and what is meant is our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). He says: "Fear Allah." "Fear Allah" means: persist in His taqwa. The author turned it away from its apparent wording, because when you command someone to do something, the default is that he is not already engaged in it. If you say, "O so-and-so, stand up," is he standing or not? No, that is the default: the default is that the command creates what did not exist. When you say, "O so-and-so, stand," or "O so-and-so, sit," at the moment the command is directed at him, he is not characterized by this attribute, is he?

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was told by Allah: "O Prophet, fear Allah." If we took the apparent wording, then the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, at the time the address was directed to him, would not have been fearing Allah, and this is impossible. Therefore the meaning of "fear Allah" is: persist in His taqwa. From here we derive that commanding something may be a command to renew it, and may be a command to persist in it. Do you understand?

It may also be a command to detail what is commanded. For example, if you say, "O believer, believe," the meaning is: persist in your faith and realize it.

In His saying: "O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger and the Book which He sent down upon His Messenger and the Book which He sent down before" [An-Nisa' 136], the command here, "O you who have believed, believe in Allah," means: persist in it. But there is detail: they are told to believe in general, then He said: "Believe in Allah and His Messenger and the Book which He sent down upon His Messenger and the Book which He sent down before."

So the command, in origin, is directed to one who is not already engaged in it; that is the default. It may be directed to request persistence, and it may be directed to explain details, as in His saying: "O you who have believed, believe in Allah and His Messenger," and His saying: "Fear Allah." Taqwa appears very often in the Noble Qur'an. What is the meaning of taqwa, and from where is it derived? We say it is derived from "wiqayah" (protection). For this reason they say the original letter of "taqwa" is a waw, so "taqwa" is originally "waqwa." If it means protection, then taqwa is for a person to take a protection from the punishment of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and there is no protection from the punishment of Allah except by doing His commands and avoiding His prohibitions. Based on this, we say that taqwa means doing the commands of Allah and avoiding His prohibitions.

It is known that when we say "doing the commands of Allah," with "commands" in construct to Allah, the person will intend by this action the fulfillment of Allah's command; likewise when we say "avoiding the prohibition of Allah," the person will avoid it because Allah prohibited it. Mere action without intention is not taqwa, and mere abstention without intention is not taqwa. But since the action and the abstention are attributed to Allah, intention becomes necessary in them.

"Fear Allah and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites" in what contradicts your Sharia. The conjunction of "and do not obey" to "fear Allah" is coordination of the specific to the general, because abandoning obedience to these people is part of the taqwa of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so its coordination with taqwa is coordination of the specific to the general. This is common in the Qur'an, the Sunnah, and Arabic speech.

"Do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites." The disbeliever is one who openly declares and proclaims his disbelief. As for the hypocrite, he is one who conceals his disbelief and shows that he is a believer. So from where is "kufr" (disbelief) or "kafir" (disbeliever) derived?

They say: "kufr" originally means covering. From it comes "kafrah," which is the sheath of the palm spathe, because it covers it. This is the original meaning. The one who does not believe in Allah was called a disbeliever because he covers the blessing of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and denies His Sharia, so he becomes one who covers the truth and covers the blessing that Allah bestowed upon him. As for hypocrisy (nifaq), it is derived from "naafiqa' al-yarbu'," the yarbu' is a well-known small creature that makes a burrow in the ground, digs a hole, and makes for it a door, and at its end it makes a door closed with some dirt. That is, it digs, and when it reaches the end of the hole, it digs until only a little of the earth's surface remains over it, so that when it pushes it with its head, or when it pushes it with its head, it opens. This is the naafiqa'. Why does it do this? So that if it is pursued from the main entrance of the burrow, it exits through this. Likewise the hypocrite: when he is addressed with faith, he says that he is a believer, and so he escapes; and when he comes to his people, he says that he is a disbeliever, and so he escapes the blame of these and the blame of those.

"Do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites." It is known that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, could not possibly obey a disbeliever, but it is possible for him to obey a hypocrite, because the hypocrite's hypocrisy and disbelief are not perceived and are not known about him, so a person may be deceived by him. For this reason Allah mentioned the disbelievers first here before the hypocrites, although in the context of threat He mentions the hypocrites before the disbelievers. Allah said: "Indeed, Allah will gather the hypocrites and the disbelievers in Hell, all together" [An-Nisa' 140], and He said: "That Allah may punish the hypocrite men and hypocrite women and the polytheist men and polytheist women" [Al-Ahzab 73].

"Do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites." The author says: "in what contradicts your Sharia." This qualification implies a restriction of the prohibition, although the prohibition is absolute: "do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites." So what led the author to restrict it to what contradicts the Sharia? It led him to that because if it were supposed that a disbeliever or hypocrite commanded what agrees with the Sharia, it would be incumbent upon us to obey him, not because he commanded, but because this is what the Sharia requires. This is one aspect.

Another aspect is to say that the author's restriction is a statement of the reality, because the disbeliever and the hypocrite, due to their enmity toward the Sharia of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, cannot command except what contradicts the Sharia. So this qualification is a clarification of the actual situation, and a qualification that is a clarification of the actual situation does not restrict, because it is not intended.

I think there are examples of this that have passed us many times. Who will bring me an example in which the qualification is a clarification of the reality and is not intended? (...) to something that does not benefit them, but this is a clarification of the reality.

Allah says: "O mankind, worship your Lord who created you and those before you that you may become righteous" [Al-Baqarah 21]. The phrase "who created you and those before you" is a qualification that clarifies the reality, and the meaning is not that there is a lord who did not create and a lord who did create. Clear? Examples of this are many. So here we can take the author's words, "in what contradicts your Sharia," as a clarification of the reality, namely that the disbeliever and the hypocrite cannot command except what contradicts the Sharia, because the disbeliever disbelieves in it, and the hypocrite also disbelieves in it, but he shows faith.

Then He said: "Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing" of what will be before it occurs, "Wise" in what He creates. "Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise." This sentence, in terms of its place relative to what precedes it, is explanatory (ta'liliyyah). The reason it is an explanation of what precedes it is that when Allah commanded His Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, to have taqwa, and forbade him from obeying the disbelievers, He clarified that this command and prohibition proceed from knowledge and wisdom, and that He, glory be to Him, is more knowing of what these enemies, the disbelievers and hypocrites, plot, so do not obey them, for they will never be people of support for you.

His saying: "Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing," of what will be before its occurrence. Is this qualification correct?

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Why? Because He knows what will be before it occurs, and what it is after it occurs while it exists, and after it ceases to exist. The knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, relates to things in their three states: before existence, during existence, and after non-existence. Right?

Before existence, during existence, and after non-existence. Do you understand? The knowledge of the created being does not relate to things in all these states. Before existence it is known that he does not know it; during existence he knows it, for example, let us suppose he knows it; and after non-existence he may forget it, right? So the knowledge of the created being is surrounded by two deficiencies: prior ignorance and subsequent forgetting. As for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, His knowledge is complete in totality and in detail in all states: before existence, during existence, and after non-existence. For this reason Moses, peace be upon him, said: "Its knowledge is with my Lord in a Record; my Lord neither errs nor forgets" [Ta-Ha 52]. So He negated from Him the error, which is ignorance, and the forgetting, which is neglect of a thing after knowing it.

His saying: "Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing," so we say: "Knowing" of what will be before its occurrence, and of what will be during its occurrence, and of what will be after its cessation, in all states.

"Wise": we have encountered it many times, and we have shown that it is derived from wisdom (hikmah) and judgment (hukm), and that the judgment of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is both cosmic (kawni) and legislative (shar'i), and that wisdom is also of two kinds: final (ghā'iyyah) and formal (suwariyyah). Formal does not mean that it is only in form, but that the thing being in this form is wisdom, and its purpose is another wisdom.

If that is so, how many divisions are there? Four? Yes, let us see: a judgment that includes wisdom in its form and its purpose; a cosmic judgment; a legislative judgment that includes wisdom in its form and in its purpose. "Indeed, Allah is ever Knowing and Wise." Here there is a difficulty in His saying "Indeed, Allah is ever," because it is known that the past has passed. Does "was Knowing" indicate that He is now not Knowing? No. Why not?

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, that is not it; because "kana" may be stripped of time (maslub al-zaman), and what is intended is the attribution of its predicate to its subject, and the realization of that attribution without regard to time in it. Do you understand? Whenever it comes with respect to Allah, His names and His attributes, it is of this type: it indicates the realization of the attribution of the described subject, which is its subject, with its attribute, which is its predicate, regardless of time. Therefore we say that the verb here is stripped of time, meaning: He has not ceased and will not cease to be Knowing and Wise.

Are knowledge and wisdom among the essential attributes or the active attributes?

* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Among the essential attributes, because Allah has not ceased and will not cease to be Knowing, and has not ceased and will not cease to be Wise. And Allah knows best. (...)

And in the wording "Indeed, Allah is ever, of what they do, Acquainted" (Khabir), "ya'malun" is according to the copy I have.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿUthaymin (Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-Karīm) on Sūrah 33, verses 1–2 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 2]. We say regarding ﴿follow what is revealed to you﴾ what we said regarding ﴿fear Allah﴾: that is, continue to follow it, and follow what is revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ). With respect to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, this following includes following him in conveying (the message), following him in calling (people to it), and following him in acting upon it, because the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is commanded in these three matters: he is commanded to convey it, to call to it, and to act upon it.

His words ﴿what is revealed to you﴾: *wahy* (revelation) originally means informing swiftly and secretly. Informing that is swift and secret is called *waḥy*, and what is meant here is the conveying to the Prophet (ﷺ) of what Allah, glorified and exalted, has legislated, whether through an intermediary or without one.

It is well known that Allah's conveying of revelation to His Prophet (ﷺ) is not apparent to people. No, because the Messenger is only known to be receiving revelation by the signs of revelation that appear, but we do not know how revelation is delivered to him unless he has informed us of that.

His words ﴿what is revealed to you﴾: *(mā)* here is a relative pronoun (*ism mawṣūl*) of general form, covering everything that is revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ).

His words ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Acquainted with what you do﴾ indicate that these disbelievers and hypocrites were trying to get the Prophet (ﷺ) to oppose his law, but the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, might not know of that. Therefore He said ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever…﴾, meaning these disbelievers and hypocrites, ﴿Acquainted with what they do﴾. The word *khabīr* (Acquainted) is derived from *khibra*, which is knowledge of the inner realities of matters. For this reason, the one who owns the crops and plantings is called *khabīr*, and sharecropping is called *mukhābara*, because the seed is buried in the earth and becomes hidden and not apparent. So the *khabīr* is the one who knows what? The inner realities of matters.

Therefore the *khabīr* is more specific than the *ʿalīm* (All-Knowing), because the *ʿalīm* includes one who knows both the outward and the inward aspects of matters, but the *khabīr* is more specific: he is the one who knows the inward aspects of matters. And one who knows the inward aspects certainly knows the outward aspects, a fortiori.

Now, the author says: *(wa fī qirāʾa bil-fawqāniyya)* (and in one reading with the upper *tāʾ*), so it is said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Acquainted with what you (pl.) do﴾. Regarding *(fī qirāʾa)* (in one reading), the terminology of the author, may Allah have mercy on him, is that when he says *(fī qirāʾa)* it is one of the canonical readings (*sabʿiyya*, the seven readings), and when he says *quriʾa* (it was read) it is an irregular reading (*shādhdha*). Accordingly, there are two canonical readings in this verse.

* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Do I have "(in one reading) with the upper *tāʾ*" and you have "with the lower *yāʾ*"?
* A student: No, with the upper *tāʾ*.
* The Shaykh: With the upper *tāʾ*, because the author affirmed ﴿*yaʿmalūna*﴾ (they do). Here we say: there are two canonical readings in the verse, and it is permissible to recite with either of them. When we say "permissible," this does not mean that the two readings are equal in standing. Rather, it means that reciting with either of them is not forbidden. The better course is to recite with this one at times and with that one at other times, because the differences in readings are like the differences in acts of worship. We have mentioned that the better course in acts of worship that come in various forms is… what is the better course? To perform this one once and that one once, so that you have acted upon the Sunnah in all its forms. Likewise in readings, the better course is to recite this way once and that way another time, on condition that you know the reading. But this statement we make applies to a person's private recitation. As for reciting before the common people, he should not depart from the reading that is in their hands, why? Because the layman does not grasp these readings, or does not grasp the difference between them. If you recite the Qurʾān in a way other than what is before him, he will object to you. Yet this objection you may be able to answer, but something of doubt will settle in his heart: he will say, "So the Qurʾān is not preserved, since one person recites this way and another recites that way, meaning it has not been preserved." Thus some doubt enters his heart. For this reason, we should speak to people in terms of what their minds can grasp, as in the hadith of ʿAlī: "Speak to the people in terms of what they know. Do you want Allah and His Messenger to be denied?"[[Reported by al-Bukhārī (127) from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, as a statement of ʿAlī (mawqūf).]]

The conclusion is that the student of knowledge who knows the readings should at times recite this way and at times that way. But does he combine the two readings? For example, here I say: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Acquainted with what they do﴾, and ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Acquainted with what you do﴾? No. The better course is to recite this once and that once, because if you combine the two readings you have contradicted, since whoever recites with the *tāʾ* does not recite with the *yāʾ*, so how can you combine them?

But some scholars say there is no harm in combining the two readings, whether they are separated or not. That is, it is permissible to recite both readings within a single verse, and it is permissible to recite one verse in one reader's reading and another verse in another reader's reading.

As for the second case, namely reciting one verse in one reader's reading and another verse in another reader's reading, it is permissible. But combining the two readings within a single verse and a single recitation, there is room for doubt about its permissibility.

* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: For example, you recite here: ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Acquainted with what they do﴾ according to one reader's reading, then in another verse you recite according to another reader who differs from him… (...).

Does mere calling (of the Prophet by name) count as honoring him?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No.
* The student: Calling (...).
* The Shaykh: Well done. (Allah calls him) by the description of prophethood, whereas the prophets other than him Allah calls by their names: "O Mūsā," "O ʿĪsā," and similar. But the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was only addressed with the description of prophethood or messengership.

If you say: Did not Allah say ﴿Muḥammad is but a messenger; [other] messengers have passed on before him﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 144], and say ﴿Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah, and those with him﴾ [al-Fatḥ 29]?
* The student: This is not a context of calling and address.
* The Shaykh: Yes, this is not a context of calling and address, but it is a context of information.

* It is derived from the noble verse: the obligation of piety (*taqwā*).
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: ﴿Fear Allah﴾, yes.
* It is derived from it: the obligation of piety upon the community (*umma*).
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: If the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is commanded to piety, then others are a fortiori. That is one point. What is another point?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: That the address directed to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is directed to him and to his community, unless there is evidence that restricts it to him.

On this occasion: address directed to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, either has evidence for generality, that the address itself indicates generality, or it contains what indicates specificity, or it contains nothing that indicates either. So what contains an indication of generality is general. Who will give an example of it?
* A student: Specificity?
* The Shaykh: No, generality.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, this has no evidence of generality.
* A student: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾.
* The Shaykh: Yes: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them at their waiting period﴾ [al-Ṭalāq 1]. Or does it contain what indicates specificity?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, correct. It has many examples. Or it contains nothing that indicates either? Like this verse, but its ruling is general: its ruling is general for the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and for his community. Is it clear?

* It is derived from the noble verse: that the Prophet (ﷺ) is a servant commanded and obligated, by what?
* A student: By his being commanded to piety and not obeying the disbelievers and hypocrites.
* The Shaykh: Yes, well done: by his being commanded to piety and not obeying the disbelievers and hypocrites.
* It is derived from this: that a person, however high his rank, the obligations do not drop from him?
* A student: That is because (...).
* The Shaykh: And upon this benefit there branches the refutation of those Sufis who say that when a person reaches the level of *muʿāyana* (direct witnessing), the obligations drop from him. Do they, or not? Because we say: no one reaches the rank of the Prophet (ﷺ) before Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and yet the obligations did not drop from him.

If they say: Allah says ﴿And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty﴾ [al-Ḥijr 99], meaning: until you reach the level of certainty, then stop. So what do we answer them?
* A student: The meaning of "certainty" here is death.
* The Shaykh: Do you have evidence that "certainty" is death?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: They say: ﴿until there comes to you the certainty﴾: until you reach the level of certainty, then halt. So now we want to find evidence showing that certainty is death.
* The student: The saying of some of the early generations: "And he strove in Allah with the striving due to Him until certainty came to him."
* The Shaykh: No, that is a saying of the early generations. We want (evidence) from the Book or the Sunnah.
* A student: ﴿until certainty came to us﴾.
* The Shaykh: Yes. Their saying, that is, the people of the Fire: ﴿and we used to deny the Day of Recompense, until certainty came to us﴾ [al-Muddaththir 46–47]. Did certainty come to them in the sense that they reached the level of certainty? Not at all; they died in denial, and they did not reach the level of certainty. And if these people say that they have reached a level of certainty by which they are among the people of Hellfire, then we agree with them about that. Is it clear?

* It is derived from the noble verse: the prohibition of obeying the disbelievers and hypocrites and inclining toward them, due to His saying ﴿and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾.
* It is derived from it: that a disbeliever or a hypocrite can never be a sincere advisor to the believers.
* A student: Here (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes. And if it were possible for them to give sincere advice, He would not have forbidden obeying them absolutely, because a sincere advisor is obeyed.
* It is derived from the noble verse: the affirmation of two of Allah's names, namely *al-ʿAlīm* (the All-Knowing) and *al-Ḥakīm* (the All-Wise).

Now the question: Is the knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, specific to the past and present, or comprehensive?
* The student: (...)
* The Shaykh: This question was not in the explanation. Is the knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, related to what is necessary (*wājib*), or to what is impossible (*mustaḥīl*), or to what is possible (*mumkin*), or to all of them?
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Is it possible that there exists in the heavens and the earth a god other than Allah? It is impossible. Likewise ﴿Allah has not taken any son, nor is there with Him any god; otherwise each god would have gone off with what he created, and some of them would have overpowered others. Exalted is Allah above what they describe﴾ [al-Muʾminūn 91]. This relates to the impossible. Is there an example of Allah's knowledge relating to the necessary? There are many, very many.
* A student: ﴿Do you not see that Allah knows what is in the heavens﴾ [al-Mujādila 7].
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: He knows (...).
* The Shaykh: My brothers, everything Allah has informed us about Himself is from knowledge of what is necessary, because for Allah the attributes of perfection are necessary. So when He informs about Himself with these attributes, it relates to the necessary. As for the possible, it is like what the brother said: ﴿Allah knows what every female carries, and what the wombs recede and what they increase﴾ [al-Raʿd 8]. Is this of the possible or of the necessary? Of the possible, because the carrying of a female, the receding of wombs, and the increase of wombs are possible, not necessary, not permissible? Possible.

So Allah's knowledge becomes comprehensive of everything, in total and in detail, present and future and past, necessary and possible and permissible. For this reason al-Saffārīnī says in his creed:

*And knowledge and speech have been related, my friend, to every thing, without restriction.*

* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: The necessary, for them, is the opposite of the impossible and the possible, because they say: things are of three kinds. Either necessary, meaning it must exist, not in the sense of an act whose doer is rewarded and whose abandoner deserves punishment; the necessary is what cannot be avoided. The impossible is what cannot occur. And the possible is what may occur or not occur.

* It is derived from the noble verse: the obligation to follow what was sent down to the Prophet (ﷺ). From where is it taken?
* A student: ﴿And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾. If you say: Is this general, that it is obligatory to follow what was sent down to the Messenger?
* Students: Yes.
* The Shaykh: Then it would be obligatory for us to raise our hands in prayer, and obligatory for us to glorify (Allah) more than once.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: So the meaning is: we say this is excepted, insofar as there is evidence that it is not obligatory. But what is authentically reported from the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, even if it is not obligatory, it is obligatory to believe in its legitimacy, even if the act itself is not obligatory. Have you understood now?

So we have belief in legitimacy and implementation of what is legislated. Implementation of what is legislated follows what the evidences indicate: either obligatory or recommended. As for believing in legitimacy regarding what is authentically established, that is obligatory.

For example: it is obligatory upon me to believe in the legitimacy of keeping the upper arms away from the sides during prostration, and we believe in the legitimacy of turning the head during prayer at the end of the prayer. But performing that depends on the detailed evidences: if the evidences indicate it is obligatory, it is obligatory; if they indicate it is recommended, it is recommended.

* It is derived from the noble verse: the establishment of the Prophet's messengership and prophethood (ﷺ).
* A student: ﴿what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾.
* The Shaykh: Due to His saying ﴿what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾, and from the beginning of the verse ﴿O Prophet﴾, yes.
* It is derived from the noble verse: that Allah, Exalted, has a special lordship with respect to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, due to His saying ﴿from your Lord﴾. It has been mentioned to us many times that lordship is of two kinds and servitude is of two kinds: general lordship and specific lordship. An example of general lordship is His saying, Exalted: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾ [Maryam 65]. Is this general or specific? General.
And an example of specificity is this verse: ﴿from your Lord﴾. Both kinds are combined in His saying, Exalted: ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Mūsā and Hārūn"﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 121–122]. Likewise servitude is of two kinds: general and specific. The general is like His saying, Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Seeing of the servants﴾ [Ghāfir 44], which is general.
And the specific: ﴿Exalted is He who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isrāʾ 1], meaning the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him.

* It is derived from the noble verse: that the knowledge of Allah, Exalted, encompasses inner matters, due to His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Acquainted with what you do﴾.
* It is derived from it: a warning to a person against opposition.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, we say: a warning to a person against opposition.
* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Because this necessitates that we do not oppose Allah. As long as we know that He is Acquainted with what we do, it is impossible for us to oppose Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Is it clear? Like if you said, for example: "Go, and I know what you are doing." What is meant by this? Threat and warning against opposition. So every text in which Allah makes clear that He knows what we do is a warning to us against opposing Him. (...)

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verse 3–8 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And put your trust in Allah﴾: in your affair. ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Trustee﴾: as Guardian for you. This is the beginning of today's lesson. ﴿Put your trust in Allah﴾. Tawakkul (complete reliance) means reliance together with confidence. For this reason the scholars defined it as the sincere reliance upon Allah in bringing about benefits and warding off harms, together with confidence in Allah the Mighty and Majestic, such that the heart relies upon Allah and not upon other than Him in bringing about benefits and in warding off harms, while trusting in Allah the Glorified and Exalted, meaning: being confident that Allah the Exalted will suffice him. For this reason He said: ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him﴾ [at-Talaq 3]: that is, sufficient for him. So when you are truthful toward Allah the Mighty and Majestic in that He, the Glorified and Exalted, will suffice you, this is the perfection of tawakkul.

As for His saying ﴿Put your trust in Allah﴾, this appears in the Quran in several places, among them His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So worship Him and put your trust in Him﴾ [Hud 123], and ﴿And upon Allah let them rely, if they are believers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 23]. Accordingly, tawakkul is part of worship, because Allah commanded it, and whatever Allah commands in the Sharia is part of worship. The divisions of tawakkul will come, God willing, in the benefits (al-fawa'id).

As for His saying ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Trustee﴾ [al-Ahzab 3], the grammarians (ahl al-i'rab) say that the bā' (in billāh) is extra (za'idah) for the sake of embellishing the expression, and that the word Allah is the subject (fa'il), and the construction is: "and Allah suffices as Trustee," with wakīlan being a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the subject. The meaning is: how great is Allah's sufficiency in this matter. Just as ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Witness﴾ [an-Nisa' 79] means: how great is Allah's sufficiency in His testimony.

I say: in this there are verses. ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Witness﴾ means: how great is Allah's sufficiency in His testimony. ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Trustee﴾ means: how great is Allah's sufficiency in His trusteeship.

As for His saying ﴿wakīlan﴾, the author says: "Guardian for you." Accordingly, fa'il here is in the sense of fa'il (active), not in the sense of maf'ul (passive). For wakīl, if you say "I appointed this wakīl," it is in the sense of maf'ul, since it is the one appointed (al-muwakkal). But here it is in the sense of fa'il, meaning that He is the Guardian. So the reliance is from the human being, and the protection and preservation are from Allah.

The author's explanation is supported by His saying: ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him﴾ [at-Talaq 3], meaning: sufficient for him, and He, the Glorified and Exalted, will undertake to protect him and to fulfil what he has entrusted to Him.

The author said: "And his ummah follows him in all of that." He only said this because the address in these verses is directed to whom? To the Prophet ﷺ. So his ummah follows him. From where do we know that his ummah follows him?

We know this from one of two paths:

The first path: Allah has commanded us to emulate him. Thus every command directed to the Messenger ﷺ, for which no evidence specifies it for him alone, applies to us as well. We are commanded to follow him: ﴿Indeed, there has been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example for whoever hopes in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Ahzab 21].

Second: it is well known in discourse that an address directed to the one who is followed is addressed to him and to his follower. For example, a commander may say to an officer in the army: "Go to such-and-such a place." Does he mean: go yourself alone, or go with those who follow you? Go with those who follow you.

So in Arabic, when an address is directed to the one who is followed, it is addressed to him and to his follower. Thus the reason the ummah is a follower of the Messenger ﷺ in these commands, and in what they contain of prohibition, is one of two paths:

The first path: we have been commanded to follow the Messenger ﷺ.

The second path: an address directed to the one who is followed is addressed to him and to his follower.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his body﴾ [al-Ahzab 4]. ﴿Ma﴾ is a negation particle, the word Allah is the subject, and ﴿two hearts﴾ is the object of ﴿ja'ala﴾. The first or the second? The first is postponed, and its second object is ﴿for a man﴾. As for ﴿min﴾ here, we say it is extra in terms of i'rab, so we parse ﴿qalbayn﴾ as an accusative object. Its sign of accusative — this is the difficulty — is the fatha, but that is not possible; it is a yā' assumed (muqaddarah) over this yā' which was brought in. Why was it brought in? It was brought in for the particle, because the action of the apparent particle is stronger than the action of the hidden particle. For example, ja'ala governs the accusative qalbayn, but it was opposed — or more precisely, opposed by a stronger, immediate operator, the genitive particle (harf al-jarr). So they say: this yā' is not the yā' of the accusative, but the yā' of the extra genitive particle.

Accordingly we say: the sign of its accusative is an assumed yā' in place of the existing yā' which was brought in for the sake of the extra genitive particle.

Regarding His saying ﴿mā ja'ala﴾: is this ja'al (making) kawni (cosmic/determinative) or shar'i (legislative)? This ja'al is kawni, because the ja'al that is attributed to Allah is divided into two kinds: legislative ja'al, meaning what He legislated, and cosmic ja'al, meaning what He created.

An example of the legislative ja'al is His saying: ﴿Allah has not instituted any bahirah or sa'ibah﴾ [al-Ma'idah 103]. This is a legislative ja'al. What is the evidence? The evidence is that it exists as something made in the cosmic sense, but was not made in the legislative sense: ﴿Allah has not instituted any bahirah or sa'ibah﴾.

As for the cosmic ja'al, it is abundant, such as His saying: ﴿And We made you more in numbers﴾ [al-Isra' 6], and ﴿And We made the night as clothing (10) and We made the day for livelihood﴾ [an-Naba' 10–11].

In this noble verse, ﴿Allah has not made for a man two hearts﴾ — which of the two kinds? The cosmic kind: ﴿Allah has not made for a man two hearts﴾. Allah emphasized this negation with the extra genitive particle, because extra particles are among the instruments of emphasis.

So it is impossible that a human being has two hearts; in one human being, two hearts is impossible. But is this sentence intended for its own sake, or intended for something else?

The author and a group of commentators hold that it is intended for its own sake, and that it is a negation of a matter that had been claimed. For this reason He said, in response to some of the disbelievers who claimed that he had two hearts with each of which he understood better than the intellect of Muhammad ﷺ — this is what a group of scholars held. That is, this is a negation of a claim: a man among the disbelievers said that he had two hearts, and if he had two hearts he would have two intellects, and if he had two intellects he would be better than the Prophet ﷺ, because he has only one heart.

Some exegetes, foremost among them al-Zuhri, may Allah have mercy on him, held that this sentence is not intended for its own sake, because it is a known matter, since no human being has two hearts. Rather, it is a preface and a preparation for what follows, because three things are mentioned in the noble verse: ﴿Allah has not made for a man two hearts within his body, nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar your mothers, nor has He made your adopted sons your sons﴾.
