Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And He has not made your wives whom you liken to your mothers your mothers﴾. We have not completed the discussion. Which of the three readings is "mudhahara" in the reading that contains the addition? Because it has an extra letter, and each letter has ten good deeds; do you know? So according to this view, which of the three readings do you choose?

* A student: ﴿tazzāharūna﴾.

* The Shaykh: ﴿tazzāharūna﴾, because this one has the most letters. Some scholars say: the best is to recite each reading, to take up every reading, to recite with this one once and with that one once. Which is preferable? The last opinion is correct: you recite with this one once and with that one once, if you know them, because every reading has been authentically transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ, so one should recite them, for two benefits (we only mentioned one):

The first benefit: acting upon both sunnas.

The second benefit: preserving these readings. That is why we, now that we rely on the reading we have, do not know the other readings. If a person is told that he should recite every authentic reading, this involves preserving the readings. Therefore the young among us should be eager for the readings, and learn them, so that this sunna is not left abandoned. Yes indeed.

His saying: ﴿ummahatikum﴾, its i'rab? (...)

﴿abna'akum﴾ — the author said: "(plural of da'iyy, who is one who is claimed as a son by one other than his father)." Ad'iya' is the plural of da'iyy, like aghniya' the plural of ghaniyy, and akfiya' the plural of kafiyy, and it has examples. And "da'iyy" is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, and its origin is da'iyyu with a waw, but the waw was changed to a yā' for a morphological reason.

So "da'iyy" means "mad'uww" (one who is called), and "da'a'" in origin is requesting approach; and the intended "ad-di'a'" here is attribution, by being attributed to other than his father, so one says, "This is the son of so-and-so," and he is not truly his son. These adopted sons, Allah did not make them sons, legislatively or by decree? Not by decree, nor legislatively. As for not by decree, it is clear that they are not sons by decree. As for legislatively, here He negated it from them, He negated it: He said, ﴿And He has not made your adopted sons your sons﴾. So if the adopted sons are not sons, neither by decree nor legislatively, the mind does not turn to them legislatively.

This statement which I make shows the weakness of the view of those who say (...) regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the wives of your sons who are from your loins﴾ [an-Nisa' 23]. They say that His saying ﴿who are from your loins﴾ is a qualification by which one guards against the adopted son, because we say: the adopted son does not enter into "son" at all, so the mind does not go to him, so that we would need a qualification to guard against him. We had already studied this issue in the chapter on the prohibited women in marriage.

The upshot is that God did not make adopted sons (adoptees, *al-ad'iya'*) into sons, neither legally nor in reality. In the Jahiliyyah, people used to ascribe a man to someone other than his father. The man might be of noble lineage and the adoptee of lowly or unknown descent, and he would be called after the noble man for the sake of that man's rank. God nullified this practice, because calling a person to other than his father has consequences. Everything that follows from lineage, such as prohibitions and permissions, inheritance, and maintenance, may pass to the adoptee merely because he was called after that man. For this reason God forbade it by law. Giving a thing a name far from its reality leads to the overturning of circumstances. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Let not the Bedouins overcome you regarding your 'Ishā' prayer; they call it *al-'Atamah*, but in the Book of God it is *al-'Ishā'*."[[Reported by Muslim (228/644) from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar (may God be pleased with them both).]]

So everything that might have different rulings if given a different name, the Law has forbidden.

﴿وَمَا جَعَلَ أَدْعِيَاءَكُمْ أَبْنَاءَكُمْ﴾ ("nor has He made your adopted sons your sons"): *ḥaqīqatan* ("in reality") explains *abnā'* ("sons"); meaning, He did not make them sons in the true sense.

﴿ذَلِكُمْ قَوْلُكُمْ بِأَفْوَاهِكُمْ﴾ ("That is your saying from your mouths"): i.e., the Jews and the hypocrites. The author intends the address here to be to the Jews and the hypocrites. The correct view is that it refers to anyone who calls a person to other than his father, whether he is a hypocrite, a Jew, a polytheist, or a Muslim. This is a statement uttered with the mouth, not a reality. The speaker himself knows that this adoptee is not the son of the one he is ascribed to, so how could he say what he believes to be otherwise?

As for His saying ﴿ذَلِكُمْ﴾ ("that"), He used the plural pronoun in the address because the addressees are a group. We have already noted regarding demonstratives that the demonstrative is matched to the thing indicated, and the *kāf* (the second-person marker) is matched to the addressee. Here the thing indicated is singular masculine, namely calling a man to other than his father, while the addressees are a group of males.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: We will discuss this in the benefits (*fawā'id*), God willing.

﴿ذَلِكُمْ قَوْلُكُمْ بِأَفْوَاهِكُمْ﴾ means: you say it with your tongues while you know the reality, that it is not so.

The author, may God have mercy on him, said: "i.e., the Jews and the hypocrites." Why did he write it with *yā'* (*ya* as a pronoun)? Because it explains His saying ﴿قَوْلُكُمْ﴾ ("your saying"), with the *kāf* in the genitive. They said: when the Prophet (ﷺ) married Zaynab bint Jahsh, who had been the wife of Zayd ibn Harithah, whom the Prophet (ﷺ) had adopted, they said: "Muhammad has married his son's wife." God refuted them in that.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: They said: "He married..." – meaning the Jews and the hypocrites. The author's statement is distant from the apparent meaning of the verse, since his words imply that after the Prophet (ﷺ) married Zaynab bint Jahsh, who had originally been with Zayd ibn Harithah, they said this statement. But the verse makes no allusion to the story at all. The verse speaks about what? About the son by adoption. God does not mention, nor allude to, a man marrying the wife of the son he adopted. This will come to us in the verse, God willing. So the correct view is that the verse concerns a person's attribution to other than his father by adoption.

(﴿وَاللَّهُ يَقُولُ الْحَقَّ﴾ "And God says the truth" in that matter, ﴿وَهُوَ يَهْدِي السَّبِيلَ﴾ "and He guides to the way": the way of truth.)

﴿وَاللَّهُ يَقُولُ الْحَقَّ﴾: the author restricted it by saying "in that matter," but the correct view is not to restrict it, even if that was the occasion, because the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause. What is the truth that God says in what He says? God explained it in the Qur'an itself when He said: ﴿وَتَمَّتْ كَلِمَةُ رَبِّكَ صِدْقًا وَعَدْلًا﴾ ("The word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice") [al-An'am 115]. This is the truth God speaks: truthfulness in reports and justice in rulings. Everything God says falls under one of two categories: either a report or a ruling. The truth of a report is its truthfulness, and the truth of a ruling is its justice. The best way to explain the Qur'an is by the Qur'an. Therefore, if someone asks, "What is the truth in God's words?" we say: the truth in God's words is what He mentioned in His saying: ﴿وَتَمَّتْ كَلِمَةُ رَبِّكَ صِدْقًا وَعَدْلًا﴾.

As for His saying ﴿وَهُوَ يَهْدِي السَّبِيلَ﴾, He did not say "and guides to the way" with an indirect object because the second verb is transitive to another (*yataʿaddā lil-ghayr*). There is a guider, a guided one, and that which is guided to and in. The guider is God; the guided one is man, for example; and that to which he is guided, and in which he is guided, is the religion, the path that leads to God, Exalted is He. Being guided *to* is guidance of indication (*hidāyat al-dalāla*), and being guided *in* is guidance of success (*hidāyat al-tawfīq*), because you say: "I showed him to such-and-such" (*dalaltuhu ilā kadhā*) and "I guided him in such-and-such" (*hadaytuhu fī kadhā*), meaning: I made him act in it. This is the wisdom in God's saying in Surat al-Fatiha: ﴿اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ﴾ ("Guide us to the straight path") [al-Fatiha 6], and He did not say "guide us to the path" with *ilā*. Why? So that it includes both guidance to it, through indicating it and explaining it, and guidance in it, through acting upon it. This is the aim of every supplicant who asks God for guidance: that God guides him to the thing so he knows and recognizes it, and guides him in it so he does not stray from it. Is that clear?

﴿يَهْدِي السَّبِيلَ﴾: which way is meant in this verse? *Al-sabīl* ("the way") with the definite article *al-* is for the mental known (*al-'ahd al-dhihnī*), and the intended meaning is the way of God, Exalted is He. What is the evidence that the way of God is meant?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿وَلَا تَتَّبِعُوا السُّبُلَ فَتَفَرَّقَ بِكُمْ عَنْ سَبِيلِهِ﴾ ("Do not follow other paths, lest they separate you from His way") [al-An'am 153].

So the way to which God guides is the way of God, Exalted is He, the path of truth. ﴿وَهُوَ يَهْدِي السَّبِيلَ﴾. Among what is included in this is that He, glory be to Him, did not make the wives whom men declare unlawful (*yuzāhirūn*) into mothers, nor did He make the adoptees into sons. So He stated the truth on this matter and guided us to the way in it. The wife is a wife, and the adopted son is not a son. God says: ﴿ادْعُوهُمْ لِآبَائِهِمْ﴾ ("Call them by their fathers' names") [al-Ahzab 5]. The author said in the tafsir: "but call them by their fathers" (*lākin ud'ūhum li-ābā'ihim*). Why did he use the corrective particle "but" (*istidrāk*) – "but call them by their fathers"? In my view, there is no need for the corrective, and the sentence is a new independent statement (*isti'nāf*). When God nullified that these adoptees be sons, He commanded us to call them by their fathers. It seems the author, may God have mercy on him, saw that the second verse, ﴿ادْعُوهُمْ لِآبَائِهِمْ﴾, is not a direct counterpart of what God negated in the first, namely: "He has not made your adopted sons your sons," but rather: "He has made them sons of their fathers, so call them by their fathers." He, may God have mercy on him, considered this to be the way of the correction ("but"): "He did not make your adopted sons your sons, but He made them sons of their fathers, so call them by their fathers."

We say: this is not needed. The sentence is a new independent statement: ﴿ادْعُوهُمْ لِآبَائِهِمْ﴾, meaning: attribute them to their fathers. So say: "O son of so-and-so." The word *ābā'ihim* is the plural of *ab* ("father"). Is the plural here taken with regard to the people called, since people are many, or is it that each person has his fathers, so that a man is ascribed to his father, his grandfather, and his great-grandfather, and so on, or does it include both?

It includes both. A person is called after his father: one says "so-and-so son of so-and-so son of so-and-so." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I am the son of 'Abd al-Muttalib."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4315) and Muslim (1776/78) from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib (may God be pleased with him).]] Muhammad, as in our *Alfiyya* verse: "Muhammad said..." – and who is Muhammad? Muhammad ibn 'Abdullah; his father is 'Abdullah. So it appears that it is inclusive: it is pluralized in regard to the individuals of people, and pluralized in regard to the fathers, since fathers include a nearer father and a father above him.

He said: ﴿هُوَ أَقْسَطُ عِنْدَ اللهِ﴾ ("that is more just in the sight of God"). The pronoun *huwa* refers to the verbal noun implied in His saying ﴿ادْعُوهُمْ﴾ ("call them"), meaning: *huwa* – i.e., their calling them by their fathers' names. This is similar to His saying: ﴿اعْدِلُوا هُوَ أَقْرَبُ لِلتَّقْوَى﴾ ("Be just; that is nearer to piety") [al-Ma'ida 8], where *huwa* means justice implied in the verb. So here *huwa* means calling them by their fathers. ﴿أَقْسَطُ عِنْدَ اللهِ﴾ means: more just.

Some exegetes interpreted it as the active participle: the active participle "just" (*qāsiṭ*) in the sight of God, meaning: it is justice in the sight of God. They resorted to this because it is known that the comparative (*ism al-tafḍīl*) shares in its basic meaning both the one preferred and the one it is preferred over. If you say: "So-and-so is braver than so-and-so," both are brave, but this one is braver. So here, if we keep the comparative in its normal sense and say: their calling them by their fathers is more just in the sight of God than calling them after those who adopted them, this implies that there is some justice in calling them after those who adopted them, though there is no justice in it at all.

For this reason some exegetes said: the comparative form here has the meaning of the active participle, so that there is nothing in the other side of the comparison.

Others said: it keeps its normal meaning, and the Arabic language uses the comparative even where there is nothing on the other side of it. Among such uses is His saying: ﴿أَصْحَابُ الْجَنَّةِ يَوْمَئِذٍ خَيْرٌ مُسْتَقَرًّا وَأَحْسَنُ مَقِيلًا﴾ ("The companions of Paradise that Day are better in their resting place and finer in their place of repose") [al-Furqan 24]. ﴿خَيْرٌ مُسْتَقَرًّا﴾ ("better in resting place"), even though the people of the Fire have no good in their resting place. Based on this, we say that keeping the verse on its apparent meaning is preferable. When this is said, a question arises: why did He use the comparative where the other side has nothing?

We answer: to show that this is the utmost of justice. Pay attention: its benefit is that calling them by their fathers is the most just thing, the utmost of justice. So the comparative here is according to the meaning, i.e., this is the most just of things.

Is the word ﴿أَقْسَطُ﴾ a comparative from the triliteral or the quadriliteral root? From the triliteral, since the comparative is formed only from the triliteral noun:
"Form them from a root that is triliteral and conjugated..."
Moreover, the quadriliteral of this root does not mean justice but injustice. Is that right? The quadriliteral means injustice? Pay attention: then it is the reverse. The *qāsiṭ* (unjust) is the oppressor, and the *muqsiṭ* (just) is the just one, or not?

God Almighty said: ﴿وَأَمَّا الْقَاسِطُونَ فَكَانُوا لِجَهَنَّمَ حَطَبًا﴾ ("As for the unjust, they will be fuel for Hell") [al-Jinn 15], and He said: ﴿وَأَقْسِطُوا إِنَّ اللَّهَ يُحِبُّ الْمُقْسِطِينَ﴾ ("And act justly; indeed God loves those who act justly") [al-Hujurat 9].

So a problem arises regarding the word ﴿أَقْسَطُ﴾ here, in ﴿هُوَ أَقْسَطُ﴾. Our answer to it: this is evidence for the correctness of the view of the Kufans, who say that the comparative form may be derived from non-triliteral roots. They say ﴿أَقْسَطُ﴾ is from the pattern of *al-iqsāṭ* (acting justly), meaning that this is more just.

His saying ﴿عِنْدَ اللهِ﴾ ("in the sight of God") means: in His ruling, since the ruling is God's ruling and is attributed to Him. This is similar to His saying concerning those who accuse chaste women: ﴿فَإِذْ لَمْ يَأْتُوا بِالشُّهَدَاءِ فَأُوْلَئِكَ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ هُمُ الْكَاذِبُونَ﴾ ("Since they did not bring witnesses, then with God they are the liars") [al-Nur 13]. Notice the phrase ﴿فَأُوْلَئِكَ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ﴾. We have now moved away from the verse. If a man accuses a woman of fornication, then in terms of the reality it may be true, and it may be false, or not? That is, it may be true that she committed adultery, and it may be a lie, but in God's ruling?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, in God's ruling it is a lie. For this reason He said: ﴿فَإِذْ لَمْ يَأْتُوا بِالشُّهَدَاءِ فَأُوْلَئِكَ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ﴾, and did not say "then they are the liars," because in reality it may be true, but in the Law of God they are liars. ﴿فَأُوْلَئِكَ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ هُمُ الْكَاذِبُونَ﴾. For this reason the *ḥadd al-qadhf* (the prescribed punishment for false accusation of unchastity) is obligatory upon them if they do not bring four witnesses.

﴿فَإِنْ لَمْ تَعْلَمُوا آبَاءَهُمْ فَإِخْوَانُكُمْ فِي الدِّينِ وَمَوَالِيكُمْ﴾ ("But if you do not know their fathers, then they are your brothers in religion and your clients"). If you do not know the fathers of whom? The fathers of these adoptees. "Then they are your brothers in religion and your clients": meaning they are not their sons. Even in the situation where a man's father is not known, it is not permissible for him to be ascribed to other than his father, but he will be a brother to us in religion, and a *mawlā* (client, freed slave, or protégé) to us, if he entered our possession and we then freed him, for example. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said, in the story of the dispute between 'Ali, Ja'far, and Zayd ibn Harithah, to Zayd: "You are our brother and our *mawlā*."[[Reported by al-Bukhari (2699) from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib (may God be pleased with him).]] So he is my brother in religion and not my son, and he is also my *mawlā* if I had freed him, and even if I did not know his father, he is not ascribed to me.

For this reason you find that scholars, may God have mercy on them, who write the names of men, when they ascribe one of the clients to the one who freed him, say: "al-Qurashi, their *mawlā*," for example, "al-Tamimi, their *mawlā*." Because if one says only "al-Qurashi," what would the listener think? That he is truly Qurashi. But if he says "their *mawlā*," it indicates he was ascribed to them by virtue of being their client. The client of a people is one of them. Scholars even said regarding alms (*ṣadaqa*) that it is forbidden for the clients of the Banu Hashim, because the client of a people is one of them. Yet they are not ascribed to them by true lineage; rather, it is necessary to qualify it.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: How?
* Student: "The sons of your paternal uncle" (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿فَإِخْوَانُكُمْ فِي الدِّينِ وَمَوَالِيكُمْ﴾.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It has no basis.
* Student: (...) that the father of Zayd ibn Harithah came to the Prophet from (...) and said (...), so the Prophet (ﷺ) gave him the choice (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, this was when his father and uncle came?
* Student: His father was recognized and his father requested him.
* Shaykh: The reason for his adoption: this was at the beginning of Islam and then it was annulled; it is *mansūkha* (abrogated). (...) ﴿وَلَيْسَ عَلَيْكُمْ جُنَاحٌ﴾ ("And there is no blame upon you") but just (...).

And it is the obligation to give precedence to revelation over personal opinion, based on His saying: ﴿وَاتَّبِعْ مَا يُوحَى إِلَيْكَ﴾ ("Follow what is revealed to you") [al-Ahzab 2]. This address is directed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and, all the more so, to his community. It indicates the obligation of giving precedence to revelation over opinion.

Giving precedence to opinion over revelation has categories, some of which reach the level of disbelief, and some of which are less than that. Those who give precedence to opinion over revelation while knowing the revelation, believing that non-revelation is equal to it or more complete than it, or that it is permissible to rule by an opinion that contradicts revelation while knowing it, these are considered disbelievers.

In these three situations, if they believe that the opinion is more complete and more beneficial than revelation, or that it is equal to it, or that it is permissible to give it precedence over revelation while knowing it, these are disbelievers, because they have judged by other than what God revealed: ﴿وَمَنْ لَمْ يَحْكُمْ بِمَا أَنزَلَ اللَّهُ فَأُوْلَئِكَ هُمُ الْكَافِرُونَ﴾ ("Whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, those are the disbelievers") [al-Ma'ida 44].

As for those who give precedence to opinion through interpretation, thinking that this does not contradict revelation, or that it is a path leading them to revelation, these do not reach the level of disbelief. This is like many of the zealots for the schools of law (*madhāhib*), who do not consider these schools to be outside of revelation, but see them as a path to acting upon revelation. They say: "This is our imam; he is more knowledgeable and more understanding than us, so we follow him and suspect our opinion relative to his opinion. Otherwise, we are adherents of the Law of God and we refer to the Book of God and the Sunna of His Messenger (ﷺ)."

To these we say: if the truth becomes clear to them, it becomes obligatory for them to follow it, even if it contradicts the imam they follow, because the truth does not err and the imams err. No one can claim infallibility (*'iṣma*) for any human except the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Only a deviant man claims infallibility for anyone other than the prophets, as the Rafidah (Rafidites) do with their imams. This is clear error, because their imams may err as others err.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verses 3–8 (part 3 of 3):

We have already mentioned what happened to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, who is the imam of the imams with respect to those people, when he made a mistake. The Prophet ﷺ gave him a silk garment (ḥullah) and he wore it, so the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, I did not give it to you for you to wear it. I only gave it to you so that you would give it to the women of Fatimah's family" [[Narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Kabir (1069) with the wording: "I did not clothe you in it so that you would wear it; I clothed you in it so that you would make it a head covering (khumur) among the Fawatim."]]. Likewise, there is what is well known from him, that a pregnant woman whose husband has died should observe the longer of the two waiting periods ('iddah). This contradicts the clear and authentic Sunnah.

The conclusion is that we say: in the noble verse ﴿And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [Al-Ahzab 2] there is an obligation to give precedence to revelation over personal opinion (ra'y), and that it is obligatory to rule by what the Shari'ah has brought in every case, whether it contradicts the opinion of those you follow or not.

﴿And rely upon Allah﴾ [Al-Ahzab 3]. Is this the beginning of the benefits?

In this there is evidence for the obligation of relying upon Allah (tawakkul). We have mentioned in the Book of Tawhid that tawakkul is divided into types:

The first: tawakkul of worship (tawakkul al-'ibadah), which is a person's sense of his need for the one he relies upon and his humility before him. This may not be directed to other than Allah, and directing it to other than Allah is shirk (associating partners with Allah), because it is associating another with Allah in what only Allah deserves. Is it major shirk or minor shirk? It is major shirk.

The second: relying on another whom you have appointed as your representative (wakil). This is permissible, and it has occurred even from the Messenger ﷺ. He appointed 'Urwah ibn al-Ja'd to buy a sacrificial animal for him, and he had an agent (wakil) in Khaybar. Likewise, he appointed 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, to slaughter what remained of the sacrificial animals (al-hady). This is permissible and there is no difficulty in it. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, when he went to Tabuk, appointed someone to be his deputy over his family. Musa, peace be upon him, appointed Harun when he went to Mount Tur, and he said: ﴿Take my place among my people and set things right﴾ [Al-A'raf 142].

So this is permissible and there is no difficulty in it, because it occurred among the prophets, and because it is a contract, and the basic ruling on contracts is permissibility unless evidence prohibits it.

The third: relying upon one who is not valid to rely upon, on a hidden power that we know has no effect in this reliance. This is shirk, which may be major or minor, such as the reliance of those who seek intercession through the dead and believe that there is benefit in relying on them. For such people the matter may reach major shirk; otherwise, merely relying on them is shirk and is not permitted.

The fourth: relying on an apparent, influential power, but relying on it not on the basis that it is a representative for him, but on the basis that it benefits him and is the source of his happiness, success, provision, and the like. This is disliked (makruh), and it may reach the level of prohibition, like a person's reliance on his salary, his pension from the ministry in which he works, the administration, the presidency, and similar things. This involves a kind of sense of need for that thing and humbling oneself before it.

Therefore you find that those afflicted with this type favor those on whom they rely: they show favoritism to their senior officials, ministers, and others, favoring them in matters that are not permitted. As for being courteous to them in what is permitted, there is no harm in that. But favoring them in what is forbidden is not permitted. Yet this may occur, because they feel they are in need of these people. The least ruling for this is disapproval (karahah), and a person should be dignified in his soul, relying only upon his Lord, glorified and exalted is He.

* From the noble verse it is derived that the sufficiency of Allah, mighty and majestic, is above every sufficiency, because of His saying: ﴿And Allah is sufficient as Disposer of affairs (wakil)﴾ [Al-Ahzab 3]. Some scholars claimed that such a construction (tarkib) expresses amazement, meaning: how great is the sufficiency of Allah! And rely upon Allah, for how great is the sufficiency of Allah, glorified and exalted is He! This is not far-fetched: that this form, changed from "Allah suffices as a disposer" to ﴿Sufficient is Allah as Disposer﴾, may be intended to show the emphasis (mubalaghah) in His sufficiency, glorified and exalted is He. What supports this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah, He is sufficient for him﴾ [At-Talaq 3].

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his chest, and He has not made your wives whom you divorce by ẓihār (zihar, a pre-Islamic form of divorce) your mothers, nor has He made your adopted sons your sons﴾ [Al-Ahzab 4].

From this context it is derived that the Qur'an has reached the utmost degree in persuasion and in establishing proof.

The reason for this is that it presented the evidence before the thing proven, in a form about which no one can doubt. What is it? ﴿Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his chest﴾. This is a known matter, and no two people dispute it: a human has only one heart, not two. Why? Because if these two hearts agreed on one matter, the second heart would be of no use. And if they disagreed, they would contradict each other regarding the same thing. So what would the person do? Would he follow the right heart or the left heart? He would remain confused. Therefore Allah did not make for a man two hearts; he has only one heart, because he is one body.

Consider His saying: ﴿within his chest﴾. It yields a benefit beyond what came before, which is that it is a description of reality: one chest cannot be managed except by one heart. Otherwise the two hearts would be in two chests, not in one chest. So there is a benefit here other than the previous one: it describes reality, that one chest cannot be governed except by one heart.

In the noble verse there is the method of establishing a matter by proof, or proving a matter by a proof that is decisive, about which no one can doubt.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the woman who is divorced by ẓihār is not a mother, because of His saying: ﴿nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by ẓihār your mothers﴾.

* It follows from this verse that making her a mother in ẓihār is a lie, falsehood, and an evil. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, said in the verse of ẓihār: ﴿And indeed, they say an objectionable word and falsehood﴾ [Al-Mujadilah 2]. It is objectionable (munkar) because it contradicts the Shari'ah, and falsehood (zur) because it contradicts reality and truth.

* It is derived from the noble verse: an indication or warning of the prohibition of ẓihār, because of His saying: ﴿nor has He made your wives﴾ ... ﴿your mothers﴾. If Allah has not made that, then it is not permissible for us to make something that Allah has not made, because the matter belongs to Allah alone.

* It is derived from the verse ﴿nor has He made your adopted sons your sons﴾ that adopted sons (da'iyy, pl. du'iyy) are not sons in reality or in the Shari'ah. They are not sons by destiny (qadar) and they are not sons by Shari'ah, and for this He said: ﴿nor has He made your adopted sons your sons﴾.

* It is derived from it: when the adopted son is not a son in the Shari'ah or in reality, he does not need a qualifier to remove him from the meaning of sonship. Why does he not need one? Because he was never included in it at all, so we would not need a qualifier to exclude him.

* From this benefit follows: the refutation of the view of those who say that the qualifier in His saying: ﴿and the wives of your sons who are from your loins﴾ [An-Nisa' 23] excludes adoptive sons (tabanni). We say: he was never included in the first place, so he does not need a qualifier to exclude him.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that a person may say a statement he does not believe: ﴿That is your saying from your mouths﴾ [Al-Ahzab 4].

* It is derived from it: it is neither manly nor reasonable for a person to say with his mouth something that he does not believe in his heart, because what is meant by His saying: ﴿your saying from your mouths﴾ is to censure them and rebuke them. How can you say something with your mouths while you acknowledge in your hearts that it does not correspond to reality?

* It is derived from the noble verse: that the speech of Allah, mighty and majestic, is entirely true and contains no falsehood, because of His saying: ﴿And Allah says the truth﴾ [Al-Ahzab 4]. It has already been stated that truth (al-haqq) in the speech of Allah is sincerity (sidq) and justice ('adl), because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ [Al-An'am 115]. It is truthful in its information and just in its rulings.

* It is derived from the noble verse: that the speech of Allah, mighty and majestic, contains no contradiction, because of His saying: ﴿says the truth﴾. Contradiction exists only in falsehood, so truth cannot be contradictory. Is it clear?

* Also among the benefits of the noble verse: that what Allah has described Himself with in His Book is upon its reality, and there is no distortion (tahrif) or interpretation (ta'wil) in it. This is because if it were contrary to its apparent meaning, then its apparent meaning would indicate what? It would indicate falsehood. If we say that it is contrary to its apparent meaning, it follows that it indicates falsehood. If the intended meaning of the verses of the divine attributes is contrary to their apparent meaning, then does their apparent meaning indicate truth or falsehood?

If we say that the intended meaning of the verses of the attributes is contrary to the apparent meaning, the apparent meaning becomes false, because it is contrary to what is intended. This contradicts the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah says the truth﴾, for He, glorified and exalted, says only the truth.

* It is derived from the verse: that although it is evident that Allah speaks the truth, people do not agree on it, because of His saying: ﴿And He guides to the way﴾ [Al-Ahzab 4]. That is, even though Allah says only the truth, not everyone is guided to that. Rather, guidance is in the hand of Allah, mighty and majestic.

* It is derived from the noble verse: that a person must turn to his Lord, glorified and exalted, asking Him for guidance, because of His saying: ﴿And He guides to the way﴾. Consider the change of form, where He said: ﴿And Allah says the truth﴾, then said: ﴿And He guides to the way﴾, and did not say: "and guides to the way" (wa yahdi al-sabil), so that the second sentence would stand independently with its two components, its subject and its predicate. Because His saying: ﴿And He guides﴾, ﴿He﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and the clause ﴿guides﴾ is its predicate. So the sentence is independent of the first, which is more eloquent in showing that guidance is in the hand of Allah, glorified and exalted.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the path of truth is one, because of His saying: ﴿the way (al-sabil)﴾, which is singular. Likewise you find that "ways" (subul) come in the plural when they oppose the truth, is that right?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Like what?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: ﴿This is My path, straight, so follow it, and do not follow the [other] ways (al-subul)﴾ [Al-An'am 153]. So He used the singular for "the path" (al-sirat), while the other path, which opposes the path of Allah, is plural: ﴿and do not follow the ways﴾. When the path of truth comes in the plural, the intended meaning is the variety of its laws (shara'i'). Likewise the guardian (wali). Regarding the disbelievers: ﴿Allah is the Guardian of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light. And those who disbelieve, their guardians are the tyrants (taghut)﴾ [Al-Baqarah 257]. This is because the ways of what is not the truth are many, and each kind of them has a tyrant who calls to it.

* Among the benefits of the following verse: the obligation to attribute a person to his father: ﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers﴾, meaning: attribute them to their fathers, both verbally and in reality. Verbally, you say: "O so-and-so son of so-and-so," attributing him to his father. And in reality, you believe that true sonship belongs to whom? To the true father from whose loins the person was born, not to the one who was claimed to be a father.

* It is derived from the noble verse: that a person should not be claimed for other than his father. This is of two types:

The first: that he is claimed for other than his father, both verbally and in reality. This is not permitted. Indeed, the Messenger ﷺ regarded this as disbelief: if a person claims to be from other than his father while knowing it, that is disbelief. "Indeed, it is disbelief in you that you should renounce your fathers" [[Agreed upon: al-Bukhari (6768) and Muslim (62/113) from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, and the wording is: "Do not renounce your fathers; whoever renounces his father has committed disbelief."]].

The second: that he is claimed for other than his father verbally, but the rulings of sonship are not established at all for the one he is claimed for. We say that this is contrary to what Allah commanded.

However, the scholars say: if a person is known by a name (with a non-biological father), while the rulings and implications of that are not taken into account, it is permissible. For this they cite the example of al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad. His father was not al-Aswad, but al-Aswad had adopted him, and he became known by this kunyah, and it continued until Allah abolished adoption. But he remained known by it. They said: this does not harm, because the rulings of adoption were removed and only the name remained.

Nevertheless, it is without doubt better that he be attributed to his father. But the difficulty is that when a thing becomes well known, if you describe it with something other than what it is known by, confusion results. Now, if we say: "from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sakhr, that the Prophet ﷺ said such and such," many people may not know who he is. But if you say: "from Abu Hurayrah," everyone knows him.

In the noble verse there is evidence that deeds vary in merit before Allah, because of His saying: ﴿it is more just in the sight of Allah﴾, meaning: more complete in justice. The reason is that this adopted man, when we attribute him to other than his father, is that unjust toward his father or not? It is unjust. How can you attribute him to a person who did not beget him, and deprive the one who begot him from being called to him? There is no doubt that this is injustice. For this reason we said in the previous lesson that the comparative form here has no counterpart on the other side, because there is no justice at all in attributing a person to other than his father. We said that the benefit of the comparative here is to show that this matter has reached the utmost degree of justice, because it was expressed with the comparative form: ﴿more just in the sight of Allah﴾. Have we taken the sentence that follows?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: If he has a father, he is called by brotherhood in religion and by religious affiliation (wala' al-din), because of His saying: ﴿But if you do not know their fathers, then they are your brothers in religion and your mawali﴾ [Al-Ahzab 5]. As for their being our brothers in religion, it is clear. As for their being mawali, if he was freed by a person, then he is that person's mawla by manumission; and if he was not freed, then he is his mawla in religion, because the believers, as Allah said: ﴿And the believing men and believing women are allies of one another﴾ [At-Tawbah 71]. So they are your brothers and your mawali. So you address him: "O my brother." If you said: "O son of my brother," is that correct? It is correct.

The author says: (﴿and your mawali﴾: your paternal cousins). He made the affiliation here one of lineage, not one of religion. But there is something in the soul about this. Affiliation is either religious affiliation or affiliation by manumission. As for affiliation by manumission, it is clear that the freed slave is the mawla of the one who freed him. As for religious affiliation, it is also clear that every believer is an ally (wali) of his believing brother. As for affiliation of lineage, such as his saying: "your paternal cousins," if the Arabic language allows this kind of expression, then we accept it, because the Qur'an is in Arabic, and there is no objection to a single word having several meanings as long as they do not contradict one another. Now the time has ended.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verse 3–8 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And put your trust in Allah﴾: in your affair. ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Trustee﴾: as Guardian for you. This is the beginning of today's lesson. ﴿Put your trust in Allah﴾. Tawakkul (complete reliance) means reliance together with confidence. For this reason the scholars defined it as the sincere reliance upon Allah in bringing about benefits and warding off harms, together with confidence in Allah the Mighty and Majestic, such that the heart relies upon Allah and not upon other than Him in bringing about benefits and in warding off harms, while trusting in Allah the Glorified and Exalted, meaning: being confident that Allah the Exalted will suffice him. For this reason He said: ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him﴾ [at-Talaq 3]: that is, sufficient for him. So when you are truthful toward Allah the Mighty and Majestic in that He, the Glorified and Exalted, will suffice you, this is the perfection of tawakkul.

As for His saying ﴿Put your trust in Allah﴾, this appears in the Quran in several places, among them His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So worship Him and put your trust in Him﴾ [Hud 123], and ﴿And upon Allah let them rely, if they are believers﴾ [al-Ma'idah 23]. Accordingly, tawakkul is part of worship, because Allah commanded it, and whatever Allah commands in the Sharia is part of worship. The divisions of tawakkul will come, God willing, in the benefits (al-fawa'id).

As for His saying ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Trustee﴾ [al-Ahzab 3], the grammarians (ahl al-i'rab) say that the bā' (in billāh) is extra (za'idah) for the sake of embellishing the expression, and that the word Allah is the subject (fa'il), and the construction is: "and Allah suffices as Trustee," with wakīlan being a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the subject. The meaning is: how great is Allah's sufficiency in this matter. Just as ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Witness﴾ [an-Nisa' 79] means: how great is Allah's sufficiency in His testimony.

I say: in this there are verses. ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Witness﴾ means: how great is Allah's sufficiency in His testimony. ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Trustee﴾ means: how great is Allah's sufficiency in His trusteeship.

As for His saying ﴿wakīlan﴾, the author says: "Guardian for you." Accordingly, fa'il here is in the sense of fa'il (active), not in the sense of maf'ul (passive). For wakīl, if you say "I appointed this wakīl," it is in the sense of maf'ul, since it is the one appointed (al-muwakkal). But here it is in the sense of fa'il, meaning that He is the Guardian. So the reliance is from the human being, and the protection and preservation are from Allah.

The author's explanation is supported by His saying: ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him﴾ [at-Talaq 3], meaning: sufficient for him, and He, the Glorified and Exalted, will undertake to protect him and to fulfil what he has entrusted to Him.

The author said: "And his ummah follows him in all of that." He only said this because the address in these verses is directed to whom? To the Prophet ﷺ. So his ummah follows him. From where do we know that his ummah follows him?

We know this from one of two paths:

The first path: Allah has commanded us to emulate him. Thus every command directed to the Messenger ﷺ, for which no evidence specifies it for him alone, applies to us as well. We are commanded to follow him: ﴿Indeed, there has been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example for whoever hopes in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Ahzab 21].

Second: it is well known in discourse that an address directed to the one who is followed is addressed to him and to his follower. For example, a commander may say to an officer in the army: "Go to such-and-such a place." Does he mean: go yourself alone, or go with those who follow you? Go with those who follow you.

So in Arabic, when an address is directed to the one who is followed, it is addressed to him and to his follower. Thus the reason the ummah is a follower of the Messenger ﷺ in these commands, and in what they contain of prohibition, is one of two paths:

The first path: we have been commanded to follow the Messenger ﷺ.

The second path: an address directed to the one who is followed is addressed to him and to his follower.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his body﴾ [al-Ahzab 4]. ﴿Ma﴾ is a negation particle, the word Allah is the subject, and ﴿two hearts﴾ is the object of ﴿ja'ala﴾. The first or the second? The first is postponed, and its second object is ﴿for a man﴾. As for ﴿min﴾ here, we say it is extra in terms of i'rab, so we parse ﴿qalbayn﴾ as an accusative object. Its sign of accusative — this is the difficulty — is the fatha, but that is not possible; it is a yā' assumed (muqaddarah) over this yā' which was brought in. Why was it brought in? It was brought in for the particle, because the action of the apparent particle is stronger than the action of the hidden particle. For example, ja'ala governs the accusative qalbayn, but it was opposed — or more precisely, opposed by a stronger, immediate operator, the genitive particle (harf al-jarr). So they say: this yā' is not the yā' of the accusative, but the yā' of the extra genitive particle.

Accordingly we say: the sign of its accusative is an assumed yā' in place of the existing yā' which was brought in for the sake of the extra genitive particle.

Regarding His saying ﴿mā ja'ala﴾: is this ja'al (making) kawni (cosmic/determinative) or shar'i (legislative)? This ja'al is kawni, because the ja'al that is attributed to Allah is divided into two kinds: legislative ja'al, meaning what He legislated, and cosmic ja'al, meaning what He created.

An example of the legislative ja'al is His saying: ﴿Allah has not instituted any bahirah or sa'ibah﴾ [al-Ma'idah 103]. This is a legislative ja'al. What is the evidence? The evidence is that it exists as something made in the cosmic sense, but was not made in the legislative sense: ﴿Allah has not instituted any bahirah or sa'ibah﴾.

As for the cosmic ja'al, it is abundant, such as His saying: ﴿And We made you more in numbers﴾ [al-Isra' 6], and ﴿And We made the night as clothing (10) and We made the day for livelihood﴾ [an-Naba' 10–11].

In this noble verse, ﴿Allah has not made for a man two hearts﴾ — which of the two kinds? The cosmic kind: ﴿Allah has not made for a man two hearts﴾. Allah emphasized this negation with the extra genitive particle, because extra particles are among the instruments of emphasis.

So it is impossible that a human being has two hearts; in one human being, two hearts is impossible. But is this sentence intended for its own sake, or intended for something else?

The author and a group of commentators hold that it is intended for its own sake, and that it is a negation of a matter that had been claimed. For this reason He said, in response to some of the disbelievers who claimed that he had two hearts with each of which he understood better than the intellect of Muhammad ﷺ — this is what a group of scholars held. That is, this is a negation of a claim: a man among the disbelievers said that he had two hearts, and if he had two hearts he would have two intellects, and if he had two intellects he would be better than the Prophet ﷺ, because he has only one heart.

Some exegetes, foremost among them al-Zuhri, may Allah have mercy on him, held that this sentence is not intended for its own sake, because it is a known matter, since no human being has two hearts. Rather, it is a preface and a preparation for what follows, because three things are mentioned in the noble verse: ﴿Allah has not made for a man two hearts within his body, nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by zihar your mothers, nor has He made your adopted sons your sons﴾. Just as you acknowledge that there are not two hearts for a man within his body, likewise a wife is not a mother, because Allah has not made for a human being two mothers, just as he does not have two hearts; and likewise there is no non-real son, meaning a human being does not have a son who was created from his water and a son who is attributed to him but was not created from his water. Rather, your son is the one who was created from your water. Is it clear?

This is what Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, chose, holding that this sentence is a preface, because the absence of two hearts in one body is a known matter. As for the story they mention, its soundness must be examined, and even if it is sound, the one who says he has two hearts, his claim that he has two hearts indicates that he has no heart, because this is an impossible matter.

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿Allah has not made for a man two hearts within his body﴾. Is His saying ﴿within his body﴾ a restrictive qualification with a conditional implication, so that it would be said to you that he has two hearts outside his body? No, rather it is to clarify the reality, because it is well known that hearts are in bodies. This is like His saying: ﴿And there is no creature moving on the earth, nor bird that flies with its two wings, but they are communities like yourselves﴾ [al-An'am 38]. For His saying ﴿nor bird that flies with its two wings﴾ is like a person saying: "nor any walker that walks on two legs," to clarify the reality.

Although some later scholars, regarding His saying ﴿nor bird that flies with its two wings﴾, said that it is a restrictive conditional qualification to exclude the known aircraft, since it flies without two wings — it may be said that this is not correct, since even the aircraft now flies with its wings; where are the jet engines that fly it? In the wings. And the propellers that existed at first are the same as the wings. But there is no doubt that the aircraft is not among the communities that are like us; rather it is of our making.

So His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿within his body﴾ is for clarifying the reality. ﴿And nor has He made your wives whom...﴾ — it is recited with hamza and yā' (al-la'i) and without yā' — with hamza and yā' (al-la'i), and without yā', meaning with hamza without yā', so that it is (al-la') and (al-la'i), as we all know, the plural of what? The plural of (allati), is it not? So it is like (alladhina) for males, the plural? Yes.

(Al-la'i) — he says: "I have (tazzahharūna) without an alif before the hā', and the second tā' is originally assimilated into the zā'," tazzahharūna, this is one reading; and the second, he says: "without an alif before the hā'," and "with it" meaning with an alif before the hā', which becomes tazzāharūna. These are two readings, and until now the author has not mentioned the well-known reading among us, which is tuzāhirūna. So there are three readings in the verse: tazzahharūna, tazzāharūna, and the third tuzāhirūna. As for tazzāharūna and tazzahharūna, he says the tā' is assimilated into the zā', and its origin is: tatazāharūna or tatazahharūna, but it became tazzahharūna, the tā' being assimilated into the zā'.

What is the meaning of tuzāhirūna minhunna? It means you say that they are upon you like the backs of your mothers. This is a formula of divorce in the Jahiliyya: when a man wanted to divorce his wife with an irrevocable divorce, he would say to her, "You are to me like the back of my mother," and she would be divorced irrevocably, because the back of his mother is never lawful to him under any circumstances. He specified the back because it is the place of riding, and does a man ride his wife or she rides him? Yes, he rides her, because she is a bed, as the Messenger ﷺ said.

So tazzāharūna, what does tazzāharūna mean? It means you say to them: "You are upon us like the back of our mothers." The people of the Jahiliyya regarded this statement as an irrevocable divorce, but in Islam it is not a divorce; in Islam it is zihar, meaning that it necessitates the prohibition of the woman until the man does what Allah has commanded him, as in Surat al-Mujadilah.

Tazzāharūna minhunna: the one who says, for example, to his wife, "You are upon me like the back of my mother." Could he say a phrase other than this? He could say, "You are upon me like the back of my sister," or he could say, "You are upon me like the belly of my mother." The consideration is the meaning, not the wording. We have already gone over in the book of zihar that a man likens his wife to someone who is forbidden to him with a permanent prohibition, by kinship or by a permissible cause; the important thing is a permanent prohibition. This is zihar according to the scholars, and the disagreement was mentioned regarding whether he forbids her or does zihar with her by likening her to someone who is forbidden to him for a period of time.

* The student: (...).

* The Shaykh: The seven readings sometimes refer to this and that without saying "and in a reading"; and sometimes they say "and in a reading." He says: (saying, for example, by a man to his wife: "You are upon me like the back of my mother").

"Ummahatikum" — what made it accusative? "Ja'ala." Where is the first object? "Azwajakum," and "al-la'i" is its adjective, and "tuzāhirūna" is the relative clause of the relative pronoun, and "ummahatikum" is the second object. "Ummahatikum" means: like mothers in their prohibition by that which was established in the Jahiliyya as a divorce; and it obligates expiation only with its condition, as mentioned in Surat al-Mujadilah.

In Islam it is not a divorce, but a prohibition that obligates expiation with its condition, which is returning, by the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Then they wish to go back on what they said — then the freeing of a slave﴾ [al-Mujadilah 3]. (...)

﴿And Allah has not made your wives whom you liken to your mothers your mothers﴾: have we taken from it any benefits, or not?
