* The Shaykh: No, here al-mu'awwiq is specific to the one who discourages: ﴿al-mu'awwiqina minkum⁠﴾.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Perhaps you mean that (hal) comes for confirmation; that is correct.
He, Exalted, says: ﴿al-mu'awwiqina minkum⁠﴾ — the address is to whom? To the Prophet, peace be upon him, and the Companions. So this exists among the Companions: there are those who discourage.
(﴿and those who say to their brothers, "Come⁠"﴾: come to us, ﴿and they do not come to battle⁠﴾: fighting, ﴿except a little⁠﴾ for show and reputation.)
﴿and those who say to their brothers﴾ — ﴿al-qa'ilina⁠﴾ is coordinated with ﴿al-mu'awwiqin⁠﴾, meaning: and He knows those who say to their brothers "come to us." This is other than hindering, because the one who hinders is the one who knows the thing which hinders a person, but does not invite him; these, however, say it to their brothers, so it is more emphatic than hindering.
As for His saying ﴿and those who say to their brothers﴾, these are other than the hinderers, so it is not coordination of attribute but coordination of essence. The basis of coordination is that it should be for difference of essences, and it may be for difference of attributes, and it may be for difference of—
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No. How quickly you forget! The coordination is for difference: either in essence or in attributes.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, or wording, my brothers; every day it strikes your ears:
................... ∗∗∗ he found her saying to be false and lying.
This is not a change of meaning; the meaning is one, but the wording has changed.
As for His saying ﴿and those who say to their brothers, "Come to us"﴾, this refers to the hypocrites. They are called "their brothers" in terms of lineage, and not their brothers in religion — unless what is meant is apparent brotherhood, since these people pretend that they are believers.
﴿Hallumma⁠﴾: come to us. Is ﴿hallumma⁠﴾ a verb in the imperative, or a noun functioning as an imperative verb (ism fi'l al-amr)? It is an ism fi'l al-amr, yes; because not everything that indicates a demand is an imperative verb. The verbal noun may indicate a demand, as when you say: "striking, Zayd!" But what indicates a demand in itself, without an external particle, either accepts the sign of the imperative verb or does not. If it accepts it, it is an imperative verb; if it does not accept it, it is an ism fi'l al-amr, or it may be a verbal noun standing in for the imperative. Do you understand?
Our phrase "without an external particle" is to exclude the present tense preceded by the imperative lam, which indicates command, but not by itself; rather by another external particle, which is the lam of command.
﴿Hallumma⁠﴾ here is an ism fi'l al-amr, because we say to 'Isa: hallumma ilayna, hallumma ila al-dars, and to Ahmad and 'Isa together we say: hallumma ilayna, all together, and we add the brother and say: hallumma ila al-dars. It does not change: singular, dual and plural, does it not?
But if we were addressing one person we would say: hallumma ilayna, and addressing two: hallumma ilayna (dual form: hallumma), and addressing three or more: hallumma ilayna (plural: hallumu), then it would be an imperative verb. For this reason we say: qum (stand, m. sing.), qumaa (stand, dual), quu (stand, plural). So it is an ism fi'l al-amr, which you address the one, the two and the group with, and it does not change. This is according to the dialect of the people of the Hijaz.
As for Banu Tamim, it is an imperative verb for them. For this reason they say to the one: hallumma ilayna; to the two: hallumma ilayna; to the group: hallumma ilayna — it is an imperative verb.

Here he indicates that it is a verb-like particle of command (ism fi'l amr), because if it were an imperative verb he would have said *halummu ilaynā* (hallumma, "come here"). He means: "Come (ta'ālaw)." This is said to others, calling them to abandon fighting: "Come on." As for them, ﴿وَلَا يَأْتُونَ الْبَأْسَ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا﴾ ("And they do not come to the fight except a little"). ﴿لَا يَأْتُونَ الْبَأْسَ﴾ means: they do not come to the fighting. ﴿إِلَّا قَلِيلًا﴾: the word "qalīl" here may mean nonexistence, or it may mean a small amount. It is possible that for some people it means nonexistence and for others a little, since among the hypocrites some never attend the fighting at all, while others attend a little for show and reputation.

It is well known that whoever seeks show (riyā') and reputation (sum'ah), if he is in a place where he finds show and reputation, he attends; and if he is in a place where he finds neither, he does not attend.

What is the difference between *riyā'* and *sum'ah*? *Riyā'* relates to actions, and *sum'ah* relates to words, because actions are seen and words are heard. For this reason the hadith says: "Whoever shows off, Allah will show off [his deeds] for him, and whoever seeks to be heard, Allah will make him heard [of]."[[Recorded by Muslim (2986/47) from Ibn 'Abbās (may Allah be pleased with them both), with the wording: "Whoever seeks to be heard, Allah will make him heard of, and whoever shows off, Allah will show off for him."]] So if a person speaks words of remembrance and raises his voice so that he may be heard and praised for it, by what do we describe his act? *Sum'ah*. And if he stands to pray so that people may see him, that is *riyā'*.

The term *riyā'* may be applied to both together, but when they occur together, *riyā'* relates to actions and *sum'ah* to words. He says: "*riyā'an wa sum'ah*" (out of show and for reputation).

(﴿أَشِحَّةً عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 19], "grudging toward you," with respect to help; it is the plural of *shaḥīḥ*, and it is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the pronoun in ﴿يَأْتُونَ﴾), ﴿وَلَا يَأْتُونَ الْبَأْسَ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا﴾.

﴿أَشِحَّةً عَلَيْكُمْ﴾: *ashiḥḥah* is the plural of *shaḥīḥ*. The *shaḥīḥ* is one who withholds with greediness, while the *bakhīl* (miser) is one who withholds without greediness. So if a person is withholding and grasping, meaning with greed, he is called *shaḥīḥ*; and if he is a miser but is not the sort of man who is greedy to accumulate wealth, for example, he is called *bakhīl*. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) warned against *shuḥḥ* (avarice), saying: "Beware of *shuḥḥ*, for it destroyed those who came before you."[[Recorded by Muslim (2578/56) from Jābir ibn 'Abdullāh (may Allah be pleased with him), with the wording: "...and beware of *shuḥḥ*, for *shuḥḥ* destroyed those who were before you."]]

He says: ﴿أَشِحَّةً عَلَيْكُمْ﴾. What put it in the accusative?

* A student: It is a circumstantial state (ḥāl).
* The Shaykh: A ḥāl of whom? It is in the accusative as a ḥāl of the subject of ﴿يَأْتُونَ﴾. Meaning: they do not come except a little, and yet they come grudging toward you, meaning: they are grudging toward you, not wanting you to attain any good, but loving to prevent every good from reaching you.

﴿فَإِذَا جَاءَ الْخَوْفُ رَأَيْتَهُمْ يَنْظُرُونَ إِلَيْكَ﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 19]. ﴿جَاءَ الْخَوْفُ﴾: fear is not a substance that comes, but it is a meaning that comes. Coming may be ascribed to meanings as well as to entities. You say: "The illness came to him" (jā'ahu al-maraḍ), and you say: "Zayd came." Here the coming is ascribed to a meaning. "Fear came" from whom? It is general: when fear comes, whether from the enemies who arrived at Madīnah, or fear of the Messenger (ﷺ) in case he learns of their conditions, fearing that Allah the Exalted will expose them through their actions, or that He will give His Messenger power over them.

He says: ﴿فَإِذَا جَاءَ الْخَوْفُ رَأَيْتَهُمْ يَنْظُرُونَ إِلَيْكَ﴾. Is the address here to the Messenger (ﷺ), or to everyone to whom the address may be directed? It may be to the Messenger (ﷺ), and this is the closer view, and it may be to everyone to whom the address is directed.

As for His saying ﴿رَأَيْتَهُمْ يَنْظُرُونَ﴾, the seeing here is visual, and accordingly it governs only one object, which is the pronoun *hā'* (them), and the clause ﴿يَنْظُرُونَ﴾ is a circumstantial state of the *hā'*: "you saw them while they were looking at you." ﴿تَدُورُ أَعْيُنُهُمْ﴾ (their eyes roll around), because the one who fears generally fixes his attention on what? On the direction of the fear, whether it is a single person or several, he looks toward the direction that is the source of fear, and his eye rolls without sound sight, meaning as if it rolls involuntarily from the intensity of fear. Then He likened their state after He had likened their eyes, saying: ﴿كَالَّذِي يُغْشَى عَلَيْهِ مِنَ الْمَوْتِ﴾ (like one overcome by death's swoon). The author said: (like a look, or like rolling).

If ﴿كَالَّذِي﴾ refers back to ﴿يَنْظُرُونَ﴾, we estimate it as "a look"; if it refers back to ﴿تَدُورُ أَعْيُنُهُمْ﴾, we estimate it as "like rolling." But what fits the Qur'an better is the first: "a look," as Allah the Exalted said in Sūrat Muḥammad: ﴿يَنظُرُونَ إِلَيْكَ نَظَرَ الْمَغْشِيِّ عَلَيْهِ مِنَ الْمَوْتِ﴾ [Muḥammad 20], "They look at you with the look of one overcome by death's swoon." Perhaps we may say: ﴿يَنْظُرُونَ إِلَيْكَ تَدُورُ أَعْيُنُهُمْ كَالَّذِي يُغْشَى عَلَيْهِ مِنَ الْمَوْتِ﴾ does not refer back to the look, but refers to their state: like a person overcome by death's swoon, unable to speak, because their throats dried and their blood drained from fear. When fear comes, their sight changes and their states change too, like one who is overcome by death's swoon. Undoubtedly, one overcome by death's swoon turns pale, does not know what he is doing, and generally cannot speak. ﴿كَالَّذِي يُغْشَى عَلَيْهِ مِنَ الْمَوْتِ﴾: ﴿مِنَ الْمَوْتِ﴾, the author said: from its agonies (sakarātihi, i.e., its agonies). ﴿يُغْشَى عَلَيْهِ مِنَ الْمَوْتِ﴾: here ﴿مِنَ﴾ indicates causation. Does *min* come to indicate causation?

The answer: Yes, it comes in many contexts. Its basic use is to indicate the starting point (ibtidā'), and some grammarians even claimed that it always indicates the starting point, even where it indicates causation, saying that it is the starting point of the cause. But the correct view is that of Ibn Mālik and other grammarians, that it comes with many meanings. He said:

"Partitive, explicative, and beginning of place—these are the uses of *min*; and it comes for the beginning of times. It is added in negation and the like, so that it makes an indefinite noun general, as in: 'There is no runaway from ...'"

He said: (﴿فَإِذَا ذَهَبَ الْخَوْفُ﴾ and the spoils were gathered, ﴿سَلَقُوكُمْ﴾: they harmed you or struck you, ﴿بِأَلْسِنَةٍ حِدَادٍ أَشِحَّةً عَلَى الْخَيْرِ﴾, meaning: they seek the spoils, ﴿أُولَئِكَ لَمْ يُؤْمِنُوا﴾ in reality, ﴿فَأَحْبَطَ اللَّهُ أَعْمَالَهُمْ﴾).

﴿إِذَا ذَهَبَ الْخَوْفُ﴾: those who were, at the time of fear, like one overcome by death's swoon, now begin to speak with fluency. ﴿سَلَقُوكُمْ﴾: meaning they struck you severely. ﴿بِأَلْسِنَةٍ حِدَادٍ﴾: meaning sharp and strong. The "tongues" here means speech, because speech is expressed by the tongue. The meaning is that they argue and dispute, and say: "We are with you, we are helping, we went out," and similar things, as Allah the Exalted said in Sūrat al-Nisā': ﴿فَإِنْ كَانَ لَكُمْ فَتْحٌ مِنَ اللَّهِ قَالُوا أَلَمْ نَكُنْ مَعَكُمْ﴾ [al-Nisā' 141], "If there is a victory for you from Allah, they say: 'Were we not with you?'" They displayed and repeated this in their victory over the Muslims, because there is no doubt that a person may overcome his opponent with speech, as Allah the Exalted said about the story of Dāwūd: ﴿فَقَالَ أَكْفِلْنِيهَا وَعَزَّنِي فِي الْخِطَابِ﴾ [Ṣād 23], "He said: 'Give him to me to take charge of,' and he overpowered me in speech," and an eloquent person with clear expression and fluency may prevail even when he is upon falsehood. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "You bring your disputes to me, and perhaps one of you is more eloquent in his argument than another, so I judge for him according to what I hear."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (2680) and Muslim (1713/4) from Umm Salamah (may Allah be pleased with her).]] Even if he is upon falsehood. A person may overcome the truth by his eloquence. For this reason, as you know, the authentic hadith says: "Indeed, some eloquence is magic."[[Recorded by al-Bukhārī (5767) from Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both).]]

These hypocrites, in the state of fear in the form which Allah the Mighty and Majestic depicted—﴿يَنْظُرُونَ إِلَيْكَ تَدُورُ أَعْيُنُهُمْ كَالَّذِي يُغْشَى عَلَيْهِ مِنَ الْمَوْتِ﴾—but when fear departs and they feel secure, ﴿سَلَقُوكُمْ بِأَلْسِنَةٍ حِدَادٍ﴾, meaning they struck you severely with these sharp tongues, ﴿أَشِحَّةً عَلَى الْخَيْرِ﴾: this is a circumstantial state of the *waw* in His saying ﴿سَلَقُوكُمْ﴾.

﴿أَشِحَّةً عَلَى الْخَيْرِ﴾: what is meant by "the good" here? The author says: the spoils which the Muslims obtained through their victory. He said: ﴿أَشِحَّةً عَلَى الْخَيْرِ أُولَئِكَ لَمْ يُؤْمِنُوا﴾ in reality; had they believed, they would not have done this act, they would not have feared the Resurrection, nor would they have claimed what they did not deserve once the battle was over.

﴿أُولَئِكَ لَمْ يُؤْمِنُوا فَأَحْبَطَ اللَّهُ أَعْمَالَهُمْ﴾: what is the meaning of "He made their deeds fruitless"? It means He nullified them, so that they gain no benefit from them.

(﴿وَكَانَ ذَلِكَ﴾, the nullification, ﴿عَلَى اللَّهِ يَسِيرًا﴾, is easy for Him by His will.) Yes, it is easy for Allah the Mighty and Majestic, because He, Glorified and Exalted, does not fear anyone, as Allah the Exalted said about the people of Ṣāliḥ: ﴿فَدَمْدَمَ عَلَيْهِمْ رَبُّهُمْ بِذَنْبِهِمْ فَسَوَّاهَا (١٤) وَلَا يَخَافُ عُقْبَاهَا﴾ [al-Shams 14–15], "So their Lord destroyed them for their sin and leveled them, and He does not fear its consequence." He, Glorified and Exalted, does not fear the consequence of it, unlike others, unlike a created being. A created being may punish a person and inflict harm on him, but he fears its consequences: he fears his tribe, fears betrayal, and similar things. As for the Lord, the Mighty and Majestic, every matter is easy for Him, and He does not fear anyone when He takes vengeance. (...)

It has two meanings: sometimes it means "be present" (uḥḍur), and sometimes it means "bring present" (aḥḍir). In this verse it means (...).

Is this the beginning of the benefits? Are you certain?

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿قُلْ مَنْ ذَا الَّذِي يَعْصِمُكُمْ مِنَ اللَّهِ إِنْ أَرَادَ بِكُمْ سُوءًا أَوْ أَرَادَ بِكُمْ رَحْمَةً وَلَا يَجِدُونَ﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 17] to the end.

* From this noble verse is derived: the execution of Allah's decree, that His decree is effective over creation, and no one can prevent it.
The basis of this: ﴿قُلْ مَنْ ذَا الَّذِي يَعْصِمُكُمْ﴾, and the interrogative here—as has already been mentioned—means negation.
* Among its benefits: the affirmation of will (irāda) for Allah, Glorified and Exalted, by His saying ﴿إِنْ أَرَادَ بِكُمْ سُوءًا﴾.
* Among its benefits: a refutation of some sects of the Qadariyyah who say that Allah does not will evil; He wills only good, and does not will evil, based on His saying ﴿إِنْ أَرَادَ بِكُمْ سُوءًا﴾.

There is a difficulty in the verse: its apparent meaning is that Allah wills evil, while the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "And evil is not attributed to You."[[Recorded by Muslim (771/201) from 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with him).]] So what is the answer?

* A student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No.
* A student: This is evil with respect to the created thing; as for with respect to the Creator (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, we say: evil is with respect to the things made (mafʿūlāt), but with respect to Allah's own act, which is His doing, it is not evil. An illness, for example, is evil with respect to the servant: it grieves him and does not gladden him, but with respect to Allah's decree concerning it, it is good and wisdom, as we have pointed out many times.

So our answer to this difficulty is: evil returns to the thing made, not to the act which is Allah's decree. A parallel: if a compassionate, merciful father's child is afflicted with a disease, and he cauterizes him with a heated iron on fire, undoubtedly this would hurt the child, because it pains and aches him. But is it an offense against him? No. With respect to the father's act it is not an offense; rather it is good, even though it pains the child.

* A student: Shaykh, is this derived from His saying ﴿وَهُوَ أَهْوَنُ عَلَيْهِ﴾ [al-Rūm 27]?
* The Shaykh: No, rather from the category that this... this is separate from this.
* The student: (...) the address is with respect to the state of the one addressed.
* The Shaykh: No, rather (...) the reality of the matter: evil does not go back to Allah; meaning that Allah's acts are not themselves evil; evil occurs only in the things made.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah the Mighty and Majestic has no one who can withhold what He gives, nor give what He withholds. By His saying ﴿إِنْ أَرَادَ بِكُمْ سُوءًا أَوْ أَرَادَ بِكُمْ رَحْمَةً﴾, no one can prevent what Allah has given, and no one can give what Allah has withheld. On this basis is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "O Allah, there is no one who can withhold what You give, and no one who can give what You withhold."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhārī (844) and Muslim (593/137) from al-Mughīrah ibn Shu'bah (may Allah be pleased with him).]]

* Among its benefits: it urges a person to attach himself to Allah, Glorified and Exalted, rather than anyone else, by His saying ﴿مَنْ ذَا الَّذِي يَعْصِمُكُمْ مِنَ اللَّهِ إِنْ أَرَادَ بِكُمْ سُوءًا أَوْ أَرَادَ بِكُمْ رَحْمَةً﴾. If the whole matter is in Allah's hand, a person attaches himself to his Lord rather than to others.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: those disbelievers will not find anyone other than Allah to help them or to be their protector, by His saying ﴿وَلَا يَجِدُونَ لَهُمْ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ وَلِيًّا وَلَا نَصِيرًا﴾. From this follows the severing of every bond between the polytheists and their idols, and that their idols do not benefit them, whatever the case.

But there is an objection to this: those who call upon idols may obtain what they asked of these idols, so how can we say that they do not benefit them?

The answer: this may occur as a trial and test from Allah the Mighty and Majestic. We know that this did not happen through these idols, or through their invocation; it happened in his presence, not because of it. What happens in the presence of a thing is not the same as what happens because of a thing. Is that clear?

If you say: "We do not accept this from you, that it happened not because of their invocation. As long as the man called and obtained his aim, how can you say it was from an external matter and not from their invocation?" What is the answer?

* A student: It is predestined (muqaddar).
* The Shaykh: It does not contradict... we know it is predestined. This is a man who invoked this grave and got what he wanted.
* A student: Does he not know that invoking at a grave is forbidden by the Sharia?
* The Shaykh: No, he invoked the grave, not at the grave; he invoked the occupant of the grave.
* The student: It is forbidden by the Sharia, and this does not happen from it.
* The Shaykh: He will tell you it happened. He says: "O my master, O my lord, O so-and-so, I am poor, I hope you will give me money." On that very day his relative died, who left millions, and no one inherited it except him. It happened.
* The student: It is from Allah's decree.
* The Shaykh: You say it is from Allah's decree, and he says: this is from the saint (walī).
* The student: ﴿سَنَسْتَدْرِجُهُمْ مِنْ حَيْثُ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ [al-Qalam 44], "We will gradually draw them in from where they do not know."
* The Shaykh: He says: who told you it is istidrāj (gradual lead-on)?
* The student: It is from the category of trial.
* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, it is a trial, my brothers, but (...).
* A student: (...) it is considered a temptation for these people.
* The Shaykh: It is a temptation and a test. We told him: this is a temptation, and your invocation did not obtain anything from Him; rather this happened at the time of your invocation, not by your invocation. So he said: "Woe to you, you do not know the worth of the saints, and I called and my aim was achieved."
* The student: Sometimes it comes once, and does not come (again)...
* The Shaykh: He says: "I have no need." Perhaps we challenge him and say: "Invoke once more," and then the decree comes in agreement (...).
* The student: All of this is not in his hand, there is no power or strength; if it were, he would have prevented death from himself.

The Shaykh: All of these are sick reasons, my brothers. We have told you: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has cut off every attachment to other than Him. ﴿And who is more astray than one who calls on other than Allah, such as will not respond to him until the Day of Resurrection?﴾ [al-Ahqaf 5]. From the noble verse we know that this one will not respond to you until the Day of Resurrection. He also said: ﴿If you call them, they will not hear your call; and if they heard, they would not respond to you. And on the Day of Resurrection they will deny your association of them﴾ [Fatir 14]. And the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Call upon those you claimed besides Allah. They do not possess an atom's weight in the heavens or on the earth, nor do they have any share in them, nor is there for Him any supporter among them. (22) And intercession with Him will not benefit except for one whom He permits﴾ [Saba' 22-23]. These are very clear verses that it is not possible for it to respond. If it is not possible for it to respond to him, then we know with certainty that what happened was not the supplication of this saint, because Allah has denied that it could respond to him.

A student: It is the very same.

The Shaykh: It is only present at the time of the supplication, and it is not by the supplication. So, at the thing, meaning it is near to it. This has passed by us, I think, the doctrine of whom?

A student: The Ash'aris.

The Shaykh: The Ash'aris. They say: Causes do not have an effect by themselves; rather the effect occurs with them, not by them. Yes indeed. So when a glass bottle is struck by a stone and shatters, they say: This did not break from the impact of the glass against the stone; it occurred at the moment of its impact with it, but not by it. In any case, this is not...

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Allah already knows those among you who hinder others and those who say to their brothers﴾ [al-Ahzab 18], to the end.

From this noble verse is derived: the comprehensive knowledge of Allah, glorified and exalted, of everything. Because this is a particular matter within the world: the saying of these people, ﴿Come to us﴾, and their hindering is one individual among the individuals of the world, a small part not attributed to the world as a whole, yet Allah knows it. And the One who knows the minute knows the great all the more so. Yes. Thus it establishes the comprehensive knowledge of Allah of everything, in total and in detail.

And among its benefits: the affirmation of Allah's knowledge in the future, since it came in the present-tense form.

And among them: the threat and warning against hindering from fighting. What is its basis?

A student: ﴿Qad ya'lamu﴾.

The Shaykh: ﴿Qad ya'lamu Allah﴾, and this is for the sake of threatening them, so that they will not do that.

And among the benefits of the noble verse: the cooperation of the hypocrites with one another, by His saying: ﴿and those who say to their brothers﴾. If that is so, then ﴿those who say﴾ is a conjunction with ﴿those who hinder﴾, as a conjunction of attributes. We mentioned in the commentary that it is possible that it is a conjunction of attributes or a conjunction of essences. If it is a conjunction of attributes, then ﴿those who hinder﴾ are the ones who say. If it is a conjunction of essences, then they become two categories: a hinderer and a sayer. The hinderer may call out and say: "Come on, leave it," and may not call out. But in any case they are among the hypocrites, because the end of the verse nullifies the possibility we mentioned yesterday, that it could be about one of the believers.

And it is derived from the noble verse: that those hinderers, toward others, are themselves cowards; by His saying: ﴿and they do not come to battle except a little﴾. So they are cowards, deterrers, and spreaders of demoralization.

And also among the benefits of the noble verse: that every person who accompanies another and mixes with him... by His saying: ﴿and those who say to their brothers﴾, for this is a brotherhood in evil and hypocrisy, not in faith.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Stingy towards you. Then when fear comes, you see them looking at you﴾ [al-Ahzab 19], to the end.

In this verse: there is evidence of the miserliness of the hypocrites with what benefits the believers, and that they do not come to them except with reluctance, like the stingy one in spending wealth; by His saying: ﴿stingy towards you﴾.

And among it: the cowardice of the hypocrites, and that they are in the utmost cowardice; by His saying: ﴿Then when fear comes, you see them looking at you with their eyes rolling﴾, to the end.

And with this we know that they are most deserving of what they described the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions with, when they said: "We have never seen the likes of these reciters of ours: more greedy in their bellies, more lying in their tongues, and more cowardly at the meeting." So we say: these descriptions are more fitting for you than anyone.

And among the benefits of the noble verse: the intensity of the hypocrites' terror at fear, because their being depicted in this manner indicates the great dread that seizes them at fear.

And also among the benefits of the noble verse: the intensity of the hypocrites' love of life, because they only reached this state through fear, out of eagerness for life and fear of death in fighting.

And among the benefits of the noble verse: the strength of the Qur'an's depiction of actual situations, because this image that Allah mentioned is an astonishing image, making a person imagine the intensity of their dread as if seen with one's own eyes.

And among the benefits of the noble verse: that death has agonies; by His saying: ﴿like one who is overcome by death﴾. This applies to ordinary death; sudden death, however, may have no agonies. A person may die suddenly, like those who die in accidents, heart failures, and the like.

And among the benefits of the noble verse: that these cowardly hypocrites, when the fear has gone, although at the time of fear they are like the dead, or like one who is overcome by death, once it goes they become eloquent speakers and masters of fluency and domination; by His saying: ﴿Then when fear departs, they assail you with sharp tongues﴾. Their speech comes once the fear is gone; they begin talking.

And among its benefits: the harshness of the hypocrites toward the believers, that they are harsh and rough against them; by His saying: ﴿they assail you with sharp tongues﴾.

And among its benefits: that the hypocrites, as the poet said:
"A lion against me, yet in wars an ostrich..." ........................
are lions against the believers, falsely of course, not in truth; and among the disbelievers they are ostriches. You know the ostrich, from its cowardice: when it sees the hunter it says, "This one will kill me," so it puts its head in the dirt so it will not see him. Yes indeed.

And among the benefits of the noble verse: the knowledge of Allah, glorified and exalted, of what is in the hearts; ﴿Those have not believed﴾. For outwardly it appears to us that they are believers, but in reality they are not believers.

And among the benefits of the noble verse: the warning against these attributes that the hypocrite is characterized by, even if the person is a believer. Why? Because they are the attributes of non-believers; by His saying: ﴿Those have not believed﴾, and the believer is forbidden from being characterized by the attributes of non-believers.

And among the benefits of the noble verse: that disbelief nullifies deeds, whether apparent or hidden; by His saying: ﴿so Allah has nullified their deeds﴾.

In general there is a difficulty in this verse, because nullification is a branch of the existence of a thing, and they are hypocrites whose deeds are void from the outset. So how do we answer this?

The answer: it is said that nullification is of two kinds: nullification of what was completed, and nullification of what was not completed. The nullification of what was completed is clear: when a thing is completed and then cancelled. The nullification of what was not completed is that it was void from the beginning. From this is the saying of some jurists: if one does not say the opening takbir, his prayer is invalid. So we say here: he did not pray such that it becomes void, but this is the invalidity of what was not completed and did not exist.

Or a second answer: we say Allah nullified their deeds. Do their deeds have outward validity or not? Because they are from a people who claim Islam and perform them according to the outward Shari'ah, but in reality they are void for lack of foundation.

And among the benefits of the noble verse: the importance of sincerity to Allah, Mighty and Majestic; by His saying: ﴿Those have not believed, so He nullified﴾. He made nullification a branch of non-belief, and this indicates that the fundamental pillar of deeds is faith.

Can it be derived from the noble verse that deeds increase in strength with the strength of faith, and in excellence?

A student: Yes indeed.

The Shaykh: How so? Because when deeds were nullified for lack of faith, this indicates that they are strengthened by the strength of faith. For this reason the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said about the Companions: "If one of you were to spend gold equal to Uhud, it would not reach the mudd of one of them nor half of it." It is the same deed, but the doer differs. There is a difference between one who acts with firm, strong faith, as if he sees the reward with his own eyes, and a person not in this state.

So the excellence of deeds is based on the excellence of what is in the hearts. It is reported from al-Hasan al-Basri, may Allah have mercy on him, that he said: "By Allah, Abu Bakr did not outstrip them through much fasting or prayer, but he outstripped them by what settled in his heart, may Allah be pleased with him," of great and firm faith.

And it should not be said that this opens a door for the sinners, who, when someone tells them, "Fear Allah, leave off sin, fear Allah, establish the obligation," says: "Piety is here," and strikes his chest a blow that echoes: "Piety is here." What do we say to him? We say: "Piety is here," true, but this is a word of truth by which falsehood is intended. We tell him: If piety were here, it would have been piety in the rest of you; because the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "When the heart is sound, the whole body is sound." If what is here were sound, the outward would be sound.

In sum, this verse is clear; the evidence in it is a clear proof that deeds vary in excellence according to the faith in the hearts, or not? And I have brought you a witness from the hadith, his saying, peace and blessings be upon him, about the Companions: "If one of you were to spend gold equal to Uhud, it would not reach the mudd of one of them nor half of it." Is the mudd of one of them of gold, or of food? It is possible.

Some say: the mudd of one of them of food, because that is what is customarily measured. That is, if one of you spent gold equal to Uhud, it would not reach the mudd of one of them of dates, because that is what is customarily measured.

Others say: it would not reach the mudd of one of them of gold, because the difference between food and gold is too great, but the difference between a small amount of gold and a large amount of gold is what is meant. (...)

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verses 13–16 (part 1 of 5):**

﴿And a faction of them said: "O people of Yathrib, there is no place for you, so return."﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 13]. ﴿And when﴾ is connected to what came before. ﴿And when the hypocrites say﴾ means: remember this abominable statement, ﴿when a faction of them said﴾. A *ṭāʾifah* (faction) is a group of people. The pronoun in ﴿minhum﴾ (of them) refers to the hypocrites, as the author said: (﴿And when a faction of them said﴾, that is, of the hypocrites).

﴿O people of Yathrib﴾. Yathrib, he says, is the land of Madinah. It was also said that it is Madinah itself. Scholars of history differed over whether Yathrib is the name of the place and the district in which Madinah lies, or whether Yathrib is Madinah itself. The apparent meaning of the hadith is that Yathrib is Madinah.

His words: (﴿O people of Yathrib﴾: it is the land of Madinah, and it is not diptoted, due to *ʿalamiyyah* (being a proper name) and the *wazn al-fiʿl* (the verbal pattern)). That is, it is prohibited from taking nunation for these two reasons: being a proper noun and having the form of a verb. The evidence that it is diptote is that it is in the genitive with a fatḥah, because it is in apposition/annexed to what follows it, and the annexed noun ought to be in the genitive. Here the word carries a fatḥah because it is in the genitive by fatḥah, like all the other nouns that are not declined.

The author's words (for *ʿalamiyyah* and *wazn al-fiʿl*): because Yathrib, which is a name, has the pattern of Yathrib, which is a verb. It has another reason besides the verbal pattern, namely the feminine form: *ʿalamiyyah* and *taʾnīth* (feminine marking), because it is the name of a locality. It seems that the author, may Allah have mercy on him, said (*for ʿalamiyyah and wazn al-fiʿl*) to indicate that this word (Yathrib) is derived from *tathrīb*, which means blame, reproach, and similar words that contain reproach. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have been commanded to go to a town that will consume the other towns. They call it Yathrib, but it is Madinah."[[Agreed upon (Muttafaq ʿalayh); al-Bukhari (1871) and Muslim (1382/488), from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him).]] This is evidence that the Messenger (ﷺ) disliked the name Yathrib, and that is one of the two opinions on the question.

As for the hadith that is narrated: "Whoever calls Madinah Yathrib, let him seek forgiveness from Allah,"[[Recorded by Abu Yaʿla in his Musnad (1688), from al-Bara' ibn ʿAzib (may Allah be pleased with him).]] it is weak. But it is sufficient to rely on the hadith in the two Sahihs: "They say, 'Yathrib,' but it is Madinah; it expels people as the bellows expels the impurities of iron."[[Agreed upon (Muttafaq ʿalayh); al-Bukhari (1871), Muslim (1382/488), from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him).]]

The summary: his words ﴿O people of Yathrib﴾ — it seems the author chose to say that it was not derived from a verb for this reason.

(﴿O people of Yathrib, there is no place for you﴾ — with a *ḍamm* and a *fatḥah* on the *mīm*, that is: there is no residence and no standing.) The word *muqām* is read with a *ḍamm* and with a *fatḥah* on the *mīm*. What does the author's statement mean? These are two readings: ﴿lā muqāma﴾ and ﴿lā maqāma﴾. He said: (there is no residence and no standing). "There is no residence" is an explanation of the *ḍamm* in ﴿muqām﴾, because it is from the quadriliteral verb, and the verbal noun of the quadriliteral is formed as *muqām*. And ﴿maqām﴾ means "no standing/position," as a noun of place. The noun of place takes a *fatḥah* on the *mīm*. The meaning is: there is no place for residing, if it is taken as a noun of place; or: there is no residence for you. Why do they say "there is no place for you"? Because they want to flee, and they do not want to remain with the Prophet (ﷺ) in battle. They are hypocrites, and the hypocrite is not patient in fighting; rather he does not want to fight. And if the matter were in his hand, whom would he fight? The Muslims.

In His words ﴿O people of Yathrib﴾ there is a clear indication of tribalism and partisanship, because He addressed them by the name of their homeland. He did not say "O our brothers," nor "O believers," but "O people of Yathrib," because he had no religion for which he would fight; he was merely a tribalist who wanted only zeal.

﴿There is no place for you, so return﴾ — return where? The author says: (to your dwellings in Madinah. They had gone out with the Prophet (ﷺ) to Sal' — a mountain outside Madinah — to fight).

His words ﴿there is no place for you﴾ are, as is known in the Arabic language, a general negation, because the *lā* of generic negation indicates generality. That is: there is no standing at all in any circumstance, so return. Such an expression, when said to a people in whose hearts there is no faith, leaves none of them behind; they must return.

Then Allah, mighty and majestic, said, based on this command and on the fact that they have no position: ﴿And a group of them asks permission of the Prophet﴾. These are lesser than the first ones, because the first ones called for flight without seeking permission, saying: ﴿there is no place for you, so return﴾. As for these, they ask the Prophet (ﷺ) for permission. But their asking permission of the Messenger (ﷺ) is not like the asking of the believers, who, when they are with him on a matter requiring assembly, do not leave until they seek his permission. Rather, they seek permission through deception and pretence. For this reason He says: ﴿a group of them asks permission of the Prophet﴾, that is, of the hypocrites, asking the Prophet (ﷺ) to let them return, ﴿saying﴾.

﴿Yastaʾdhinu﴾ means: seeks permission, because the form *istafʿala* often means seeking something, as in *istaghfara* (sought forgiveness), i.e., sought forgiveness; and *istaʿtaba* (sought reproach/admonition), i.e., sought to be admonished.

His words ﴿yaqūlūna﴾ (saying): this clause is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from ﴿farīq﴾ (a group), meaning while they are saying, or it is an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) or a substitute (badal) for ﴿yastaʾdhinu﴾. Both have a basis. As for taking it as a circumstantial clause, that is because the indefinite noun here has been described, and an indefinite noun, when described, becomes specified, so a circumstantial clause may come from it. Is this not so? As for taking it as a substitute or explanatory apposition, it follows the saying of Ibn Malik, may Allah have mercy on him. What did he say?

*And a verb may be substituted for a verb, like: whoever reaches us, seeks help from us, and he will be helped.*

So two possibilities are allowed: it may be a substitute for ﴿yastaʾdhinu﴾, or an explanatory apposition like a substitute, or a circumstantial clause from the subject of ﴿yastaʾdhinu﴾.

﴿They say: "Indeed our houses are exposed"﴾. He said: (not fortified, and feared for). They say to the Messenger (ﷺ), as a justification for the request for permission: ﴿Indeed our houses are ʿawrah﴾, and we fear for them from the enemy. *ʿAwrah* here means not fortified, because a fortress protects and covers them, just as a garment covers a man's nakedness. So this is the meaning of their saying that it is *ʿawrah*: exposed, and it is impossible for us to be safe from the enemy's attack upon it.

In a reading that is not among the seven canonical readings, it is read *ʿawira* with a *kasrah* on the *wāw*, meaning: defective.

Allah, exalted, said refuting their claim: ﴿And they are not exposed; they only intend to flee﴾. Here it is necessary to pause at His words ﴿Indeed our houses are exposed﴾, because if you continued, it would give the impression that the words ﴿and they are not exposed﴾ are part of the hypocrites' speech, and this would produce contradiction and corruption of the meaning. So you pause at ﴿They say: Indeed our houses are exposed﴾, then you resume reading and say: ﴿And they are not exposed﴾.

His words ﴿wa-mā hiya bi-ʿawrah﴾ (and they are not exposed): I would like to hear its grammatical analysis from one of you, O grammarians of Basra.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Is it indeclinable with a *kasrah*?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: With a sukūn.
* Student: A fatḥah.
* Shaykh: A fatḥah? Correct.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Grammatically superfluous.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Suppose someone said: who says it is the Ḥijāzī construction, since the text is not explicit about the predicate? Could ﴿bi-ʿawrah﴾ not be the predicate of the subject, in the nominative with a presumed ḍamm on its last letter, prevented from showing because of the occupation of the position (by the preposition)? So what shall we answer him?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: What is the evidence? We want a witness from the Qur'an supporting your view.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿This is not a human being﴾ — it is in the accusative. This shows that the Qur'an was revealed according to the usage of the people of the Ḥijāz.

Allah, exalted, said: ﴿And they are not exposed; they only intend to flee﴾. As for ﴿in﴾, the author said: *mā* (not). What is the meaning of this *mā*?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: An explanation of ﴿in﴾? So here ﴿in﴾ is what?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Negative, because it has been explained by *mā*, and *mā* is negative. And the evidence for that is that ﴿illā﴾ (except) comes after it, is that not so? ﴿They only intend to flee﴾. This is evidence that it is negative. *In* comes as a negative, as here, and it comes as a conditional. What is an example? ﴿And if you return, We will return﴾ [al-Anfāl: 19]. It also comes as a lightened form of the heavy (*an*). Like what?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: That is *an*.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, that is conditional.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: *An*.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: ﴿Indeed these two are certainly magicians﴾ [Ṭāhā: 63]. This is a lightened form of the heavy. These are three. Does it also come as superfluous?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: That is *an*. There is no contradiction in it. If there were nothing in the Arabic except the Qur'an, bring us something from the speech of the Arabs or from outside the Qur'an.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh:
*... mā in antum dhahabun*
*wa-lā ṣarīfun wa-lakin antumu l-khazafu*

*You are not gold, nor refined silver, but you are only clay pottery.*

This *in* is superfluous, or not? That is, *mā in antum* means *mā antum* (you are not). What determines these meanings? Context determines them, and this is agreed upon among the scholars: the existence of homonymous words that are specified by context is established in the Arabic language.

But they differed on the question of literal and figurative meaning. Some affirmed it and some denied it, and they said that figurative and literal meaning are like homonymy. You (the students) hold to homonymy, and this is the preferred view, as was mentioned several times before: the correct view is that there is no figurative usage in the Arabic language.

He says: ﴿in yurīdūna﴾ — this is the speech of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿And they are not exposed; they only intend to flee﴾. That is, they intend nothing but flight. As you see, this sentence is restrictive; it indicates exclusivity: these people have no intention at all except to flee from fighting. Their houses are fortified, and nothing is feared for them more than for Madinah. They have no excuse except one, namely fleeing from battle, because they do not want to face the enemy; rather they are the enemy, as Allah said of them.

Allah, exalted, said: ﴿And if it had been entered upon them from its sides, and then they were asked for fitnah, they would have given it﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 14]. ﴿Wa-law﴾ (and if) is conditional here; its condition is ﴿dukhilat﴾ (it were entered), and its response is ﴿la-ātawhā﴾ (they would have given it).

﴿If it had been entered upon them from its sides﴾: the agent was explained by the author as Madinah. That is, if Madinah were entered upon them from its sides. His explanation of it as Madinah is supported by His words at the beginning of the verse: ﴿O people of Yathrib, there is no place for you﴾. Some explained it as the houses, that is: if the houses were entered upon them from their sides.

This interpretation is supported by their saying: ﴿Indeed our houses are exposed﴾. But the first is preferred, that it is Madinah, because of His words ﴿from its sides﴾, since ﴿min aqṭārihā﴾ (from its sides) generally does not refer to houses, because houses are small, and their directions are not called *aqṭār*. The term *aqṭār* is used only for large things.

For this reason he said: (﴿from its sides﴾, that is, its regions), meaning if the enemy entered Madinah from all its regions, or from any one of its regions. (﴿Then they were asked﴾, that is, those who entered asked them ﴿for fitnah﴾; ﴿they would have given it﴾, with a long vowel and with a short vowel, that is: they would have given it and done it).

﴿Then they were asked for fitnah﴾ — the agent? The deputy agent is the hypocrites. But the one who asks, the agent in meaning, is the one who entered Madinah from its sides. If this entrant asked them for *fitnah*, the author says *fitnah* means *shirk* (polytheism). The evidence that *fitnah* means *shirk* is His words: ﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 193], that is, until there is no shirk.

Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said regarding His words: ﴿Let those who oppose His command beware lest a fitnah befall them﴾ [al-Nūr: 63]: Do you know what *fitnah* is? *Fitnah* is shirk. These people, if Madinah were entered upon them, would not have sincere adherence to Islam and steadfastness in it. As soon as the entrants ask them for disbelief, they would agree to it, because they are people who want only this world; they want to live in this world even the life of a donkey. As for living the life of the believers, they do not want this. For this reason He says: ﴿If they were asked for fitnah﴾, (...).

Short vowel; *ātawhā* is the long vowel. The difference between them: *atā* means "came," and *ātā* means "gave." The explanation of the two readings, or the combined explanation, shows that they would give what they were asked, and come to it submissively. That is, *atā al-shayʾ* means it came to them by their choice, while *ātāhu* means he gave him, even if unwillingly. Nevertheless, these are people who give what they are asked — by choice. For this reason, in the second reading ﴿la-ātawhā﴾ means they would come to it (*lajāʾūhā*).

So these people who make excuses, or who ask the Prophet (ﷺ) for permission on the pretext that their houses are exposed, the matter has turned contrary to what they said, because Allah informed about them, and He, glory be to Him, knows what is in their hearts. This is from Allah's knowledge of what is in the hearts. He informed about a future matter that had not occurred, which would proceed from people whose hearts we do not know, but Allah knows. Allah, mighty and majestic, knows what His servant would do if what would bring about this intent happened to them.

Indeed, He, glory be to Him, knows even more than that. He said about those who say that if they were returned to the world they would do righteous deeds: ﴿And if they were returned, they would return to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-Anʿām: 28], because He, glory be to Him, knows what is in a person's heart. He said: ﴿And they would not remain therein except briefly﴾. ﴿They would have come to it, and they would not have lingered therein except briefly.﴾ *Talabbathū* means *tarayyathū*, that is, they would not hesitate in giving and accepting *fitnah* except briefly.

His words ﴿illā yasīran﴾ (except briefly): it was said that this means *illā ʿadaman* (except [almost] nothing), because "little" and "few" may be intended to mean nonexistence.

Some said: ﴿illā yasīran﴾ means except a little in the true sense, and this brief time is the interval between the question and the answer. That is, the interval between being asked and answering. Is this period long or not? It is very short. It is like the interval between a seller saying, "I have sold you this item," and the buyer saying, "I accept." That is, they — may Allah protect us — do not delay or hesitate at all; rather they accept immediately. Between their acceptance and the asking of the *fitnah* there is nothing except the interval between the asking and the answering.

In reality this short period is like nothing, and for this reason His words ﴿illā yasīran﴾ were explained as meaning "except [almost] nothing."

﴿And they had already promised Allah before, that they would not turn their backs, and the promise of Allah will be questioned﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 15]. ﴿And they had already﴾ — this sentence is emphasized with how many emphatic particles?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The *wāw* is not an emphasis.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: With *lām* and *qad*. What comes after? We said three.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: An implied oath. Whenever such an expression occurs in the Qur'an, it is emphasized with the three emphatic particles: "By Allah, they had certainly promised Allah before." An oath was previously mentioned to us: Allah swears about something not in the sense of denial, but in the sense of importance. He may also swear about something in the sense of denial, like: ﴿Those who disbelieved claim that they will not be resurrected. Say: Yes, by my Lord, you will certainly be resurrected﴾ [al-Taghābun: 7].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verse 13–16 (part 2 of 5):

Here Allah, exalted is He, emphasizes this covenant from them: that they had earlier made a covenant with Allah not to turn their backs. This covenant was between them and the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and making a covenant with the Messenger ﷺ is making a covenant with Allah, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, [O Muhammad], they are actually pledging allegiance to Allah﴾ [al-Fath 10]. So they had covenanted with the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, that they would not flee and would not turn their backs, but they broke the covenant. Breaking covenants, betrayal and lying are traits of whom? They are traits of the hypocrites; that is their nature. We ask Allah for well-being.

﴿They had earlier made a covenant with Allah not to turn their backs﴾. What is the grammatical position (i'rab) of His saying: ﴿not to turn their backs﴾? Some of them said: it has no grammatical position, because it is an answer to the statement "they covenanted" (ʿahada). Others said: it is an explanation of the covenant, meaning: the covenant that took place was that they would not turn their backs.

The phrase ﴿لَا يُوَلُّونَ الأَدْبَارَ﴾ (lā yuwallūna al-adbār, "not turn their backs") requires two objects: the first object is al-adbār (the backs), and the second object is omitted, and the implied meaning is: not turn their backs toward their enemy. Turning the back (tawliyat al-dubur) means departing and deviating; instead of their faces being toward the enemy, their backs would be toward the enemy. They swore first and covenanted that they would not turn their backs when meeting the enemy, but they broke the covenant. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the covenant of Allah is ever questioned﴾. The author said: (﴿And the covenant of Allah is ever questioned﴾ concerning its fulfillment).

Based on this, the questioning is not about the covenant itself, but about fulfilling it. The covenant is "questioned", meaning it is questioned about its fulfillment, and questioning about its fulfillment is also questioning about its occurrence. It is said, for example: "Is there not a covenant between me and you? Did you not break the covenant?" So the question is about the covenant itself and about its fulfillment. When does this accountability take place: in this world or in the Hereafter?

As for the accountability between a person and his Lord, it is in the Hereafter, and as for the accountability between him and people, it is in this world: he is required to fulfill the covenant. ﴿And the covenant of Allah is ever questioned﴾.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say, "Flight will not benefit you if you flee from death or killing"﴾ [al-Ahzab 16]. The word ﴿لَنْ﴾ (lan) conveys three things, which the brother will mention for us.

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Negation, and the subjunctive (naṣb).
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: And futurity: that is, the present-tense verb is ambiguous between the present and the future; when ﴿لَنْ﴾ (lan) precedes it, it is necessarily future. Does ﴿لَنْ﴾ (lan) indicate perpetual negation? That is, does it necessitate and entail perpetual negation, or does it come for perpetuity and for non-perpetuity?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Always for non-perpetuity?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: And does it come for perpetuity?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: That is, it comes for this and for that? Give an example of perpetuity.
* Student: ﴿فَإِنْ لَمْ تَفْعَلُوا وَلَنْ تَفْعَلُوا﴾ [al-Baqarah 24]?
* The Shaykh: ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do it﴾, and the verse we have is for perpetuity: ﴿Flight will not benefit you if you flee from death or killing﴾. And does it come for non-perpetuity?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Apparently it is for perpetuity here, or perhaps they may harm them with more than harm. What do you say about this verse: is it for perpetuity or for non-perpetuity? ﴿They will not harm you except with a little injury﴾ [Ali 'Imran 111]. Could they harm the believers with something other than injury, or do they only harm them with injury?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿But they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have sent ahead﴾ [al-Baqarah 95]. Is this for perpetuity?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Do they not wish for death? In the torment of the Fire they wish for death.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, in this world they do not wish for death; but even in this world it is emphasized by His saying: "never" (abadan). The correct view is that ﴿لَنْ﴾ (lan) does not necessarily entail perpetuity, as Ibn Malik said:

"Whoever sees the negation with lan as perpetual, / Then reject his statement, and support the other."

It cannot always be for perpetuity; that is, its meaning does not necessitate perpetuity, though it may convey it. For this reason the People of the Sunnah said that the words of Allah to Musa: ﴿You will never see Me﴾ do not necessitate that Allah is not seen either in this world or in the Hereafter. As for the Mu'tazilah and those who deny the seeing of Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, they say: ﴿لَنْ﴾ (lan) conveys perpetuity, so it indicates that Allah is never seen. Yes indeed.

﴿Say, "Flight will not benefit you if you flee from death or killing"﴾, meaning: if you do not flee from death or killing, would flight benefit you? This condition is to explain the actual situation, because there is no flight unless they flee, so it benefits them nothing from death or killing.

He said: ﴿وَإِذًا﴾ (wa-idhan), meaning: even supposing that you fled from death or killing, (﴿وَإِذًا﴾ if you fled, ﴿لَا تُمَتَّعُونَ﴾ you would not be given enjoyment in the world after your flight, ﴿إِلَّا قَلِيلًا﴾ except for a little, namely the remainder of your lifespans).

That is: on the supposition that you fled from death or from killing, will you remain alive? No, they will not remain; if they flee, they will not be given enjoyment except for a little, which is the remainder of their lifespans. This is on the assumption of their fleeing. Then what is the benefit of a person abandoning the fighting that is obligatory upon him and turning his back, for a matter that may benefit him or may not benefit him? He may die while turning away, and he may remain and be granted a long life. But if he remains and is granted a long life, will he remain forever? No, he is not given enjoyment except for a little; however long his term is, it is little. For this reason the whole of this world, compared to the Hereafter, is nothing. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿But you prefer the worldly life, while the Hereafter is better and more lasting﴾ [al-A'la 16-17].

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, informed that the place of a person's whip in Paradise is better than this world and all that is in it. So the enjoyment of this world is in reality nothing compared to the time of the Hereafter. For this reason He said: ﴿And then you would not be given enjoyment except for a little﴾.

Furthermore, there is something else: if they are killed in the way of Allah, they have been killed but they are alive. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah, "They are dead." Rather, they are alive, but you do not perceive﴾ [al-Baqarah 154]. We have been forbidden from saying this with the tongue, and even from thinking it in the heart: ﴿And never think of those who have been killed in the way of Allah as dead. Rather, they are alive with their Lord, being provided for﴾ [Ali 'Imran 169].

So it is not permissible to say or think that one who is killed in the way of Allah is dead; rather, his body is dead, but his soul is alive with a barzakh life, which is not like the life of this world. Had it been like the life of this world, it would not have been permissible to bury them, because if we buried them while they were alive with worldly life, we would have killed and destroyed them. From this we recognize the error of those who say that they are alive, that they hear you when you ask them to supplicate to Allah for you, and that they respond to you, and who use this matter as a means to associating partners with them, with the prophets, and with those whom they call "awliya'."

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: For the generalization of circumstances, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say, "Indeed, the death from which you flee will surely meet you"﴾ [al-Jumu'ah 8]. Or it may also be said: those who came to fight may die without being killed.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It is specific to the martyrs and to those who are better than them. This is the apparent view, and it is possible that this is specific to the martyrs, because the martyr is not like others: the martyr exposed himself to death and sold himself, so he is rewarded by being alive. But the well-known view is that whoever is higher than the martyrs has that ruling, and the prophets have another distinction that is not shared by others: the earth does not consume their bodies.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: This does not happen to them (...); they exposed themselves but were not killed.
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: We do not affirm this matter with certainty. The matter is as I said: the view of most of the scholars I have examined is that whoever is higher in rank than them is more entitled to that ruling. (...)

﴿So little do they believe﴾ [al-Baqarah 88]; ﴿so they do not believe except a little﴾ [al-Nisa' 46]. Such an expression, the exegetes mentioned, is intended to mean non-existence; that is: they do not believe at all.

﴿And when a faction of them said﴾. Have we finished the previous one?

* In this noble verse: an explanation of the hypocrites' spreading of alarm among the believers. Irjaf (spreading alarm) is that a person mentions what causes fear and anxiety; this is irjaf. In matters of fighting there is the "murjif" (alarmist) and the "mukhadhdhil" (discourager), and the difference between them is that the murjif is one who frightens, and the mukhadhdhil is one who reduces the desire for good. This is the difference between them: the murjif terrifies them, while the mukhadhdhil weakens their resolve, saying: "What is the point? What is the benefit of such and such?" So there is a difference between them. Are these alarmists or discouragers? Alarmists. There is no position here, because it is a danger to you; for this reason they said: ﴿So return﴾. It is thus derived from this that the hypocrites' nature is to spread alarm among the believers.

* And among the benefits of the noble verse: that pride in the homeland is a trait of the hypocrites, since their saying: ﴿O people of Yathrib﴾ was intended to stir up their national zeal. As for the hadith that is narrated: "Love of the homeland is part of faith" [[See Kashf al-Khafa' (1/398).]], it is a lie upon the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him; it is not authentic.

* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the permissibility of calling the city Yathrib. Some have derived this.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What is derived? The argument of this speaker is that Allah related it from them and approved it. But some scholars said: this does not indicate that; rather it indicates the opposite. Calling it Yathrib comes from the hypocrites, because Allah, exalted is He, relates the disbelief of the disbelievers; He relates everything these disbelievers, including the hypocrites and others, say. Does relating their disbelief from them constitute approval of it? No.

So it is derived from the verse that calling the city Yathrib is a trait of the hypocrites. For this reason the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "They say: Yathrib, and it is al-Madinah" [[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1871) and Muslim (1382/488), from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]], and this clearly shows that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, did not approve of this name.

* A corollary of this benefit: a clarification of the state of those historians, not the Arabs, rather the Islamists who are imitators. The orientalists came and spoke of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, only by the name Muhammad, saying "Muhammad," just as the disbelievers said in the time of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and they speak of the city as Yathrib. Then these wretched people came, imitating those orientalists, and began to refer to the Messenger by the word Muhammad and to refer to the city by the word Yathrib, as though this were pride and progress.

* And among the benefits of the noble verse: that those alarmists did not limit themselves to alarm, but misled people with their saying: ﴿So return﴾.

* A corollary of this: that everyone who calls to turning back from the truth has a resemblance to whom? To the hypocrites, because of His saying: ﴿So return﴾. Those people first spread alarm, then called to abandonment: ﴿So return﴾.

* And among the benefits of the noble verse: ﴿And a faction of them asks permission of the Prophet﴾ and so on: a clarification of the hypocrites' deceit, since they came asking the Messenger ﷺ for permission as a pretense, while in their intention they had no intention of staying, but they disguised it. ﴿A faction of them asks permission of the Prophet﴾. In this there is evidence of the hypocrite's disguise and his showing his state as that of the believer who submits and does not leave except after seeking permission. Yet seeking permission in such a matter, or in such a situation, is the practice of whom? Seeking permission in truth is the practice of the believers, or not? As Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿The believers are only those who have believed in Allah and His Messenger, and when they are with him on a matter of common concern, they do not leave until they have asked his permission﴾ [al-Nur 62].

* And among the benefits of the noble verse: that it is the nature of the hypocrites to lie, due to His saying: ﴿They say, "Indeed, our houses are exposed"﴾, while they are liars.

* And among its benefits: a clarification of Allah's comprehensive knowledge of what is in the hearts, due to His saying: ﴿They intend only to flee﴾. As for His saying: ﴿And they were not exposed﴾, this may be known, because it is evident that the houses are secure and there is no threat from the enemy to them. But ﴿they intend﴾: intention in the heart is known only to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, or to its owner, or to whomever Allah has informed of it.

* And among the benefits of the noble verse: the obligation to refute the one who speaks falsehood. Now, see whether it is correct to use the word "obligation" here, or whether we should say "legislated permissibility."
If we look at the fact that falsehood must be refuted, we say: it is obligatory. But the discussion is about whether it is derived from the verse. The verse contains the legislation of that, the refutation of the statement of one who speaks falsehood, because Allah refuted it in His saying: ﴿And they were not exposed﴾.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if they had been entered upon from its surroundings, and then they had been asked for fitnah, they would have given it﴾ and so on.

* It is derived from the noble verse: that the hypocrites are the most terrified of people, due to His saying: ﴿And if they had been entered upon﴾, and ﴿then they had been asked for fitnah, they would have given it﴾, because they have terror of those who entered from its surroundings.

* And it is also derived from the verse: the hypocrites' closeness to disbelief and polytheism, due to His saying: ﴿they were asked﴾ and ﴿they would have given it﴾, hastening without delay, not saying: "Let us consider the matter." No.

Is it derived from this verse that there is no ruling for coercion, and that if a person disbelieves under compulsion, the ruling of disbelief applies to him? I say: is it derived from the verse that there is no ruling for coercion, and that whoever disbelieves under compulsion bears sin? It is not derived. Why? Because these people were asked and were not compelled; by mere asking they agreed. So there is no conflict with His saying: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief, except one who has been forced﴾ [al-Nahl 106]; this verse does not contradict it.

* And among the benefits of the noble verse: a clarification that the life of the hypocrite is a material life; he wants to live whether he is a disbeliever or not.

Its basis from the verse: because when these people were asked for fitnah, they gave it. So their faith is not genuine faith; otherwise, a true believer, if asked for polytheism, would not commit it.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they had already covenanted with Allah before, not to turn their backs, and the covenant of Allah is ever questioned﴾ [al-Ahzab 15].

* It is derived from the noble verse: that the hypocrites are people of treachery and betrayal, due to His saying: ﴿And they had already covenanted with Allah before, not to turn their backs﴾, and they are now trying to turn their backs, but they disguise it by asking the Prophet ﷺ for permission.

* So a corollary of this benefit: that everyone who breaks a covenant has a resemblance to the hypocrites, and to the Jews as well. For this reason the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "The sign of the hypocrite is three," and among them: "When he makes a covenant, he betrays it" [[Narrated by Ahmad (6879) from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, may Allah be pleased with them both.]].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verse 13–16 (part 3 of 5):

* It follows from this: if treachery is among the characteristics of the hypocrites, then it is obligatory for the believer to keep far from it. Even if treachery were only (wrong) because it is a characteristic of the hypocrites, that would be sufficient to make keeping far from it and guarding against it obligatory.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the hypocrite's disregard for the right of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; His saying ﴿they had covenanted with Allah﴾ means: breaking a covenant with a human being like you may be lighter, but breaking a covenant with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is more severe and more grave.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the prohibition of turning one's back when meeting the enemy.
The reason for this is that Allah, Exalted, mentioned this of the hypocrites as a warning against it. The noble verse in Surat al-Anfal has shown that it is one of the major sins, by the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, when you meet those who have disbelieved advancing [for battle], do not turn your backs to them. And whoever turns his back to them on such a day—unless swerving [as a strategy] for war or joining [another] company—then he has returned with anger from Allah, and his refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination﴾ [Al-Anfal 15–16]. And there are hadiths which count this among the destructive sins (al-Mubiqat), meaning those which bring ruin, because it is a major sin.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of accountability, by His saying ﴿And the covenant of Allah will be questioned﴾. So everything between you and Allah of rights, you will be held accountable for on the Day of Resurrection. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers. Then We will surely relate to them [their deeds] with knowledge, and We were not absent﴾ [Al-A'raf 6–7].

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿Say, "Flight will not benefit you if you should flee from death or killing; and then you will not be given enjoyment except for a little."﴾

* In this verse there is evidence that there is no escape from the decree of Allah, by His saying ﴿Say, "Flight will not benefit you if you should flee from death or killing"﴾.
The phrase ﴿from death or killing﴾ — is it connected to ﴿you fled﴾ or to ﴿the flight﴾? This is a parenthetical clause (jumla mu'tarida); in reality, it is not among the benefits. ﴿Say, "Flight will not benefit you if you should flee from death or killing"﴾ — is it connected to ﴿you fled﴾ or to ﴿the flight﴾? Say: flight will not benefit you from death or killing if you flee, and the conditional clause ﴿if you should flee﴾ is a parenthetical clause. This is clearer in meaning.
* It is derived from it: there is no escape from the decree of Allah.
Does the noble verse imply the nullification of causes? That is, if a person sees a fire consuming trees coming towards him, does he flee or not? He flees; so he flees, and perhaps he is saved. It is other than this, but what is the means of deliverance?
That is, if someone were to say: does this verse negate acting upon causes?
The answer to that is: if acting upon a cause nullifies a legislated ruling, then it is not permissible, like in this verse, or like this situation. So nullifying the natural (qadari) causes by violating the legislated rulings is not permissible. That is, for a person to abandon an obligatory legislated ruling out of fear of its consequences — is that permissible for him? It is not permissible.
But a real cause that is permitted by the Law — is it done or not? If it is a real cause permitted by the Law, then do it. We do not say to a man: "If you see the fire coming towards you, stand still, do not flee; fleeing will not benefit you." This is not correct. Rather, we say: in this situation, flee, because this is a permissible cause, permitted by the Law, and a real cause. But to make causes nullify the legislated rulings — this is not permissible.
* It is derived from the noble verse: the demonstration of the force of the ruling of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, both legislated and decreed. As for the decreed, you have no will in it; as for the legislated, you have a will in it. For this reason we say, regarding the legislated: it is obligatory to implement the legislated ruling of Allah, because Allah, Exalted, blamed those who fled, since their fleeing entails the cancellation of a legislated ruling. Yes, indeed.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that remaining in this world, however long, is little; by His saying ﴿and then you will not be given enjoyment except for a little﴾. Allah, Exalted, said in another verse: ﴿Say, "The enjoyment of this world is little, and the Hereafter is better for those who fear Allah, and you will not be wronged even as much as the thread in a date-stone"﴾ [An-Nisa' 77].
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the rebuke of those who fled to preserve their lives. From Allah's command to His Prophet to say to them: ﴿Flight will not benefit you if you should flee from death or killing﴾, there is no doubt that this is in the manner of rebuke to them. For this reason He said: ﴿and then﴾, meaning: even if you flee and escape from this incident, you will not escape death, ﴿and you will not be given enjoyment except for a little﴾. Yes, from the cowardice of the hypocrites is that they are people of cowardice, humiliation, fear and terror.
This also gives rise to a difficulty: fear of death is a natural matter. Allah, Exalted, said about Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿He said, "My Lord, I have killed a soul among them, so I fear that they will kill me"﴾ [Al-Qasas 33]. There is a problem with this.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: The word (...) says: what is the difference between saying: this is other than this, is it not sufficient?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: The point of the objection is that he feared being killed, and these feared being killed. Fear of being killed — as we have indicated just now — which entails the nullification of a legislated ruling, this is not permissible. As for this one, he feared being killed because he took a step which could lead to his being killed, correct? Musa — yes, indeed — it was possible he would be killed, because he had done what, according to them, entails being killed. (...)
We say: ﴿Say, "Who is it that can protect you from Allah if He intends for you harm or intends for you mercy?"﴾ [Al-Ahzab 17].
The author said regarding the meaning of ﴿yaʿṣimukum﴾: (yujirukum, "will protect you"). But the correct meaning is: will prevent you, because 'iṣma (protection) is prevention; from it comes al-ma'sum, that is, one who is prevented from error. So the correct reading is that ﴿yaʿṣimukum﴾ means: will prevent you from Allah.
As for His saying ﴿Say, "Who is it that...﴾, what is the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of ﴿man dha alladhi﴾? Who will parse it for us?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It is obligatorily concealed (pronoun); if it begins with the letter ya' then it is optionally concealed; if it begins with the letter ta' then it depends on the situation — it may be obligatory, like: "you (masc.) thank" (tashkuru anta); it may be optional, like: "she thanks" (tashkuru hiya).
﴿dha⁠﴾ — now the two men differed in its i'rab: one said it is a demonstrative noun (ism ishara), and the other said it is annulled (mulgha). Which is correct? The correct view is that it is annulled, because when a relative pronoun (ism mawsul) follows it, it is annulled, like: ﴿Who is it that intercedes...﴾ [Al-Baqarah 255], and like: ﴿Say, "Who is it that can protect you...﴾.
As for His saying ﴿Say, "Who is it that can protect you...﴾, the interrogative here is intended to mean negation; that is, no one can protect you. When negation comes in the form of a question, it is more emphatic than bare negation, because it becomes a negation imbued with challenge, as if he were saying: tell me, can anyone protect you from Allah if He intends you harm? Do you understand? This is a rule for every case in which an interrogative carries the meaning of negation: we say that it has been turned away from plain negation to interrogation, so that it carries the meaning of challenge.
﴿Who is it that can protect you from Allah﴾, meaning: who can prevent you from Him, ﴿if He intends for you harm﴾ — what is the answer? No one. He says: (﴿if He intends for you harm﴾: destruction or defeat). (Destruction) if there is no fighting, or if there is fighting and you are killed; (or defeat) if you are overcome and remain alive. All of that is harm, but it is harm with respect to the one held accountable; as for with respect to the act of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, it is good, because it is for a wisdom.
﴿or intends﴾ — the author said: (or afflicts you with harm if Allah intends mercy for you). The author, may Allah have mercy on him, supplied this clause, because he, may Allah have mercy on him, was very perceptive. He said: (or afflicts you with harm). ﴿afflicts you﴾ is coordinated with ﴿protects you﴾, meaning: or who is it that can afflict you with harm if Allah intends mercy and good for you? The answer is also as before: no one. The author supplied "or afflicts you with harm" contrary to the apparent context, because mercy is not counted as a calamity that requires protection from it. When Allah intends mercy for a person, one does not say: who can protect him from it? Why? Because mercy is desired; a person does not seek anyone to protect him from it. Therefore he supplied "or afflicts you with harm," meaning: no one can afflict you with harm if Allah intends mercy for you.
But the correct view is that there is no need for this supplying. If we take 'iṣma to mean prevention, then the meaning is: who can prevent you from Allah if He intends harm for you, and who can prevent you from His mercy if He intends mercy for you? Fleeing does not prevent you from the evil which Allah intends for you, and staying does not bring you the mercy which Allah intends for you. Everything is in the hand of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; neither fleeing nor staying will benefit you.
As for His saying ﴿or if He intends for you mercy﴾, the author said: (khayran, "good"). And since we interpreted the first as destruction and defeat, the meaning of "good" here is victory and survival.
Allah, Exalted, said: (﴿And they will not find for themselves besides Allah any ally﴾, meaning: other than Him, ﴿wali⁠﴾ who benefits them, ﴿nor any helper﴾ who repels harm from them).
﴿They will not find for themselves﴾ — meaning: these who fled from fighting will never find anyone who benefits them, or brings them good, or repels harm from them. ﴿They will not find﴾ ﴿wali⁠﴾ — and the wali is the one who takes charge of your affairs and cares for you. So these will not find anyone except Allah.
As for His saying ﴿wali⁠﴾, it means in the general sense of guardianship, because the guardianship of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, is divided into two kinds: a general guardianship which includes everyone, and a special guardianship for the believers only. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Allah is the Wali of those who have believed; He brings them out from darknesses into light﴾ [Al-Baqarah 257], and He, Exalted, said: ﴿That is because Allah is the Mawla of those who believe, and because the disbelievers have no Mawla﴾ [Muhammad 11].
As for the general sense, it is like His saying, Exalted: ﴿Then they are returned to Allah, their true Mawla﴾ [Al-An'am 62]. This is general guardianship, because Allah, Exalted, is Wali over everyone in the general sense, which is management, dominion and sovereignty.
As for His saying ﴿nor any helper﴾… ﴿min nasir⁠﴾ [Al-Hajj 71]: it is the one who supports you when you meet enemies, and so prevents them from you. So these have no one who takes charge of them by bringing good to them, nor who supports them by repelling harm from them, because the whole matter belongs to Allah.
Then He, Exalted, said: (﴿Already Allah knows those among you who hinder⁠﴾ [Al-Ahzab 18]: the discouragers, ﴿and those who say to their brothers, "Come to us"﴾ ) [Al-Ahzab: 18]. ﴿Qad⁠﴾ here is for confirmation (tahqiq).
