Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verses 17–21 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They think﴾ means "they suppose." It takes two objects, which originally were the subject and predicate of a nominal sentence. The first object here is ﴿the confederates﴾, and the second object is the clause ﴿they have not gone away﴾. The meaning is: these hypocrites think that the confederates have not gone away. This shows their cowardice, their fear, and their terror, because even after the confederates have departed and dispersed, these hypocrites still think that they have not gone.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: (﴿they have not gone away﴾ to Makkah, out of their fear of them. ﴿And if the confederates come﴾ again ﴿they would wish﴾: they would desire ﴿that they were living among the desert Arabs﴾, that is, dwelling in the desert ﴿asking about your news﴾: about your reports with the disbelievers).

The phrase ﴿And if they come﴾ is stated as a hypothetical supposition. ﴿The confederates﴾ is the plural of ḥizb (a faction), and they were the groups who formed a coalition against the Prophet ﷺ: the Quraysh, Ghatafan, Asad, and others. If these confederates came a second time, these hypocrites would wish ﴿that they were living among the desert Arabs﴾. The bādī (desert dweller) is one who lives in the desert. From this comes the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "A town dweller should not sell on behalf of a desert dweller." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2150) and Muslim (1413/52), from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.] So bādī here is an active participle, and its meaning is one who dwells in the desert. These people would wish that they were dwelling in the desert among the Arabs, that is, living in the desert. Why would they wish to be dwelling in the desert? To be saved from these confederates.

The phrase ﴿asking about your news﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back to the subject in ﴿living among the desert Arabs﴾. The meaning is: these hypocrites would wish to be in the desert, ﴿asking about your news﴾, and not taking part with you in the fighting. You have now grasped the meaning. Allah, glorified and exalted, has thus made clear the terror of these hypocrites in two respects:

The first respect: they think the confederates are still present, even though the confederates have already withdrawn.

The second respect: even if it were supposed that the confederates had returned, they would wish to be in the desert, where they would not be exposed to skirmishes or fighting, but would only ask about your news.

Therefore, the clause ﴿asking﴾ is, we say, in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the subject of ﴿living among the desert Arabs﴾.

Allah, the Exalted, says: (﴿And if they were among you﴾ on this occasion ﴿they would not fight except a little﴾, out of ostentation and out of fear of reproach).

That is, the ﴿if﴾ here is conditional (law), and its answer is linked with ﴿mā﴾ (not). When the conditional ﴿law﴾ is linked with ﴿mā﴾, the answer most commonly does not take the particle lām. Why? Because ﴿mā﴾ is for negation and lām is for emphasis, and combining a particle that indicates emphasis with one that indicates negation involves some conflict and contradiction. So you say: "If Zayd had come, I would not have spoken to him," and you do not say: "If Zayd had come, I would not have spoken to him" with lām (*la-mā*).

However, when the answer is affirmative, it most commonly takes lām. You say: "If Zayd had come, I would have spoken to you," which is the most common form, and it is also permissible to say: "If Zayd had come, I would have spoken to him" (without lām). Allah, blessed and exalted, says in Surah al-Waqi'ah: ﴿If We willed, We would have made it crumbled debris﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 65]; here lām is attached. ﴿If We willed, We would have made it bitter, so why do you not give thanks?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 70]. As for ﴿mā﴾, as you have just seen, lām is not attached to it, but sometimes lām is attached to it, rarely. From this is the poet's saying:

"Had we been given the choice, we would not have parted,
but there is no choice with the nights."

The evidence (shāhid) is the phrase: *"lamā iftaraqnā"* (we would not have parted).

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And if they were among you, they would not fight except a little﴾. The word ﴿a little﴾ here means: except in a nonexistent way (i.e., hardly at all), or it may be taken in its apparent sense, that they would fight but only a little. This is the closer view, because the basic principle is to keep the speech in its apparent meaning, unless there is evidence that the apparent meaning is not intended. So if these people were among us when the confederates came, you would find that, because of their cowardice, they would fight only a little.

The author explained this little fighting as being for the sake of ostentation and fear of censure. That is, they would show off to people that they were fighting in the way of Allah, while fearing people's reproach of them. They would not fight so that the word of Allah would be supreme. This is among the most important matters, namely a person making his worship sincerely for Allah, the Exalted. This is among the most important things and among the hardest to treat in the soul, because outward deeds are something everyone can make as good as possible. Is that not so?

Everyone can stand and pray with a calm recitation, a calm bowing, a calm prostration, a calm standing, and a calm sitting. But reforming the heart is the difficult part. For this reason, the soundness of the heart brings about the soundness of the body, but not the reverse, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (52) and Muslim (1599/107), from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, may Allah be pleased with them both.]

These hypocrites have no genuine desire for the fighting in which they could hope for one of the two good outcomes: either martyrdom or victory and happiness. No, they fight only out of ostentation and fear of reproach, not for Allah. Whoever has this intention will not fight the fight that should be fought, because it will be lukewarm. This is unlike the person whose intention is sincerely for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; rather, he will have a strong motive driving him to act according to what he sees as obedience to Allah, the Glorified and Exalted.

Then Allah, the Exalted, says: (﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah there has been for you an excellent example﴾, with the hamzah pronounced with a kasra and with a ḍammah).

﴿Indeed there has been﴾: the lām is a lām introducing an oath (lām al-muwaṭṭi'ah lil-qasam), and ﴿qad﴾ is for confirmation. On this basis, the sentence is emphasized with three emphatic elements: the implied oath, the lām, and ﴿qad﴾.

As for ﴿Indeed there has been for you in the Messenger of Allah﴾: ﴿kāna﴾ is a past-tense verb. How can it be a past-tense verb, when following the Messenger ﷺ is continuous and perpetual, while it is well known that a past-tense verb refers to a time that has ended? It is said, and Allah knows best: "There has been for you in the knowledge of Allah and in the law of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, an excellent example."

As for ﴿in the Messenger of Allah﴾: He did not say "in Muhammad" or "in the Prophet," which points to the fact that the example lies in him, peace and blessings be upon him, because he is the Messenger of Allah. This description indicates causation: the cause of the example is that he is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Otherwise, it would not be incumbent upon us to follow him as an example, since he is a man among men. But because he is the Messenger of Allah, there is for us in him an excellent example.

As for ﴿uswah﴾ (example), with a kasra or a ḍammah on the hamzah, these are two canonical (sab'iyyah) recitations. When the author expresses it in this way, the two recitations are canonical and equal. But when he says "it is recited," the second recitation is irregular (shādhdh).

So it is permissible for me to say *Iswah* and *Uswah*. Is it better to limit oneself to one of its recitations, or to recite one at times and the other at other times?

It has been established earlier that the better course, for one who knows the recitation and is sure of it, is to recite one at times and the other at other times. But not in front of the general public. If we recite these recitations in front of ordinary people, confusion and reaction result from it. They say: "How can this change the Qur'an and distort it?!"

But in private, between a person and himself, if he knows that there are two recitations, it is better to recite this one at one time and that one at another, because both recitations are established from whom? From the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. So we should not limit ourselves to just one, because if we limit ourselves to only one, we abandon the others.

* The Shaykh: By learning. If someone comes wanting to learn the recitations, we teach him. But a layman who knows nothing about these matters will undoubtedly become confused, and on the other hand he may become bold enough to recite it incorrectly.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed. And let it not be harmful; because by consensus, limiting oneself to one is permissible. It is not obligatory. So if reciting the second recitation would cause harm, there is no blame in not reciting it.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, it does not disappear. As regards the expression in the past tense, it does not disappear. The difficulty is the expression in the past tense.

As for the phrase ﴿an excellent example﴾, the author said: ("an imitation of him in fighting, and steadfastness in its places"). This explanation by the author, may Allah have mercy on him, is open to question. What is the point of objection to it? That he restricted it to fighting. In reality, he is an excellent example in everything he does. Everything that was part of his sunnah, we have in it an excellent example. The phrase ﴿an excellent example﴾ has two meanings:

The first meaning: following the Messenger ﷺ is entirely good, because he, peace and blessings be upon him, is protected from error in legislation. So every following of him is good, unlike following others, which may be good and may be not good.

The second meaning: he is an excellent example in terms of our following him, not in terms of what he himself is. The excellent following of him, in terms of our imitating him, is that we agree with him in speech, action, and intention, which is the creed. We agree with him in these three matters: in creed, speech, and action. This is the excellent example. Whoever agrees with him in his speech but not his action has not followed him with an excellent example. Whoever agrees with him in his action but not his speech has not followed him with an excellent example. And whoever follows him in speech and action but not in creed and intention has not followed him with an excellent example.

Included in the excellent example is calling people to the religion of Allah. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, undoubtedly called to the religion of Allah. ﴿Say: This is my way; I call to Allah with insight, I and whoever follows me﴾ [Yusuf 108].

From this we learn that the student of knowledge should be active in his society, not merely a copy of a book. That is, he should be one who stirs people's consciences, feelings, and guidance, and has determination to reform creation, so that he is not merely a copy. A mere copy, what is the benefit of it? He says: "By Allah, I have memorized, for example, *Matn al-Zad*, I have memorized *Bulugh al-Maram*, I have memorized *al-Muntaqa*, and the like, but (...)." What is the benefit? Or he says: "I want to sit in my house; if anyone comes asking me, I will teach him, and if not..."

No. It is necessary to spread awareness among the Muslims, especially at this time in our age, because people have begun to move. They have grown tired of the previous way of life, and they have now started to move, but they need a starting point and guidance, because they may move toward something bad. When the students of knowledge, whom Allah has granted knowledge, take on the task of directing people to these matters, much good comes of it, just as our Prophet ﷺ used to do. So the excellent example in the Messenger includes calling to the religion of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

He says: ﴿for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day﴾. The good example is good in itself and in its application: in itself, meaning that following him is good, and it is impossible that any of his actions is not described as good; and good in applying this following in creed, speech, and action.

But He says: ﴿for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day﴾. ﴿For whoever was﴾: the author says ("a substitute for ﴿for you﴾"). ﴿Indeed there has been for you﴾ ﴿an excellent example﴾, but specifically for whoever hopes for Allah. It is a partial substitution (badal ba'ḍ min kull) with repetition of the governing element (ʿāmil). Is that right? Brothers, answer: a partial substitution with repetition of the governing element. ﴿For you﴾: the address includes those who hope for Allah and the Last Day and those who do not hope for Him. And ﴿for whoever was﴾ restricts it to those who hope for Allah and the Last Day. So it is a partial substitution.

Is it a partial substitution in essence or in meaning and attributes?

If you say, "Honor the people, some of them," this is a partial substitution in essence. But here, is it in essence or in attributes? In attributes: ﴿for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day﴾. And when we say "with repetition of the governing element," where is the governing element that was repeated? It is the lām, the preposition, which is present both in the substitute and in the substituted element: present in the substituted element in ﴿for you﴾, and in the substitute in ﴿for whoever was﴾.

As for ﴿for whoever hopes for Allah﴾, the author says: ("fears Allah").

Someone may say: How do we explain hope as fear? Because hope is seeking or wishing for something that is close to being attained, so how can we explain it as fear?

It is said: hope is applied to fear and also to expectation. Hope is for what is loved, and fear is for what is disliked. It is not necessary to interpret it as the author did, that hope here means fear, because hoping in Allah and the Last Day is also established, which is the wish for the attainment of what is sought. What Allah has of reward for those who follow the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, necessitates hope, and what there is of happiness in the Last Day also necessitates hope. So what appears is that hope here has its real meaning, which is seeking that a person expect what is beneficial and good for him.

As for ﴿and the Last Day﴾: what is meant by it? It means the Day of Resurrection. It is called "the Last Day" because there is no day after it, since that day is the final stage of creation. For a person in this world there are four stages: a stage in his mother's womb, a stage in this world, a stage in the barzakh, and a fourth stage on the Day of Resurrection. Four states.

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: There is no (...) in it.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: All of it has no night and day, because the sun will be wound up and thrown into the Fire.

The phrase ﴿for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day﴾: Allah, the Exalted, frequently in the Qur'an joins faith in Him with faith in the Last Day, ﴿Believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Nisa' 39]. Why? Because faith in the Last Day necessitates action. When you believe that there is a day on which you will be recompensed for your deeds, you will work for that day. This is unlike the person who denies it, for the one who denies the Last Day does not work, because he believes there is nothing but this world: wombs that expel and earth that swallows, and nothing more. But when a person believes in the Last Day, it obliges him to act. For this reason He says: ﴿for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day﴾.

He says: ﴿and remembers Allah much﴾, in contrast with one who is not like that. ﴿And remembers Allah﴾: the waw here is a conjunctive particle, and ﴿remembered﴾ is conjoined to what? To ﴿for whoever hopes﴾. That is: and for whoever remembers Allah. Or it is conjoined to ﴿was﴾: ﴿for whoever was﴾, and for whoever remembers Allah, conjoined to ﴿was﴾, because a past-tense verb is conjoined to a past-tense verb. Also, if you make it conjoined to ﴿was﴾, the meaning becomes clearer: ﴿for whoever was hoping for Allah﴾ is an inner act, and ﴿and remembered Allah﴾ is an outward act. He says: conjoined to ﴿was﴾: ﴿for whoever was hoping for Allah﴾, and for whoever ﴿remembers Allah much﴾.

As for ﴿and remembers Allah much﴾: ﴿much﴾ is an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq), meaning remembrance much. The remembrance of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, occurs with the heart, with the tongue, and with the limbs. With the heart, by a person reflecting on the signs of Allah and on His names and attributes; this is remembrance with the heart. With the tongue, such as glorification, declaring Allah's oneness, and praising Him, and the like. With the limbs other than the tongue, such as prayer, which contains bowing, prostration, standing, and sitting, and it is remembrance.

So remembrance occurs in the heart, in the tongue, and in the limbs. The wise, resolute, believing person never ceases to remember Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, because in every one of His creations there is a sign indicating His oneness, glorified and exalted, and His wisdom. Whatever you observe in this universe will remind you of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Likewise, regarding your actions: if you are resolute, you can avoid doing any action except that it becomes worship. The resolute person makes habits into acts of worship, while the heedless person makes acts of worship into habits. So if a person is resolute, not a moment of his life will be wasted on him; he must use it in the remembrance of Allah, the Glorified and Exalted.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verses 17–21 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They think﴾ means "they suppose." It takes two objects, which originally were the subject and predicate of a nominal sentence. The first object here is ﴿the confederates﴾, and the second object is the clause ﴿they have not gone away﴾. The meaning is: these hypocrites think that the confederates have not gone away. This shows their cowardice, their fear, and their terror, because even after the confederates have departed and dispersed, these hypocrites still think that they have not gone.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: (﴿they have not gone away﴾ to Makkah, out of their fear of them. ﴿And if the confederates come﴾ again ﴿they would wish﴾: they would desire ﴿that they were living among the desert Arabs﴾, that is, dwelling in the desert ﴿asking about your news﴾: about your reports with the disbelievers).

The phrase ﴿And if they come﴾ is stated as a hypothetical supposition. ﴿The confederates﴾ is the plural of ḥizb (a faction), and they were the groups who formed a coalition against the Prophet ﷺ: the Quraysh, Ghatafan, Asad, and others. If these confederates came a second time, these hypocrites would wish ﴿that they were living among the desert Arabs﴾. The bādī (desert dweller) is one who lives in the desert. From this comes the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "A town dweller should not sell on behalf of a desert dweller." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2150) and Muslim (1413/52), from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.] So bādī here is an active participle, and its meaning is one who dwells in the desert. These people would wish that they were dwelling in the desert among the Arabs, that is, living in the desert. Why would they wish to be dwelling in the desert? To be saved from these confederates.

The phrase ﴿asking about your news﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back to the subject in ﴿living among the desert Arabs﴾. The meaning is: these hypocrites would wish to be in the desert, ﴿asking about your news﴾, and not taking part with you in the fighting. You have now grasped the meaning. Allah, glorified and exalted, has thus made clear the terror of these hypocrites in two respects:

The first respect: they think the confederates are still present, even though the confederates have already withdrawn.

The second respect: even if it were supposed that the confederates had returned, they would wish to be in the desert, where they would not be exposed to skirmishes or fighting, but would only ask about your news.

Therefore, the clause ﴿asking﴾ is, we say, in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the subject of ﴿living among the desert Arabs﴾.

Allah, the Exalted, says: (﴿And if they were among you﴾ on this occasion ﴿they would not fight except a little﴾, out of ostentation and out of fear of reproach).

That is, the ﴿if﴾ here is conditional (law), and its answer is linked with ﴿mā﴾ (not). When the conditional ﴿law﴾ is linked with ﴿mā﴾, the answer most commonly does not take the particle lām. Why? Because ﴿mā﴾ is for negation and lām is for emphasis, and combining a particle that indicates emphasis with one that indicates negation involves some conflict and contradiction. So you say: "If Zayd had come, I would not have spoken to him," and you do not say: "If Zayd had come, I would not have spoken to him" with lām (*la-mā*).

However, when the answer is affirmative, it most commonly takes lām. You say: "If Zayd had come, I would have spoken to you," which is the most common form, and it is also permissible to say: "If Zayd had come, I would have spoken to him" (without lām). Allah, blessed and exalted, says in Surah al-Waqi'ah: ﴿If We willed, We would have made it crumbled debris﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 65]; here lām is attached. ﴿If We willed, We would have made it bitter, so why do you not give thanks?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 70]. As for ﴿mā﴾, as you have just seen, lām is not attached to it, but sometimes lām is attached to it, rarely. From this is the poet's saying:

"Had we been given the choice, we would not have parted,
but there is no choice with the nights."

The evidence (shāhid) is the phrase: *"lamā iftaraqnā"* (we would not have parted).

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And if they were among you, they would not fight except a little﴾. The word ﴿a little﴾ here means: except in a nonexistent way (i.e., hardly at all), or it may be taken in its apparent sense, that they would fight but only a little. This is the closer view, because the basic principle is to keep the speech in its apparent meaning, unless there is evidence that the apparent meaning is not intended. So if these people were among us when the confederates came, you would find that, because of their cowardice, they would fight only a little.

The author explained this little fighting as being for the sake of ostentation and fear of censure. That is, they would show off to people that they were fighting in the way of Allah, while fearing people's reproach of them. They would not fight so that the word of Allah would be supreme. This is among the most important matters, namely a person making his worship sincerely for Allah, the Exalted. This is among the most important things and among the hardest to treat in the soul, because outward deeds are something everyone can make as good as possible. Is that not so?

Everyone can stand and pray with a calm recitation, a calm bowing, a calm prostration, a calm standing, and a calm sitting. But reforming the heart is the difficult part. For this reason, the soundness of the heart brings about the soundness of the body, but not the reverse, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (52) and Muslim (1599/107), from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, may Allah be pleased with them both.]

These hypocrites have no genuine desire for the fighting in which they could hope for one of the two good outcomes: either martyrdom or victory and happiness. No, they fight only out of ostentation and fear of reproach, not for Allah. Whoever has this intention will not fight the fight that should be fought, because it will be lukewarm. This is unlike the person whose intention is sincerely for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; rather, he will have a strong motive driving him to act according to what he sees as obedience to Allah, the Glorified and Exalted.

Then Allah, the Exalted, says: (﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah there has been for you an excellent example﴾, with the hamzah pronounced with a kasra and with a ḍammah).

﴿Indeed there has been﴾: the lām is a lām introducing an oath (lām al-muwaṭṭi'ah lil-qasam), and ﴿qad﴾ is for confirmation. On this basis, the sentence is emphasized with three emphatic elements: the implied oath, the lām, and ﴿qad﴾.

As for ﴿Indeed there has been for you in the Messenger of Allah﴾: ﴿kāna﴾ is a past-tense verb. How can it be a past-tense verb, when following the Messenger ﷺ is continuous and perpetual, while it is well known that a past-tense verb refers to a time that has ended? It is said, and Allah knows best: "There has been for you in the knowledge of Allah and in the law of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, an excellent example."

As for ﴿in the Messenger of Allah﴾: He did not say "in Muhammad" or "in the Prophet," which points to the fact that the example lies in him, peace and blessings be upon him, because he is the Messenger of Allah. This description indicates causation: the cause of the example is that he is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Otherwise, it would not be incumbent upon us to follow him as an example, since he is a man among men. But because he is the Messenger of Allah, there is for us in him an excellent example.

As for ﴿uswah﴾ (example), with a kasra or a ḍammah on the hamzah, these are two canonical (sab'iyyah) recitations. When the author expresses it in this way, the two recitations are canonical and equal. But when he says "it is recited," the second recitation is irregular (shādhdh).

So it is permissible for me to say *Iswah* and *Uswah*. Is it better to limit oneself to one of its recitations, or to recite one at times and the other at other times?

It has been established earlier that the better course, for one who knows the recitation and is sure of it, is to recite one at times and the other at other times. But not in front of the general public. If we recite these recitations in front of ordinary people, confusion and reaction result from it. They say: "How can this change the Qur'an and distort it?!"

But in private, between a person and himself, if he knows that there are two recitations, it is better to recite this one at one time and that one at another, because both recitations are established from whom? From the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. So we should not limit ourselves to just one, because if we limit ourselves to only one, we abandon the others.

* Student: If we do not recite the recitations among ordinary people, how will ordinary people know the recitations?
* The Shaykh: By learning. If someone comes wanting to learn the recitations, we teach him. But a layman who knows nothing about these matters will undoubtedly become confused, and on the other hand he may become bold enough to recite it incorrectly.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed. And let it not be harmful; because by consensus, limiting oneself to one is permissible. It is not obligatory. So if reciting the second recitation would cause harm, there is no blame in not reciting it.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, it does not disappear. As regards the expression in the past tense, it does not disappear. The difficulty is the expression in the past tense.

As for the phrase ﴿an excellent example﴾, the author said: ("an imitation of him in fighting, and steadfastness in its places"). This explanation by the author, may Allah have mercy on him, is open to question. What is the point of objection to it? That he restricted it to fighting. In reality, he is an excellent example in everything he does. Everything that was part of his sunnah, we have in it an excellent example. The phrase ﴿an excellent example﴾ has two meanings:

The first meaning: following the Messenger ﷺ is entirely good, because he, peace and blessings be upon him, is protected from error in legislation. So every following of him is good, unlike following others, which may be good and may be not good.

The second meaning: he is an excellent example in terms of our following him, not in terms of what he himself is. The excellent following of him, in terms of our imitating him, is that we agree with him in speech, action, and intention, which is the creed. We agree with him in these three matters: in creed, speech, and action. This is the excellent example. Whoever agrees with him in his speech but not his action has not followed him with an excellent example. Whoever agrees with him in his action but not his speech has not followed him with an excellent example. And whoever follows him in speech and action but not in creed and intention has not followed him with an excellent example.

Included in the excellent example is calling people to the religion of Allah. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, undoubtedly called to the religion of Allah. ﴿Say: This is my way; I call to Allah with insight, I and whoever follows me﴾ [Yusuf 108].

From this we learn that the student of knowledge should be active in his society, not merely a copy of a book. That is, he should be one who stirs people's consciences, feelings, and guidance, and has determination to reform creation, so that he is not merely a copy. A mere copy, what is the benefit of it? He says: "By Allah, I have memorized, for example, *Matn al-Zad*, I have memorized *Bulugh al-Maram*, I have memorized *al-Muntaqa*, and the like, but (...)." What is the benefit? Or he says: "I want to sit in my house; if anyone comes asking me, I will teach him, and if not..."

No. It is necessary to spread awareness among the Muslims, especially at this time in our age, because people have begun to move. They have grown tired of the previous way of life, and they have now started to move, but they need a starting point and guidance, because they may move toward something bad. When the students of knowledge, whom Allah has granted knowledge, take on the task of directing people to these matters, much good comes of it, just as our Prophet ﷺ used to do. So the excellent example in the Messenger includes calling to the religion of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

He says: ﴿for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day﴾. The good example is good in itself and in its application: in itself, meaning that following him is good, and it is impossible that any of his actions is not described as good; and good in applying this following in creed, speech, and action.

But He says: ﴿for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day﴾. ﴿For whoever was﴾: the author says ("a substitute for ﴿for you﴾"). ﴿Indeed there has been for you﴾ ﴿an excellent example﴾, but specifically for whoever hopes for Allah. It is a partial substitution (badal ba'ḍ min kull) with repetition of the governing element (ʿāmil). Is that right? Brothers, answer: a partial substitution with repetition of the governing element. ﴿For you﴾: the address includes those who hope for Allah and the Last Day and those who do not hope for Him. And ﴿for whoever was﴾ restricts it to those who hope for Allah and the Last Day. So it is a partial substitution.

Is it a partial substitution in essence or in meaning and attributes?

If you say, "Honor the people, some of them," this is a partial substitution in essence. But here, is it in essence or in attributes? In attributes: ﴿for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day﴾. And when we say "with repetition of the governing element," where is the governing element that was repeated? It is the lām, the preposition, which is present both in the substitute and in the substituted element: present in the substituted element in ﴿for you﴾, and in the substitute in ﴿for whoever was﴾.

As for ﴿for whoever hopes for Allah﴾, the author says: ("fears Allah").

Someone may say: How do we explain hope as fear? Because hope is seeking or wishing for something that is close to being attained, so how can we explain it as fear?

It is said: hope is applied to fear and also to expectation. Hope is for what is loved, and fear is for what is disliked. It is not necessary to interpret it as the author did, that hope here means fear, because hoping in Allah and the Last Day is also established, which is the wish for the attainment of what is sought. What Allah has of reward for those who follow the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, necessitates hope, and what there is of happiness in the Last Day also necessitates hope. So what appears is that hope here has its real meaning, which is seeking that a person expect what is beneficial and good for him.

As for ﴿and the Last Day﴾: what is meant by it? It means the Day of Resurrection. It is called "the Last Day" because there is no day after it, since that day is the final stage of creation. For a person in this world there are four stages: a stage in his mother's womb, a stage in this world, a stage in the barzakh, and a fourth stage on the Day of Resurrection. Four states.

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: There is no (...) in it.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: All of it has no night and day, because the sun will be wound up and thrown into the Fire.

The phrase ﴿for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day﴾: Allah, the Exalted, frequently in the Qur'an joins faith in Him with faith in the Last Day, ﴿Believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Nisa' 39]. Why? Because faith in the Last Day necessitates action. When you believe that there is a day on which you will be recompensed for your deeds, you will work for that day. This is unlike the person who denies it, for the one who denies the Last Day does not work, because he believes there is nothing but this world: wombs that expel and earth that swallows, and nothing more. But when a person believes in the Last Day, it obliges him to act. For this reason He says: ﴿for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day﴾.

He says: ﴿and remembers Allah much﴾, in contrast with one who is not like that. ﴿And remembers Allah﴾: the waw here is a conjunctive particle, and ﴿remembered﴾ is conjoined to what? To ﴿for whoever hopes﴾. That is: and for whoever remembers Allah. Or it is conjoined to ﴿was﴾: ﴿for whoever was﴾, and for whoever remembers Allah, conjoined to ﴿was﴾, because a past-tense verb is conjoined to a past-tense verb. Also, if you make it conjoined to ﴿was﴾, the meaning becomes clearer: ﴿for whoever was hoping for Allah﴾ is an inner act, and ﴿and remembered Allah﴾ is an outward act. He says: conjoined to ﴿was﴾: ﴿for whoever was hoping for Allah﴾, and for whoever ﴿remembers Allah much﴾.

As for ﴿and remembers Allah much﴾: ﴿much﴾ is an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq), meaning remembrance much. The remembrance of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, occurs with the heart, with the tongue, and with the limbs. With the heart, by a person reflecting on the signs of Allah and on His names and attributes; this is remembrance with the heart. With the tongue, such as glorification, declaring Allah's oneness, and praising Him, and the like. With the limbs other than the tongue, such as prayer, which contains bowing, prostration, standing, and sitting, and it is remembrance.

So remembrance occurs in the heart, in the tongue, and in the limbs. The wise, resolute, believing person never ceases to remember Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, because in every one of His creations there is a sign indicating His oneness, glorified and exalted, and His wisdom. Whatever you observe in this universe will remind you of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Likewise, regarding your actions: if you are resolute, you can avoid doing any action except that it becomes worship. The resolute person makes habits into acts of worship, while the heedless person makes acts of worship into habits. So if a person is resolute, not a moment of his life will be wasted on him; he must use it in the remembrance of Allah, the Glorified and Exalted.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verse 17–21 (part 2 of 2):

Does "the remembrance of Allah" include enjoining good and forbidding evil? Yes, it is part of the remembrance of Allah. Reciting the Qur'an is part of the remembrance of Allah. Every statement or action that brings one closer to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is part of the remembrance of Allah.

* Shaykh: By Allah, I do not know (...).
He, the Exalted, said: ﴿They think the confederates have not withdrawn﴾ [al-Ahzab 20].
* It is derived from this: the great cowardice of these hypocrites, for they think the enemy is still present when it has gone. Or not? If you say: is there evidence for this? I say: yes. If a coward saw a lion in a cave, and the lion left the cave and was taken out, and you said to this coward: "Go ahead, walk past this cave," what would he say? He would say: "No, there is a lion in it." That is because he is a coward. The coward thinks his enemy has not left its place, and he fears even his own shadow.
* It is also derived from this noble verse: that if the confederates returned again, these hypocrites would wish that they were among the Bedouins rather than in the cities, based on His saying: ﴿And if the confederates should come, they would wish that they were out among the Bedouins﴾ [al-Ahzab 20]. Which is the better life: life in the desert or life in the cities? The cities. But because of their cowardice, they wish to go off to the Bedouins, to the desert, and not to be present with these confederates.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: these hypocrites do not want to share in the battles of the believers, based on His saying: ﴿They ask about your news﴾. They love to be far from the battles; they only seek out news.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: if the hypocrite were to take part in fighting alongside the believers, he would fight only a little, ﴿and they would not fight except a little﴾.
Here is a question: may we include hypocrites in our fighting if we know they are hypocrites, or should we not include them? We should not include them, because their harm to us is far greater than their benefit. As for those whose condition we do not know, the principle is that a person is judged by his outward state.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent pattern for anyone whose hope is in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Ahzab 21].
* It is derived from this noble verse: the obligation to follow the Prophet ﷺ (ﷺ). From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿for anyone whose hope is in Allah and the Last Day﴾, because hoping in Allah and the Last Day is obligatory.
* And it is derived from this noble verse: that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, based on His saying: ﴿in the Messenger of Allah﴾.

* It is derived from this noble verse: the obligation of hoping in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the Last Day. But look, we say "obligation." From where is it taken?

* Shaykh: Yes, that does not contradict it, but the obligation, I mean, if someone said: from where do we take the obligation?

The world is such-and-such, or the last of the stages of a human being? The last stage of a human being, as we have already mentioned in the tafsir.

Allah, the Exalted, has explained in Surah Ali 'Imran about the people of understanding that they remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides. A person is either standing, sitting, or lying on his side, and they remember Allah in all these states.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verses 17–21 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They think﴾ means "they suppose." It takes two objects, which originally were the subject and predicate of a nominal sentence. The first object here is ﴿the confederates﴾, and the second object is the clause ﴿they have not gone away﴾. The meaning is: these hypocrites think that the confederates have not gone away. This shows their cowardice, their fear, and their terror, because even after the confederates have departed and dispersed, these hypocrites still think that they have not gone.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: (﴿they have not gone away﴾ to Makkah, out of their fear of them. ﴿And if the confederates come﴾ again ﴿they would wish﴾: they would desire ﴿that they were living among the desert Arabs﴾, that is, dwelling in the desert ﴿asking about your news﴾: about your reports with the disbelievers).

The phrase ﴿And if they come﴾ is stated as a hypothetical supposition. ﴿The confederates﴾ is the plural of ḥizb (a faction), and they were the groups who formed a coalition against the Prophet ﷺ: the Quraysh, Ghatafan, Asad, and others. If these confederates came a second time, these hypocrites would wish ﴿that they were living among the desert Arabs﴾. The bādī (desert dweller) is one who lives in the desert. From this comes the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "A town dweller should not sell on behalf of a desert dweller." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2150) and Muslim (1413/52), from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.] So bādī here is an active participle, and its meaning is one who dwells in the desert. These people would wish that they were dwelling in the desert among the Arabs, that is, living in the desert. Why would they wish to be dwelling in the desert? To be saved from these confederates.

The phrase ﴿asking about your news﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back to the subject in ﴿living among the desert Arabs﴾. The meaning is: these hypocrites would wish to be in the desert, ﴿asking about your news﴾, and not taking part with you in the fighting. You have now grasped the meaning. Allah, glorified and exalted, has thus made clear the terror of these hypocrites in two respects:

The first respect: they think the confederates are still present, even though the confederates have already withdrawn.

The second respect: even if it were supposed that the confederates had returned, they would wish to be in the desert, where they would not be exposed to skirmishes or fighting, but would only ask about your news.

Therefore, the clause ﴿asking﴾ is, we say, in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the subject of ﴿living among the desert Arabs﴾.

Allah, the Exalted, says: (﴿And if they were among you﴾ on this occasion ﴿they would not fight except a little﴾, out of ostentation and out of fear of reproach).

That is, the ﴿if﴾ here is conditional (law), and its answer is linked with ﴿mā﴾ (not). When the conditional ﴿law﴾ is linked with ﴿mā﴾, the answer most commonly does not take the particle lām. Why? Because ﴿mā﴾ is for negation and lām is for emphasis, and combining a particle that indicates emphasis with one that indicates negation involves some conflict and contradiction. So you say: "If Zayd had come, I would not have spoken to him," and you do not say: "If Zayd had come, I would not have spoken to him" with lām (*la-mā*).

However, when the answer is affirmative, it most commonly takes lām. You say: "If Zayd had come, I would have spoken to you," which is the most common form, and it is also permissible to say: "If Zayd had come, I would have spoken to him" (without lām). Allah, blessed and exalted, says in Surah al-Waqi'ah: ﴿If We willed, We would have made it crumbled debris﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 65]; here lām is attached. ﴿If We willed, We would have made it bitter, so why do you not give thanks?﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 70]. As for ﴿mā﴾, as you have just seen, lām is not attached to it, but sometimes lām is attached to it, rarely. From this is the poet's saying:

"Had we been given the choice, we would not have parted,
but there is no choice with the nights."

The evidence (shāhid) is the phrase: *"lamā iftaraqnā"* (we would not have parted).

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And if they were among you, they would not fight except a little﴾. The word ﴿a little﴾ here means: except in a nonexistent way (i.e., hardly at all), or it may be taken in its apparent sense, that they would fight but only a little. This is the closer view, because the basic principle is to keep the speech in its apparent meaning, unless there is evidence that the apparent meaning is not intended. So if these people were among us when the confederates came, you would find that, because of their cowardice, they would fight only a little.

The author explained this little fighting as being for the sake of ostentation and fear of censure. That is, they would show off to people that they were fighting in the way of Allah, while fearing people's reproach of them. They would not fight so that the word of Allah would be supreme. This is among the most important matters, namely a person making his worship sincerely for Allah, the Exalted. This is among the most important things and among the hardest to treat in the soul, because outward deeds are something everyone can make as good as possible. Is that not so?

Everyone can stand and pray with a calm recitation, a calm bowing, a calm prostration, a calm standing, and a calm sitting. But reforming the heart is the difficult part. For this reason, the soundness of the heart brings about the soundness of the body, but not the reverse, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (52) and Muslim (1599/107), from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, may Allah be pleased with them both.]

These hypocrites have no genuine desire for the fighting in which they could hope for one of the two good outcomes: either martyrdom or victory and happiness. No, they fight only out of ostentation and fear of reproach, not for Allah. Whoever has this intention will not fight the fight that should be fought, because it will be lukewarm. This is unlike the person whose intention is sincerely for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; rather, he will have a strong motive driving him to act according to what he sees as obedience to Allah, the Glorified and Exalted.

Then Allah, the Exalted, says: (﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah there has been for you an excellent example﴾, with the hamzah pronounced with a kasra and with a ḍammah).

﴿Indeed there has been﴾: the lām is a lām introducing an oath (lām al-muwaṭṭi'ah lil-qasam), and ﴿qad﴾ is for confirmation. On this basis, the sentence is emphasized with three emphatic elements: the implied oath, the lām, and ﴿qad﴾.

As for ﴿Indeed there has been for you in the Messenger of Allah﴾: ﴿kāna﴾ is a past-tense verb. How can it be a past-tense verb, when following the Messenger ﷺ is continuous and perpetual, while it is well known that a past-tense verb refers to a time that has ended? It is said, and Allah knows best: "There has been for you in the knowledge of Allah and in the law of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, an excellent example."

As for ﴿in the Messenger of Allah﴾: He did not say "in Muhammad" or "in the Prophet," which points to the fact that the example lies in him, peace and blessings be upon him, because he is the Messenger of Allah. This description indicates causation: the cause of the example is that he is the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Otherwise, it would not be incumbent upon us to follow him as an example, since he is a man among men. But because he is the Messenger of Allah, there is for us in him an excellent example.

As for ﴿uswah﴾ (example), with a kasra or a ḍammah on the hamzah, these are two canonical (sab'iyyah) recitations. When the author expresses it in this way, the two recitations are canonical and equal. But when he says "it is recited," the second recitation is irregular (shādhdh).

So it is permissible for me to say *Iswah* and *Uswah*. Is it better to limit oneself to one of its recitations, or to recite one at times and the other at other times?

It has been established earlier that the better course, for one who knows the recitation and is sure of it, is to recite one at times and the other at other times. But not in front of the general public. If we recite these recitations in front of ordinary people, confusion and reaction result from it. They say: "How can this change the Qur'an and distort it?!"

But in private, between a person and himself, if he knows that there are two recitations, it is better to recite this one at one time and that one at another, because both recitations are established from whom? From the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. So we should not limit ourselves to just one, because if we limit ourselves to only one, we abandon the others.

* Student: If we do not recite the recitations among ordinary people, how will ordinary people know the recitations?
* The Shaykh: By learning. If someone comes wanting to learn the recitations, we teach him. But a layman who knows nothing about these matters will undoubtedly become confused, and on the other hand he may become bold enough to recite it incorrectly.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, indeed. And let it not be harmful; because by consensus, limiting oneself to one is permissible. It is not obligatory. So if reciting the second recitation would cause harm, there is no blame in not reciting it.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, it does not disappear. As regards the expression in the past tense, it does not disappear. The difficulty is the expression in the past tense.

As for the phrase ﴿an excellent example﴾, the author said: ("an imitation of him in fighting, and steadfastness in its places"). This explanation by the author, may Allah have mercy on him, is open to question. What is the point of objection to it? That he restricted it to fighting. In reality, he is an excellent example in everything he does. Everything that was part of his sunnah, we have in it an excellent example. The phrase ﴿an excellent example﴾ has two meanings:

The first meaning: following the Messenger ﷺ is entirely good, because he, peace and blessings be upon him, is protected from error in legislation. So every following of him is good, unlike following others, which may be good and may be not good.

The second meaning: he is an excellent example in terms of our following him, not in terms of what he himself is. The excellent following of him, in terms of our imitating him, is that we agree with him in speech, action, and intention, which is the creed. We agree with him in these three matters: in creed, speech, and action. This is the excellent example. Whoever agrees with him in his speech but not his action has not followed him with an excellent example. Whoever agrees with him in his action but not his speech has not followed him with an excellent example. And whoever follows him in speech and action but not in creed and intention has not followed him with an excellent example.

Included in the excellent example is calling people to the religion of Allah. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, undoubtedly called to the religion of Allah. ﴿Say: This is my way; I call to Allah with insight, I and whoever follows me﴾ [Yusuf 108].

From this we learn that the student of knowledge should be active in his society, not merely a copy of a book. That is, he should be one who stirs people's consciences, feelings, and guidance, and has determination to reform creation, so that he is not merely a copy. A mere copy, what is the benefit of it? He says: "By Allah, I have memorized, for example, *Matn al-Zad*, I have memorized *Bulugh al-Maram*, I have memorized *al-Muntaqa*, and the like, but (...)." What is the benefit? Or he says: "I want to sit in my house; if anyone comes asking me, I will teach him, and if not..."

No. It is necessary to spread awareness among the Muslims, especially at this time in our age, because people have begun to move. They have grown tired of the previous way of life, and they have now started to move, but they need a starting point and guidance, because they may move toward something bad. When the students of knowledge, whom Allah has granted knowledge, take on the task of directing people to these matters, much good comes of it, just as our Prophet ﷺ used to do. So the excellent example in the Messenger includes calling to the religion of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

He says: ﴿for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day﴾. The good example is good in itself and in its application: in itself, meaning that following him is good, and it is impossible that any of his actions is not described as good; and good in applying this following in creed, speech, and action.

But He says: ﴿for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day﴾. ﴿For whoever was﴾: the author says ("a substitute for ﴿for you﴾"). ﴿Indeed there has been for you﴾ ﴿an excellent example﴾, but specifically for whoever hopes for Allah. It is a partial substitution (badal ba'ḍ min kull) with repetition of the governing element (ʿāmil). Is that right? Brothers, answer: a partial substitution with repetition of the governing element. ﴿For you﴾: the address includes those who hope for Allah and the Last Day and those who do not hope for Him. And ﴿for whoever was﴾ restricts it to those who hope for Allah and the Last Day. So it is a partial substitution.

Is it a partial substitution in essence or in meaning and attributes?

If you say, "Honor the people, some of them," this is a partial substitution in essence. But here, is it in essence or in attributes? In attributes: ﴿for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day﴾. And when we say "with repetition of the governing element," where is the governing element that was repeated? It is the lām, the preposition, which is present both in the substitute and in the substituted element: present in the substituted element in ﴿for you﴾, and in the substitute in ﴿for whoever was﴾.

As for ﴿for whoever hopes for Allah﴾, the author says: ("fears Allah").

Someone may say: How do we explain hope as fear? Because hope is seeking or wishing for something that is close to being attained, so how can we explain it as fear?

It is said: hope is applied to fear and also to expectation. Hope is for what is loved, and fear is for what is disliked. It is not necessary to interpret it as the author did, that hope here means fear, because hoping in Allah and the Last Day is also established, which is the wish for the attainment of what is sought. What Allah has of reward for those who follow the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, necessitates hope, and what there is of happiness in the Last Day also necessitates hope. So what appears is that hope here has its real meaning, which is seeking that a person expect what is beneficial and good for him.

As for ﴿and the Last Day﴾: what is meant by it? It means the Day of Resurrection. It is called "the Last Day" because there is no day after it, since that day is the final stage of creation. For a person in this world there are four stages: a stage in his mother's womb, a stage in this world, a stage in the barzakh, and a fourth stage on the Day of Resurrection. Four states.

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: There is no (...) in it.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: All of it has no night and day, because the sun will be wound up and thrown into the Fire.

The phrase ﴿for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day﴾: Allah, the Exalted, frequently in the Qur'an joins faith in Him with faith in the Last Day, ﴿Believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Nisa' 39]. Why? Because faith in the Last Day necessitates action. When you believe that there is a day on which you will be recompensed for your deeds, you will work for that day. This is unlike the person who denies it, for the one who denies the Last Day does not work, because he believes there is nothing but this world: wombs that expel and earth that swallows, and nothing more. But when a person believes in the Last Day, it obliges him to act. For this reason He says: ﴿for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day﴾.

He says: ﴿and remembers Allah much﴾, in contrast with one who is not like that. ﴿And remembers Allah﴾: the waw here is a conjunctive particle, and ﴿remembered﴾ is conjoined to what? To ﴿for whoever hopes﴾. That is: and for whoever remembers Allah. Or it is conjoined to ﴿was﴾: ﴿for whoever was﴾, and for whoever remembers Allah, conjoined to ﴿was﴾, because a past-tense verb is conjoined to a past-tense verb. Also, if you make it conjoined to ﴿was﴾, the meaning becomes clearer: ﴿for whoever was hoping for Allah﴾ is an inner act, and ﴿and remembered Allah﴾ is an outward act. He says: conjoined to ﴿was﴾: ﴿for whoever was hoping for Allah﴾, and for whoever ﴿remembers Allah much﴾.

As for ﴿and remembers Allah much﴾: ﴿much﴾ is an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq), meaning remembrance much. The remembrance of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, occurs with the heart, with the tongue, and with the limbs. With the heart, by a person reflecting on the signs of Allah and on His names and attributes; this is remembrance with the heart. With the tongue, such as glorification, declaring Allah's oneness, and praising Him, and the like. With the limbs other than the tongue, such as prayer, which contains bowing, prostration, standing, and sitting, and it is remembrance.

So remembrance occurs in the heart, in the tongue, and in the limbs. The wise, resolute, believing person never ceases to remember Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, because in every one of His creations there is a sign indicating His oneness, glorified and exalted, and His wisdom. Whatever you observe in this universe will remind you of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Likewise, regarding your actions: if you are resolute, you can avoid doing any action except that it becomes worship. The resolute person makes habits into acts of worship, while the heedless person makes acts of worship into habits. So if a person is resolute, not a moment of his life will be wasted on him; he must use it in the remembrance of Allah, the Glorified and Exalted.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verse 17–21 (part 2 of 2):

Does "the remembrance of Allah" include enjoining good and forbidding evil? Yes, it is part of the remembrance of Allah. Reciting the Qur'an is part of the remembrance of Allah. Every statement or action that brings one closer to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is part of the remembrance of Allah.

He, the Exalted, said: ﴿They think the confederates have not withdrawn﴾ [al-Ahzab 20].
* It is derived from this: the great cowardice of these hypocrites, for they think the enemy is still present when it has gone. Or not? If you say: is there evidence for this? I say: yes. If a coward saw a lion in a cave, and the lion left the cave and was taken out, and you said to this coward: "Go ahead, walk past this cave," what would he say? He would say: "No, there is a lion in it." That is because he is a coward. The coward thinks his enemy has not left its place, and he fears even his own shadow.
* It is also derived from this noble verse: that if the confederates returned again, these hypocrites would wish that they were among the Bedouins rather than in the cities, based on His saying: ﴿And if the confederates should come, they would wish that they were out among the Bedouins﴾ [al-Ahzab 20]. Which is the better life: life in the desert or life in the cities? The cities. But because of their cowardice, they wish to go off to the Bedouins, to the desert, and not to be present with these confederates.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: these hypocrites do not want to share in the battles of the believers, based on His saying: ﴿They ask about your news﴾. They love to be far from the battles; they only seek out news.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: if the hypocrite were to take part in fighting alongside the believers, he would fight only a little, ﴿and they would not fight except a little﴾.
Here is a question: may we include hypocrites in our fighting if we know they are hypocrites, or should we not include them? We should not include them, because their harm to us is far greater than their benefit. As for those whose condition we do not know, the principle is that a person is judged by his outward state.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent pattern for anyone whose hope is in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Ahzab 21].
* It is derived from this noble verse: the obligation to follow the Prophet ﷺ (ﷺ). From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿for anyone whose hope is in Allah and the Last Day﴾, because hoping in Allah and the Last Day is obligatory.
* And it is derived from this noble verse: that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, based on His saying: ﴿in the Messenger of Allah﴾.

The world is such-and-such, or the last of the stages of a human being? The last stage of a human being, as we have already mentioned in the tafsir.

A person is either standing, sitting, or lying on his side, and they remember Allah in all these states.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verses 22–27 (part 1 of 5):

Allah the Exalted said, at the start of today's lesson: (﴿When the believers saw the confederates, they said, "This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us"﴾, of trial and victory, ﴿and Allah and His Messenger had spoken truly﴾ in the promise, ﴿and it increased them not except in faith﴾, meaning affirmation of Allah's promise, ﴿and submission﴾ [Al-Ahzab 22] to His command.)

﴿لَمَّا رَأَى الْمُؤْمِنُونَ الْأَحْزَابَ﴾ Here ﴿لَمَّا﴾ is conditional (shartiyyah) but does not apply jazm (jussive). The conditional verb in the verse is ﴿رَأَى﴾, and its response is ﴿قَالُوا هَذَا مَا وَعَدَنَا اللَّهُ﴾. It has already passed us that (lamma) in the Arabic language has several uses: among them the conditional, as in this verse; among them the jussive (jazimah), as in His saying: ﴿Nay, they have not yet tasted My punishment﴾ [Sad 8], this is jussive; and among them that it means (illa, "except"), as in His saying: ﴿There is no soul but that over it is a guardian﴾ [At-Tariq 4], meaning: except that over it is a guardian.

﴿وَلَمَّا رَأَى الْمُؤْمِنُونَ الْأَحْزَابَ﴾. The word "al-ahzab" here refers to the confederates who banded together against the Prophet ﷺ: from Quraysh, Ghatafan, Banu Asad and others. When they saw them, was it a visual seeing or a seeing of the heart? A visual seeing. When they saw them, ﴿they said, "This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us."﴾ How? Where did Allah and His Messenger promise that these confederates would come? Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise without the example of those who passed on before you? They were touched by misfortune and hardship and were shaken until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When is the help of Allah?" Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near﴾ [Al-Baqarah 214]. Allah the Exalted has made clear in this verse that they cannot enter Paradise except after these matters, so the promise of Allah the Exalted to them includes that they would see such things that shake them.

He says: ﴿This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us﴾, and this is evidence of their steadfastness, their faith and the sincerity of their intentions. But the hypocrites, as has already been mentioned, used to mock the Messenger ﷺ when he struck the rock that obstructed them while digging the trench, and said that he had seen the cities of Kisra, the palaces of Caesar and Yemen. What did they say? ﴿Allah and His Messenger promised us nothing but delusion﴾ [Al-Ahzab 12]. How can this one possess Yemen, Sham and Iraq when he is now confined? This is a lie and is not true. But the believers said: ﴿This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us, and Allah and His Messenger have spoken truly﴾, the opposite of those hypocrites who said: ﴿Allah and His Messenger promised us nothing but delusion﴾.

﴿وَصَدَقَ اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ﴾. Truthfulness (al-sidq) is the reporting of a matter in accordance with how it actually is. If you wish, say: it is a report that corresponds to reality. This is truthfulness, and its opposite is falsehood. It is said: ṣadaqanī al-ḥadītha and ṣaddaqanī al-ḥadīth, and there is a difference between them. ṣadaqanī al-ḥadītha means: he told me the truth. ṣaddaqanī al-ḥadīth means: he said that what I related to him is true. Do you understand?

﴿وَلَقَدْ صَدَقَكُمُ اللَّهُ وَعْدَهُ إِذْ تَحُسُّونَهُمْ بِإِذْنِهِ﴾ [Al 'Imran 152]. What is the meaning of ﴿صَدَقَكُمُ﴾? It means: He informed you of the truth and made clear to you that what He promised you was true, when you were killing them by His permission.

He says: ﴿وَصَدَقَ اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ﴾. In this sentence, ﴿مَا وَعَدَنَا اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ وَصَدَقَ اللَّهُ وَرَسُولُهُ﴾, was this speech stated as a dispraise or as a praise? As a praise. But it may be puzzling to you how the promise of the Messenger of Allah was joined with the promise of Allah by the conjunction "and" (wa), and how the truthfulness of the Messenger of Allah was also joined with the truthfulness of Allah by "and". The Prophet ﷺ said to a man who said to him: "What Allah wills and you will," the Prophet ﷺ said to him: «Have you made me a rival (nid) to Allah?». So how do we reconcile this with what is in this verse?

The answer is that what belongs to the matters of the Sharia (law) may be attributed to Allah and His Messenger with "and", because what the Prophet ﷺ legislated is part of the legislation of Allah, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [An-Nisa 80]. As for what belongs to the matters of qadar (divine decree), it is not permissible to attribute it to Allah and His Messenger with "and"; rather, it must be with (thumma, "then"), because the capability and will of a human being follow the will and power of Allah.

For example, if a man asks you: "What is the ruling on such and such?", meaning the ruling on congregational prayer, and you do not know its ruling, you say: "Allah and His Messenger know best", because this is a legislated ruling. But if the matter belongs to the matters of qadar, it is not possible to associate anyone other than Allah with Allah using "and", because the will and power of other than Allah follow the will of Allah, and it is not possible for them to be equal to it.

He says: ﴿وَمَا زَادَهُمْ إِلَّا إِيمَانًا وَتَسْلِيمًا﴾. The doer of ﴿زَادَهُمْ﴾ refers to what? That is, the sight of the confederates. That is, the sight of the confederates and their gathering against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not increase them except in ﴿إِيمَانًا﴾. The author says: (affirmation of Allah's promise ﴿وَتَسْلِيمًا﴾ to His command). Faith (iman) is in the heart and submission (taslim) and compliance (inqiyad) are in the limbs, because faith has its locus in the heart, and submission and compliance have their locus in the limbs. A person does not complete his religion except by these two matters: faith and submission. Whoever submits without believing is a hypocrite, and whoever believes without submitting is arrogant. When faith and submission are combined in a person, he becomes a true believer and a true worshipper.

So a believer who does not submit, we say: this is arrogant. And a submitter who is not a believer, we say: this is a hypocrite, because the hypocrites submit outwardly. Faith is not complete except by these two matters, faith and submission. The Sharia is not complete except by these two matters, faith and submission.

He says: ﴿وَمَا زَادَهُمْ إِلَّا إِيمَانًا وَتَسْلِيمًا﴾. ﴿إِيمَانًا﴾ here is a maf'ul li-ajlihi (object of purpose)? What is its i'rab (grammatical analysis)?
