We say: whoever harms the Prophet (ﷺ) harms the believers. Also, whoever opposes the messengers will oppose their followers and harm them.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of patience upon the harm of the disbelievers and the hypocrites, from His saying: ﴿And leave off their harm﴾, for this is a command to be patient with their harm.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of relying upon Allah, from His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And rely upon Allah﴾, and the command implies obligation.

* Among its benefits: that the Prophet (ﷺ) does not possess for himself any benefit or harm, nor for others, all the more so. From His saying: ﴿And rely upon Allah﴾: he is in need of his Lord and is commanded to rely upon Him.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the greatness of Allah's, Mighty and Majestic, sufficiency for those who rely upon Him, from His saying: ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Disposer of affairs﴾. We have mentioned earlier that this is meant to express wonder at the sufficiency of Allah for whoever relies upon Him.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿O you who have believed, when you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them﴾ [Al-Ahzab 49] ... to the end.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the importance of marriage (nikah) and divorce (talaq), because Allah, the Exalted, opened it with the call that seeks to alert the one being addressed to what will be delivered to him.

* Among them: that adherence to the rulings of the law in marriage and divorce is one of the requirements of faith. Its basis: from His saying: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, for it is one of the requirements of their faith that they carry out what they were commanded.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that there is no divorce before marriage, from His saying: ﴿when you marry believing women, then﴾, and "then" indicates sequence. So there is no divorce before marriage. There is no difference in this between a divorce directed at a specific woman and one in general terms. So if a man says to a woman: "If I marry you, you are divorced," and then he marries her, she is not divorced, why? Because the divorce occurred before the marriage.

Likewise, if he says: "Every woman I marry is divorced," then when he marries a woman she is not divorced, because there is no divorce except after marriage.

* Among its benefits: there is no ila' (oath of abstention, ), no zihar (a form of divorce by likening the wife to a forbidden relative, ), and no prohibition on a woman except after marriage. Since divorce, which is the greatest separation, is only after marriage, then so is what is less than it, except that if a man prohibits a specific woman and then marries her afterwards, he owes an expiation of an oath (kaffarat yamin, ). Likewise, zihar, if he intends prohibition by it and makes zihar on a woman before marrying her, he owes an expiation of an oath, and he does not owe the expiation of zihar, because zihar is valid only from one's wife.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of divorce, from His saying: ﴿then you divorced them﴾. Allah did not blame the believers for divorce, and if it were forbidden, He would have blamed them for it.

* Among its benefits also: is divorce before consummation permissible or not? From His saying: ﴿then you divorced them before you had touched them﴾. This is a benefit other than (the permissibility of divorce in general), because divorce before consummation may involve some diminishment of the woman's right. So it is said: this man, had he not known that there was some affliction in her, would not have divorced her before he consummated the marriage and touched her, because the custom is that when a person marries, he marries out of desire. So if he divorces her before touching her, it is evidence that there is something in her.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that if he divorces her before intercourse, there is no 'iddah (waiting period, ) owed by her. There is disagreement about this. Some scholars, who are the majority (al-jumhur), hold that if he was alone with her (khalwah, ), then she must observe the 'iddah. They placed seclusion in the position of intercourse. This is what the Rightly Guided Caliphs ruled, and it is the position of the majority of the Companions, indeed the majority of the Ummah. Only a small group opposed this, among them al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, in his new opinion. He held that if he did not have intercourse with her, there is no 'iddah upon her, even if he was alone with her. There is no doubt that this is the apparent meaning of the verse. But what is transmitted from the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, especially the Rightly Guided Caliphs, establishes that she must observe the 'iddah if he was alone with her.

* One of the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of a provision (mut'ah) for a woman divorced before consummation. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿so provide for them﴾. This is qualified by another verse, which concerns the case where a dowry has been specified for her. If a dowry has been specified for her, then he owes only half of the dowry, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them, and you have already specified a dowry for them, then half of what you specified [is due], unless they forgo it or the one in whose hand is the marriage contract forgoes it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:237].
* Another benefit of this noble verse: the use of euphemism for what is shameful to mention, based on His saying: ﴿before you have touched them﴾.
* Another benefit of this noble verse: that a woman widowed by her husband must observe the waiting period ('iddah) in all cases, even if he did not consummate the marriage with her. From where is this taken? From His saying: ﴿then you divorce them﴾. God attached this ruling to what? To divorce. So His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, they shall wait for four months and ten days﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:234] remains upon its general application: that a widow must observe the waiting period even if he did not consummate the marriage with her.
* Another benefit of this noble verse: the mercy of God, glorified and exalted is He, toward His servants and creation, in that He made the provision obligatory for the woman divorced before consummation. The reason is that it consoles her heart and removes the worry and grief that overcome her after the divorce.
* Another of its benefits: the obligation of releasing [the wife] in a good manner when parting, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and release them with a fair release﴾.
* Another benefit of this noble verse: that the waiting period is a right of the husband. Its basis is His saying: ﴿then you have no right over them﴾, so it is a right of the husband over the woman.
* Another of its benefits: that a person should keep count of his wife's waiting period, take care of it, and not leave her neglected, not knowing about her. This is based on His saying: ﴿that you count﴾. This is evidence that it is part of the duty of husbands to count their wives' waiting periods, keep track of them, and monitor them, because she is his bed as long as she is in the waiting period, if it is a revocable divorce.

Does the phrase ﴿when you marry believing women﴾ imply that if they marry women from the People of the Book, the ruling changes? No. Why? Because this is a qualifier that describes the usual case, and the scholars of usul (principles of jurisprudence) have mentioned that a qualifier describing the usual case has no implied meaning (mafhum). From where is this taken?

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: From His saying: ﴿believing women﴾, because this ruling covers believing women and others.

Also among its benefits: there is no waiting period for a divorce before consummation, even if a long time has passed, based on His saying: ﴿then you divorce them﴾.

And another benefit in it: divorce is in the hand of the husband, based on His saying: ﴿then you divorce them﴾. So neither the father, nor the grandfather, nor the paternal uncle, nor the maternal uncle, nor anyone else may divorce on behalf of a person.

And another benefit in it: there is no waiting period for a woman who is not divorced, such as one whose marriage is annulled by khul' (divorce initiated by the wife) or otherwise? Or is there some debate about this? What do you say about this benefit: that there is no waiting period for one who is separated during life by other than divorce?

* Student: It is not derived.
* The Shaykh: It is not derived. Why?
* The student: Because it did not say: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, but in the case of divorce, its implied meaning is that the waiting period applies only to divorced women. This is the Prophet's ruling. If the waiting period is for divorced women, then the meaning is that khul'd women have no waiting period. What do you say, everyone?
* The student: Because (...) its attributes?
* The Shaykh: How?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Is it not, for example, ﴿Then if you divorce them before you have touched them, then you have no waiting period for them﴾? Its meaning is: if you divorce them after consummation, then they must observe a waiting period. So He made the waiting period one of the rulings of divorce. Fine, what about other than divorce?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, that is not possible, because divorce has its own rulings. For this reason they say: a widow must observe the waiting period even if her husband did not consummate the marriage with her.

In any case, it may not be apparent to everyone, but the preponderant view is that a woman separated by other than divorce has no waiting period. The woman who obtains khul' only needs to be cleared by one menstrual cycle, and then she is free to remarry.

Do we also say that the verse includes combining financial and practical kindness? From where?

* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: What is this? Is this financial or practical?
* Student: Practical.
* The Shaykh: Practical. And the financial?
* Student: ﴿so provide for them﴾.
* The Shaykh: ﴿so provide for them﴾.

Fine, there is also a benefit here: the verse excludes the woman for whom a dowry has been specified.

* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: It is there? Where?
* Student: In the explanation.
* The Shaykh: The explanation?
* Student: What is the benefit?
* The Shaykh: The benefit: the woman for whom a dowry has been specified receives half of the dowry, and the husband owes her no provision.
* The student: (...) provision for the one for whom no dowry was specified (...)?
* The Shaykh: Yes, good.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verse 50 (part 1 of 4):

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: (﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful for you your wives whom you have given their due compensation﴾ [al-Ahzab: 50] i.e. their dowries (mahur, the marriage gift)). ﴿O Prophet﴾: this form of address indicates the honouring of the one addressed, since the address is directed to him by the vocative, this being one aspect; and another aspect is that he is described with prophethood, ﴿O Prophet﴾. In this there is honour and exaltation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

His saying: ﴿Indeed We have made lawful for you your wives whom you have given their due compensation﴾. ﴿We have made lawful﴾ means: We have made them lawful (ḥill) for you. Is the intended meaning "your wives whom you wish to marry," or "your wives whom you have already married"?

On this there are two opinions among the scholars. Some of them said: ﴿Indeed We have made lawful for you your wives whom you have given their due compensation﴾ means: your wives whom you wish to marry and give their due compensation to. The argument of these scholars is that if we take it to refer to those he has already married, it would be an instance of obtaining what is already obtained (taḥṣīl al-ḥāṣil), because when the wife is already with him and Allah has permitted her to him, there is no need to say ﴿We have made lawful for you﴾, since they are already married to him.

The second opinion: the intended meaning is "We have made lawful your wives whom you have married," based on His saying ﴿whom you have given their due compensation﴾. This second opinion is the one that agrees with the apparent meaning of the verse, because His saying ﴿you have given﴾ is a past-tense verb, whereas on the first opinion one would have to interpret the past-tense verb as a present-tense verb, meaning "whom you give their due compensation." This contradicts the apparent meaning of the verse.

As for the objection of those scholars, that if the intended meaning is the wives who are in his marriage, then mentioning the making lawful is obtaining what is already obtained, this is answered by saying that mentioning the making lawful is for emphasis: its meaning is that these women are lawful to you, there is no doubt about them and no conflict regarding them.

* Student: Could it be for expressing favour (imtinan)?
* Shaykh: It may be for expressing favour, but the manifest meaning is the removal of any blame that might be directed at him.

He says: ﴿whom you have given﴾: ﴿ātayta﴾ means "given" (a'ṭayta). As for (atayta) without the long vowel, it means "came."

So we say: ﴿ātayta﴾, i.e. "you have given," ﴿their due compensation (ujūrahunna)﴾. The author says: (i.e. their dowries).

The dowry (mahr) is called a due compensation (ajr) because it is a return for the benefit of the wife and for enjoying her, and not a return for her essence. Had it been a return for her essence it would have been called a price (thaman), but it is a return for enjoying her and benefiting from her; for this reason it is called a wage (ujrah).

His saying: ﴿ātayta ujūrahunna﴾: when ﴿ātayta﴾ means "gave," it takes two objects. Where is the first object? The first object is omitted, and the estimate is "ātaytahunna" (you gave them), and ﴿ujūrahunna﴾ is the second object. Have you understood? It is permissible to omit the object when it is known.

He says: ﴿ātayta ujūrahunna wa-mā malakat yamīnuka﴾: the waw is a conjunctive particle, and ﴿mā﴾ is coordinated with His saying ﴿your wives (azwājaka)﴾, meaning: and We have made lawful for you what your right hand possesses; that is, does it possess her essence or the benefit of her?

It possesses her essence, and possession of the essence entails possession of its benefits, because whoever possesses a thing possesses its benefits, but whoever possesses benefits does not necessarily possess the substances or the essences.

He says: ﴿and what your right hand possesses of what Allah has given you as spoils (mimmā afā'a Allāhu 'alayka)﴾. "Right hand," "hands," and the like are used to denote the essence, because they are generally the means of taking and giving. So His saying, exalted is He, ﴿by what your hands have earned﴾ [al-Shura: 30] means: by what you have earned. ﴿And what your right hand possesses﴾ means: what you possess; but He expressed it by "right hand" to denote the essence, because taking and giving is generally done by the hand, and the right is more honourable than the left, so it is the one by which one takes and gives. ﴿And what your right hand possesses﴾.

* Student: His saying ﴿their due compensation﴾: the maintenance by the wage in exchange for enjoyment, meaning the dowry in exchange for enjoyment...
* Shaykh: Yes, in exchange for possessing the benefit and enjoyment.
* Student: Meaning, O Shaykh, is the Hanbali view correct that a man does not wash his wife when she dies?
* Shaykh: Afterwards the benefits have come, may Allah bless you.

He says: ﴿and what your right hand possesses of what Allah has given you as spoils﴾: ("of" here, min, is explanatory (bayaniyyah)). What is the thing explained?
* Student: (﴿what Allah has given you as spoils﴾)?
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: ﴿what your right hand possesses﴾.
* Shaykh: Yes, but where is the thing explained? ﴿malakat﴾ is the explained item, the known possession. The explained item is the relative pronoun; the relative pronoun, the conditional noun and the interrogative noun are all vague words after which the explanation comes; as in His saying: (min) is explanatory of ﴿mā﴾ in His saying ﴿and what your right hand possesses of what Allah has given you as spoils﴾. The author says: (from the unbelievers by captivity).

﴿Afā'a﴾ means "returned," and from it comes al-fay', which is the shade after the sun, because it returns after the sun had abrogated it, becoming shade as it was before the sun reached it.

His saying: ﴿what Allah has given you as spoils (mimmā afā'a Allāhu 'alayka)﴾ here means the booty (ghanīmah), because booty is in reality the return of property from those who do not deserve it to its rightful people; for we Muslims are the ones who rightfully deserve what Allah has provided for creation, while the unbelievers enjoy it unjustly; for this reason they are called to account for it. It has passed with us that the unbelievers are held to account for eating, drinking and clothing, and we mentioned a proof for that from the Qur'an. What is the proof from the Qur'an that they are held to account for clothing?
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, this applies even to Muslims.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, glory be to Allah! The proof that unbelievers are held to account for clothing?
* Student: (...) in Surah al-A'raf (...)?
* Shaykh: ﴿Say: Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah which He has brought forth for His servants, and the good things of provision? Say: They are for those who believed in the life of this world, purely for them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-A'raf: 32]. This also includes clothing and food ﴿and the good things of provision﴾; ﴿for those who believed﴾: the lam is for permission and entitlement; ﴿purely on the Day of Resurrection﴾: for whom? For the believers. As for those, they are not entitled to it and it is not purely theirs on the Day of Resurrection; so in this world it is forbidden for them, and they are called to account for it on the Day of Resurrection.

And what is the verse that is the proof that eating and drinking are forbidden to the unbelievers?
Recite it.
* Student: (﴿there is no blame upon those who believed﴾)?
* Shaykh: No, it is not (﴿there is no blame upon those who believed﴾).
* Student: ﴿Those who believed﴾..?
* Shaykh: No, yes, ﴿and did righteous deeds﴾ in full?
* Student: ﴿there is no blame upon them for what they have eaten﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 93]?
* Shaykh: Its implication is that those who did not believe and did not do righteous deeds are blameworthy for what they have eaten.

Thus it becomes clear why the booty is a return (fay'), and fay' means what? Return and restoration. Therefore the property in the hands of the unbelievers, when the Muslims seize it, has returned to its people, as if they had been taking the property without right; when we take it from them, it returns to its entitled owner.

His saying: ﴿and what your right hand possesses of what Allah has given you as spoils﴾: he said: (from the unbelievers by captivity, like Safiyyah and Juwayriyah). Safiyyah is from which captivity?
* Students: Khaybar.
* Shaykh: Yes, from the captives of Khaybar, and Juwayriyah from the captives of the battle of Banu al-Mustaliq; both of them are Mothers of the Believers.

His saying: ﴿of what Allah has given you as spoils﴾ apparently means that what his right hand possesses from other than that is not lawful to him, but this is not intended... intended; the proof is that Maria the Copt was made lawful by the Prophet (peace be upon him), and she bore him a son, and the benefits will come, God willing.

He says: (﴿and the daughters of your paternal uncles, the daughters of your paternal aunts, the daughters of your maternal uncles, and the daughters of your maternal aunts, who emigrated with you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 50], unlike those who did not emigrate).
* Student: Safiyyah and Juwayriyah (...)?
* Shaykh: They were from those whom his right hand possessed first, then he freed them and married them.

His saying: ﴿the daughters of your paternal uncles, the daughters of your paternal aunts, the daughters of your maternal uncles, and the daughters of your maternal aunts﴾: these four are the permitted wives from among the relatives, and other relatives are forbidden, as in Surah al-Nisa. Thus relatives now become both permitted and forbidden. The forbidden ones are those mentioned in Surah al-Nisa in His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, the daughters of the brother, and the daughters of the sister﴾ [al-Nisa: 23]. How many? Seven. The permitted relatives are four: the daughters of the paternal uncle, the daughters of the paternal aunt, the daughters of the maternal uncle, and the daughters of the maternal aunt. Is that right? These are the permitted relatives.

(The daughters of the paternal uncle) means: even if they descend (in generations); (the daughters of the paternal aunt) even if they descend; (the daughters of the maternal uncle) even if they descend; (the daughters of the maternal aunt) even if they descend; all of these are lawful.

His saying: ﴿the daughters of your paternal uncles, the daughters of your paternal aunts﴾: the exegetes discussed His saying "your paternal uncles, your paternal aunts, your maternal uncles, your maternal aunts," and they said: why is the male singular and the female plural? Where are the males? "Your paternal uncle and your maternal uncle"; and for the females He said "your paternal aunts and your maternal aunts."

Some said: this is a matter of honouring the masculine, as if one man is matched by a plural of women; this is the view of Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him. Others said: since the word "paternal uncle" and "maternal uncle" is like a verbal noun (maṣdar), it is appropriate not to pluralize them, because verbal nouns are known not to be pluralized or dualized; but there is something in the soul about this.

The closer view is what Ibn Kathir mentioned, that the bond of the paternal uncle with a person is stronger than the bond of the paternal aunt with him; for this reason the plural was used. Otherwise, it is well known that a person has paternal uncles, not just one; and the daughters of his paternal uncles are all lawful, are they not? Lawful.

﴿the daughters of your paternal uncles, the daughters of your paternal aunts, the daughters of your maternal uncles, and the daughters of your maternal aunts﴾ contains an added condition relating to the Messenger (ﷺ), which is His saying: ﴿who emigrated with you﴾. ﴿Who emigrated with you﴾ means: who emigrated from Makkah to Madinah; whether they were with him directly or with him in the sense of the emigration, it is not necessary that the daughter of the paternal uncle or the daughter of the maternal uncle be directly with the Messenger (ﷺ), travelling with him; rather, if she emigrated before him or after him, she is included in this. ﴿Who emigrated with you﴾.

He says: (﴿and a believing woman if she gives herself to the Prophet, if the Prophet wishes to take her in marriage﴾ [al-Ahzab: 50] seeking marriage with her without dowry; ﴿exclusively for you, apart from the believers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 50]: marriage in the wording of a gift without dowry, meaning exclusively, and marriage) ﴿We know what We have enjoined upon them concerning their wives﴾ [al-Ahzab: 50], and so on to the end.

He says: ﴿and a believing woman﴾: meaning, We have made lawful for you a believing woman. This is an indefinite noun in an affirmative context, and it is well known that an indefinite noun in an affirmative context does not imply generality; but since the context is one of favour (imtinan), it becomes general. The default for an indefinite noun in an affirmative context is that it is not general; when you say to someone, "Strike a man," it does not mean that I command you to strike all men; but when an indefinite noun in an affirmative context is intended to express favour, it becomes general, because if it were restricted to a single one, the favour would not be complete; the favour is not complete unless it is intended generally.

So ﴿a woman (imra'ah)﴾: although its form is singular, what is intended by it is generality, why? Because it was brought for the purpose of favour, and favour through singularity is not complete unless it is favour with every item or every individual of this indefinite noun.

So the meaning of the verse becomes: We have made lawful for you any woman.

His saying ﴿believing﴾: this is a condition by which a non-believing woman is excluded, even if she is a Christian or Jewish woman, for she is not lawful to the Prophet (ﷺ). For this reason some scholars held that among the particularities of the Prophet (ﷺ) in marriage is that he did not marry a scripturist woman; but this did not occur: the Prophet (ﷺ) never married a scripturist woman.

It is known that among the particularities of the Messenger in marriage are both facilitations and restrictions: the facilitation is marriage by gift and marrying more than four, and the restriction is that he may not take as lawful from the daughters of his paternal uncles, paternal aunts, maternal uncles and maternal aunts except those who emigrated with him; and likewise, according to the preponderant view, after the Prophet (ﷺ) gave his wives the choice, women are no longer lawful to him, as will come, God willing.

He says: ﴿if she gives herself to the Prophet﴾: ﴿if she gives herself﴾: she herself, without a guardian; ﴿gives herself﴾, i.e. she gave herself to the Prophet (ﷺ) without compensation, because the definition of a gift is giving up property without compensation. The meaning of ﴿gives herself﴾ is that she came to the Messenger (peace be upon him) and said to him: "I have given myself to you," and so she becomes lawful to him. But since the Messenger (peace be upon him) had the choice in this and it was not obligatory upon him to accept, He said: ﴿if the Prophet wishes to take her in marriage﴾, and this condition falls under the first condition.

It is known that the second condition is a qualification of the first condition; so it is later in wording but earlier in meaning. The overlapping of conditions: whenever conditions overlap, make the last condition a qualification of what precedes it; it is later in rank but earlier in meaning. Now, are we speaking in Arabic or in Persian? Is it clear to you or not?

When conditions are multiplied, whether introduced by "if," "when," or similar, the following last condition is a condition on what precedes it, so it is later in wording but earlier in meaning and rank. For example, if you say: "Tell me when Zayd strikes you if he wrongs you," the wronging precedes the striking, though it is later in mention. This is fully clarified by the words of the poet:

If you seek help from us, if you are terrified, you will find from us
Strongholds of honour, whose adornment is generosity.

Where is the first condition? "If you seek help" and the second: "if you are terrified." The second condition is later than the first in wording but earlier in meaning and rank, because the terror precedes the seeking of help. This is a rule: whenever conditions are multiplied, the second condition precedes the first, that is, the one before it; if there are three conditions, four conditions, the third precedes the second, and the second precedes the first; that is, in reverse.

Here, ﴿a believing woman, if she gives herself to the Prophet, if he wishes﴾: the wish precedes permissibility and acceptance; therefore He said: ﴿if the Prophet wishes to take her in marriage﴾. The benefit of this condition is that, since the Prophet's rejection of a woman who gives herself to him would be a very difficult matter, and the Prophet (ﷺ) was the most modest of people, a woman offering herself to the Messenger (ﷺ) might be almost binding upon him by the demands of his character. Since this is so, Allah opened the door wide for His Messenger, granting him choice and will in this situation, so He said: ﴿if the Prophet wishes to take her in marriage﴾.

So what is the benefit of mentioning the wish, given that the one to whom the gift is made may accept or refuse it? This is a known matter. The benefit is that the Prophet (ﷺ) is not obligated to accept, since his character (ﷺ) was known to be the most modest of people; and it is well known that a person refusing a woman's gift of herself is difficult, since she comes desiring you with the utmost desire, to the extent that she has ransomed you with herself; how could you reject her? This is indeed difficult in reality, and rejecting her may be contrary to manliness, while the Prophet (peace be upon him) was the most eager of people for manliness and the most modest of people in such matters. But Allah willed to open the door for him, so that no one would object or say, "How did he reject her?", and so that the Messenger would have complete freedom in this matter, in accepting her or rejecting her.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verse 50 (part 2 of 4):

He says: ﴿If the Prophet wishes to marry her﴾. The author said: (seeks to marry her). The correct meaning is: agrees to marry her. Is he the one seeking, or the one being sought? He is the one sought, so the correct meaning is that what is intended by ﴿wishes to marry her﴾ is: that he accepts her marriage.

﴿who have emigrated with you﴾: those who embraced Islam along with you.

He says: ﴿specially for you, to the exclusion of the believers﴾. Regarding ﴿specially for you﴾, it may be an adjective modifying ﴿and a believing woman﴾, or it may be an object of a verb that is omitted, with the sense: We have made it specially for you; that is, this ruling We have made specially for you. What is "khalis" (sincere, exclusive) of a thing is that which is not mixed with anything else, so the meaning of ﴿specially for you﴾ is: no one shares it with you, in the case where a woman gives herself in marriage to someone, for she is not lawful to him.

Is what is meant by "khalis" here that he marries without a dowry and without a guardian, or that it occurs through the wording of a gift (hibah)?

The correct view is the first: that what is exclusive is that it be without a dowry, without a guardian, and without witnesses according to the view that witnesses are a condition. For what is a gift? It is a donation without compensation. So what is meant is the meaning, not the wording. That is, what the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was singled out for is that a woman comes to him and says: "I have given myself to you," and he accepts her. This indeed happened in fact more than once: women came to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and gave themselves to him. So what is exclusive to and specific to the Messenger is that the marriage is without payment, without a guardian, and without witnesses.

As for a gift-worded marriage, the scholars differed on whether a marriage is valid with the wording of a gift, such as saying: "I have given you my daughter in exchange for a dowry of such and such," or "I have made my daughter yours in exchange for a dowry of such and such."

On this the scholars hold two opinions: some hold that it is not valid, and that the marriage contract must be worded with "tazwij" or "inkah"; others hold that it is valid. This has another place for its discussion.

﴿specially for you, to the exclusion of the believers﴾: ﴿dun﴾ means "other than"; that is, apart from them. The meaning is that it is not lawful for believers, and for disbelievers it is even more so, for a disbeliever is not lawful to marry by gift, and likewise a believer.

The author said: ﴿If the Prophet wishes to marry her﴾, he said: (seeks to marry her), and we corrected yesterday that what is meant by ﴿yastankihaha﴾ is: agrees.

He says: ﴿specially for you, to the exclusion of the believers﴾: marriage by the wording of a gift without a dowry is specific to the Messenger ﷺ, to the exclusion of the believers.

(﴿We have known what We have ordained for them﴾: that is, the believers, ﴿concerning their wives﴾: of the rulings.) ﴿We have known﴾: ﴿qad﴾ here is for confirmation. It has been said that "qad" when it precedes a past verb is for confirmation, and when it precedes a present verb it is for diminution, though it may sometimes be intended for confirmation. So when you say "qad qama" (he has indeed stood), this is for confirmation; and when you say "qad yajud al-bakhil" (the miser may give) and "qad yasdiq al-kaddhab" (the liar may speak truth), this is for diminution. But it comes for confirmation in such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He knows what you are upon﴾ [An-Nur 64], and ﴿Allah already knows the hinderers﴾ [Al-Ahzab 18]; these are without doubt for confirmation.

His saying: ﴿We have known what We have ordained for them﴾ means that We have indeed ordained things for them, and We knew that the benefit requires what We ordained rather than anything else. So the verse does not mean merely knowledge, or merely informing that God has known what He ordained, because that God has known what He ordained is a known matter.

﴿We have known what We have ordained for them﴾: I say: the intended meaning is not merely the information that God knows, because that God ordained it is known to proceed from knowledge; rather, what is meant is that what We ordained proceeded from knowledge on Our part of what suits them regarding their wives, and not from ignorance. That is why He said: ﴿We have known what We have ordained for them﴾. ﴿Ordained﴾ here means "made obligatory." (﴿for them﴾: that is, upon the believers, ﴿concerning their wives﴾: of the rulings.) ﴿Their wives﴾ is the plural of "zawjah" or the plural of "zawj." (Of the rulings: that they not exceed four wives, and not marry except with a guardian, witnesses, and a dowry), and other matters that differ from the rulings established for the Messenger ﷺ. For the Prophet ﷺ was singled out in marriage with rulings, and the believers were singled out with rulings, and all of that proceeds from the knowledge of God, Glorified and Exalted, and from wisdom.

As for His saying, that is, the author's: (that they not exceed four): it is not lawful for a believer to exceed four wives, based on the saying of God, Exalted: ﴿And if you fear that you will not be just with the orphans, then marry what seems good to you of women, two, three, or four﴾ [An-Nisa 3]. He made the last of it "rubaʿ," that is, four, while knowing that the context would call for more if there were more, as evidenced by the fact that the verse mentions only the permissible number, because it was arranged upon a condition, which is ﴿if you fear that you will not be just with the orphans﴾; that is, if you fear you will not be just among the women before you, such as a paternal cousin and the like, then there are many other women available to you. If there were more than four, God would have mentioned them so that the scope would be wider. Are you understanding this or not?

The verse was revealed restricted by the condition ﴿if you fear that you will not be just with the orphans﴾, meaning: that you will not be just in marrying them. In the Jahiliyyah, if a man had an orphaned paternal cousin, he would wrong her in marriage: either by preventing her, or by tying her to himself. So God revealed this verse.

﴿Then marry﴾: that is, other women are many; marry what seems good to you of women, two, three, or four. So if a number above four were permissible, it would have been mentioned here, and it would have said, for example: "Then marry whomever you wish of women," or it would have said: "Then marry what seems good to you of women" without restriction. Since it restricted, it is known that more than four is not permitted.

None dissented on this except some anomalous scholars or the Rafidah. The Rafidah have a looseness in matters of marriage, of which this matter is one: they permit a person to marry up to nine. Among them is also the matter of temporary marriage (mut'ah), and this is what leads weak-faithed people to adopt their school, because they find in it satisfaction of their desires. If they permit temporary marriage, so that when a person arrives in a city he may go to a woman and say: "Marry yourself to me for a period of seven days, or ten days, or a month," they permit that, and they also permit a person to marry up to nine.

Likewise the author says: (and not marry except with a guardian). Yes, marriage is not permitted except with a guardian. The evidence for this from the Qur'an is ﴿And marry off the single among you﴾ [An-Nur 32]: marry; ﴿And do not marry the polytheists﴾: do not give in marriage; ﴿Do not prevent them from marrying their husbands﴾ [Al-Baqarah 232]. And if the guardian were not a condition, his preventing would have no ruling.

Second: (and no witnesses). The requirement of witnesses in marriage is disputed. The well-known view is that witnesses are necessary, because the marriage contract is serious and entails matters and rights: lineage, property, and rights. That is, other contracts you find are either financial or rights-related other than property, but this one combines property, lineage, and rights, or not?

Property is like the dowry, the maintenance, and inheritance; lineage is like attributing the child to his father in marriage; and rights are what is owed between the husband and wife of kind companionship. So witnesses are necessary.

Ibn Taymiyyah, may God have mercy on him, does not require witnesses; rather, what is required is public declaration of the marriage or witnesses. So if public declaration exists, even without witnesses, it suffices.

The divisions are: either both witnessing and public declaration are present, which is the highest division; or both are absent, which is not valid; or witnessing exists without public declaration, and he said: the validity of marriage here is doubtful and subject to consideration; or public declaration exists without witnessing, and this is valid according to him. So the divisions are four: both public declaration and witnessing exist; both are absent; witnessing exists without public declaration; public declaration exists without witnessing.

* Student: Do the witnesses testify to the consent or to the contract?
* Shaykh: They testify to the contract.
* Student: To the consent or to the contract?
* Shaykh: No, to the contract. As for witnessing the consent, that is a sunnah and not obligatory.
* Student: (...) weddings (...) simply (...) the family of the wife (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, public declaration is not necessarily by a feast. Public declaration may be, for example, by walking on the wedding night through the markets as was done in the past, and likewise now with cars; now it is clear. Likewise placing lights on the husband's house and the wife's house; this too is public declaration.
* Student: If that does not happen?
* Shaykh: If that does not happen, it is not public declaration.
* Student: (...) with the presence of some relatives?
* Shaykh: If it does not appear to be a wedding, it is not public declaration; but if it appears so, such that the gathering is larger than usual, this is public declaration.

As for His saying: (except with a guardian, witnesses, and a dowry): what is the dowry? The dowry is the mahr. The apparent meaning of the author's words is that the dowry is a condition of the marriage's validity. Know that the dowry has three states: sometimes it is stated specifically, sometimes it is negated, and sometimes it is left unmentioned, three states: sometimes it is negated, sometimes it is affirmed as specific, and sometimes it is left silent, neither specified nor negated.

An example of a specified dowry: he says, "I marry you my daughter for ten riyals." Is it valid or not? It is valid. "I marry you my daughter for one riyal," is it valid? Do not laugh; people have married for less than a riyal. A man married a woman for one riyal, and when it was midmorning and he was with her, a man knocked on the door; he went to open it, and they argued, and their voices rose. When he returned to her, she said: "Who is this man who comes to dispute with you on the first day of your marriage?" He said: "This is a man claiming one riyal from me." She said: "Take this riyal, give it to him," her dowry. But now it is apparent that no one marries for one riyal. This is affirming it as specific, by saying: "I marry you my daughter for one riyal, or for ten riyals, or for a hundred riyals, or more, or less."

The second state: it is negated, as when he says, "I marry you my daughter," and says, "I accept, without a dowry." The scholars, may God have mercy on them, differed on whether this contract is valid or not. The well-known view of the school is that the contract is valid, and she has the mahr al-mithl (the customary dowry). Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah chose that the contract is not valid, because he married on other than the condition God mentioned, for God, Exalted, says: ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that, that you seek with your wealth, as chaste, not as fornicators﴾ [An-Nisa 24]. And what comes after it? ﴿that you seek with your wealth﴾.

The third state: it is left silent, neither specified nor negated, as when he says, "I marry you my daughter," and he says, "I accept." Here the contract is valid and she has the mahr al-mithl. God has stated this in His saying: ﴿There is no blame on you if you divorce women before you have touched them or specified for them a dowry; but provide for them﴾ [Al-Baqarah 236]. Here, if he consummates with her, the customary dowry becomes due; if he divorces her before consummation, the provision (mut'ah) becomes due. Do you now know the divisions?

The apparent meaning of the author's words, "and witnesses and a dowry," is that the dowry is a condition of the contract's validity, which agrees with the words of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may God have mercy on him.

(...) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We have known what We have ordained for them concerning their wives﴾. When "faradha" is followed by "li," it means "ahalla" (made lawful), as in His saying earlier: ﴿There is no fault upon the Prophet concerning what God has ordained for him﴾ [Al-Ahzab 38], that is, what He made lawful; and as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿God has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths﴾ [At-Tahrim 2], that is, made it lawful and prescribed it. But when it is followed by "ʿala" (upon), it means "obligation," as here: ﴿We have known what We have ordained for them concerning their wives﴾.

The author mentioned that what God has ordained for us concerning wives is that we not exceed four, and that we not marry except with a guardian, witnesses, and a dowry. We have already discussed what relates to the dowry, and that it has three states...

* Student: (...) negated (...) silent about it?
* Shaykh: Silent about it. Its example when specified?
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: When specified, is it permissible or not permissible?
* Student: When specified, it is permissible.
* Shaykh: Permissible, and it is also better; naming it in the contract is better. And when negated?
* Student: Not permissible.
* Shaykh: What do you mean by "not permissible"?
* Student: Forbidden, not allowed.
* Shaykh: Is the contract forbidden and invalid? Or is the contract valid and she is owed the customary dowry?
* Student: There is a difference of opinion (...) the contract is valid and she has the customary dowry.
* Shaykh: And Shaykh al-Islam says the contract is not valid.
Which is more correct when the dowry is negated: that the contract is valid and she has the customary dowry, or that the contract is void?
* Student: Valid, and she has the customary dowry.
* Shaykh: Yes, as if Isa wants to disagree.
* Student: The correct view is the words of Shaykh al-Islam.
* Shaykh: That the contract is not valid? What is the evidence?
* Student: (...) ﴿that you seek with your wealth﴾.
* Shaykh: God, Exalted, says: ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that, that you seek with your wealth﴾ [An-Nisa 24]. This indicates that there must be wealth involved.

Now, is the guardian a condition of marriage?

* Student: (...) The guardian is a pillar; there must be a guardian in marriage: "There is no marriage except with a guardian and two just witnesses" [narrated by Ibn Hibban (4075) from the hadith of 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her].
* Shaykh: Good. What is the evidence from the Qur'an and the Sunnah?
* Student: As for the Qur'an, the saying of God, Glorified and Exalted, in Surat al-Baqarah...
* Shaykh: (...) Negation is first applied to the negation of existence; if that is not possible, then to the negation of validity; if that is not possible, then to the negation of perfection. Clear? An example of negation of existence?
* Student: From the Sunnah?
* Shaykh: Whichever you want, from the Sunnah, the Qur'an, or yourself.
* Student: There is no god but God.
* Shaykh: Is there any god other than God?
* Student: There is no god but God, in truth.
* Shaykh: That is, there is no true god but God.
An example for negation of validity?
* Student: "There is no prayer without ablution" [narrated by Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi (240) from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd, may God be pleased with him].
* Shaykh: "There is no prayer without ablution" is for negation of validity, because a person could pray without ablution.
An example for negation of perfection?
* Student: The saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "There is no prayer in the presence of food" [narrated by Muslim (560/67) from the hadith of 'A'ishah, may God be pleased with her].
* Shaykh: "There is no prayer in the presence of food" means: no complete prayer; otherwise, if he prayed, it would be valid.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: It cannot be taken as perfection, and it can be taken as negation of validity. "There is no valid marriage except with a guardian": as long as it can be taken as negation of validity, it is required. We first apply negation to what? To negation of existence, because this is the apparent sense of the wording. If that is not possible, because it exists, we take it as negation of validity, since negation of validity is legal negation of existence. If that is not possible, because the texts establish validity, it is taken as negation of perfection.

Alright, let us read the tafsir, starting from now. We will discuss what came before, God willing.

He says: (﴿concerning their wives and what their right hands possess﴾: of the female slaves). That is, and We have known what We ordained for them concerning what their right hands possess.

(Of the female slaves): the author restricted the general word ﴿mā﴾ to female slaves. Is "mā" in ﴿mā malakat﴾ a relative pronoun or not? "Mā" is a relative noun that conveys generality, and a person owns female slaves, livestock, money, buildings, and land, does he not? So is "mā" here general, meaning: of what their right hands possess of every kind, or of female slaves as the author said?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verse 50 (part 3 of 4):

We say: a general term (lafz 'amm) cannot be restricted by us except with evidence; otherwise it is obligatory to keep the general term in its generality. Here we have restricted it to the female slaves (imaa') by evidence. What is the evidence? Its being coupled with "wives" (azwaj), and the discussion now concerns marital rights. So He says: ﴿We have certainly known what We have enjoined upon them concerning their wives and those whom their right hands possess﴾ (from among the female slaves). Thus the indication of restriction comes from His words ﴿their wives﴾. On this basis we say: every place in which "wives" and "what the right hand possesses" are mentioned together, what is meant by "what the right hand possesses" is female slaves.

He says (by purchase and otherwise), meaning: We have known what We have enjoined upon them regarding the female slaves, by purchase and by other than purchase. Is it possible for a person to own a female slave other than by purchase? It is possible by what? By capture in war (sabi), by gift, by inheritance, and the causes of ownership are many.

The point is that the causes of ownership by right hand (milk al-yamin) are multiple.

(provided the slave is of those who are lawful to her owner, such as a kitabiyya, unlike a Magian or an idolatress) The author, may God have mercy on him, has informed us that it is not lawful for a person to have a slave woman other than a kitabiyya. Of female slaves, only a kitabiyya is lawful, namely a Jewess or a Christian. As for a Magian slave woman, she is not lawful; that is, if we take captives of women from the Magians, it is not lawful for us to have intercourse with them, and likewise the idolatress. And what is the idolatress? She who worships idols; she is not lawful to us by right hand ownership.

What is the difference between Magianism and idolatry? The difference between them is that the Magians worship fire, while idolaters worship idols made of trees, stones and the like, and likewise one who worships graves. And likewise a woman who does not pray; but a woman who does not pray and is an apostate must be killed if she does not repent.

The author's statement "unlike the Magian and the idolatress" is one of the two opinions on this question. The correct view is that the Magian and the idolatress are lawful by right hand ownership, because of the generality of His words, exalted is He: ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Mu'minun 6]. So the phrase ﴿what their right hands possess﴾ is general and includes what is owned of kitabiyyat, what is owned of Magian and idolatrous women, and communist women and others. There is no evidence for restricting it to the kitabiyya. Yes, marriage (nikah) is what is lawful only with a kitabiyya, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you, when you have given them their bridal payments﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5]. He did not say "when you have owned them"; He said ﴿when you have given them their bridal payments﴾. This indicates that what is meant here is marriage, because it is they who are given their payment. As for an owned woman, she is bought; so the correct view is that owned women are lawful to us if they are Magian or kitabiyya, because of the generality of the Scripture reference.

He says: (and that she be istabra'ed before intercourse). This too is among what is enjoined upon us: that we must make sure a female slave we have acquired is cleansed before we have intercourse with her, because the Prophet ﷺ, at the battle of Awtas, «forbade that a pregnant woman be had intercourse with until she gives birth, and that a woman who menstruates be had intercourse with until she has menstruated»[[Abu Dawud (2157) with his chain from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may God be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said concerning the captives of Awtas: «A pregnant woman is not to be had intercourse with until she gives birth, nor a non-pregnant one until she has had one menstrual period.»]]. So istibra' is necessary: if she is pregnant, then by the birth of the child; and if she menstruates, then by one menstrual period.

Is istibra' obligatory in every case, or is a virgin not subjected to it?

Some scholars held that istibra' is obligatory even for virgins, while some scholars, among them Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, said: a virgin is not subjected to istibra'. Why?

Because the purpose of istibra' is knowledge of the womb's being clear, and the virgin's womb is known to be clear; the possibility that she might conceive by means other than intercourse is conceivable but remote. That is, it is possible that she is a virgin yet conceives by the semen of some man and becomes pregnant, but this is remote.

If he acquires her from a trustworthy man and that man informs him that he has already performed istibra' on her (...), is istibra' obligatory? The school's position: istibra' is obligatory. The second view on the matter is that istibra' is not obligatory, since the seller is trustworthy.

Now I ask you about the grammatical analysis (i'rab) of (kay). Who knows it? Do you know it?

* Student: It is a masdariyya (verbal particle).

* Shaykh: It is masdariyya. Is it not valid for it to be a preposition of causation (harf jarr lil-ta'lil)?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes indeed, as when you say: "I came in order to read" (ji'tu kay aqra'). By what?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: And when it is preceded by the lam.

* Student: Then it is masdariyya.

* Shaykh: It is necessarily masdariyya, correct. (Kay) when joined with the lam must be masdariyya, so that two particles of causation are not combined. If it is not preceded by the lam, it becomes a particle of causation and the verb after it is in the subjunctive by (an).

So: ﴿li-kayla﴾: the lam is a preposition, (kay) is masdariyya, ﴿la﴾ is a negative particle, and ﴿yakuna﴾ is an imperative verb built on fatha in a position of genitive?

* Student: No, it is an imperfect verb.

* Shaykh: How? An imperfect verb in what state, governed by what?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: By (kay), and its sign of the accusative is the fatha visible at its end.

﴿So that there will not be upon you any discomfort; and ever is Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾. That is, upon the Prophet ﷺ; the address is to the Messenger ﷺ. ﴿Haraj﴾ means constraint in marriage.

The author said regarding ﴿li-kayla﴾: (it is connected to what precedes it). What precedes it?

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: The author is good. (What precedes it) may mean that it is connected to ﴿ahlalna﴾: ﴿Indeed We have made lawful for you your wives﴾ up to His words ﴿so that there will not be upon you any discomfort﴾. It may also be connected to ﴿khalisatan laka min dun al-mu'minin﴾ (a privilege for you, so that there is no discomfort upon you). Both meanings are correct; for this reason some said it is connected to ﴿ahlalna﴾, and some said it is connected to ﴿khalisatan﴾, and the author's statement is suitable for both. ﴿So that there will not be upon you any discomfort﴾ means: We made this lawful for you so that there is no constraint upon you in marriage. It is known that the Prophet ﷺ is sought after; women may come to him offering themselves to him. If he does not find lawful the woman who gives herself, he would face constraint from two angles: if he desires her, there is constraint in not being able to marry her; and if he does not desire her, there is constraint in rejecting her. So Allah, mighty and majestic, gave him the choice if the Prophet wished to take her in marriage, so that there would not be upon him what? Discomfort, constraint; so that the scope is open to him. The Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, was singled out with this, namely to marry whom he wishes, even from those who gave themselves to him, because his connection with them carries a great benefit to whom? To them, to their families, and to the Muslims. To them, clearly; to their families, because there is no doubt that for those among them whom the Prophet ﷺ married there is the honour of being related by marriage to the Prophet ﷺ; and to the Muslims, because this woman would have knowledge of the Sunnah of the Messenger ﷺ, is that not so? This knowledge she would not have acquired were it not for her connection to him; that is why many household Sunnahs were transmitted from whom? From the wives of the Messenger ﷺ.

﴿So that there will not be upon you any discomfort; and ever is Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾. Allah, exalted, always joins these two noble names, because with forgiveness the disliked thing is removed, and with mercy the desired thing is attained; and when the disliked thing is removed and the desired thing is attained, matters are complete.

﴿And ever is Allah Forgiving﴾: ﴿kana﴾ refers to the past? No, because (kana) here has been stripped of indicating time, and what is meant by it is the realisation of the attribute in the one described, that this attribute is truly in this described subject.

﴿Ghafuran﴾: is it an intensive form (sigha mubalagha) or an attributive adjective (sifa mushabbaha)? It may be an intensive form and it may be an attributive adjective; in either case it is derived from forgiveness (maghfirah), which is concealing sin and what else? And overlooking it.

And ﴿Rahiman﴾ is derived from mercy, which is an attribute connected to the Essence of Allah, mighty and majestic, whose consequence is beneficence and bounty. "The Forgiving" and "the Merciful" are among the names of Allah, glorified and exalted. Every name of Allah indicates three matters if it is transitive, and two matters if it is intransitive.

What are the three matters that a name indicates when it is transitive?

* Student: (...)?

* Shaykh: And know that knowledge is not an easy matter; knowledge requires toil. For this reason some of the predecessors said: knowledge is not attained through physical ease. Whoever wants to rest is not a seeker of knowledge. Whoever wants to sleep does not say "I am a seeker of knowledge." The seeker of knowledge must truly be a seeker of knowledge, and he will find its fruit afterward, will find the result and attainment. It may be difficult for him at first to restrain himself to knowledge, but when he becomes accustomed to restraining himself to knowledge, it becomes a disposition and nature for him, so that if he loses that restraint he feels restrained. Try it and you will find: I have tried, and others have tried; if you restrain yourself from knowledge, you will lose that restraint if you fall behind in it. But if you accustom yourself to neglect and indifference, know that you will remain like one afflicted with feminine tuberculosis (as-sull al-mu'annath). Do you know the one afflicted with feminine tuberculosis? Masculine tuberculosis takes its sufferer within two or three months to the grave, but the calamity of feminine tuberculosis keeps him for many years, neither alive nor dead. Likewise the seeker of knowledge, if he does not strive in seeking knowledge, remains neither alive nor dead. So, O my brothers, be keen, be keen in seeking knowledge, if you truly want knowledge. But if you want to pass the time and let time pass by, that is another matter. Whoever wants knowledge must devote himself to it and strive. If he tires his body now, he will find rest afterward, especially you young people. The young person who memorises knowledge, God willing, does not forget it; but be assured that when age advances upon you, you will study today and forget tomorrow. It is true that when a person advances in knowledge his understanding becomes greater, broader and more precise, but in memorisation there is no memorisation except in youth. So, God willing, you are keen on seeking knowledge. Do not think you are on a leisure trip except one leisure trip, which is the leisure of the sciences, because in them is "of every fruit two kinds": this is fiqh, this is hadith, this is tafsir, this is tawhid, this is grammar, masha'Allah, varied fruits. So let your leisure be this knowledge. I ask Allah for success for me and for you. As for me, we studied the issue yesterday and come to question on it today, and no one answers, or one cannot answer; not all of you, all of you may be able to answer, but among you are those who do not answer, though the matter is not far off.

We mentioned that the name of Allah, mighty and majestic, yields three matters if it is transitive, and two if it is intransitive. The three, if transitive?

* Student: The name, the attribute, and the effect?

* Shaykh: Yes: the name, the attribute, and the effect. An example of this with "Forgiving": "the Forgiving" is one of Allah's names; the attribute in "the Forgiving" is forgiveness; and the effect is that He forgives sins entirely, glorified and exalted is He.

"The Merciful" is similar: the name "the Merciful," the attribute mercy, and the effect that He shows mercy. Do you understand, everyone? As for when it is intransitive and does not transfer its effect, it yields two benefits: the name and the attribute. The name, such as "the Exalted, the Mighty": from "the Exalted" we derive the name and the attribute, which is loftiness, and it does not extend to anyone, so we do not say we derive an effect; and likewise "the Mighty."

("﴿And ever is Allah Forgiving﴾" for what is difficult to guard against; "﴿Merciful﴾" in widening in that matter.) This is part of forgiveness and mercy, and not the whole of forgiveness and mercy; forgiveness is in what corresponds to sins, and mercy is in what attains the desired. Now let us return to the benefits.

* Student: His words "﴿so that there will not be upon you any discomfort﴾": what is the cause in this, and its relation to the effect "﴿We have certainly known what We have enjoined upon them﴾"?

* Shaykh: This cause is a cause for what came before; it is not for His words "﴿We have certainly known﴾".

* Student: What is the reason for this separation?

* Shaykh: It is a cause for His words "﴿We have made lawful for you﴾" or "﴿khalisatan﴾".

* Student: What separates the cause from the effect?

* Shaykh: The separator is that when He said: "﴿And a believing woman if she gives herself to the Prophet—if the Prophet wishes to marry her—a privilege for you, not for the believers﴾", when He mentioned that this is among his particular privileges, He explained what was enjoined upon him; meaning, this is specifically for you, and they have other rulings specific to them.

Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful for you your wives﴾.

* From this noble verse is derived: the high rank of the Prophet ﷺ, from His words ﴿O Prophet﴾; for addressing him with the call combined with the description of prophethood, as already mentioned, indicates the elevation of his station ﷺ.

* Among its benefits: that permitting and prohibiting belong to Allah, mighty and majestic, from His words ﴿Indeed We have made lawful for you﴾. This does not contradict that the Prophet ﷺ may at times exercise ijtihad and judge; the preponderant view is that the Messenger ﷺ has the right to legislate, and then if Allah approves it, it becomes sharia, and if He does not approve it, it is in accordance with what Allah willed. The evidence that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, independently legislates is several hadiths, and also from the Qur'an: His words, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has obeyed Allah﴾ [al-Nisa' 80], which indicates that the Prophet ﷺ has an independent command. And from the Sunnah, such as his words ﷺ: «Had it not been that I would burden my ummah, I would have commanded them to use the siwak»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (887) and Muslim (252/42), and the wording is his, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. This indicates that he commands and forbids; otherwise he would have said: "Had Allah not not commanded me, I would have commanded them." That is, he does not tie it to his own will, but to the will of Allah. And among them his words ﷺ: «I had intended to forbid ghilah (nursing while pregnant), but I looked and found that the Romans and Persians do it and it does them no harm»[[Muslim (1442/140) from the hadith of Judamah bint Wahb al-Asadiyyah, may Allah be pleased with her, that she heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: «I had intended to forbid ghilah, until I mentioned that the Romans and Persians do it, and it does not harm their children.»]], and other examples, such as his words concerning the night prayer: «It is indeed its time, were it not that I would burden my ummah»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (570) and Muslim (638/219) from the hadith of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her.]]. The conclusion is that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, may command, forbid, make lawful and make unlawful; but if Allah approves it, it is part of the sharia of Allah, and otherwise the matter returns to Allah, mighty and majestic.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that marriage requires a bridal payment (mahr); from His words ﴿those to whom you have given their bridal payments﴾.

* Among its benefits: that marriage is a contract over usufruct and not over the substance itself; from His words ﴿their bridal payments﴾, and hire (ijarah) is a contract over benefits, not over substances. For this reason a woman owns herself by sale, purchase, gift and other means, and her husband has no right to object to her in these matters, since he only owns the benefit of enjoyment.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of intercourse by right of ownership (milk al-yamin); from where is it taken? From His words ﴿or what your right hand possesses﴾.

* Among its benefits: the validity of attributing a thing to a part of it; from His words ﴿what your right hand possesses﴾, and this is common in the Qur'an, such as His words ﴿for what your hands have earned﴾ [al-Shura 30], and His words ﴿then the freeing of a neck﴾ [al-Nisa' 92], for a person does not free a neck alone but frees the whole slave.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the cause of ownership by right hand is fay' (war booty and spoils); from His words ﴿of what Allah has returned to you (afa'a)﴾.

* Among its benefits: that the wealth of disbelievers, when it comes back to the Muslims, has returned to its rightful people, derived from His word ﴿afa'a﴾, because fay' means return. The disbelievers enjoy their wealth but without right, and for this they will be held accountable on the Day of Resurrection; as for the wealth, it is truly for the Muslims.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of these four categories of relatives: daughters of paternal uncles, daughters of paternal aunts, daughters of maternal uncles, and daughters of maternal aunts; and as for other relatives, they are forbidden, as in the verse of al-Nisa'.

* Among its benefits: the lawfulness for the Prophet ﷺ of marrying these relatives requires that they have emigrated with him, as indicated by His words: ﴿who have emigrated with you﴾. From this benefit follows that the Prophet ﷺ may be singled out with regard to marriage, with restrictions or with extensions. From where is this derived? From His words: ﴿who have emigrated with you﴾. This is a restriction, because for others the daughters of paternal uncles, maternal uncles and maternal aunts are lawful without condition, unlike for the Prophet ﷺ.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the lawfulness of the Prophet ﷺ marrying by way of a gift. From where is this taken?

* Student: ﴿And a believing woman if she gives herself [in gift] to the Prophet﴾.

* Shaykh: ﴿If she gives herself [in gift]﴾ to whom?

* Student: ﴿To the Prophet﴾ ﷺ.

* Shaykh: Good, to the Prophet.

* Among its benefits: the lawfulness of the Prophet ﷺ marrying by way of a gift, because of His words: ﴿And a believing woman if she gives herself [in gift] to the Prophet﴾. It is required of this woman who gives herself that she be what? Believing, because of His words: ﴿And a believing woman﴾. So if a woman of the People of the Book had given herself to the Prophet ﷺ, she would not have been lawful to him.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the subtle kindness of Allah the Exalted toward His Prophet ﷺ, because of His words: ﴿if the Prophet wishes to marry her﴾.

* Also among its benefits: the demonstration of the exalted status of the Prophet ﷺ, in that He said: ﴿if the Prophet wishes﴾ and did not say, "if you wish", although the context would require him to say, "if you wish to marry her", because the address is to him: ﴿Indeed, We have made lawful to you your wives whom you have given their due compensation, and those your right hand possesses from what Allah has returned to you as spoils, and the daughters of your paternal uncles and the daughters of your paternal aunts and the daughters of your maternal uncles and the daughters of your maternal aunts who emigrated with you, and a believing woman if she gives herself [in gift] to the Prophet, if the Prophet wishes to marry her﴾. The context would have required him to say: "And a believing woman if she gives herself to you, if you wish to marry her", but He mentioned the Prophet to show the exaltation of his status and rank.

* Among its benefits, and among the benefits [of this verse] is that the explicit mention here shows the reason for the ruling. The explicit mention in a place where a pronoun would be expected has as one of its benefits showing the reason for the ruling. How? If He had said: "And a believing woman if she gives herself to you, if you wish to marry her", we would not have understood the reason for the distinction. But when He said: ﴿if she gives herself [in gift] to the Prophet, if the Prophet wishes to marry her﴾, the reason for the distinction becomes clear, because he was a prophet. So the reason is that he is a prophet, and therefore this woman who gives herself was made lawful to him.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the refutation of the Jabriyyah (the determinist sect), in His words: ﴿if he wishes﴾, where He affirmed will for the Prophet ﷺ, whereas the Jabriyyah do not affirm will for the human being. They say that he is compelled in his actions.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the lawfulness of marriage by way of a gift is one of the distinctive privileges (khasa'is) of the Prophet ﷺ, because of His words: ﴿exclusively for you, not for the [other] believers﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that a ruling established for the Messenger ﷺ is established for his community unless there is evidence otherwise. From where is it derived that a ruling established for the Messenger is established for the community unless there is evidence? From His words: ﴿exclusively for you, not for the [other] believers﴾. If the ruling established for him were not established for his community, then His words ﴿exclusively for you, not for the [other] believers﴾ would be pointless, with no benefit in it. Since He excluded the believers from that ruling, it is known that the basic principle is that his community shares with him in the rulings.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that Allah the Exalted may single out whomever He wills with His rulings. By singling out the Prophet ﷺ with this ruling, Allah the Exalted may single out whatever He wills with His rulings.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that singling out a ruling must have a reason that requires singling out that particular person to whom the ruling applies. From where is this derived?

* Student: (...)?

* Shaykh: No, pay attention. Singling out must have a reason that requires that singling out.

* Student: ﴿We have already known what We have enjoined upon them﴾.

* Shaykh: No.

* Student: (...).

* Shaykh: Yes, yes. ﴿If she gives herself [in gift] to the Prophet, if the Prophet wishes﴾. The reason for that is that he is a prophet, and this reason does not apply to the believers.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of knowledge for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because of His words: ﴿We have already known what We have enjoined upon them concerning their wives﴾.

* Among its benefits: that Allah the Exalted has enjoined upon us obligations concerning our wives which we must observe, because of His words: ﴿We have already known what We have enjoined upon them﴾. Likewise we say concerning those whom the right hand possesses: ﴿or those whom their right hands possess﴾.

* Among its benefits: the lawfulness of intercourse with a slave woman one possesses, as has already been mentioned.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the rulings of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, are grounded in wisdoms or accompanied by their wisdoms, because of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿so that there will be no discomfort for you﴾.

* Among its benefits: the care of Allah the Exalted for His Messenger and His kindness toward him, in that He made lawful for him that by which hardship is removed from him, because of His words: ﴿so that there will be no discomfort for you﴾.

* Among the benefits also: the affirmation of two of Allah's names, al-Ghafur (the Forgiving) and al-Rahim (the Merciful), and the affirmation of what they contain of attribute, quality and effect: ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾.

Shall we derive from it the benefit: whether a marriage contracted with the wording of a gift is valid or not? If someone said, "I have given you my daughter," and the other said, "I accept," it is not valid. The apparent view is that it is valid, because the cause in ﴿if she gives herself [in gift] to the Prophet﴾ is that he marries without a bridal gift (mahr); the cause is not the wording. The cause is that the marriage be without a bridal gift, and that is what is specific to the Prophet ﷺ. As for the wording of the gift, it has come in one of the wordings of the hadith (prophetic report) of Sahl ibn Sa'd concerning the woman who gave herself, that the Prophet ﷺ said to the man: "I have made her yours in marriage (mallaktukaha) in exchange for what you have of the Qur'an."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5087) and Muslim (1425/76) from the hadith of Sahl ibn Sa'd al-Sa'idi, may Allah be pleased with him.]] This is one of the wordings in al-Bukhari, and it indicates the permissibility of concluding a marriage contract with such wording.

* Student: Is there (...)?

* Shaykh: No, there is nothing in that, not at all.

* Student: Do you mean what happens with stealing children of disbelievers and then selling them?

* Shaykh: It is not permissible (...).

* Student: What happens with stealing children of disbelievers and then selling them to Muslims?

* Shaykh: Yes, this is not permissible, and they do not become slaves by this.

* Student: A gift in exchange for a consideration (...), I have given you in marriage?

* Shaykh: A gift in exchange for a consideration has the same ruling as a sale in every respect.

* Student: Marriage (...) in exchange for a consideration (...)?

* Shaykh: Then this is a marriage with a bridal gift. That is, the wording does no harm. The correct view is that all contracts are concluded with whatever indicates them.

* Student: Shall we say that it is a gift in exchange for a consideration?

* Shaykh: Here, no, no. We say: it is a marriage with a bridal gift, even if the wording is that of a gift, but it is a marriage.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verses 51–52 (part 1 of 3):

Then He said: ﴿You may defer whom you wish of them, and take to you whom you wish, and whomever you seek out of those you had set aside, there is no blame upon you.﴾ [Al-Ahzab 51] ﴿تُرْجِي﴾ The author says: (with a hamzah and a yā' in its place, meaning "tu'akhkhir," "delays"). ﴿تُرْجِئُ﴾ and ﴿تُرْجِي﴾ mean "delay."

His saying ﴿مَنْ تَشَاءُ﴾ is the object of ﴿تُرْجِي﴾.

(﴿مَنْ تَشَاءُ مِنْهُنَّ﴾ means: your wives, regarding their turn. ﴿وَتُؤْوِي﴾ means: takes in. ﴿إِلَيْكَ مَنْ تَشَاءُ﴾ means: from among them, so that you go to her. ﴿وَمَنِ ابْتَغَيْتَ﴾ means: you seek. ﴿مِمَّنْ عَزَلْتَ﴾ means: from the division (qasm, the equal allotment of nights among wives). So there is no blame upon you in seeking her and taking her to you. He was given the choice in this, after the division had been obligatory upon him.)

The author's words now indicate that His saying ﴿تُرْجِي مَنْ تَشَاءُ مِنْهُنَّ﴾ refers to the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) who were under his care, and that the meaning of ﴿تُرْجِي﴾ is to delay them, so that he does not allot a night to them, and ﴿وَتُؤْوِي﴾ is to take them in, so that he allots a night to them. Thus the verse was revealed concerning the Prophet's (ﷺ) division among his wives, and Allah the Exalted gave him the choice between deferring and taking in; that is, He gave him the choice between dividing among the wives and not dividing. In this there is latitude for the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding the division: if he wished he divided, and if he wished he did not divide. This is one of the two opinions in the interpretation of the noble verse, and the context may support it: ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful to you your wives to whom you have given their bridal payments﴾ up to His saying ﴿You may defer whom you wish of them﴾, meaning: of your wives, ﴿and take to you whom you wish﴾. So deferring means leaving off the division, and taking in means dividing.

The second opinion regarding the matter is that ﴿تُرْجِي مَنْ تَشَاءُ مِنْهُنَّ﴾ means: of those women who gave themselves to you (as a gift). That is, if you wish you accept, and if you wish you refuse. ﴿وَمَنِ ابْتَغَيْتَ مِمَّنْ عَزَلْتَ﴾ means: if you had refused her first and then wanted her again, there is no blame upon you. We have already mentioned a principle of tafsir: if a verse can bear two meanings that do not contradict each other, then the obligation is to take it as bearing both meanings. For this reason Ibn Jarir, may Allah have mercy on him, chose that the verse includes both meanings together: that the Messenger (ﷺ) was given the choice between dividing and not dividing, and was given the choice between accepting a gift and not accepting it. And also, if he did not divide and then wished to divide, he may do so; and if he refused a gift and then wished to accept it, he may do so. The woman, if he did not divide for her and then he wished to divide for her, has no right to refuse, because the choice is in the hand of the Prophet (ﷺ).

* Student: Shaykh, (...) is taken to mean abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of an earlier ruling by a later one) (...) the Messenger was (...) which indicates that he used to divide?
* Shaykh: Yes, but he divided from himself. A division from himself, peace and blessings be upon him, that was not obligatory from Allah. That is, he divided of his own accord, even though he had the choice.
* Student: What is the evidence that he had the choice?
* Shaykh: This verse.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, but it is suitable, and the early scholars (salaf) interpreted it that way, so it is suitable for both meanings.
* Student: (...) evidence for (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, there is a specific evidence. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has two wives and leans toward one of them will come on the Day of Resurrection with one side of him inclining."[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (2133) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him.]] This is a threat.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No, leaving it entirely, and if he wished, he may return (to her).

(﴿مِنْهُنَّ﴾ means: your wives, regarding their turn. ﴿وَتُؤْوِي﴾ means: takes in to you. ﴿مَنْ تَشَاءُ﴾ means: from among them, so that you go to her.)

(﴿وَمَنِ ابْتَغَيْتَ﴾ means: you sought. ﴿مِمَّنْ عَزَلْتَ﴾ means: from the division. So there is no blame upon you in seeking her and taking her in. He was given the choice in this, after the division had been obligatory upon him.)

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, has informed us that the verse concerns the ruling on division with respect to the Prophet (ﷺ), and that Allah the Exalted gave him the choice between dividing among his wives and not dividing, and that whoever he did not divide for, if it became apparent to him to divide for her, there is no hardship upon him. This is one of the two opinions on the verse.
