The second category: those who deny slavery absolutely, even where its lawful causes exist. This is said by those civilised nations that claim civilisation and progress. But it is strange that they deny the slavery that has lawful, divine causes, while they enslave the servants of Allah with a slavery harsher than Islamic slavery, without any lawful cause. The present problem of South Africa is only one example of this, for they enslave black people in a shameful manner and deprive them of their rights, and this is far more repugnant than lawful Islamic slavery. Moreover, lawful Islamic slavery contains no repugnance, because when you reflect on the texts concerning the rules of slaves, you find that the Shariah permitted their enslavement only for their own benefit, since the causes of slavery are one while the causes of freedom are many, and because the slave is obligated to be treated with kindness by his owner. On this basis, the third path, which is affirming slavery through the lawful divine causes, is the truth. It is indicated by the Qur'an, the Sunnah and the consensus, and none denies it except an obstinate person, and whoever denies it is a disbeliever.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of expressing the whole by a part, based on His saying: ﴿what your right hand possesses﴾ [al-Ahzab 52].
* From it also: the preference of the right hand over the left, in that ownership is attributed to it rather than to the left. The left hand is never used to express the whole self; rather, the general term "hands" is used and the right hand is used, but the expression with the left is not reported.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of one of Allah's names, al-Raqib (the Watchful), in His saying: ﴿and Allah is ever Watchful over all things﴾ [al-Ahzab 52]. Al-Raqib means al-Hafiz (the Preserver). Belief in Allah's watchfulness, glorified and exalted is He, necessitates for the servant perfect vigilance of Allah and fear of Him, and that he not dare to disobey Him nor fall short in His obedience. For if one of the kings, the kings of this world, had appointed a watcher over you, which is what is called the intelligence and investigation men, could you speak or do anything that would cause your punishment before that king? The answer: No. Indeed, they warn one another, saying: "Let there not be among you any of the intelligence men, let there not be among you any of the security men," and the like, and they fear him. This is with respect to the created being, so the watchfulness of the Creator, Mighty and Majestic, is more perfect and greater.
* It is derived from this noble verse: the eloquence of the Qur'an, in that it concludes the verses with what suits the rulings contained in them. Since the context is one of permitting and forbidding, it concluded with His saying: ﴿and Allah is ever Watchful over all things﴾, meaning: He watches you if you oppose what has been legislated for you.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: (﴿﴿O you who believe, do not enter the houses of the Prophet unless you are given permission﴾﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53] "to enter, by an invitation ﴿to a meal﴾ so that you enter, ﴿without waiting for it﴾ waiting for it, ﴿its ripeness﴾ its cooking, a verbal noun of أنى يأني (anā, ya'nī)"). ﴿O you who believe﴾: We have already discussed phrases like this, and we explained that opening a ruling with the vocative (nidā') indicates its importance and the care given to it, because the vocative requires the attention of the one addressed. Describing this address as "belief" indicates that adhering to this ruling is one of the requirements of faith, and that neglecting it causes a deficiency in faith. Moreover, the expression "belief" contains encouragement and urging, because the truly believing person adheres to what he is commanded and abstains from what he is forbidden. An example of this is when you say, "O man, do such-and-such." The meaning is: by virtue of your manhood it is incumbent upon you to do such-and-such. So "O believer, do such-and-such" means: by virtue of your faith it is incumbent upon you to do such-and-such. Thus it contains encouragement and urging.

﴿O you who believe﴾: meaning, because of your faith We have directed this address to you. ﴿Do not enter the houses of the Prophet﴾: "the houses of the Prophet" is a plural construction in the genitive, attributed to the Messenger ﷺ, because his houses were nine; each of his wives had a house. The Prophet ﷺ did not gather them together in one house, but assigned a house to each wife.

As for its attribution to the Prophet ﷺ, "the houses of the Prophet," although it is also attributed to the women themselves, as previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿And remember what is recited in your houses of the verses of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 34]. Does this contradict that? No, it does not contradict it. It is attributed to each of them according to a particular relationship. Since these houses are the refuge and dwelling of the Prophet ﷺ, they are attributed to him; and since they, i.e. these houses, are the property of his wives, they are attributed to the wives.

The scholars differed: are the houses of the Messenger's wives their property or the property of the Messenger ﷺ? There are two opinions among the people of knowledge. We have already mentioned that the more apparent view is that they are the property of the wives, based on the fact that they inherited these houses. Had they been the property of the Prophet ﷺ, they would not have inherited them, because the Prophet ﷺ said: "We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from; what we leave is charity"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3093) and Muslim (1759/52) from Abu Bakr.]].

It is not an objection to this that these houses were later incorporated into the mosque, because either they were incorporated in exchange for compensation, or they were incorporated with the consent of those entitled to them, and this does not contradict ownership.

﴿the houses of the Prophet, unless you are given permission﴾ ﴿to a meal, without waiting for its ripeness﴾: ﴿unless you are given permission﴾ is in the passive voice, and He did not say "unless the Prophet gives you permission," because a wife of his may give permission to someone, and he then enters. So it is not a condition that the permission come from the Messenger ﷺ. Rather, Allah, Exalted, has stipulated three conditions: the permission, ﴿to a meal﴾, and third, ﴿without waiting for its ripeness﴾.

Let us examine these restrictions: are they binding or not? His saying ﴿unless you are given permission﴾ includes both customary permission and verbal permission. Verbal permission is that one is told, "Enter." Customary permission is that there be a sign indicating that the situation is one of permission, such as opening the door and the like. Can one enter without permission? No, one cannot. So permission is a valid and binding restriction.

He said ﴿to a meal﴾. Does this indicate that if they were given permission to enter for something other than a meal, it would be impermissible? No. ﴿To a meal﴾: if they are invited for something other than a meal, may they enter or not? If we look at the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿to a meal﴾, we would say they may not enter, because Allah, Exalted, said ﴿to a meal﴾. But we say that this restriction is a clarification of the actual situation, and what is a clarification of the actual situation has no implied meaning (mafhūm). The verse was revealed concerning a specific case, which is the entry of these people to a meal without an invitation, so it was restricted by His saying ﴿to a meal﴾.

The third: ﴿without waiting for its ripeness﴾. (ناظر): if it is followed by (إلى), it is from looking with the eye; if it is followed directly by its object, it means waiting. You say, "I looked at him" (nazartu ilayhi), and you say, "I looked for him" (nazartuhu), meaning "I waited for him." Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Do they wait except for the angels to come to them?﴾ [al-An'am: 158], ﴿Do they await except its interpretation?﴾ [al-A'raf: 53]. The meaning is: do they wait? Because it is followed directly by its object.

﴿Some faces that day will be radiant, looking at their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22–23]: this is from looking with the eye. Here, ﴿nāẓirīn﴾ is transitive directly or by (إلى)? It is directly transitive, so it means "waiting." His saying ﴿its ripeness﴾, i.e. its cooking: is this a condition or not? We say it is a condition for the permissibility of entering: that they enter for a meal without waiting for its ripeness. They used to watch for the food to ripen, and when they judged that it had ripened and was about to be served or had been served, they would enter the houses in order to eat. There is no doubt that catching a person by surprise at his meal harms him. The one who surprises people at the time the food is served is called a ṭufaylī (a hanger-on) and a ḍayfan (an unwelcome guest). He is not a guest (ḍayf); ḍayfan is with the letter nūn, because that nūn is like the one who leans on a stick as if he were heavy.

If someone has a guest and you do not like that he be with you, and you say to your companion, and he says, "Do you have a guest?" you say, "No, I have a ḍayfan," meaning a heavy, parasitic person who came without an invitation, who sleeps on the host's ... and does not budge or leave, and keeps asking, "Bring water, bring a drink, bring this, I want the bathroom, I want that," and wears you out.

The point is that His saying ﴿without waiting for its ripeness﴾ is a condition, meaning it is not permissible for you to watch for the cooking of the food in order to enter, because that causes hardship to the Prophet ﷺ. It is possible that the meaning is: do not enter early such that you remain in the houses until the food is ready, because that also burdens the owner of the house. If lunch is being prepared at one o'clock and these people arrive at twelve, do they wait or not? How long do they wait? An hour. This causes hardship to the Prophet ﷺ. The Prophet ﷺ was modest and generous. If they asked permission to enter an hour before the food was ready, he ﷺ would not turn them away, even though he would be bothered by it, but because of his generosity and modesty he would not turn them away.

Thus it is shown by this that the prohibition is against entering the houses of the Messenger ﷺ except under three conditions: permission, that it be for a meal, and that they not wait for its ripeness. As for "to a meal," we said this is not a condition, because it is a restriction clarifying the actual situation, so it has no implied meaning. Every restriction that clarifies the actual situation has no implied meaning. For this reason, if they are invited to something other than a meal, there is no harm in their entering.

Now let us return to the verse ﴿unless you are given permission﴾. The author said: (in entering by invitation ﴿to a meal﴾). The author's words ﴿unless you are given permission﴾ tell us about what relates to ﴿is given permission﴾ only by way of tadmīn (implicit meaning, where a verb carries the sense of another verb). This is because yu'dhana (is given permission) is not followed by (إلى); it is followed by (في) or by the (لام). But with the (لام) it is for the one given permission, not for the one to whom it is given. So it would be followed by (في), "unless you are given permission in a meal." However, it came with (إلى), because permission here is implicitly given the meaning of invitation; meaning: unless you are invited to a meal.

His saying ﴿without waiting for its ripeness﴾: why is it in the accusative when the preceding word is in the genitive? That is, it was not in the form "to a meal, without waiting for its ripeness," because it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the kāf in His saying ﴿you are given permission﴾: "to a meal, in a state of your not waiting for its ripeness." So if you were waiting for its ripeness and watching for it, then do not enter on that basis either, because that causes hardship and harm.

As for His saying ﴿its ripeness﴾: the author says it is (a verbal noun of anā ya'nī ina), and it is not something elided; that is, it is not originally "his vessel" (ināʾahu). Rather, ﴿ināhu﴾ is originally and in derivation a verbal noun of anā ya'nī ina.

His saying: ﴿But when you are invited, then enter; and when you have eaten, disperse﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53]. Since His saying ﴿do not enter the houses of the Prophet unless you are given permission﴾ might lead someone to think that they may never enter, He said: ﴿But when you are invited, then enter.﴾ So in His saying ﴿But when you are invited, then enter﴾ there is a benefit: whenever they are invited, they enter. When they are invited, they enter. Their entering on their own initiative is not permissible except under the previously mentioned conditions. But when they are invited, they enter. Then when they have eaten, they disperse. For this reason He said: ﴿But when you are invited, then enter﴾, and do not enter without an invitation.

This differs from His saying ﴿unless you are given permission to a meal﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53], because (yu'dhana) means that they came and asked permission. As for what we have here, the second clause: ﴿But when you are invited﴾, these are the ones who were invited. The Messenger ﷺ used to invite people to his meal, as he invited Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) when he found him hungry one day. "Abu Hurayrah went out of his house, hungry, until he nearly fell unconscious from hunger. When people went out, he followed 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, asking him about a verse from the Book of Allah. Abu Hurayrah, when he asked him about the verse, knew the verse, but he was hoping, perhaps 'Umar would say: follow me. But 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) did not think about this matter; he informed him of the verse and went on. [Abu Hurayrah] said: When the Messenger ﷺ came and saw me, he recognized what was in my face, so he invited him, and he entered. Milk was brought to the Prophet ﷺ, and he commanded him to call the people of the Suffah. The people of the Suffah were the poor emigrants who had no shelter in Medina; they had a place in the mosque where they gathered. Sometimes they reached eighty, sometimes more, and sometimes fewer." He said: When he said, "Call the people of the Suffah," and the milk was little, he seemed hesitant, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: What will this milk do for the people of the Suffah? If I call the people of the Suffah and they drink the milk, I will remain hungry. He said: But I had no choice but to obey Allah and His Messenger. So he went and called the people of the Suffah, and they came and drank. Each one drank from the milk, and each one drank, and each one drank. When a remainder was left, he said, "Drink." He said: So I drank until I was satisfied. Then he said, "Drink, Abu Hirr." I said: By Allah, O Messenger of Allah, I cannot find any way for it to go down. Then a remainder was left, and the Prophet ﷺ drank it[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6452) from Abu Hurayrah.]].

In this account there is a general invitation and a specific invitation. Similarly, in the hadith of Anas: "When the Prophet ﷺ prepared food, he said: 'Go out and invite for me whomever you meet'"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5163) and Muslim (1428/94) from Anas ibn Malik.]]. So when the Muslims are invited to a meal, then enter: ﴿But when you are invited, then enter; and when you have eaten, disperse﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53]. He did not say, "when you are satisfied," but said ﴿when you have eaten﴾, because food may satisfy and may not satisfy. His saying ﴿disperse﴾ means: scatter.

(And do not linger, seeking familiar conversation﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53]). The author informed us with his saying "and do not linger" that the phrase ﴿seeking familiar conversation﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from an elided subject along with its verb, and the estimate is: "and do not linger, seeking familiar conversation." Being familiar with a thing means being at ease with it. That is: do not remain after eating, talking, relaxing, and feeling at ease. As for brief conversation, there is no harm in it after eating. But this is not, in any case, the etiquette of one who has eaten, because He gave the reason, saying: ﴿Indeed, that was causing harm to the Prophet, and he is shy of you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53].

He (the author) said: (﴿seeking familiar conversation﴾ with one another ﴿Indeed, that﴾ the lingering ﴿was causing harm to the Prophet, and he is shy of you﴾ to have you leave; ﴿but Allah is not shy of the truth﴾ to have you leave). Based on this, they are forbidden to remain at ease for conversation, for a reason, which is causing harm, the harm to the Prophet ﷺ. And based on this reason: if it were assumed that he is not harmed by it, there would be no blame on a person for remaining. Later, God willing, in the lessons (fawā'id) there will be an explanation of what some people use: that when one has eaten, they say to him, "Sit a little," and "when you have eaten, disperse," that this is an improper inference.

(...) ﴿Indeed, that was causing harm to the Prophet﴾: he repeated the explicit noun in place of the pronoun to elevate the status of the Messenger ﷺ. Otherwise, one would expect him to say, "Indeed, that was causing him harm," but He said ﴿was causing harm to the Prophet﴾ to elevate his status ﷺ, and as an indication that, because of his prophethood, one must avoid harming him because of his great merit. His saying ﴿Indeed, that﴾: why was it pluralized in the address ﴿Indeed, that﴾?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No. Why was it pluralized? Because those addressed are plural. When the demonstrative is accompanied by the kāf, the demonstrative takes into account the one pointed to, and the kāf takes into account the one addressed. The demonstrative changes according to the one pointed to, and the kāf changes according to the one addressed. Have you understood this rule? When the kāf is attached to the demonstrative, the demonstrative takes into account the one pointed to, and the kāf takes into account what? The one addressed.

Let us suppose I point to a group and address one person. I say: ﴿ulā'ika﴾ (those). And conversely, I point to one and address a group, I say: ﴿dhalikum﴾. I point to a group and address a group, I say: ﴿ulā'ikum﴾. I point to a group and address a group of women, I say: ﴿ulā'ikunna﴾. I point to one and address a group of women, I say: ﴿dhalikunna﴾: ﴿She said: That is the one about whom you blamed me﴾ [Yusuf: 32].

The point is, when the demonstrative is accompanied by the kāf, the kāf takes into account the one addressed, and the demonstrative takes into account the one pointed to: if it is plural, make it plural; if it is dual, make it dual; if it is singular, make it singular. If you point to two and address two, how do you say it?

* Student: Dhālik.
* Shaykh: No. You point to two and address two?
* Student: Dhālikumā.
* Shaykh: Dhālikumā, no; dhānikumā. Yes.
You point to two women and address two women?
* Student: I don't know.
* Shaykh: How don't you know?
* Student: Tānikumā.
* Shaykh: Tānikumā, yes, correct, because the feminine dual is said tān. Ibn Mālik said:
"...... ∗∗∗ and dhān, tān for the dual in the nominative"

Have you understood, everyone? Many students make a mistake here: the one pointed to becomes confused with the one addressed.

So, ﴿Indeed, that﴾: is the one pointed to here singular or plural? The one pointed to is singular, and the addressee is plural, because He addresses the group of believers and points to a mentioned thing, that this mentioned thing causes harm to the Prophet, and he is shy of you.

His saying ﴿causing harm to the Prophet﴾: harm (adhā) is not the same as damage (ḍarar), since one may be harmed without being damaged by it. For this reason, Allah, Exalted, is described as being harmed, but not described as being damaged. Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who harm Allah and His Messenger, Allah has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Ahzab: 57], and He said in the hadith qudsi: "The son of Adam harms Me; he curses time"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4826) and Muslim (2246/2) from Abu Hurayrah.]]. As for damage, in the hadith qudsi He said: "O My servants, you will never reach My harm so as to harm Me, nor will you reach My benefit so as to benefit Me"[[Narrated by Muslim (2577/55) from Abu Dharr.]]. We now observe in ourselves that we are harmed by a thing without being damaged by it: a person is harmed by a foul smell, like the smell of onions, leeks, dirt, sweat, and the like, but is not damaged by it. Therefore, harm does not necessarily entail damage.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verse 53–54 (part 2 of 4):

﴿Indeed, that was [a matter that] would hurt the Prophet, but he would be shy of [asking] you to leave,﴾ [al-Ahzab 53]. The fa' (فاء) here is conjunctive, coordinated with His words ﴿would hurt﴾; meaning, he would also be shy of you, that he should have you leave, when you had entered in this state. As for His words ﴿but he would be shy of you﴾: what is al-hayaa' (الحياء, shyness)? Define al-hayaa'? For al-hayaa', we write beside it "(م)" in bold, meaning "well-known." In the dictionary, when a well-known word comes, one writes "(م)", meaning ma'ruf (معروف, well-known). It does not need us to define it, just as if you were asked: what is al-mahabba (المحبة, love)? You cannot [define it]. As Ibn al-Qayyim says in Rawdat al-Muhibbin: love cannot be defined by anything clearer than its own word; love is love.
What is al-karaha (الكراهة, dislike)? It is dislike; you cannot define it, because these are psychological states that a person feels within himself and cannot express. So al-hayaa' is al-hayaa'. What is sleep (النوم)? Sleep is sleep, well-known. Some say it is a heavy faintness that overtakes the brain, causing it to lose awareness and sensation. I, if I imagine that this is sleep, sleep does not come to me. If I imagine it is a faint... may God ward off affliction. The upshot is that when you say, "Sleep is well-known," this is well-known to everyone.
Hunger, or the contraction of the stomach from lack of food: this is its effect; as for itself, it is well-known. Thus these psychological meanings cannot in reality be defined by anyone; they cannot be defined by anything clearer than their own word. So al-hayaa' is well-known, and the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was shy of these people, because he (ﷺ) was the most perfect of people in faith, and shyness is part of faith; and because he (ﷺ) was the most generous of people, and the generous person is shy before his guest, lest he expel him or show weariness at his presence or dislike for him. Therefore the Messenger (ﷺ) would endure, even though he was hurt by it, because of the perfection of faith and perfection of generosity with which God created him ﴿but he would be shy of you﴾.

The author said: (﴿but he would be shy of you﴾ to have you leave). His words "to have you leave" are in the position of a genitive substitute (badal ishtimal), because the meaning is "he would be shy of your leaving."

﴿And God is not shy of the truth﴾ [al-Ahzab 53]. God, Mighty and Majestic, is not shy of the truth, which is justice in rulings and truthfulness in reports. The Lord, Mighty and Majestic, is not shy of the truth, because shyness from the truth means abandoning the truth, or it entails abandoning the truth, weakness, and lack of resolve. God, Mighty and Majestic, is not shy of making the truth clear.

The author says: ﴿is not shy of the truth﴾ (to have you leave). Thus the author said that God is not shy to have you leave. There is something to be considered in what he said. Rather, the correct reading is: ﴿is not shy of the truth﴾ to make it clear to you, because the context here is not one of expulsion; the context is one of clarification, of what is obligatory upon those who asked permission to enter upon the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him. So the meaning is: He is not shy of the truth. I say: the truth is truthfulness in reports and justice in rulings, and what is meant by "the truth" here, according to the author's view, is expulsion; that is, He is not shy to have you leave. But the correct view is: He is not shy to make clear to you what is required of you, so that you leave.

Then the author, may God pardon him, said: (i.e., He does not abandon its clarification). That is, He does not abandon the clarification of the truth. This is a distortion, since he explained shyness by its consequence, which is abandonment; for among the consequences of being shy of something is that the shy person leaves it. The author explained shyness by its consequence, which is abandonment; that is, He does not abandon the clarification of the truth.

There is some contradiction between his words "He does not abandon the clarification of the truth" and his words "He is not shy to have you leave," because he made the object of shyness here the clarification of the truth, and in the first he made it expulsion. The correct view is the second; his second statement is correct, that is, He is not shy of clarifying the truth. But his explanation of shyness as abandonment is false, since it contradicts the apparent wording. What is obligatory upon us regarding the names and attributes of God is that we apply them to their apparent meaning, fitting for God, Glorified and Exalted, believing that He has no equal in this attribute, and keeping away from specifying their modality (takyif).

As for the obligation to apply them to their apparent meaning: God addressed us in a clear Arabic tongue, and if He had intended something other than that apparent meaning, the expression would have been one that conveys, in its apparent sense, disbelief or likeness, or else the expression would have been clarification or the opposite of clarification. God, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿God desires to make clear to you﴾ [al-Nisa' 26]. How could He, Glorified and Exalted, speak in a way contrary to clarity regarding what is considered the core of belief, which concerns the names and attributes of God?!

For this reason, the path of these distorters is among the most grave forms of attack upon the speech of God, Mighty and Majestic, indeed among the most grave forms of attack upon God Himself, since their method entails that God did not make the truth clear regarding His names and attributes, and left the truth to be determined by what their minds require. Then they try to refer the speech of God and the speech of His Messenger back to what these corrupt, contradictory minds require. The safest, most knowledgeable, and most wise path is the path of the Salaf: to take the speech of God and His Messenger according to its apparent meaning; for we know with certainty that no one knows God better than God Himself, and no one among creation knows God better than the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him. We also know that no one's speech is more truthful than God's, and no one among created beings is more truthful in speech than the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him. This too is established.

The third matter: no one is clearer in expression than God, Mighty and Majestic, and no one among created beings has greater clarity than the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him. These are three matters.

The fourth matter: we also know that no one has a more sound intention and purpose than God, Mighty and Majestic, for God wills of His servants only that He make the truth clear to them. Likewise, regarding the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, we know of no one more sincere to creation, or more truthful in his intention to make the truth clear.

When these four matters are fulfilled in any speech, whatever speech it is, what its apparent wording indicates is the intended meaning that we must follow. These are four matters; when they are combined in speech, that speech must be taken according to its apparent meaning. What are the four?
* Student: Knowledge, intention, truthfulness...
* Shaykh: Yes, and truthfulness and clarity; four matters.

Their opposites are not accepted nor considered. If an ignorant person came to you speaking with the most eloquent speech, while being a man we know to be most sincere and truthful, would you trust his words? We would not trust his words. If a man spoke about medicine, while we know he never studied medicine, and began explaining medicine to us, would we trust him? We would not, because he is ignorant.

If a scholar, whom we know is knowledgeable in what he speaks, but is a liar, came to us, would we trust his speech?
* Students: No.
* Shaykh: Why? Because he is a liar; he may have lied to us.

If a knowledgeable and truthful man came to us but with bad intention, perhaps deceiving and intending the misguidance of people, we also would not trust him, because we fear he deceived us in what he said.

Fourth: if a knowledgeable, sincere, and truthful person came to us but does not express himself well, like a Persian who does not know Arabic and tries to express himself in Arabic, would we trust his speech? No, we would not, because he does not know how sometimes to say... if he wants to attach the pronoun to himself he says "you ate," and if he wants to say "I ate," he says "you ate," and if he wants to say "you ate," he says "I ate." We do not trust his speech, since he may reverse the speech, because he is incapable. But the speech of God and the speech of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, combines the four qualities of acceptance. Therefore it is obligatory upon us to believe in every attribute with which God has described Himself.

If someone says: the verse and what resembles it contain negation of shyness, and negation is the opposite of affirmation, so how do you say the verse affirms shyness? We say: the explicit wording of the verse is ﴿He is not shy of the truth﴾ [al-Ahzab 53], and its implicit meaning is: He is shy of what is other than the truth, is He not? For if the matter were not so, negating shyness regarding the truth would be idle speech with no meaning. Then we say: the attribute of shyness has been affirmed for God, Mighty and Majestic, in affirmative form, as in the hadith in the Musnad: "Indeed God is Shy and Generous" [Narrated by al-Tirmidhi (3556), and the wording is his, and Ahmad (23714), from the hadith of Salman]. This is the affirmation of shyness for God, Glorified and Exalted.

So every attribute God has affirmed for Himself, it is obligatory upon us to accept it, but we purify our belief from two grave prohibitions, which are?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, likening (tamthil) and modality (takyif). Tamthil is better than tashbih; that is, expressing with tamthil is better than expressing with tashbih, because this is what God negated of Himself, and because the absolute negation of tashbih is not correct, since we have mentioned that there are no two existents that do not share the attribute of existence, though they differ in what this attribute requires and entails. And there are no two hearing beings that do not share the attribute of hearing, though they differ in its implications and requirements. And there are no two seeing beings that do not share the attribute of sight; so there is some resemblance between them in what they share. Therefore, the negation of tamthil is what we, the students of knowledge, should express, because it is what came in the Qur'an, and it is safer.

He said: ﴿And God is not shy of the truth﴾, then he said: ﴿And when you ask them﴾, meaning: He does not abandon its clarification. The reading ﴿yastahyi﴾ with one yaa' (بياء واحدة) is it shadh or sab'i? It is shadh, because the author's rule, may God have mercy on him, is that when he says "wa-qari'a" (وقرئ, and it was read), it is an irregular reading. Unlike when he says "wa-fi qira'a" (وفي قراءة, and in a reading), or says "with yaa' and nuun," or "with yaa' and taa'," and similar, which are two canonical readings.
* Student: Does it have a deficiency, or does it not fulfill the requirement?
* Shaykh: It does not fulfill the requirement and has a deficiency, because it contradicts the Qur'anic expression, and because this led to denying many attributes under this claim.
* Student: The expression of al-Tahawi?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed. For this reason Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya, may God have mercy on him, in al-'Aqida al-Wasitiyya did not say "without likening," but said: "without distortion, denial, modality, or likening," and this is the better.

﴿And when you ask them﴾: the subject refers to the Companions, and the object refers to the wives of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, who had not been mentioned in the verse before; but his words ﴿the houses of the Prophet﴾ indicate this, because the residents of the Prophet's houses are the wives of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him.

(﴿And when you ask them﴾: i.e., the wives of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him.) ("i.e.") here is explanatory, and ("wives") is an explicative apposition to the pronoun in his words: (﴿And when you ask them﴾: i.e., the wives of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him.) ﴿an article﴾: the meaning of mata' (متاع, article) is what one enjoys of clothing, food, drink, and other things, even dirhams are considered mata', so everything one enjoys is mata'.

(﴿And when you ask them an article, ask them from behind a screen﴾: a cover.) ﴿ask them﴾ takes two objects: the first is the pronoun in His words ﴿ask them﴾, and the second is omitted, indicated by what precedes it; that is, ask them the article from behind a screen. His words ﴿from behind a screen﴾: hijab means a cover, and the word ﴿from﴾ indicates that this cover must be separate, and that it is not covering the face or body with garments, but is another cover, a hijab. The hijab of the Mothers of the Believers is different from the hijab of the women of the believers, because the hijab of the believing women may be attached to the body, like the khimar, the milhafa, and similar garments. But the hijab of the Mothers of the Believers is a separate, different hijab that stands between a man and seeing the Mothers of the Believers. For this reason He said ﴿from behind a screen﴾, indicating that this hijab is separate from what it covers. Compare God's words about the disbelievers saying to the Messenger: ﴿and between us and you is a hijab﴾ [Fussilat 5], as if...

Why did He say (dhalika) and (kum)? (dhalika) is for the singular and (kum) for the plural; how does the plural agree with the singular?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: You don't know? Do you understand the question? How does the plural fit with the singular?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: That is, because of the difference in referent: the demonstrative refers to the one pointed at, and the "kaf" of address refers to the addressee; so the one pointed at may be singular and the addressees plural, as here.

﴿That﴾: i.e., what was mentioned. The address is to the Companions, may God be pleased with them.

﴿That is purer for your hearts and their hearts﴾ [al-Ahzab 53]. ﴿purer﴾: i.e., more effective in purifying hearts. ﴿for your hearts﴾: O askers; ﴿and their hearts﴾: i.e., the ones asked (from disquieting thoughts). Look, the address now is to whom? To the Companions, who are the purest hearts of this nation, regarding whom? Regarding the wives of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, who are the most chaste of women and the furthest from what is disliked. So if this address concerns such people and these women, what about others, if the possibility of the heart being soiled by addressing a woman without a screen exists? If this possibility exists among such people, what about those far below them by stages, neither in time nor in rank? This would be even more severe; therefore one who says that the hijab is specific to the Mothers of the Believers is sharply denounced. We say to him: where is the specificity? If God gave as the reason that it is purer for their hearts, that is, the hearts of those addressed and those addressing, and they are undoubtedly the purest and most chaste of women, and likewise those who address them are the best of people, as in the hadith: "The best of people is my generation" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2652), Muslim (2533/212), from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud], what about those beyond them? Is it not so? The possibility of the heart being defiled by addressing a woman without a hijab is nearer for those after the Companions than otherwise, much nearer; and if this is the case regarding the Companions with the wives of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, then others with women below them are all the more so by way of a fortiori.

As for His words ﴿That is purer for your hearts and their hearts﴾: the author, may God have mercy on him, says: (from disquieting thoughts). The thoughts that come to the heart: if a person does not settle upon them and indulge in them, he is not held accountable for them, since they are the speech of the self. Rather, they are what assails the self, and guarding against them is stricter; for the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is reported to have said: "God has overlooked for my community what their selves whisper, so long as they do not act upon it or speak it" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5269), Muslim (127/201), from the hadith of Abu Hurayra]. If this applies to the whisperings of the self, what about what assails the self without intention? Pardon for it is all the more fitting. So thoughts that come to the heart, if a person does not indulge in them or settle upon them, do not harm him, whether these thoughts concern the majesty of God, or His Messenger, or the desires and urges of the self, provided he does not indulge. Indeed, these thoughts only come to a sound heart which Satan attacks in order to corrupt it. For this reason, when the Companions complained to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, of such thoughts, he said: "Have you found this?" They said: "Yes." He said: "That is the clear faith" [Narrated by Muslim (132/209), from Abu Hurayra], meaning its pure essence; for Satan does not attack a corrupt heart, but attacks righteous hearts to corrupt them. The remedy for this is to seek refuge in God from the accursed Satan, to cease, and to praise God, Mighty and Majestic, as is due to Him; say: "God is One, the Eternal Refuge; He neither begets nor is begotten, and there is none equal to Him" [al-Ikhlas]: seeking God's protection and ceasing, and attributing perfection to God, and after that it will leave you little by little.

Qur'an 33:53 says: "And it is not for you to harm the Messenger of Allah..." The address is to the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them), and those who came after them are included all the more so. "It is not for you" (مَا كَانَ لَكُمْ) and similar expressions indicate that something is absolutely impermissible. This is why the author (may Allah have mercy on him) said: ("And it is not for you to harm the Messenger of Allah" in any way), meaning: no specific thing is identified or explained. That is, it is not proper, suitable, or possible for you to harm the Messenger of Allah. Such an expression indicates the impossibility of something, like the verse: ﴿Allah has not taken any son, nor was there with Him any god﴾ [al-Mu'minun 91]. The meaning is that this is impermissible and unsuitable. Thus it is impossible, improper and unfitting for any believer to harm the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), whether by word or by deed.

﴿Indeed, those who harm Allah and His Messenger, Allah has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter, and has prepared for them a humiliating punishment﴾ [al-Ahzab 57]. Harming the Messenger (ﷺ) is among the deeds of the polytheists, those who harm the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by word and by deed.

﴿It is not for you to harm the Messenger of Allah﴾. Here He says: ﴿the Messenger of Allah﴾, while at the beginning of the verse He says: ﴿the Prophet﴾. This indicates that the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) is honoured because of the greatness of the One who sent him, Allah. Since he is the Messenger of Allah, it is impossible for him to be harmed, because he is a messenger from Allah, blessed and exalted. Harming the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) during his life relates to his person, and harming him after his death relates to his Sunnah. It is not befitting or suitable for any believer to act against the Sunnah of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) in a way that hurts him, such as rejecting it, distorting it, and the like.

He says: ﴿It is not for you to harm the Messenger of Allah﴾. So, may we sit enjoying conversation after the meal, in respect of the Messenger? No, because Allah said: ﴿Indeed, that used to harm the Prophet﴾. Therefore, we may not sit as long as there is harm to the Messenger (ﷺ).

﴿Nor that you should marry his wives after him, ever﴾. That is: and it is not for you to marry his wives after him, ever. The word ﴿marry﴾ (تَنْكِحُوا) here means the contract (العقد), i.e., you cannot contract marriage with his wives after him. Every instance of nikah in the Qur'an means the contract, contrary to those who say that every nikah in the Qur'an means intercourse (al-wat') except the verse: ﴿And do not marry those women whom your fathers married﴾ [an-Nisa' 22]. The correct view is that every nikah in the Qur'an means the contract. As for those who say it means intercourse except in this verse: ﴿O you who believe, when you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them﴾ [al-Ahzab 49], this is not correct.

As for His saying: ﴿his wives﴾: when does a woman become a man's wife? By the contract with her. His saying: ﴿after him﴾ means after his separation from them. The Prophet's (ﷺ) separation from them occurs either during life or at death, and separation during life occurs either before consummation or after consummation. So there are three situations:

The first situation: one who is separated from her after his death, or separated from her by his death. She is not lawful to anyone after him, by consensus, and no one has disagreed about this.

The second situation: one who is separated from her during his life without consummation. She is lawful, and there is no dispute about it, as Ibn Kathir mentioned in his Tafsir.

The third: one who is separated from her during his life after consummation with her. This is a matter of disagreement among the scholars. Some said she is lawful, and some said she is not lawful. According to the opinion that says she is not lawful, it applies to her that she is his wife and that she is "after him." Were it not for the consensus regarding one who contracted with a woman and then separated from her before consummation, we would also say she is not lawful for anyone after him. So the situations become three. What are they?

One who separates from her after his death: she is not lawful, by consensus.
One who separates from her during his life before consummation: she is permissible and lawful to others. Ibn Kathir said: there is no dispute about this.
One who separates from her during his life after consummation: there is disagreement among the scholars; some say she is lawful, and some say she is not lawful. The topic is finished; there is no need to correct or to correct.

* Student: Do we not say that the more correct view is (...)?
* Shaykh: Actually, we do not know that anyone married one of the Prophet's wives after consummation with her. The apparent meaning of the verse, ﴿after him﴾, may be apparent regarding a matter after his life.
* Student: Shaykh, but what about the woman who sought refuge (al-mustaʿidhah) whom the Prophet (ﷺ) entered upon?
* Shaykh: Yes, he did not have intercourse with her; he did not consummate the marriage.
* Student: Do we take that consummation suffices, meaning seclusion (khalwah)?
* Shaykh: No, he says: "consummated with her" means: had intercourse with her.

He says: ﴿Nor that you should marry his wives after him, ever. Indeed, that is in the sight of Allah an enormity﴾ [al-Ahzab 53]. ﴿Indeed, that﴾ refers to harming the Prophet (ﷺ) and marrying his wives after him.

His saying: ﴿was in the sight of Allah an enormity﴾: the word "was" (كان) here is stripped of indicating time; the purpose is to affirm the greatness of that in the sight of Allah.

﴿Indeed, that was in the sight of Allah an enormity﴾. That this matter is great in the sight of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is evidence of Allah's protection of His Messenger (ﷺ), especially regarding marriage. This is why Allah said regarding the incident of the slander: ﴿When you received it with your tongues and said with your mouths that of which you had no knowledge, and you thought it trivial, while it was in the sight of Allah great﴾ [an-Nur 15]. Here He says: ﴿Indeed, that was in the sight of Allah an enormity﴾. ﴿An enormity⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ (عظيمًا)⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠ means in its rank and elevation, or great in its sin and crime? In its sin and crime. Accordingly, "greatness" means the greatness of the thing, i.e., its magnitude, and it includes what is praiseworthy and what is blameworthy. Here, it was great in the sight of Allah in its sin, so He said: (He will recompense you for it), according to the sin you committed, because recompense is of the same kind as the deed (...).

The wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) after him: that it is great in the sight of Allah. He warned against opposing that by His saying: ﴿Whether you disclose a thing or conceal it﴾ [al-Ahzab 54]. The sentence here is conditional, and ﴿a thing﴾ (شيئًا) is indefinite in a conditional context, so it denotes generality: ﴿Whether you disclose a thing﴾.

His saying: ﴿Whether you disclose a thing or conceal it﴾: the author said: (regarding their marriage after him). The correct view regarding the verse is that it is not restricted, and that it is general to everything: regarding the marriage of the Prophet's wives after him and in other matters.

His saying: ﴿or conceal it﴾ means: do not reveal it to anyone; conceal it within yourselves or conceal it among yourselves and your relatives. Concealment and disclosure are relative matters: the most intense concealment is what a person keeps within himself, then what he reveals to his family and companions while concealing it from others, then what he reveals to the people of his town, then what he reveals to people in general. In any case, everything a person discloses or conceals, ﴿indeed Allah is ever, of all things, Knowing﴾. This clause is the answer of the condition, and it is joined with "fa" (then) because it is a nominal sentence; ﴿indeed Allah﴾ is a nominal sentence, even though it is preceded by "inna," which denotes emphasis. Its connection with what precedes it, i.e., the conditional verb, is that when Allah, exalted is He, knows it, He will recompense you for it: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil. After completing this verse, since it is connected to what precedes it, we return to explaining the lessons from the previous verse, since we had not taken them. Does the apparent meaning of ﴿O you who believe, do not enter the houses of the Prophet﴾ [al-Ahzab 53] fit, or not?

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who believe, do not enter the houses of the Prophet unless you are permitted﴾.

* It is derived from this noble verse that it is not lawful for any believer to enter the houses of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) except under the conditions mentioned, due to His saying: ﴿do not enter﴾. The default in a prohibition is prohibition until evidence shows it is for something other than prohibition. Supporting prohibition here is that this relates to the right of a human being, and what relates to the right of a human being is not treated with leniency.

* It is derived from the noble verse that idafah (attribution) is made on the basis of the slightest connection: attributing a thing to another is for the slightest association, whether it is ownership, specific association, companionship, nearness, or otherwise. Therefore, among their well-known principles is that idafah is for the slightest connection, but there must be some connection between the attributed and that to which it is attributed. This is taken from His saying: ﴿the houses of the Prophet﴾, since their attribution to the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) is because they are his dwelling, although according to the preponderant view they belong to his wives.

* It is derived from the noble verse that permission to enter is valid whether it comes from the owner of the house or from one he has delegated, due to His saying: ﴿unless you are permitted﴾, and He did not say: (unless the Prophet permits you). So if a person is permitted to enter, whether by the owner of the house, or by his servant, or by his son, or the like, entry is permitted. Can it be derived from this that entry is permitted when you find the door open, even if there was no prior arrangement between you and your companion, or not? 

If we say that customary permission is like verbal permission, then it is derived from this; and His saying supports this: ﴿O you who believe, do not enter houses other than your houses until you have asked permission and greeted their inhabitants﴾ [an-Nur 27]. Indeed, seeking familiarity (isti'nas), which is being at ease, includes permission by word, seeking permission by action, and custom.

* It is derived from the noble verse that entry into the houses of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) is permitted under these conditions: permission, and that it not be waiting for food to be ready, because surprise causes harm; if your food is ready and then a person comes asking permission, this is a kind of harm, for if you refuse him it burdens you, and if you permit him it burdens you as well. Therefore, entering for one who is waiting for food to be ready is not permitted.

* It is derived from the verse: is prohibiting parasitism (tatafful) also derived? Yes, because the parasite's habit is to wait for when the food will be served; when it is served he asks permission or rushes in without permission. Before the food is ready and served, he could enter and then be told: leave; but once the food is served he must eat.

* It is derived from this noble verse: the legislated nature of accepting an invitation, due to His saying: ﴿but when you are invited, then enter﴾. Can it be derived from it that an invited person may enter even if he has not been given permission, when he finds the door in a state that indicates permission?

The answer: Yes, and it is clear, because He said: ﴿when you are invited, then enter﴾, and He did not say: when you are invited, then respond. Entering is more specific. Accordingly, if I am invited and I have come to the door, I may enter if we know by context that the door has been placed in the position of permission, as if it were open.

* It is derived from the noble verse that a person, when he has satisfied his need for food, should leave, due to His saying: ﴿and when you have eaten, disperse﴾. This applies to the houses of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) and equally to the houses of others: it is more virtuous for one invited to a meal, when he has eaten, to disperse, because his staying may burden the host, and because the need for which he came has ended. If you reflect on the Shari'ah, you will find that a person's good manners and conduct is that whenever he finishes his need, he completes it and departs for other needs. This is why the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said regarding the traveler who has finished his need: "When one of you has finished his need, let him hasten to his family and not delay." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1804), Muslim (1927/179), from Abu Hurayrah.] If we preserved our times with such manners, our times would be blessed, but we find our time wasted, and we do not observe this condition: whenever work is finished, we do not wait but walk to other work, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So when you are relieved, then strive, and to your Lord direct your longing﴾ [ash-Sharh 7-8]. Do not waste time.

* It is derived from the noble verse that whoever enters the houses of the Prophet (ﷺ) by invitation and then eats, should not sit to converse, due to His saying: ﴿nor staying for conversation﴾. This is beyond His saying: ﴿and when you have eaten, disperse﴾, because that is a command, whereas this is a prohibition: those invited are forbidden to remain conversing after finishing the meal.

* It is derived from the verse that this ruling applies only when the host is harmed, due to His saying: ﴿Indeed, that used to harm the Prophet﴾. As for when he is not harmed by it but is rather pleased by it, and may even request it, saying after they have eaten: "Wait, sit, let us be at ease and talk," then is this prohibited or not? It is permissible and there is no harm in it, because the principle among the scholars is that a ruling revolves with its cause in existence and in absence: when the cause exists, the effect exists, and when the cause is absent, the effect is absent.

* It is derived from the noble verse that the Prophet (ﷺ), like other human beings, is harmed as others are harmed, due to His saying: ﴿Indeed, that used to harm the Prophet﴾. However, he differs from others in the strength of his patience and forbearance (ﷺ), unlike other human beings who do not endure patiently as the Prophet (ﷺ) endures. This is why the Messenger would be harmed by their remaining in conversation, and he would not forbid them until Allah, exalted is He, forbade them.

* It is derived from the noble verse: Allah's care for His Prophet (ﷺ), by defending him against everything that harms him, due to His saying: ﴿Indeed, that used to harm the Prophet, so he is shy of you﴾.

* It is derived from it: the perfection of the Messenger's modesty (peace and blessings be upon him) and generosity, due to His saying: ﴿so he is shy of you﴾. He was shy because of his intense modesty; he was described as "more modest than a virgin in her chamber" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3562), Muslim (2320/67), from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri], and "modesty is part of faith" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (24), Muslim (36/59), from Abdullah ibn Umar], as the hadith from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) confirms. It is also evidence of his generosity, because the generous person is shy to embarrass his guests by saying: "Leave," or by showing weariness of them and displeasure at their conduct. Therefore the Messenger (ﷺ) treated them as if he were pleased with them, until Allah, exalted is He, made this clear to the Companions.

* It is derived from the noble verse that the Qur'an encompasses everything, even the manners of entering, sitting, eating and the like, which the Qur'an has explained; this is an elucidation of His saying: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things﴾ [an-Nahl 89].

The Qur'an's indication of things is of two kinds: a specific indication, meaning that it indicates the thing itself, which is clear; and an indication of comprehensiveness, verbal or semantic. Verbal comprehensiveness means that the wording is general in its form and includes everything the word can bear as meaning. Semantic generality is what is known among the scholars as analogy (qiyas), because the analogue and the original analogy agree in the cause, so there is generality in meaning between them. Thus the Qur'an's indication of this matter is in this manner, either as verbal indication or semantic indication, through verbal or semantic comprehensiveness.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verse 53–54 (part 4 of 4):

There is also the indication by implication (dalalat al-iltizam), which is a branch of, or included within, the two indications we have mentioned. If you say: "It may be objected that the Qur'an does not specify the amounts of the zakat portions, nor the amount that is obligatory, nor the number of units of prayer (rak'at), nor the amount of dhikr that is recommended in them. So what is the answer?" The answer is that the Sunnah has explained all of that, and Allah the Exalted has commanded us in His Book to adhere to what has come from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He said: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾ [al-Hashr 7]. His words ﴿whatever he gives you﴾ include what has reached us of wealth and what has reached us of knowledge. Is knowledge called "giving" (iytaʾ)? Yes, it is called iytaʾ: ﴿And those who were given knowledge and faith said: "You have indeed remained within the Book of Allah until the Day of Resurrection"﴾ [al-Rum 56]. Just as the giving of wealth is called iytaʾ, so too the giving of knowledge is called iytaʾ. Therefore His words ﴿whatever the Messenger gives you﴾ [al-Hashr 7] include what has reached us of wealth and what has reached us of knowledge. Likewise Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Whoever obeys the Messenger has indeed obeyed Allah﴾ [al-Nisa' 80], and He said: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger has certainly strayed into clear error﴾ [al-Ahzab 36]. All of this indicates that what the Sunnah has brought is among what the Qur'an has brought.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the description of Allah the Exalted with modesty (haya'); based on His words:
* Student: ﴿And Allah does not feel shy of the truth﴾.
* Shaykh: From His words ﴿And Allah does not feel shy of the truth﴾, what is the point of the indication, given that this is a negation?
* Student: Is it that Allah feels shy of what is not the truth?
* Shaykh: The point of the indication is that if Allah the Exalted were not described with modesty, it would not be valid to negate modesty from Him in one situation but not in the other. On this basis, the verse is evidence that Allah the Exalted is described with modesty, but the modesty of Allah is not like the modesty of a human being, because Allah says in His Book: ﴿There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾ [al-Shura 11].
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that among matters there is what is true and what is false. The truth in reports is truthfulness (sidq), and in rulings it is justice ('adl); the falsehood in both is the opposite of that. Falsehood in reports is lying (kadhib), and in rulings it is oppression (jawr).
* Among the benefits of the noble verse, His words ﴿And when you ask them for a possession﴾ to the end: it is not permissible to ask the wives of the Prophet ﷺ for anything except from behind a barrier (hijab), and the verse is explicit on this: ﴿ask them from behind a barrier﴾.
* Among its benefits: the permissibility of speaking with the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, its basis being ﴿ask them﴾. Allah permitted asking them. Is the asking here the asking of enquiry or the asking of begging?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, "possession" (mata') is not all one thing; He said ﴿when you ask them for a possession﴾, so it is asking of begging. But asking for knowledge is more fitting. Can it be deduced from it that it is permissible to speak with women other than the wives of the Messenger ﷺ?
The answer: Yes, it can be deduced, because if it is permissible with the wives of the Messenger ﷺ, despite the respect and honour they have, then with others it is more fitting. However, it is conditional on safety from temptation (fitnah). If temptation is feared from the speaker or from the woman, it becomes forbidden. Likewise, it is conditional that a person should not take pleasure in speaking with a woman, even if it is not pleasure of desire; because a person may take pleasure in addressing a woman, not in a sexual or instinctive sense, but he wishes to continue the conversation with her. This too is not permissible, except when she is one of his mahram and he wishes to speak with her to make her feel at ease or to be at ease with her; this is not objectionable.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the barrier mentioned here is not merely covering the face, but is something beyond that; based on His words ﴿from behind a barrier﴾, and He did not say "veiled women." This indicates that this barrier is separate and is not part of a woman's clothing, but is something separate, like when she is in her private chamber (khidr) and people speak to her.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the establishment of the causation (ta'lil) of legal rulings from His words ﴿That is purer﴾, and from His earlier words ﴿Indeed, that was causing harm to the Prophet﴾.
* It is derived from it: that a person must strive in everything that purifies his heart, and must keep away from everything that defiles his heart; because He gave as the cause of the prohibition or the command regarding the barrier that it is purer for hearts. There is no difference in this between purifying the heart from vile morals such as adultery and sodomy, or purifying it from corrupt beliefs or evil intentions. All of this is obligatory upon a person: he must purify his heart from it and keep away from everything that defiles his heart in that regard.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that temptation in addressing women may come from the man alone, from the woman alone, or from both together; based on His words ﴿for your hearts and their hearts﴾. A man may be the one who takes pleasure in addressing the woman, while the woman has no such thought in mind, has not been concerned with it, and has not reflected on the matter; but he takes pleasure in this address, so the defilement is in the man's heart. It may also be the reverse: the woman speaks to the man while she takes pleasure in this address, and the man has no such thought in mind, so the defilement is then in her heart. It may also be from both sides, so the defilement is in both their hearts.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: prohibition.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: It is possible. How? We have mentioned it.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: That is three.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: From the heart of the man alone, or the woman alone, or both together.
* Student: Or both together.
* Shaykh: Yes indeed.
* Student: Meaning: is it not possible, for example, that neither the man nor the woman takes pleasure?
* Shaykh: No, it is possible. How? That fourth one is not what we meant; we meant that the defilement arises from this.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the prohibition of marrying the wives of the Prophet ﷺ after him; based on His words ﴿nor that you should marry his wives after him﴾.
* It is also derived from it: that the prohibition concerning them is perpetual; based on His word ﴿ever﴾. Accordingly, how many categories are the perpetually prohibited women? They are prohibited by lineage (nasab), by suckling (rada'), by marriage relationship (sihr), by mutual cursing (li'an), and by honour (ihtiram): five types. Is that right? Prohibited by lineage, by suckling, by marriage relationship, by li'an, and by honour: five.
The women prohibited by lineage are seven, mentioned in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, your brothers' daughters, and your sisters' daughters﴾ [al-Nisa' 23].
By suckling, in His words: ﴿And your mothers who nursed you, and your sisters through nursing﴾, and the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "What is forbidden by lineage is forbidden by suckling"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2645), and Muslim (1447/12), from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas.]].
By marriage relationship, in His words: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already passed; indeed it was an indecency and hateful and an evil way﴾ [al-Nisa' 22], and in His words: ﴿And the mothers of your wives, and your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship, born of your wives with whom you have consummated marriage; but if you have not consummated marriage with them, there is no blame upon you; and the wives of your sons who are from your loins﴾.
* Student: "The wives of your sons who are not from your loins" – was this excluded by this verse?
* Shaykh: Excluded what? 
* Student: Your sons other than those from your loins; meaning, through suckling?
* Shaykh: Yes, it is excluded by it; it is excluded by the verse.
The prohibited by li'an: this is that when a man accuses his wife of adultery and she does not confess to it, and it is not established by evidence, he performs li'an with her; when the li'an is completed, she becomes forbidden to him permanently.
As for those prohibited forever by honour, they are the wives of the Prophet ﷺ.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the greatness of the sin of one who marries one of the wives of the Messenger ﷺ after him, based on His words ﴿Indeed, that was in the sight of Allah an enormity﴾.
* It is also derived from it: that sins differ in their magnitude; based on His words ﴿Indeed, that was in the sight of Allah an enormity﴾. This is so: sins are of major and minor kinds, and among major sins some are greater than others, and minor sins likewise vary; and acts of obedience also vary, some of them being among the foundations of Islam and others being less than that.
Can it be deduced from the noble verse that a guest should not ask about the host's food when he serves it, or not? Does it follow that a guest should not ask his host about his food when it is served, saying for example, if he is served chicken: "Is this chicken imported or not imported?"
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Based on His words ﴿And when you have eaten, disperse﴾. Allah did not command asking about the food, and it is so: it is neither prescribed nor part of good manners for you to ask your companion who served you food, saying: "By Allah, where is this from? Is it lawful or unlawful?" Because this contradicts the guidance of the Prophet ﷺ: "A Jewish woman presented the Prophet ﷺ with a sheep, and he ate from it and did not ask"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (2617), and Muslim (2190/45), from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]], and "a Jew invited him to a meal, and he ate from it and did not ask"[[Related by Ahmad in al-Musnad (13201) (13860), from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]]. Moreover, if you ask, you embarrass your companion: a man who has honoured you with hospitality, and you say to him: "Where is this from?! Where did you buy this?! Is it halal or imported?!" And if we open this door, then we would say: "Come, where did the origin of this food come from to you? Perhaps it is usurped? Stolen?" And if that is ruled out, perhaps this man has earnings that are unlawful, of which we do not know, and we say to him: "Where did you get this?" "By Allah, I bought it from the market." "Fine, bring witnesses that you bought it." It is a problem: if we open this door, many doors will be opened upon us. For this reason, it is part of the wisdom of the Law that a person is never prescribed to ask, no matter what; even if the one who serves you is a Jew or a Christian, do not ask him about his food, because this is excessive scrutiny and over-investigation, and it is a burden on your companion and a burden on yourself; for if you accustom yourself to eating only after investigation, then it means you will be doubtful about everything you eat. Praise be to Allah for safety, since the Messenger (...).
He says: "Peace be upon you," and enter.
* Student: (...) we said: if we know (...).
* Shaykh: Yes, we have entered; and when we arrive, we greet him, or we greet as we enter through the door.
* Student: The verse ﴿And when you have eaten, disperse﴾ is specific to the Messenger, or general?
* Shaykh: We mentioned before you arrived that in meaning it is general; meaning, even for someone other than the Messenger ﷺ, if we do not know that he is pleased by our staying, we leave; and every person who invites you to a meal, you disperse after it, unless he says: "Rest, let us talk"; then that choice is his.
* Student: Is it not asked about camel meat?
* Shaykh: Not at all; one does not ask about camel meat. Firstly, camel meat is usually recognisable, unless it is from a young camel, and a person who is not accustomed to eating meat might be confused about it.
* Student: If it is (...).
* Shaykh: It is not valid; if he is compelled and does not eat at all, what embarrasses him?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: This may be something we ask about to avert harm, not for excessive scrutiny. Meaning: if he has been told: "Do not eat camel meat," and he doubts whether this is camel meat or not, then this is something we may say: the asking is not for the sake of making it lawful, nor for the sake of whether ablution is obligatory upon him or not; this is for averting harm, and it is not objectionable (...).
The prohibition of harming the Messenger ﷺ, and his being most strongly protected from the believers; based on His words ﴿And it is not for you to harm the Messenger of Allah﴾. The reference to the prohibition of that is that harming him is prohibited because he is the Messenger of Allah; and because he is a messenger from Allah, the believers are most strongly prohibited from harming him.
* Among the benefits of the verse: the Law's concern for whatever causes the purity of hearts. I do not know whether you have written this down or not: the Law's concern for whatever causes the purity of hearts; based on His words ﴿That is purer for your hearts and their hearts﴾.
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that if Allah obligated in that age what causes complete purity of hearts, then in our age it is all the more so; so everything that causes the purity of hearts and their remoteness from base morals is obligatory. I do not know whether this was written down or not. It was not written? I think we wrote that the rulings of the Law are causally grounded (ma'lalah); did we write it? And we wrote an explanation of the benefits of mentioning the cause, or linking the cause to the ruling; did we not write it? It falls under the benefit; look, what is its number in your notes?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Thirty-three. The rulings are tied to their causes and their wisdom?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No, you wrote that the rulings are tied to their causes and their wisdom; in which benefit? What is its number?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: Seventeen.
* Student: (...) the establishment of the causes of the legal rulings (...).
* Shaykh: What is its number?
* Student: Seventeen.
* Another student: (...).
* Shaykh: You have twenty-one, yes. And, in commentary on what preceded regarding linking the rulings with their wisdom, we say: among the benefits of that is the tranquillity of a person in the ruling, and the showing of the exaltedness of the Law, that its rulings are not vain or void. The third: attaching to the ruling whatever agrees with it in its cause, meaning that what agrees with that cause is attached to this ruling. These are three benefits, or not? And they are?
* Student: The exaltedness of the Law, the tranquillity of a person, attaching to the ruling what agrees with it in the cause.
We mentioned among the benefits of the verse: the establishment of modesty for Allah?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: We mentioned it; we mentioned that it is appropriate to leave the place as soon as the meal ends?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: We mentioned it; we mentioned the variation in the magnitude of sins before Allah?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Then we take the last verse: ﴿If you disclose a thing or conceal it﴾ [al-Ahzab 54].
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: We do not say: legislation (mashru'iyyah); because the scholars differ regarding this outside the wedding feast; they differ regarding it.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: It is not so in any case; even the right of a Muslim over a Muslim, of which is accepting an invitation, is clearer and more manifest.
But we mentioned that the difference between (but when you are invited, then accept) and His words ﴿When you are invited, then enter﴾.
Allah the Exalted said: ﴿If you disclose a thing or conceal it, indeed Allah is ever, of all things, Knowing﴾.
* It is derived from the noble verse: the all-encompassing knowledge of Allah the Exalted regarding everything; based on His words ﴿indeed Allah is ever, of all things, Knowing﴾.
* It is also derived from it: warning the accountable person against opposing Allah the Mighty and Majestic, in little or in much; because the benefit of mentioning His knowledge is warning against opposition.
* Among its benefits: a refutation of the Qadariyyah, the extreme Qadariyyah who deny Allah's knowledge, glorified and exalted is He, of the actions of the servant; based on His words ﴿indeed Allah is ever, of all things, Knowing﴾, since it includes what a person will do and what he has already done.
* It is derived from the noble verse: that whatever a servant does, good or evil, he is held accountable for it, either for him or against him; based on the generality of the word ﴿thing﴾. In another verse: ﴿If you disclose good or conceal it﴾ [al-Nisa' 149], but this verse is more general.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: (﴿﴿O you who believe, do not enter the houses of the Prophet unless you are given permission﴾﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53] "to enter, by an invitation ﴿to a meal﴾ so that you enter, ﴿without waiting for it﴾ waiting for it, ﴿its ripeness﴾ its cooking, a verbal noun of أنى يأني (anā, ya'nī)"). ﴿O you who believe﴾: We have already discussed phrases like this, and we explained that opening a ruling with the vocative (nidā') indicates its importance and the care given to it, because the vocative requires the attention of the one addressed. Describing this address as "belief" indicates that adhering to this ruling is one of the requirements of faith, and that neglecting it causes a deficiency in faith. Moreover, the expression "belief" contains encouragement and urging, because the truly believing person adheres to what he is commanded and abstains from what he is forbidden. An example of this is when you say, "O man, do such-and-such." The meaning is: by virtue of your manhood it is incumbent upon you to do such-and-such. So "O believer, do such-and-such" means: by virtue of your faith it is incumbent upon you to do such-and-such. Thus it contains encouragement and urging.

﴿O you who believe﴾: meaning, because of your faith We have directed this address to you. ﴿Do not enter the houses of the Prophet﴾: "the houses of the Prophet" is a plural construction in the genitive, attributed to the Messenger ﷺ, because his houses were nine; each of his wives had a house. The Prophet ﷺ did not gather them together in one house, but assigned a house to each wife.

As for its attribution to the Prophet ﷺ, "the houses of the Prophet," although it is also attributed to the women themselves, as previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿And remember what is recited in your houses of the verses of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 34]. Does this contradict that? No, it does not contradict it. It is attributed to each of them according to a particular relationship. Since these houses are the refuge and dwelling of the Prophet ﷺ, they are attributed to him; and since they, i.e. these houses, are the property of his wives, they are attributed to the wives.

The scholars differed: are the houses of the Messenger's wives their property or the property of the Messenger ﷺ? There are two opinions among the people of knowledge. We have already mentioned that the more apparent view is that they are the property of the wives, based on the fact that they inherited these houses. Had they been the property of the Prophet ﷺ, they would not have inherited them, because the Prophet ﷺ said: "We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from; what we leave is charity"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3093) and Muslim (1759/52) from Abu Bakr.]].

It is not an objection to this that these houses were later incorporated into the mosque, because either they were incorporated in exchange for compensation, or they were incorporated with the consent of those entitled to them, and this does not contradict ownership.

﴿the houses of the Prophet, unless you are given permission﴾ ﴿to a meal, without waiting for its ripeness﴾: ﴿unless you are given permission﴾ is in the passive voice, and He did not say "unless the Prophet gives you permission," because a wife of his may give permission to someone, and he then enters. So it is not a condition that the permission come from the Messenger ﷺ. Rather, Allah, Exalted, has stipulated three conditions: the permission, ﴿to a meal﴾, and third, ﴿without waiting for its ripeness﴾.

Let us examine these restrictions: are they binding or not? His saying ﴿unless you are given permission﴾ includes both customary permission and verbal permission. Verbal permission is that one is told, "Enter." Customary permission is that there be a sign indicating that the situation is one of permission, such as opening the door and the like. Can one enter without permission? No, one cannot. So permission is a valid and binding restriction.

He said ﴿to a meal﴾. Does this indicate that if they were given permission to enter for something other than a meal, it would be impermissible? No. ﴿To a meal﴾: if they are invited for something other than a meal, may they enter or not? If we look at the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿to a meal﴾, we would say they may not enter, because Allah, Exalted, said ﴿to a meal﴾. But we say that this restriction is a clarification of the actual situation, and what is a clarification of the actual situation has no implied meaning (mafhūm). The verse was revealed concerning a specific case, which is the entry of these people to a meal without an invitation, so it was restricted by His saying ﴿to a meal﴾.

The third: ﴿without waiting for its ripeness﴾. (ناظر): if it is followed by (إلى), it is from looking with the eye; if it is followed directly by its object, it means waiting. You say, "I looked at him" (nazartu ilayhi), and you say, "I looked for him" (nazartuhu), meaning "I waited for him." Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿Do they wait except for the angels to come to them?﴾ [al-An'am: 158], ﴿Do they await except its interpretation?﴾ [al-A'raf: 53]. The meaning is: do they wait? Because it is followed directly by its object.

﴿Some faces that day will be radiant, looking at their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22–23]: this is from looking with the eye. Here, ﴿nāẓirīn﴾ is transitive directly or by (إلى)? It is directly transitive, so it means "waiting." His saying ﴿its ripeness﴾, i.e. its cooking: is this a condition or not? We say it is a condition for the permissibility of entering: that they enter for a meal without waiting for its ripeness. They used to watch for the food to ripen, and when they judged that it had ripened and was about to be served or had been served, they would enter the houses in order to eat. There is no doubt that catching a person by surprise at his meal harms him. The one who surprises people at the time the food is served is called a ṭufaylī (a hanger-on) and a ḍayfan (an unwelcome guest). He is not a guest (ḍayf); ḍayfan is with the letter nūn, because that nūn is like the one who leans on a stick as if he were heavy.
