Among it: annoying the neighbor, to the extent that the scholars say: a person may not drive a stake into the wall shared between him and his neighbor in a way that harms his neighbor; nor may he water his palm trees if the water seeps into his neighbor's land; nor may he place a millstone that grinds next to his neighbor, because that harms him.
So annoyance is numerous. Among this type is that he humiliates him when he comes to seek his right; for some employees, we seek refuge in Allah, when people come to them to complete their transactions, you find them demeaning and harming them. This too is among annoying the believers without their having earned it.
Its individual instances, indeed its types, cannot be enumerated, and the general matter is that the believer is harmed by an act or a statement; so those who annoy believers without their having earned it have borne a slander and a manifest sin. We ask Allah for well-being (...) ﴿And His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ [al-Ahzab 56].
* In this verse there are benefits:
* Among them: the affirmation of the angels, by His saying: ﴿and His angels﴾.
* Among them: the nobility of the angels in their being attributed to Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala; by His saying: ﴿and His angels﴾, their attribution to Allah is an attribution of honor.
* Among its benefits: the demonstration of the exalted status of the Prophet (ﷺ), since Allah and His angels send blessings upon him; this is undoubtedly from the elevation of his rank and the loftiness of his remembrance.
* Among its benefits: the command to send blessings and peace upon the Messenger (ﷺ), by His saying: ﴿O you who believe, send blessings upon him and greet him with peace﴾.
* Among its benefits: that sending blessings and peace upon him is a requirement of faith, and that it is an increase in faith; by His saying: ﴿O you who believe﴾.
* Among them: that sending blessings and peace upon him are obligatory, because the basic meaning of a command is obligation; and because that is from fulfilling the right of the Prophet (ﷺ) which he holds over his Ummah, for his right over his Ummah is greater than the right of parents over their children. But the obligation is fulfilled by doing it once; if a proof indicates repetition, we must act according to what the proof requires.
Many scholars have said that sending blessings upon him (ﷺ) in the prayer is obligatory, in the tashahhud; the person says: "Peace be upon you, O Prophet," and says: "O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad."
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that it is prescribed for a person to send blessings upon him verbally: ﴿O you who believe, send blessings upon him and greet him with peace﴾.
Peace or blessings in the heart alone is not sufficient; accordingly, when we write hadith, we should write: ﷺ.
As for what some people do in writing (ص) or writing (صلعم), the scholars disliked that and said: the better course is to write ﷺ.
Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, would sometimes write a hadith without mentioning ﷺ.
Some scholars answered this: that he would omit it out of eagerness to seize time, and that he would send blessings upon him with his tongue rather than his pen.
It has passed with us in the explanation or the tafsir that sending blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ) is divided into two kinds: absolute and restricted; and that in restricted contexts it may be obligatory and may be recommended, and that in some places it may be disliked.
There are also discussions, not within the verse itself, but related to it:
Is it permissible to send blessings upon other than the prophets?
On this the scholars have three positions: permissibility, prohibition, and permissibility when it is not made a symbol (shi'ar). The last is the correct view: it is permissible to send blessings upon a person provided you do not make it a symbol for him, such that whenever you mention him you bless him or greet him.
The scholars have stated that what appears in some books when mentioning 'Ali, radiya Allahu 'anhu, saying "'Ali 'alayhi al-salam" or "'Ali karram Allahu wajhahu," that this is the work of some copyists, and that the better course is to say of him what is said of the other Companions: "'Ali radiya Allahu 'anhu," even though 'Ali radiya Allahu 'anhu is more complete than "'Ali 'alayhi al-salam" and more complete than "'Ali karram Allahu wajhahu," because radiya (being pleased) is a great rank.
As for sending blessings upon non-prophets as a consequence, this is permissible by consensus, and the Prophet (ﷺ) taught his Ummah to say: "O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and upon the family of Muhammad" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3370) and Muslim (406 / 66) from the hadith of Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah].
It also passed with us: supplicating for mercy for the Messenger, whether one may pray for mercy for him. Some scholars disliked that, and the correct view is that it is not disliked.
Then He said: ﴿Indeed, those who annoy Allah and His Messenger, Allah has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter, and has prepared for them a humiliating punishment﴾.

Alright. ﴿Indeed, those who annoy Allah and His Messenger﴾ to the end [al-Ahzab: 57].

* From this noble verse is derived: that harming Allah and His Messenger is one of the major sins (kaba'ir). The reason is that Allah threatened it with curse and punishment, and everything for which Allah threatens curse or punishment is one of the major sins.

The scholars have differed regarding the major sins: are they to be enumerated or defined? Some of them enumerated them, and some of them defined them.

He said: The major sin is every act for which a specific punishment has been prescribed. This is the definition of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him: every thing or every sin for which a specific punishment has been prescribed, whether worldly or otherworldly, is one of the major sins, whether that is a curse, or wrath, or negation of faith, or disavowal from it, or punishment, or what is similar to that. Everything for which a specific punishment has been set is one of the major sins.

* And from the noble verse is derived: the description of Allah, blessed and exalted, as being harmed, by His saying: ﴿who annoy Allah and His Messenger﴾.

* And from it is derived: the demonstration of Allah's perfection, may He be glorified and exalted, because if He is harmed by reprehensible things that do not befit Him, this indicates His perfection. For this reason, among people it is considered a fault that a person is not harmed by being described with a defect. The fault is that he is not harmed by being described with a defect. For this reason, such a man is called a donkey for his dullness and his unimportance, meaning he does not distinguish between one who praises him and one who disparages him; it is all the same to him. But the person who is harmed by a defect is the one who has feeling and emotion. Then, if he is patient and seeks reward, and uses wisdom in that, it is better.

The point is that being harmed by what is not praiseworthy is considered a perfection.

* And from the benefits of the noble verse: that harming the Messenger ﷺ is like harming Allah, because Allah joined them with the conjunction "and": ﴿who annoy Allah and His Messenger﴾. Just as obeying the Messenger is like obeying Allah, and disobeying the Messenger is like disobeying Allah, harming the Messenger is like harming Allah, meaning in terms of prohibition and that it is one of the major sins. Otherwise, harming Allah is greater in terms of the aspect to which blame and defect are attributed.

* And from the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of cursing, that is, the curse of Allah, which is His expulsion and distancing. Is it one of the essential attributes or the active attributes? It is an active attribute, because every attribute of Allah that is linked to a cause is an active attribute, since that cause renews itself, so the attribute comes into being after its cause exists. This is what is (...).

﴿And He has prepared for them﴾, and the humiliating punishment, we all know, is in the Fire, because it is the Fire whose punishment is humiliating.

* And from the benefits of the noble verse: that recompense is of the same kind as the deed. Just as these people exalted themselves and became arrogant and humiliated the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, by harming him, Allah punished them with what humiliates and abases them of torment.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And those who annoy the believing men and believing women without their having earned it have certainly borne a slander and a clear sin﴾ [al-Ahzab: 58].

* From this noble verse is derived: the prohibition of harming believers without right, by His saying: ﴿they have certainly borne a slander and a clear sin﴾.

* And from it is derived: the prohibition of every form of harm, whatever its type, whether verbal or physical, by the generality of the wording in His saying: ﴿those who annoy﴾, and the relative pronoun is among the forms of generality.

* And from it is derived: that harming a believer for what is from his own earning does not carry a threat, and it is neither a sin nor a slander, by His saying: ﴿without their having earned it﴾.

* And from it is derived: that it is not permissible to harm someone beyond what he deserves. If he insults you, do not insult him more; for if you insult him more, you have harmed him without his having earned it, and if you insult him with the like of what he insulted you, you have harmed him to the extent he earned. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40].

* And from the benefits of the verse: the refutation of the Jabriyyah, by His saying: ﴿without their having earned it﴾, where He attributed the act to them. The Jabriyyah say that man is compelled in his deeds, that he has no power or strength, that he does a thing without his choice and leaves it without his choice.

* And from the benefits of the noble verse: the dispraise of lying, by His saying: ﴿they have certainly borne a slander﴾, especially when the lie leads to harming others.

* And from the benefits of the noble verse: the permissibility of harming non-believers, by His saying: ﴿And those who annoy the believing men and believing women without their having earned it﴾. However, if the non-believer is a dhimmi, or one with a covenant (mu'ahad), or one granted safe conduct (musta'man), then it is not permissible to harm him in a way that violates his covenant.

So the non-believer has a distinction: harming a believer is forbidden in every case, while regarding the non-believer there is a distinction. What is the distinction? If we harm him more than the covenant requires, it is forbidden and not permissible; and if we harm him within the limit that the covenant requires, he has no sanctity except in what his covenant requires.

* And from the benefits of the noble verse: that a sin may combine two blameworthy attributes, by His saying: ﴿they have certainly borne a slander and a clear sin﴾. By their lying they bore slander, and by their transgression they bore a clear sin (...).

﴿ ﴾

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ [al-Ahzab 56]. ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels﴾: this is a report emphasized with (inna), and the angels are conjoined to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, with the conjunction (wa), because they share with Allah, glorified and exalted be He, in this action. For this reason He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels﴾.

As for His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels﴾, the angels (al-mala'ika): it has already been stated that they are the plural of malak (angel), and that the root of malak is ma'lak, from al-alukah, which means message. But there occurred in it a change (i'lal) by transposition, so that instead of ma'lak it became mal'ak, then the hamza was dropped for ease because of frequent usage, so it became malak. As for the plural, the hamza was restored, and it is said: mala'ika.

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: This is a morphological explanation, which does not belong in a lesson on jurisprudence. They say: from where is malak derived? From al-alukah. Al-alukah in the language means message, and the angels are messengers. So its original form is ma'lak, meaning from al-alukah, then it underwent i'lal by transposition and became mal'ak, then the hamza was dropped for ease because of frequent usage, and its vowel was transferred to the lam, so it became malak. As for the plural, it is mala'ika. The angels are those whom Allah, the Exalted, made messengers, and they are an unseen world, created from light, obedient to the command of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, devoted to His worship night and day, as Allah mentioned about them: ﴿They glorify Him night and day, never tiring﴾ [al-Anbiya 20], and they, moreover, ﴿do not disobey Allah in what He commands them﴾ [al-Tahrim 6], because of the strength of their obedience to Allah's command.

﴿And they do what they are commanded﴾: because of their strength in carrying it out. So ﴿they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them﴾ is considered in terms of their wills: they have no will that opposes the command of Allah. ﴿And they do what they are commanded﴾ is considered in terms of execution and action. They, that is the angels, are of various kinds in their forms, their deeds and their attributes. We know of this only what Allah and His Messenger have informed us of, and the rest is unknown to us, so we believe in what we know of their names, forms, attributes and deeds, and for what we do not know we believe in it in a general manner (ijmal). We say: we believed in Allah and His angels.

﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels﴾, the report: ﴿send blessings upon the Prophet﴾. ﴿The Prophet﴾: who? Muhammad ﷺ; for this reason he said: (Muhammad ﷺ). What is the meaning of ﴿send blessings﴾? It is well known among many scholars that the blessing (salah) from Allah is mercy, and from the angels is seeking forgiveness. On this basis, ﴿send blessings﴾ is explained as relating to Allah in the sense of mercy, and relating to the angels as seeking forgiveness. But this explanation is incorrect, for mercy is more general than blessing, because mercy is invoked for everyone, whereas blessing is specific to the prophets; it is their distinctive sign, and it is not said of anyone other than them except in a manner that is not a distinctive sign. As for mercy, it is general, to the extent that some scholars say: it is not permissible to invoke mercy for the Messenger; you do not say: Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, or: the Messenger of Allah, may Allah have mercy on him. But this view is weak, because the Prophet ﷺ himself used to invoke mercy for himself, saying: «My Lord, forgive me and have mercy on me»[[Narrated by Abu Dawud (850), al-Tirmidhi (284), and Ibn Majah (898), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Abbas.]], and in the story of the Bedouin he said: «O Allah, have mercy on me and on Muhammad»[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (6010), from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]], and the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, did not reject it from him. But among the early scholars (al-salaf), the Messenger ﷺ is invoked with what? With blessing (salah), and others are invoked with mercy and good pleasure, and what is similar to that.

The correct view is that Allah's blessing upon His Messenger means His praise of him in the highest assembly, and it is not His mercy toward him, as evidenced by His words, exalted be He: ﴿Those upon them are blessings from their Lord, and mercy﴾ [al-Baqarah 157]. He said: ﴿blessings﴾ and ﴿mercy﴾, so this indicates that mercy is other than blessing, and so it is. As for the blessing of the angels upon the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, it may mean that they invoke blessing for him, and it may mean that they praise him along with Allah, and this is closer, so that the meaning is not divided within the word ﴿send blessings﴾; the meaning then is that Allah praises him and the angels likewise praise him. This is from the exaltation of the rank of the Messenger ﷺ, and for this reason He placed this declarative sentence before the imperative sentence in His words: ﴿O you who have believed, send blessings upon him﴾ [al-Ahzab 56], because when the soul knows the nobility of this Prophet, and that Allah, the Exalted, Himself and His angels, both those brought near and others of the angels, send blessings upon him, then they send blessings upon him. I said: the angels brought near, because all the angels are brought near in the general sense, but there are angels who are brought near to Allah in a particular sense, such as the bearers of the Throne and the like, and all of these send blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ.

And in the attribution of the angels to Allah ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings﴾..
the Prophet ﷺ.
﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ [al-Ahzab 56]. And when this was established in souls, the exalted status of the Messenger ﷺ through this sentence, Allah directed the address to the believers, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, send blessings upon him and greet him with peace in full submission﴾.

The opening of the sentence with the vocative indicates its importance and the care given to it, because the vocative requires the attention of the one addressed, and there is no need to alert the listener except for a matter of importance.

Then, this vocative with this description, ﴿O you who have believed﴾, contains an incitement to comply, that is, to comply with the address directed to them. For this reason Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: «When Allah says: O you who have believed, then lend him your ear, meaning listen to it, for it is either a good thing you are commanded to, or an evil thing you are forbidden from»[[Narrated by Sa'id ibn Mansur in his Tafsir (50).]].

And in describing them with faith, while it is an incitement, is evidence that complying with this command is among the requirements of faith, and that disobeying it is a deficiency in faith.

He said: ﴿O you who have believed, send blessings upon him﴾ [al-Ahzab 56]. We want to merge the hadith with the tafsir, since I have not brought the rules.

﴿O you who have believed, send blessings upon him﴾: ﴿send blessings upon him﴾ means, invoke blessing for him. The intended meaning of "blessing" when you say: send blessings upon so-and-so, is not general invocation, but invocation with blessing. For this reason, when Allah commanded His Prophet to send blessings upon the one who gave him charity, he would say: «O Allah, send blessings upon him»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (1497) and Muslim (1078/176), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa, with similar meaning.]].

So salah in the language is invocation, which is correct, but when I command you to send blessings upon a person, the meaning is that you invoke for him with what? With Allah's blessing upon him. So the meaning of ﴿O you who have believed, send blessings upon him﴾ is a command to send blessings upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and it is an absolute, unrestricted command. Thus sending blessings upon the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is absolute and unrestricted: we send blessings upon him in whatever form we pray, and we send blessings upon him at all times and in all places. But there are places where it is emphasized, and places where it is not fitting, and places where it is recommended absolutely, meaning it is not emphasized.

Among the situations in which sending blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ is emphasized is when his name is mentioned, for then sending blessings upon him is obligatory, because of his ﷺ saying in the hadith of Abu Hurayrah: «Jibril came to me and said: May a man be humbled, in whose presence you are mentioned and he does not send blessings upon you»[[Narrated by Muslim (2551/9), and al-Tirmidhi (3545), and the wording is his.]]. This is an invocation against him that Allah humble his nose in the dust, and humbling the nose in the dust is evidence of abasement and humiliation, and this indicates the obligation of sending blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ when his name is mentioned.

Secondly: sending blessings upon him in the final tashahhud is a pillar without which the prayer is not valid, according to the school of the Hanbalis and the Shafi'is, and there is no difference between an obligatory prayer and a voluntary one.

* Among them: it is recommended, in the sending of blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ in supplication, to place it before or after it.
* Among them: at the adhan: «Say the same as he says, then send blessings upon me»[[Narrated by Muslim (384/11), from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Amr.]]. And there are multiple occasions, but some of them are obligatory and some are recommended.

As for disliking the sending of blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ, they mentioned that it is disliked to send blessings upon him at the slaughter: when you say, "In the name of Allah, and Allah is greatest," you do not say, "O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad." They said: because the situation is one of sincerity and monotheism, so it is not appropriate to mention anything else alongside the name of Allah. So you say, "In the name of Allah, and Allah is greatest," and you do not send blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ.

As for His words: ﴿O you who have believed, send blessings upon him﴾, I told you that it is absolute, in whatever manner it is done. As for what was reported from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, when the Companions asked him: How should we send blessings upon you? He said: «Say: O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad»[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3369) and Muslim (407/69), from the hadith of Abu Humayd al-Sa'idi.]]. This is by way of recommendation, not obligation; for this reason the scholars agreed that sending blessings upon the family of the Messenger ﷺ is not obligatory, although the formula that the Prophet ﷺ taught his community includes blessings upon his family, though it is not obligatory, which indicates that it is by way of recommendation.

Perhaps one may also cite as evidence for this that the formulas the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, commanded regarding how to send blessings upon him differ; they are not all one formula. This indicates that whatever formula you use is sufficient.

As for His words: ﴿Send blessings upon him and greet him with peace in full submission﴾ [al-Ahzab 56]: that is, say: "Peace be upon you," meaning invoke peace for him, so say: "Peace be upon you, O Prophet."

Greeting the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, with peace even though he is absent is a lawful matter; for this reason we say in our prayer: "Peace be upon you, O Prophet," although he is absent, and the Companions used to say: "Peace be upon you, O Prophet," although he was absent, and he does not hear them, even if they were with him in prayer, for he does not hear them. But there are wandering angels who convey to the Prophet ﷺ the greetings of his community; and because when a person has strong faith in the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, he becomes as though he is present before him, addressing him.

As for His words: ﴿O you who have believed, send blessings﴾ ﴿and greet him with peace﴾, the verse places blessing before peace, although in the tashahhud peace is placed before blessing. So is there any contradiction between the verse and what is established in the hadith of the tashahhud? Is there a contradiction between them?

The answer: No, because coordination with the conjunction (wa) does not necessitate the obligation of precedence, although it may suggest it, but it does not necessitate it, because the conjunction, as the linguists said, indicates mere joint association without order. For this reason, if you say, "What Allah wills and you will," although you placed Allah's will first, this is a form of shirk, because the conjunction implies equality and does not necessitate ordering.

If someone asks: why was the greeting emphasized with a verbal noun? He said: ﴿greet him with peace in full submission﴾, and the blessing was not emphasized?

The answer: the blessing was preceded by something that emphasizes it, namely Allah's report that He and His angels send blessings upon him, and this gives a person strength in sending blessings upon him once he knows that the Messenger ﷺ is blessed by Allah and His angels. Therefore the emphasis came on the greeting and not on the blessing; for the blessing was emphasized with a semantic emphasis by mentioning that Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet, while the greeting was emphasized with a verbal emphasis, because His words ﴿tasliman﴾ ("in full submission") is a verbal noun emphasizing His words ﴿greet﴾.

The author said: (﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾: Muhammad ﷺ), and he did not explain ﴿send blessings﴾, may Allah have mercy on him, and this is a deficiency in the explanation.

Then he said: (﴿O you who have believed, send blessings upon him and greet him with peace in full submission﴾: that is, say: "O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and grant peace") and he did not explain the greeting.

So what is the meaning of the greeting (taslim)? Some scholars said: when you say, "Al-salamu 'alayka," al-salam is one of the names of Allah; meaning, "Allah is over you." And what is the meaning of "Allah is over you"? That is, Allah is watchful over you, observing you and protecting you.

Some scholars said: "Al-salamu 'alayka" means "al-taslim 'alayka," so it is a declarative sentence with the meaning of supplication, and al-salam is a verbal noun of (sallama), like al-kalam is a verbal noun of (kallama). So the meaning of "al-salamu 'alayka" is "Allah's greeting of safety upon you," that is, your safety from afflictions.

This meaning is more correct; this is the sound meaning: that when you say to a person, "Al-salamu 'alayka," you are asking Allah, exalted be He, to keep him safe from afflictions. Afflictions that are sensory and moral, or one of them? Sensory and moral safety: the safety of the body, honor and wealth is sensory, and the safety of religion from afflictions is moral. For a person is surrounded by two afflictions: an affliction in religion and an affliction in worldly life, and safety from both together is among the greatest blessings of Allah upon the servant.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: The meaning must be present; one must be mindful of it, otherwise it becomes idle speech.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Most people, when they give the greeting, consider it merely a salutation, and this is not what is required. Rather, what is required is that you be mindful that it is a supplication for him for safety from afflictions; for if you are only mindful that it is a greeting, then there is no difference between it and your saying "Ahlan wa sahlan," indeed the greeting may be more eloquent than this with "Ahlan wa sahlan, marhaban ya Aba Fulan, hayyaka Allah wa bayyaka," and what is similar to such welcoming words. Therefore, for us, as long as we do not intend the meaning that the Lawgiver intended, it becomes a bare utterance; so when we greet someone, we should be mindful that we are invoking for him safety from afflictions; and therefore, if you were to bring every welcome, it would not equal this supplicatory sentence in which you ask Allah for his safety.

So the upshot is that what the brother mentioned is correct: most people say "Al-salamu 'alaykum" merely as a salutation.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes indeed, he moves it, because it is a supplication.
* Student: And the reply as well?
* Shaykh: And the reply as well. That is, we should be mindful of the meanings in everything we say. Even now, the "at-tahiyyat lillah" – may Allah grant us and you repentance – do we be mindful of the meaning of at-tahiyyat, the meaning of as-salawat, and the meaning of at-tayyibat, or do the words pass as things recited? Sometimes one way, sometimes another. This too is not what is required; rather, one should be mindful of the meaning of each word, or else they become hollow words, garments with no bodies, or bodies with no spirits. What benefit is there in your reciting "at-tahiyyat lillah, as-salawat, at-tayyibat" while your mind is wandering and you have nothing but words passing over the heart? This is something that, whenever you recite these, you must be mindful while you pray: what is the meaning of at-tahiyyat? What is the meaning of as-salawat? What is the meaning of at-tayyibat, or not? And, God willing, we will test you on them some day. What is the meaning of at-tahiyyat? What is the meaning of as-salawat, unless you are now ready, so that we can finish the rest of the lesson?
* Students: Explain it.
* Shaykh: Should I explain it?! If I explain it, it will not be a test.
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: No objection. Now let us see about at-tahiyyat. Who knows the meaning of at-tahiyyat?
* Student: Remaining (...)?
* Shaykh: That is, every word indicating permanence, glorification and honor, since tahiyyah is known as glorification of the one greeted and honoring him.
Alright, (lillah): it is known that it is due to Allah and specific to Him.
As for as-salawat, what is the meaning of as-salawat? Are the prayers for Allah?
* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The obligatory and voluntary prayers, which is the specific worship; or even supplication is included, so as-salawat means the specific worship, and also means supplication; all of it belongs to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; nothing is invoked except Allah, and none is worshipped through prayer except Allah. At-tayyibat, are they for Allah?
* Student: At-tayyibat are the good sayings and deeds that belong specifically to Allah, glorified and exalted be He.

Shaykh: Yes, and likewise the attributes. The good things (al-tayyibat) are from us, and they are from Him; all His attributes are good, all His actions are good, and all His statements are good. Also, from us there are things that are for Allah, and Allah accepts only what is good. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah is Good (tayyib) and accepts only what is good." [Narrated by Muslim (1015 / 65) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.] Who keeps these two meanings in mind while praying? That the good things, as an attribute of Allah, and as a description of the creature's action?
* Student: The second is more prevalent.
* Shaykh: The more prevalent second meaning is that the good things that come from us are for Allah; Allah accepts nothing but them. No, the truth is that both meanings are correct. "Indeed Allah is Good" refers to what relates to Allah, and "He accepts only what is good" refers to what the servant does. Now, what is the meaning of "Peace be upon you, O Prophet"? We have said it.
(And the mercy of Allah and His blessings), "mercy" (al-rahmah) means supplicating for him with mercy, which is the attainment of what is sought; and with "peace" (al-salam) is the removal of what is disliked.
("And His blessings") means abundant, enduring goodness. So after you have supplicated for him with mercy, you ask Allah, exalted is He, to make that a continuous blessing upon him.
As for "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah," the Prophet (ﷺ) explained it and said: "When you say that, you have greeted every righteous servant in the heaven and on the earth." [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6230) and Muslim (402 / 55) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.] Who keeps in mind, when we say "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah," whether the meaning is that we greet the prophets or not? And the angels, the saints, and the righteous of this Ummah and of others, so that by these words we greet the disciples whom 'Isa chose, the seventy whom Musa chose, the few who believed with Nuh, and the People of the Cave? Who keeps this in mind? And Adam and others, do we keep this in mind? The apparent and prevalent situation is that it is not kept in mind.
* Student: The Messenger's (ﷺ) statement does not indicate that the Companions (...) this is obtained if it is mentioned, when he said: if you say it, you have greeted every righteous servant.
* Shaykh: No; because they used to say: "Peace be upon Jibril, and upon Mika'il, and upon so-and-so, and upon so-and-so." (...) The statement of specification: you specified what had a need; when you say "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah," what you did not specify enters into this.
* Student: So its meaning is as if they did not keep it in mind?
* Shaykh: No, it is not as if they did not keep it in mind; that is why they specified.

And his saying: "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger" is clear.
("I bear witness") means I affirm, but an affirmation like one who witnesses with the eye, not a weak affirmation of that sort. That is, "ashhadu" originally means witnessing or testimony regarding what is seen or heard with the ear, but here what is in the heart is expressed by testimony, as if the person is witnessing what he affirms.
As for "that there is no god but Allah," the common people err in it, saying "ashhadu [anna] la ilaha illa Allah," and this is an error from the standpoint of the language, because "anna" with the doubled nun does not have its noun omitted; rather it is the lightened "an."
("There is no god but Allah") means there is no true god; that is, there is no true object of worship except Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and the objects worshipped besides Him are false.
("And I bear witness that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger") also contains a certain affirmation, as if witnessing that Muhammad is the servant of Allah and His Messenger; he is a servant who has no share of lordship, and a Messenger in whom there is no treachery; he is truly a Messenger.
This is the meaning of the tashahhud, and beyond the meaning that is the whole meaning there are only apparent, passing meanings, yet most people do not keep them in mind.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No; because this is information and praise.

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, those who annoy Allah and His Messenger, Allah has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Ahzab 57].
The author said: (﴿Indeed, those who annoy Allah and His Messenger﴾ — they are the disbelievers who attribute to Allah what is far above Him, such as offspring and partners, and who deny His Messenger) this is from annoyance.
﴿Indeed, those who annoy﴾ is a declarative sentence emphasized by "inna," and the predicate of "inna" is His saying: ﴿Allah has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter﴾.
He said: ﴿Indeed, those who annoy Allah﴾. How do they annoy Allah? They annoy Allah by ascribing to Him defects that are not fitting for Him, like the saying of some of them: "Allah is poor," and like reviling time: "The son of Adam annoys Me; he reviles time" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4826) and Muslim (2246 / 2) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah], and like their saying that Allah has taken a consort or a son, or that Allah, exalted is He, when He created the heavens and the earth, grew weary and rested on Saturday, and the like.
So annoying Allah, exalted is He, consists of what? Of ascribing to Him what is not fitting for Him.
Among it is denying His names and attributes, for negating perfection from Him undoubtedly implies deficiency, since perfection and deficiency are opposites; nothing exists without being described by perfection or by deficiency, so when the attributes of perfection are negated from Him, it necessarily follows that He is described by deficiency, and this is a kind of annoyance.
As for annoying the Messenger (ﷺ), it occurs by speech and by action. By speech: that the Messenger (ﷺ) is described as a sorcerer, a poet, a soothsayer, or a madman.
Strikingly, sorcery and madness were ascribed to all the prophets; every prophet sent to his people was described with this. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Thus, no messenger came to those before them but they said: "A sorcerer or a madman"﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 52]. These descriptions undoubtedly annoy the Messenger (ﷺ), and they annoy every friend of Allah and His Messenger, that the Prophet (ﷺ) be described with these false attributes.
Likewise annoying the Messenger by action: "as the Quraysh did to him (ﷺ) when they brought the entrails of a she-camel while he was prostrating in the Sacred Mosque in front of the House of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and they placed the entrails of the she-camel on his back while he was prostrating." What annoyance could be greater than this? A man who had not troubled them, but who was worshipping Allah, exalted is He, in the safest place on the face of the earth, in front of the House of Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala, and nearest to his Lord; then these wrongdoing transgressors come and place these filths upon him. I believe this is among the most severe forms of annoyance. "Until his young daughter, a little girl, came and removed it from him" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (240) and Muslim (1794 / 107) from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud]. This is among the annoyances.
Likewise, among the annoyances is what they mention: that they used to throw foul things and filth on the threshold of his door (ﷺ) in Makkah, until he would come out and say: "What kind of neighborliness is this? What kind of neighborliness is this?!" [Mentioned by Ibn Hisham in al-Sirah (1/76), and Ibn Kathir in al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah (4/305).] That is, if you were neighbors to us and not of us, you would not do this to me.
So those who annoy Allah and His Messenger, ﴿Allah has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Ahzab 57], and we seek refuge in Allah. That is, Allah has removed them far from His mercy in this world and in the Hereafter, because la'n (cursing) means expulsion and distancing from the mercy of Allah.
In His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who annoy Allah﴾, and He did not say "those who annoyed Allah," the meaning is that they are persistent in annoyance; so as long as they persist in annoyance, they will have the curse in this world and the Hereafter. But if Allah bestows guidance upon them, and they return to Allah, exalted is He, and repent from their shirk, the curse will be lifted from them, because the ruling revolves with its cause.
﴿Allah has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter﴾ (He removed them far away), ﴿and has prepared for them a humiliating punishment﴾. ﴿Prepared﴾ means readied, and "punishment" means retribution.
As for ﴿humiliating﴾, the author said: (possessing humiliation), and it is the Fire. Yes indeed, the punishment of the Fire, we seek refuge in Allah, is a bodily, sensory humiliation and a psychological humiliation. For this reason it is said to the people of the Fire: ﴿Seize him and drag him into the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾ [ad-Dukhan 47]. ﴿Seize him and drag him﴾ means push him with severity and force, ﴿into the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾, that is, its depths and its base. ﴿Then pour over his head﴾, the head that never bowed to anyone or to Allah, ﴿pour over his head of the punishment of scalding water﴾ [ad-Dukhan 48]. ﴿Scalding water﴾ is water of extreme heat. Then, after the humiliation in deed, it is said to him: ﴿Taste! Indeed you were the mighty, the noble﴾ [ad-Dukhan 49]. This is the utmost mockery; that is, you were in yourself mighty and noble, but now you are abject and humiliated, the opposite of might and nobility. This humiliating punishment prepared for the disbelievers, we ask Allah to save us and you from it, has thus made the punishment of these who annoy Allah and His Messenger two great matters:
The first: the curse, which is expulsion and distancing from the mercy of Allah.
The second: the humiliating punishment which brings them into degradation and abasement.
The believing men and women?
He said: ﴿And those who annoy the believing men and believing women without their having earned it﴾ [al-Ahzab 58] (they accuse them of what they did not do), ﴿have certainly borne a slander and a manifest sin﴾ [al-Ahzab 58] (they have borne a lie), ﴿and a manifest sin﴾ (clear).
Reflect on the difference between annoying Allah and His Messenger and annoying the believers, and you will find a great difference in the punishment.
﴿Those who annoy the believing men and believing women without their having earned it﴾: ﴿without their having earned it﴾ — the cause was not mentioned in the first verse, because it is impossible that from Allah's act, or from His Messenger's act, there would be something that deserves annoyance, is that not so? But believers may commit something that deserves annoyance; for this reason He said: ﴿without their having earned it﴾, because the believer may earn something for which he deserves to be annoyed, is that not so?
Also He said: ﴿Then they have certainly borne a slander and a manifest sin﴾, and He did not say "Allah has cursed them," nor "He has prepared for them a humiliating punishment," but rather said: ﴿they have borne a slander﴾, that is, a lie, and they have borne it. And slander (buhtan) is that you mention your brother with what is not in him. For this reason, when the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about backbiting, he said: "It is your mentioning your brother with what he dislikes." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, what if what I say is in my brother?" He said: "If what you say is in him, you have backbitten him; and if what you say is not in him, you have slandered him" [Narrated by Muslim (2589 / 70) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah].
How is the annoyance of the believers effected? By speech and by action, and it is numerous, without limit; the annoyance of the believer is numerous without limit. Among it: annoying the neighbor, to the extent that the scholars say: a person may not drive a stake into the wall shared between him and his neighbor in a way that harms his neighbor; nor may he water his palm trees if the water seeps into his neighbor's land; nor may he place a millstone that grinds next to his neighbor, because that harms him.
So annoyance is numerous. Among this type is that he humiliates him when he comes to seek his right; for some employees, we seek refuge in Allah, when people come to them to complete their transactions, you find them demeaning and harming them. This too is among annoying the believers without their having earned it.
Its individual instances, indeed its types, cannot be enumerated, and the general matter is that the believer is harmed by an act or a statement; so those who annoy believers without their having earned it have borne a slander and a manifest sin. We ask Allah for well-being (...) ﴿And His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ [al-Ahzab 56].
* In this verse there are benefits:
* Among them: the affirmation of the angels, by His saying: ﴿and His angels﴾.
* Among them: the nobility of the angels in their being attributed to Allah, subhanahu wa ta'ala; by His saying: ﴿and His angels﴾, their attribution to Allah is an attribution of honor.
* Among its benefits: the demonstration of the exalted status of the Prophet (ﷺ), since Allah and His angels send blessings upon him; this is undoubtedly from the elevation of his rank and the loftiness of his remembrance.
* Among its benefits: the command to send blessings and peace upon the Messenger (ﷺ), by His saying: ﴿O you who believe, send blessings upon him and greet him with peace﴾.
* Among its benefits: that sending blessings and peace upon him is a requirement of faith, and that it is an increase in faith; by His saying: ﴿O you who believe﴾.
* Among them: that sending blessings and peace upon him are obligatory, because the basic meaning of a command is obligation; and because that is from fulfilling the right of the Prophet (ﷺ) which he holds over his Ummah, for his right over his Ummah is greater than the right of parents over their children. But the obligation is fulfilled by doing it once; if a proof indicates repetition, we must act according to what the proof requires.
Many scholars have said that sending blessings upon him (ﷺ) in the prayer is obligatory, in the tashahhud; the person says: "Peace be upon you, O Prophet," and says: "O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad."
* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that it is prescribed for a person to send blessings upon him verbally: ﴿O you who believe, send blessings upon him and greet him with peace﴾.
Peace or blessings in the heart alone is not sufficient; accordingly, when we write hadith, we should write: ﷺ.
As for what some people do in writing (ص) or writing (صلعم), the scholars disliked that and said: the better course is to write ﷺ.
Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, would sometimes write a hadith without mentioning ﷺ.
Some scholars answered this: that he would omit it out of eagerness to seize time, and that he would send blessings upon him with his tongue rather than his pen.
It has passed with us in the explanation or the tafsir that sending blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ) is divided into two kinds: absolute and restricted; and that in restricted contexts it may be obligatory and may be recommended, and that in some places it may be disliked.
There are also discussions, not within the verse itself, but related to it:
Is it permissible to send blessings upon other than the prophets?
On this the scholars have three positions: permissibility, prohibition, and permissibility when it is not made a symbol (shi'ar). The last is the correct view: it is permissible to send blessings upon a person provided you do not make it a symbol for him, such that whenever you mention him you bless him or greet him.
The scholars have stated that what appears in some books when mentioning 'Ali, radiya Allahu 'anhu, saying "'Ali 'alayhi al-salam" or "'Ali karram Allahu wajhahu," that this is the work of some copyists, and that the better course is to say of him what is said of the other Companions: "'Ali radiya Allahu 'anhu," even though 'Ali radiya Allahu 'anhu is more complete than "'Ali 'alayhi al-salam" and more complete than "'Ali karram Allahu wajhahu," because radiya (being pleased) is a great rank.
As for sending blessings upon non-prophets as a consequence, this is permissible by consensus, and the Prophet (ﷺ) taught his Ummah to say: "O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and upon the family of Muhammad" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3370) and Muslim (406 / 66) from the hadith of Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah].
It also passed with us: supplicating for mercy for the Messenger, whether one may pray for mercy for him. Some scholars disliked that, and the correct view is that it is not disliked.
Then He said: ﴿Indeed, those who annoy Allah and His Messenger, Allah has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter, and has prepared for them a humiliating punishment﴾.
* Student: You did not mention what our sending blessings upon the Messenger (ﷺ) means?
* Shaykh: We mentioned our sending blessings upon the Messenger; we said its meaning is seeking praise, the request from Allah that He praise him in the exalted assembly.
* Student: Writing (ص) (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes; because they say either write it in full or leave it.
* Student: You read it in full?
* Shaykh: Leave aside reading; but writing: if a person comes, for example, reading and he does not know the conventions of these scribes, he will say: "The Messenger of Allah said (ص)," "The Messenger of Allah said (صلعم)!"
* Student: Their saying about 'Ali radiya Allahu 'anhu: "karram Allahu wajhahu," how (...)?
* Shaykh: They say: he never prostrated to an idol, and that he is "karram Allahu wajhahu" for this. But the origin of those who write this is to make a distinction for 'Ali ibn Abi Talib alone. This is the most important thing for them, whether that is better or not; they want to give him a distinction.
* Student: (...) in a book I read (...)?

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verse 56–58 (part 3 of 3):

* The Shaykh: Strange. What does it say, written there with you?
* The student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: I mean, when they mention the Companions, they write (r) or (ḍ).
* The student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: And 'Ali, when they write 'Aliyyan, what do they say?
* The student: (...).
* The Shaykh: But do you not think that the (r) and the (ḍ) are like the (ṣ) in ﷺ? Do you not think these are symbols?
* The student: I do not think it is a symbol.
* The Shaykh: Yes, this is the apparent view, that they are symbols.
* The student: Did he write that in a book for the Shi'a (...)?
* The Shaykh: Perhaps. Allah knows best.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: Does no one see it except Him? And when he dies?
* The student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: It seems that when he dies, it is placed in his shroud, so there is no harm.

Alright. ﴿Indeed, those who annoy Allah and His Messenger﴾ to the end [al-Ahzab: 57].

* From this noble verse is derived: that harming Allah and His Messenger is one of the major sins (kaba'ir). The reason is that Allah threatened it with curse and punishment, and everything for which Allah threatens curse or punishment is one of the major sins.

The scholars have differed regarding the major sins: are they to be enumerated or defined? Some of them enumerated them, and some of them defined them.

He said: The major sin is every act for which a specific punishment has been prescribed. This is the definition of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him: every thing or every sin for which a specific punishment has been prescribed, whether worldly or otherworldly, is one of the major sins, whether that is a curse, or wrath, or negation of faith, or disavowal from it, or punishment, or what is similar to that. Everything for which a specific punishment has been set is one of the major sins.

* And from the noble verse is derived: the description of Allah, blessed and exalted, as being harmed, by His saying: ﴿who annoy Allah and His Messenger﴾.

* And from it is derived: the demonstration of Allah's perfection, may He be glorified and exalted, because if He is harmed by reprehensible things that do not befit Him, this indicates His perfection. For this reason, among people it is considered a fault that a person is not harmed by being described with a defect. The fault is that he is not harmed by being described with a defect. For this reason, such a man is called a donkey for his dullness and his unimportance, meaning he does not distinguish between one who praises him and one who disparages him; it is all the same to him. But the person who is harmed by a defect is the one who has feeling and emotion. Then, if he is patient and seeks reward, and uses wisdom in that, it is better.

The point is that being harmed by what is not praiseworthy is considered a perfection.

* And from the benefits of the noble verse: that harming the Messenger ﷺ is like harming Allah, because Allah joined them with the conjunction "and": ﴿who annoy Allah and His Messenger﴾. Just as obeying the Messenger is like obeying Allah, and disobeying the Messenger is like disobeying Allah, harming the Messenger is like harming Allah, meaning in terms of prohibition and that it is one of the major sins. Otherwise, harming Allah is greater in terms of the aspect to which blame and defect are attributed.

* And from the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of cursing, that is, the curse of Allah, which is His expulsion and distancing. Is it one of the essential attributes or the active attributes? It is an active attribute, because every attribute of Allah that is linked to a cause is an active attribute, since that cause renews itself, so the attribute comes into being after its cause exists. This is what is (...).

﴿And He has prepared for them﴾, and the humiliating punishment, we all know, is in the Fire, because it is the Fire whose punishment is humiliating.

* And from the benefits of the noble verse: that recompense is of the same kind as the deed. Just as these people exalted themselves and became arrogant and humiliated the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, by harming him, Allah punished them with what humiliates and abases them of torment.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And those who annoy the believing men and believing women without their having earned it have certainly borne a slander and a clear sin﴾ [al-Ahzab: 58].

* From this noble verse is derived: the prohibition of harming believers without right, by His saying: ﴿they have certainly borne a slander and a clear sin﴾.

* And from it is derived: the prohibition of every form of harm, whatever its type, whether verbal or physical, by the generality of the wording in His saying: ﴿those who annoy﴾, and the relative pronoun is among the forms of generality.

* And from it is derived: that harming a believer for what is from his own earning does not carry a threat, and it is neither a sin nor a slander, by His saying: ﴿without their having earned it﴾.

* And from it is derived: that it is not permissible to harm someone beyond what he deserves. If he insults you, do not insult him more; for if you insult him more, you have harmed him without his having earned it, and if you insult him with the like of what he insulted you, you have harmed him to the extent he earned. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40].

* And from the benefits of the verse: the refutation of the Jabriyyah, by His saying: ﴿without their having earned it﴾, where He attributed the act to them. The Jabriyyah say that man is compelled in his deeds, that he has no power or strength, that he does a thing without his choice and leaves it without his choice.

* And from the benefits of the noble verse: the dispraise of lying, by His saying: ﴿they have certainly borne a slander﴾, especially when the lie leads to harming others.

* And from the benefits of the noble verse: the permissibility of harming non-believers, by His saying: ﴿And those who annoy the believing men and believing women without their having earned it﴾. However, if the non-believer is a dhimmi, or one with a covenant (mu'ahad), or one granted safe conduct (musta'man), then it is not permissible to harm him in a way that violates his covenant.

So the non-believer has a distinction: harming a believer is forbidden in every case, while regarding the non-believer there is a distinction. What is the distinction? If we harm him more than the covenant requires, it is forbidden and not permissible; and if we harm him within the limit that the covenant requires, he has no sanctity except in what his covenant requires.

* And from the benefits of the noble verse: that a sin may combine two blameworthy attributes, by His saying: ﴿they have certainly borne a slander and a clear sin﴾. By their lying they bore slander, and by their transgression they bore a clear sin (...).

﴿ ﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verses 59–61 (part 1 of 3):

﴿O Prophet, say to your wives and your daughters and the women of the believers that they should draw their outer garments over themselves.﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:59] The address "﴿O Prophet﴾" has already been noted: Allah, exalted is He, addressed Muhammad (ﷺ) by his attribute of prophethood, and a prophet carries out what is revealed to him and does not delay in it.

It has already been mentioned that the word nabi (prophet) is derived either from naba' (news), or from nubuwwah (elevated status), or from both together. He is one who gives news (munbi'), one who receives news (munba'), and one of elevated rank (dhu rif'ah). So it is derived from naba', whether the news is issued by him or given to him, and from nubuwwah, which means elevation; thus "al-shay' al-nabi" means an elevated thing.

﴿Say to your wives and your daughters and the women of the believers that they should draw their outer garments over themselves.﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:59]

"﴿Say﴾" is an imperative verb. It is well known that the Messenger (ﷺ) was commanded to recite and convey the entire Qur'an, but when a ruling is introduced with "qul" (say), it is an indication of special concern for it, since he was commanded to convey this particular matter specifically. So this indicates that what the Messenger (ﷺ) was commanded to say, namely this matter, is an important one.

"﴿To your wives﴾": the plural of zawj (spouse). The word zawj is applied both to the husband and to the wife, because it is derived from izdiwaj, which means pairing or mixing.

The eloquent usage of the word is that there is no distinction between male and female in it. However, the specialists in inheritance (al-fara'iyyin), may Allah have mercy on them, adopted the practice of making the feminine form with the ta' (zawjah) and the masculine form without it, to distinguish between the cases. For when they said, "A dead person died leaving a spouse and a son," and intended the wife, it would be unclear whether the husband or the wife was meant. So they committed themselves to distinguishing male and female with the ta'. It has been said that this is a dialect form, but it is rare.

"﴿To your wives﴾": he began with the wives because protecting them and the jealousy regarding them is stronger and more emphatic.

"﴿And your daughters﴾": how many were they? They were four. But if this verse was revealed in the sixth year after the Hijrah, some of them had already died, so what is meant is those of them who were alive.

"﴿And the women of the believers﴾" is general, covering every woman among the believers. He said "﴿the women of the believers﴾" rather than simply "the women," in order to incite and encourage, like his saying (ﷺ): "It is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day..." Otherwise, non-believing women are also obligated to observe the hijab that believing women are obligated to observe, so that people are not tempted by them.

And His saying "﴿the women of the believers﴾" includes the wives of believers, and those women over whom believers have guardianship: daughters, sisters, paternal aunts, maternal aunts, mothers, and others.

In His saying "﴿the women of the believers﴾" there is evidence that men are in charge (qawwamun) over women; otherwise He would have sufficed with saying "and the believing women."

"﴿They should draw their outer garments over themselves﴾": the clause "﴿yudnina 'alayhinna min jalabibihinna﴾" may be read as marfu' (nominative) or majzum (jussive). In either case it is now mabni (indeclinable). Why is it mabni? Because it is joined to the nun of the feminine plural (nun al-niswah). The imperfect verb is mabni in two situations: when it is joined to the nun of the feminine plural or to the emphatic nun (nun al-tawkid). Here it is joined to the nun of the feminine plural, so it is built on sukun. But is it in a position of raf' or a position of jazm?

If "﴿yudnina﴾" is the object of the saying (maqul al-qawl), then it is in a position of raf': "Say to them, 'Let them draw...'" And if it is a response to the imperative (jawab al-amr), then it is in a position of jazm, because the response to an imperative is jussive.

It has also been said that it is jussive by the implied lam (lam al-amr); that is, "Say to your wives, daughters and the women of the believers, let them draw their outer garments over themselves," meaning the implied lam of command, like the poet's words:

"Muhammad, may every soul be ransomed for you..." [the verse continues]

"Tafdi" is jussive by the implied lam, meaning "li-tafdi nafsaka" (so that it may ransom your soul).

Which of the two possibilities is stronger: that it is the object of the saying in the position of raf', or that it is in the position of jazm?

Let us see whether the Qur'an clarifies this. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say to My servants that they should say that which is best﴾ [al-Isra' 17:53]. This indicates that it is jussive as a response to the imperative. For if it were marfu', He would have said "yaqulun" (they say) and not "yaqulu" (let them say)... Since He said "﴿yaqulu﴾" it indicates that it is a response to the imperative.

It is also more eloquent in meaning when it is a response to the imperative, as if they carry it out directly, meaning as if their action is their response to the command, which is caused by it. That makes it more effective in compliance than if they were commanded with a command they might or might not carry out.

"﴿Say to the believing men that they should lower their gaze﴾" [al-Nur 24:30]. What supports which? That it is a response to the imperative or that it is the object of the saying? It is a response to the imperative. That is why He said "﴿yaghuddu﴾" (they should lower), and He made it jussive by dropping the nun, and did not say "yaghuddun" (they lower).

"﴿And say to the believing women that they should lower their gaze﴾" [al-Nur 24:31]. What supports which? There is no evidence here, because it is mabni (indeclinable), so there is no proof either way.

The main point is that it is better for us to take His saying "﴿they should draw their outer garments over themselves﴾" as a response to the imperative. This is supported by the context in the Book of Allah, and by the fact that it is stronger in compliance and implementation, since it is a response to the mere saying, as if they are acting and complying immediately.

"﴿They should draw their outer garments over themselves﴾": "﴿min jalabibihinna﴾". His saying "﴿min﴾" is not superfluous (za'idah), as some have claimed, because "min" is only added (as a superfluous particle) in negation, as Ibn Malik said:

"And it is added after negation or what resembles it, so it governs..."

[Complete the verse:] "...a indefinite noun, like 'ma li-baghin min mafarr'" (there is no escape for the seeker).

Based on this, "min" is not superfluous. The meaning is not "they draw their outer garments over themselves," but rather "min" is partitive (lil-tab'id): "they draw over themselves some of their outer garments," meaning part of their garments.

Is this partitive a partitive of part of a whole, or a partitive of one individual from among individuals? That is, does His saying "﴿min jalabibihinna﴾" mean from among the outer garments they have, since a woman may have two or more jilbabs, or does it mean part of the outer garment she is wearing? The latter is closer. That is, she draws over herself part of her jilbab. The jilbab is the cloak, wrap or mantle, meaning the wide garment that covers the whole body or most of it.

"﴿Yudnina 'alayhinna﴾" and not "ilayhinna" (toward them). He said "'alayhinna" (over them) so that the drawing is close against them. For example, if you say "adnaytu ilayya" (I drew it toward me), but if you say "'alayya" (over me), it is as if it implies the meaning of "yadummunna" (they wrap, gather), so that it is drawn over them.

"﴿Yudnina 'alayhinna min jalabibihinna﴾" means they bring it near so as to gather it over themselves.

His saying "﴿yudnina 'alayhinna min jalabibihinna﴾": "﴿'alayhinna﴾" He did not say "over their faces," nor "over their necks," nor "over their chests," so that it covers the whole body.

"﴿Yudnina 'alayhinna﴾" means over the whole body. However, it is well known that the jilbab covers most of the body, and their custom was that a woman would uncover her face and go out with her face and neck uncovered. So Allah the Mighty and Majestic commanded that "﴿they draw their outer garments over themselves﴾," meaning over this exposed part which is customarily uncovered, namely the face and the neck, as Ibn 'Abbas and others said: by covering her face and showing only one eye to look through when necessary. This applies when the jilbab is thick, such that when she covers her face with it she cannot see. But if it is thin, as is well known among us at the present time, then there is no need to show the eye, because showing the eye is only permitted out of necessity. The evidence is that the Companions, such as Ibn 'Abbas and others, permitted showing one eye, because that is the measure of necessity; otherwise they would have said, "She should bring out both eyes." In any case, the meaning of "﴿they draw their outer garments over themselves﴾" concerns what they uncover of their bodies, namely the face. This is what custom had established.

This uncovering was general for both slave women and free women. So some of those in whose hearts is a disease, from among the hypocrites who harm the believing men and women, began pursuing them. When they found any woman, they said, "This is a slave woman; we thought she was a slave, so we mocked her," when she was in fact free. This was reported to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Allah revealed this verse: ﴿O Prophet...﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:59]. Some have said this regarding the occasion of revelation, but it is not traced back to a chain of transmission (ghayr musnad). What matters to us is not whether the verse has an occasion of revelation or not; what matters is the ruling it indicates.

He said: (﴿They draw their outer garments over themselves﴾: the plural of jilbab, which is the wrap with which a woman wraps herself, meaning they let some of it down over their faces when they go out for their needs, except for one eye.) Why? For the necessity of looking.

His saying "(the plural of jilbab, which is the wrap)" is as he said. It resembles the 'abayah (cloak) among us. When the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded women to go out to the 'Eid prayer, Umm 'Atiyyah said: "O Messenger of Allah, one of us does not have a jilbab." He said: «Let her sister clothe her with one of her jilbabs»[1]. He did not say, "Let her go out without a jilbab." This indicates that a woman must go out with something that covers her and does not reveal the shape of her body.

(﴿That is more suitable﴾: closer to ﴿that they will be known﴾ as free women ﴿and not be harmed﴾ by being molested.)

His saying "(that they will be known as free women)" is based on what I said. But we may also say: "﴿that they will be known﴾" as modest women, far from suspicion, who do not want evil or indecency. For when a woman is modest and veiled, this indicates the perfection of her chastity, and that she does not wish to put herself in places of suspicion. This is in contrast to a woman who is a prostitute, may Allah protect us, who displays herself, uncovers her face, shows her hands, her arms, her jewelry, and the like. When a woman is veiled, it is known that she is a modest, chaste woman. For this reason He said "﴿that they will be known﴾." When a woman is chaste and modest, the immoral do not approach her, because they know she is not among their kind, but is a woman protecting and guarding herself. This is one aspect. It is also possible that what the author said, "(that they will be known as free women)," and the verse is suitable for this as well as for that.

He said: (﴿That they will be known and not be harmed﴾: by being molested, unlike slave women, who do not cover their faces, so the hypocrites molested them.)

This was the state of slave women in the time of the Messenger (may Allah's prayers and peace be upon him), and in the time of the caliphs they did not veil, because they were owned, and only a base-minded person would pursue them.

However, Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This applies to slave women from whom temptation is not feared. But beautiful slave women who tempt people are obligated to cover their faces, because of the fear of temptation, not because they are being equated with free women.

What he said, may Allah have mercy on him, is correct, and the meaning supports it. For everything from which temptation is feared must be avoided. This is why Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And let them not stamp their feet so as to reveal what they conceal of their adornment﴾ [al-Nur 24:31]. For the anklet that is heard when a woman strikes her foot on the ground is feared as a source of temptation, and the fear of temptation from a concealed anklet when a woman strikes her foot is far less than the fear from a woman showing her face, that beautiful face adorned with kohl and rouge and the like. Everyone knows that this is a greater temptation than a hidden anklet whose sound is heard when struck with the foot. The wisdom of Allah the Mighty and Majestic would not permit Him to forbid a woman to strike her foot lest her anklet be heard, and then permit a woman of the most beautiful women to uncover her face and hands. This is something the wisdom of Allah the Mighty and Majestic refuses.

* Student: "'Umar struck a slave woman because she covered her head"[2]?
* Shaykh: Yes. He struck her so that she would not imitate free women, out of fear that these would be mixed with those, and then the distinction and difference between them would have no effect. If slave women covered their faces, free women would be unidentifiable.
* Student: This might be used as evidence for Shaykh al-Islam's view?
* Shaykh: No, it is not evidence, because we have general principles, namely that exposing oneself to temptation is forbidden in the Shari'ah.
* Student: Shaykh, then is wearing one eye showing considered a sunnah until now?
* Shaykh: No, it is not a sunnah, because the jilbabs at that time were thick, and a woman could not see through them. But in our time they are thin, and a woman can see, walking with her sight, even if she covers her whole face.
* Student: If she wears this jilbab herself, meaning she puts it on?
* Shaykh: Now the women among us wear the jilbab and do not uncover even one eye, and affairs go on.
* Student: (...) wearing (...)?
* Shaykh: With the Nile?
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, that is the apparent meaning. That is why the Companions made showing one eye a matter of necessity, and confined themselves to the measure of necessity, which is only one eye. This indicates that if a woman can see without showing an eye, it is not permissible to show the eye.
* Student: Shaykh, does His saying "﴿That is more suitable that they will be known﴾" not indicate the obligation of covering the face, since a woman is only recognized by her face?
* Shaykh: No, according to the author's explanation, "﴿they will be known﴾" means distinguished, that free women are distinguished from...
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, if we take the apparent wording, especially with the interpretation we mentioned, that they are known as modest and far from suspicion. Yes.

﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:59].

(﴿Allah is ever Forgiving﴾: for what has passed of their leaving off covering. ﴿Merciful﴾: to them, in that He covered them.)

"﴿Allah is ever Forgiving﴾": We have already explained "al-Ghafur" (the Forgiving) and "al-Rahim" (the Merciful), and that Allah the Exalted always combines them, so that the two names together imply the removal of what is disliked and the attainment of what is desired. The removal of what is disliked is by forgiveness, and the attainment of what is desired is by mercy. Allah the Mighty and Majestic always mentions forgiveness and mercy regarding a matter that has already passed and for which no ruling has yet been revealed, such as His saying: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already passed. Indeed, it was an immorality and hateful and an evil way﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:22], and the verse continues: ﴿And that you combine two sisters, except what has already passed. Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:23]. For were it not for Allah's forgiveness and mercy, He would punish us for the unbecoming violation. But Allah the Mighty and Majestic, in His forgiveness and mercy, does not hold us accountable for what He did not legislate for us.

Then He said: ﴿If the hypocrites do not desist, and those in whose hearts is a disease, and the agitators in Al-Madinah, We will surely incite you against them﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:60].

"﴿la-in﴾": The author says it is the lam of oath (lam al-qasam), meaning a lam preceding the oath, not the particle of oath itself. Rather, the oath is implied, and the sense is: "By Allah, if they do not desist," or "By your Lord, if they do not desist." So it is a lam that precedes the oath.

The author said "(lam al-qasam)" so that no one would suppose it is the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida').

His saying "(in)" is a conditional particle. "﴿la-in lam yantahi al-munafiqun﴾": is "﴿lam yantahi﴾" jussive or marfu'?

* Student: (...).
* Shaykh: The evidence? The weak letter, the yā', was dropped, and what governs it as jussive, "in" or "lam"? "Lam," because it is the immediate governor.

"﴿la-in lam yantahi al-munafiqun﴾" means "(from their hypocrisy)," as the author said. The author said "(from their hypocrisy)" because that is the attribute from which the name "al-munafiqun" (the hypocrites) is derived. Otherwise, its meaning could be: "If the hypocrites do not desist from their hypocrisy, and from their harming of the believers, and other things."

[1] Agreed upon (Bukhari, 324; Muslim, 890/12), from the hadith of Umm 'Atiyyah.
[2] Reported by 'Abd al-Razzaq in al-Musannaf (5064), from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verse 59–61 (part 2 of 3):

His saying: ﴿those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ (with fornication), and this is based on the view that His saying ﴿That is more suitable that they will be known and not be abused﴾ means that the harm intended is harassment by propositioning them for immorality. So the meaning of ﴿those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ is those who approach women seeking immorality and fornication. However, the meaning may be more general than what the author said; that is, those in whose hearts is a disease of doubt, bad character, and other things. This is more general and better.

﴿And the agitators in the city﴾: the believers are the object of (agitators), because it derives from arjafa yurjifu, and it is taken from ar-rajfah, and ar-rajfah is the earthquake. The murjif (agitator) is the one who says: "The enemy has come upon you," "Indeed you have a great enemy," "Your expeditions have been killed," "The armies have been routed," and whatever is similar to that, bringing fear and terror into people's hearts. This is called irjaf because it shakes a person's confidence in himself and in his brothers; and because it shakes his security and tranquility. Some of them said: and because it has no stability, since it is a false statement. All these meanings may be the derivation of irjaf or indicate it.

So the murjif is the one who reports what? What shakes the tranquility of the believers: defeat, the killing of an enemy, a multitude of troops, or whatever is similar. Some people of this kind existed in Madinah; when the Prophet ﷺ sent out the expeditions, they would spread such statements, that the expedition had been defeated, captured, killed, and whatever is similar.

﴿Then We would surely incite you against them﴾: the lam in His saying ﴿la-nughriyannaka﴾ falls in the answer to an implied oath; so the sentence is an answer to an oath and not to a condition, because the rule is that when an oath and a condition come together, the answer belongs to whichever precedes them, as Ibn Malik said:
"Omit, when a condition and an oath gather, the answer of what comes later, for it is then obligatory."

As for His saying ﴿la-nughriyannaka﴾, the author said: (we will certainly empower you over them). This explanation is an explanation by necessary consequence, because incitement (al-ighra') means urging with agitation to take vengeance on them, and from it is inciting a person against an enemy, meaning he urges him against it with agitation so that he falls upon them and kills them, defeats them, or whatever is similar.

﴿Then they will not remain your neighbors therein﴾ ((﴿then they will not remain your neighbors﴾) they will not dwell with you -﴿therein﴾ meaning in the city- ﴿except for a little﴾ then they will leave ﴿cursed﴾ (distanced from mercy)). Meaning: We will incite you against them by empowering you over them, either by reprimand, or discipline, or killing, or otherwise. So when the city becomes too constricted for them, they will leave. This is why He said ﴿then they will not remain your neighbors﴾ and did not say "so they will not remain your neighbors"; this is because the cessation of neighborhood is delayed after the incitement, since Allah incites him against them, and so they receive from discipline, reprimand, and humiliation what makes it impossible for them to remain in the city; for this reason ﴿then﴾ was used.

His saying ﴿Then they will not remain your neighbors therein except for a little﴾ may mean a little time, or a little of them. In either case:
His saying ﴿cursed﴾ is a circumstantial state of the subject in ﴿they remain as neighbors﴾. And according to the author's estimation, it is a circumstantial state of a subject that was omitted along with its governing word, when he said: then they will leave cursed.

But the closer view is not to estimate anything; rather the meaning is: then they will not remain your neighbors except for a little, while being cursed during the time of neighborhood; that is, even during their staying with you they will be cursed, expelled, distanced, no one will be fond of them or show them kindness.

Then He said: ﴿Wherever they are found, they will be seized and massacred with massacre﴾ ((﴿wherever they are found﴾) they are found ﴿they will be seized and massacred with massacre﴾).
﴿Wherever﴾ is a conditional particle indicating generality in place; the conditional verb is ﴿are found﴾ and the answer of the condition is ﴿will be seized﴾.
He said: ﴿they will be seized and massacred with massacre﴾, saying: (meaning the ruling concerning them is this, by way of command).

The sentence ﴿Wherever they are found, they will be seized and massacred﴾ is it a declarative or an imperative sentence? It is declarative, since it is conditional, and a conditional sentence is declarative; but it is declarative in the sense of imperative, that is, in the sense of command and request: wherever you find them, seize them and kill them.

In His saying ﴿taqtil﴾ (massacre), the emphatic verbal noun is evidence that they will be killed individually and in groups.

There is no doubt that this verse contains a threat to those who combined these attributes: the hypocrites, those in whose hearts is a disease, and the agitators in the city. It is a threat. The discussion concerning it is:

First: Are these attributes for one described person, or for several different people? Is the meaning that they are hypocrites, and in their hearts is a disease, and agitators? The attributes here belong to one described person, and the coordination is correct, because it is coordination of attributes, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned, and who destined and guided, and who brings out the pasture﴾ [al-A'la 1–4]. Is it one or many? One; so the coordination here is coordination of attributes. Should we say that these are coordinated attributes of one described person? Or should we say that they are coordinated individuals who are described, not one described person? This latter is more correct and also more general; because the hypocrite may have a disease in his heart inclining him to immorality and fornication, and may not; and he may be an agitator or not; and he may combine hypocrisy, heart disease, and agitation; and a person may have a disease in his heart without being a hypocrite; and he may be an agitator without being a hypocrite or having a disease in his heart.
