* Shaykh: That is, applying the meaning of His saying: ﴿But perhaps you dislike a thing and it is good for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 216]. But this was not mentioned in the Qur'an, so we did not make it a separate lesson. Otherwise it is a great lesson: a person may dislike a thing and it is good for him.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: He did not put it first, because he said: "and in one reading." 
* Student: In the context?
* Shaykh: Yes, because he, may Allah have mercy on him, interpreted according to this reading, since the copy of the Qur'an he had was according to this reading.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No.

* Student: His saying, the Most High: ﴿And you will never find any change in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab 62] (...) that Allah, glorified and exalted, may change His practice regarding His creation?
* Shaykh: No, he says: ﴿you will never find﴾, and this is a negation.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, because he did not say, for example, "and you will not find Allah changing," as in the other verse: ﴿There is no changer of His words﴾ [al-An'am 115].
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Never, it is tied to its causes.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: It never differs, it is tied to its causes. When the cause differs, the practice differs. But if the cause is one, it cannot differ.

**Student:** Why do we not say, regarding His saying ﴿And He has prepared for them a blaze﴾ (...), that its occurrence is certain?

**Shaykh:** This goes against the basic principle, and the existence of the Fire is already established. We do not resort to saying that He used the past tense for the future to indicate the certainty of its occurrence except in a matter that has clearly not yet happened, such as His saying: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [al-Nahl 1]. His saying ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾ means that it has not occurred yet.

**Student:** (...) the refutation of (...) ﴿And you will never find any change in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab 62] (...) relies on (...) the honours from Allah, glory be to Him (...)?

**Shaykh:** By Allah, I do not know. This appears to be a lame point. Look, if the lame man had an honour, we might accept it from you.

**Student:** (...)?

**Shaykh:** No, because *wijaha* (standing, rank, status) is a non-physical matter. So the nearness here is a nearness of rank. But physical nearness is like His saying (...): ﴿Those who are with your Lord do not disdain His worship, and they glorify Him, and to Him they prostrate﴾ [al-A'raf 206].

**Student:** (...)?

**Shaykh:** In this verse? No (...), because standing and rank are non-physical.

**Student:** (...)?

**Shaykh:** Yes, physical, yes. There is no doubt that those among the angels who are close to Allah, the bearers of the Throne, are nearer than others.

**Student:** (...)?

**Shaykh:** It is not (...). As long as it exists, it is not (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verse 62–69 (part 1 of 4):

Then He said: ﴿The way of Allah concerning those who passed away before, and you will not find any change in the way of Allah.﴾ [al-Ahzab 62].
Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿The way of Allah concerning those who passed away before, and you will not find any change in the way of Allah.﴾ ﴿The way of Allah﴾: sunnah (way, custom, practice) means the path or manner. The sunnah of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is of two kinds: the cosmic sunnah (sunnah kawniyyah) and the legislative sunnah (sunnah shar'iyyah).
As for the legislative sunnah, it is according to the interests of the servants and differs with the differing of nations, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a way﴾ [al-Ma'idah 48]. Although all these laws agree on the foundations of monotheism concerning the Essence of Allah, His Names and His Attributes, they are in agreement.
Likewise, in the general principles of the Shari'ah, which Allah indicated in His saying: ﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden indecencies, whether apparent or concealed, and sin, and oppression without right, and that you associate with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority, and that you say about Allah what you do not know﴾ [al-A'raf 33]. How many are these? ﴿The indecencies, whether apparent or concealed, and sin, and oppression without right, and associating with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority, and saying about Allah what you do not know﴾. These are the five foundations. The scholars have mentioned that all the laws agree upon them. But as for the laws whose interests differ with the difference of time, place and nations, their rulings must necessarily differ according to what wisdom requires, the wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
As for the cosmic sunnah, it is what Allah, Blessed and Exalted, causes to occur by decree, of punishments and other things. This sunnah does not change or alter. Although Allah, Mighty and Majestic, may double the punishment for some people and not others, as we have already explained regarding the wives of the Prophet: ﴿Whoever of you commits a clear indecency, the punishment will be doubled for her, twofold﴾ [al-Ahzab 30]. Allah, Exalted, may also reward some doers of deeds more than others, as in this Ummah, which was given a double portion of reward over the nations before it, and as with the Companions of the Messenger, peace be upon him, about whom the Messenger ﷺ said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, if one of you were to spend gold equal to Uhud, it would not reach the mudd of one of them nor half of it"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3673), and Muslim (2541 / 222) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]].
But regarding punishments, Allah says: ﴿The way of Allah﴾. The author said: (That is, Allah has prescribed that). From this estimation, the author informed us that ﴿sunnah﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun whose verb is omitted; i.e., We have prescribed for them the way of Allah; i.e., We have prescribed for these hypocrites, those in whose hearts is a disease, and the rumour-mongers in Medina, the way of Allah concerning those before them, for whoever opposes the servants of Allah and His allies, Allah empowers over them.
(﴿The way of Allah concerning those who passed away before﴾ from the nations), ﴿passed away﴾ means departed. For this reason the author said: (from the earlier nations, concerning their hypocrites who spread rumours against the believers, ﴿and you will not find any change in the way of Allah﴾ from Him) — and not from others? Yes, and not from others: the cosmic sunnahs. Yes indeed.
As for the legislative, Allah erases what He wills and establishes, and it may be changed. But the cosmic sunnah of Allah, you will not find any change in it, neither from Him nor from others, in sending punishment upon those who deserve it. And although this punishment may differ, the opponents must necessarily face a punishment. And Allah knows best.
(...) Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿The people ask you about the Hour﴾ [al-Ahzab 63]. ﴿The people ask you﴾: the author said: (i.e., the people of Makkah). The correct view is that it is more general. In His saying ﴿asks you﴾ rather than ﴿asked you﴾ is evidence that this questioning continued to be directed at the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, people asking him about the Hour. Questioning about the Hour may be motivated by denying it and considering it far-fetched; and this comes from whom? If the motive is denial and considering it far-fetched, it comes from whom? From the disbelievers. At other times it is asked about in the form of a question: when will it be? while being certain of it; and this may come from whom? From the believers. At other times it is asked about in order to show people that its knowledge cannot be attained, as Jibril asked the Prophet ﷺ about the Hour, and said: "When is the Hour?"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50), and Muslim (9 / 5) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.]] He asked not out of denial or disbelief, nor seeking guidance as to when its time would be, but to inform that its time is known only to Allah.
But someone may say: the saying ﴿The people ask you﴾ does not include the question of Jibril, since Jibril is not one of the people? It is answered that when Jibril asked, he was in the form of a man.
(﴿The people ask you about the Hour﴾, when will it be?) Allah commanded His Prophet to answer with His saying: ﴿Say: Its knowledge is only with Allah﴾. ﴿Say﴾ in answer. This is an instruction from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, instructing His Messenger in the answer that he should say this. Allah instructed him so that it would be clear to people in general that His saying ﴿Its knowledge is only with Allah﴾ comes from Allah and not from his own accord, so that people might be convinced of it and be certain of it.
And His saying ﴿Its knowledge is only with Allah﴾: this sentence contains restriction (hasr). By what means?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, it is not fronting; the means is ﴿innama﴾ (only). ﴿Its knowledge is only with Allah﴾ means: no one knows it except Allah alone. This is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman 34]. So no one knows when the Hour will come except Allah, Mighty and Majestic. And everything said about its time by those before and after is nothing but baseless fabrication, which we know with certainty, because Allah said: ﴿Say: Its knowledge is only with Allah﴾. And who is the most knowledgeable of the messengers of Allah, among humans and angels? Muhammad ﷺ and Jibril, and both do not know. When Jibril asked the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "The one asked about it is no more knowledgeable than the one asking"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50), and Muslim (9 / 5) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.]]. So if you, O questioner, are ignorant, then I am like you, more ignorant than you.
﴿Say: Its knowledge is only with Allah﴾. And this encompasses not only the general Hour, when people are raised from their graves to the Lord of the worlds, but also includes the specific hour, which is the death of each person, for whoever dies, his resurrection and his hour have come, since he has passed from the world to the abode of recompense. The saying of Allah, Exalted, indicates this: ﴿No soul knows in what land it will die﴾ [Luqman 34]. What is the point of evidence?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, but what is the point of evidence from the verse you mentioned?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What is the point of evidence that no one knows when he will die?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: The point of evidence is (...) a certain land he has not gone to (...).
* The Shaykh: I say: the point of evidence is that if his knowledge of which land he will die in is negated, then in which time is more so; because a person has the ability to go to a land or not go, whereas time is not within his control. So if his knowledge of what is within his control, which is moving from one place to another, is negated, then the negation of his knowledge of what is not within his control is all the more so.
Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: (﴿And what will make you know﴾ informs you of it; i.e., you do not know it), ﴿And what will make you know﴾: ﴿what﴾ may be negative, meaning nothing informs you of it; and it may be interrogative, meaning what makes you know of it so that you are asked about it. Either way, Allah, Exalted, negates the knowledge of His Messenger ﷺ of it and says to him: ﴿What will make you know﴾.
And His saying: (﴿Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ it exists ﴿soon﴾) the author's or commentator's wording indicates that the saying ﴿Perhaps the Hour﴾ is a new independent clause, unconnected to the preceding verb, and that it is a new statement from Allah: that is, you do not know about it, but it is near: ﴿Perhaps the Hour will be soon﴾, and ﴿perhaps﴾ here indicates expectation, i.e., it is anticipated.
Some grammarians held that the saying ﴿Perhaps the Hour﴾ is the object of ﴿will make you know﴾, a second and third object, but it is suspended, suspended by what? By ﴿perhaps﴾, since ﴿perhaps﴾ is among the suspending words; that is: what will make you know about the expectation of its nearness; i.e., you do not know about its nearness either, and whoever does not know about its nearness does not know about its occurrence all the more.
In any case, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, negated that the Prophet ﷺ knew it or its nearness, and if the Prophet's ﷺ knowledge of that is negated, then the knowledge of others is all the more negated.
Furthermore, the question about the Hour is not of great value. The great value is what the Prophet ﷺ indicated, when a man asked him about the Hour and he said: "Look at what you have prepared for it"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3688), and Muslim (2639 / 163) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]]. That is the value. As for when it will come or not, it is not of great value; the true value is that a person looks at what he has prepared for it.
Therefore Allah, Exalted, followed this with His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blazing fire﴾ [al-Ahzab 64], and so on; i.e., beware lest the Hour come upon you while you are among them.
﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers﴾..
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, the suspension occurs only after the operator.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Where is this?
* Student: (...) ﴿Do the people think they will be left﴾ [al-Ankabut 2].
* The Shaykh: No operator precedes it, so there is no suspension.
* Student: The interrogative hamzah?
* The Shaykh: The hamzah is for interrogation, but the sentence is initial, like if you say: Did Zayd stand? Did Amr sit? There is no suspension.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Its object is "an" (that) and what follows it.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, it is not suspended; this is a verbal "an" (masdariyyah), so the verbal noun takes the place of the two verbs; i.e., "Do the people think their leaving alone?"
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: It is for emphasis, and it may also be for causation, like: ﴿And follow him that you may be guided﴾ [al-A'raf 158] and similar. But it is not for expectation. Some said it is for expectation when considering the addressee rather than the speaker.
Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blazing fire﴾ [al-Ahzab 64]. ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed﴾: la'n (cursing), the people of knowledge said, means expulsion and distance from the mercy of Allah. This sentence is emphasized by ﴿indeed﴾ (inna). And His saying ﴿the disbelievers﴾: disbelievers in whom? Disbelievers in Allah and in what must be believed in. And His saying ﴿has cursed the disbelievers﴾ means He has distanced them from mercy.
Then He said: ﴿and prepared for them a blazing fire﴾: meaning they are not merely distanced from mercy and spared from sin, but rather there is combined for them both distance from mercy and punishment. ﴿Prepared for them﴾ means He made ready for them. ﴿A blazing fire﴾: (a fierce fire they enter), a fire kindled for them, and Allah protect us, they are its fuel and the stones; a fire that rises over the hearts, reaching their hearts within their bodies, and Allah protect us. They will not remain in it for a day or two, or a year or two. He says: ﴿Abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Ahzab 65]. He said: (determining their eternal abiding). The author indicated that the state here is a determined state (hal muqaddarah), because eternal abiding is not the state of their disbelief but the state of their recompense on the Day of Resurrection, so this state is a determined state: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾. And ﴿abadan﴾ (forever) indicates the continuation of time into the future, and ﴿azalan﴾ (without beginning) indicates its continuation into the past. For this reason we say that Allah's knowledge is established for Allah without beginning and without end.
And His saying ﴿abiding therein forever﴾ is one of three verses in which Allah explicitly declared the eternity of the abiding of the people of the Fire. The second verse is in Surat an-Nisa: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and wronged, Allah would never forgive them, nor guide them to a path, except the path of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [an-Nisa 168-169]. The third verse is in Surat al-Jinn: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, then indeed for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Jinn 23]. In some of these verses, indeed in one of them, there is a clear refutation of the view that the Fire is not eternal. For this reason the creed of Ahl as-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah is that the Fire is eternal like the Garden. This does not contradict the mercy and wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, nor does it nullify His saying in the hadith qudsi: "Indeed My mercy precedes My wrath"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7422), and Muslim (2751 / 15) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.]]. This is because this punishment has been warned of to those who did what deserves it and upon whom the proof has been established, so they have no excuse. They are thus treated according to justice; their punishment is a justice from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, with no oppression in it. Whoever is warned of something and then, by his own choice, does what leads to it, is the one who has brought harm upon himself.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: He said: ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ [Hud 107]; i.e., beyond that.
Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: (﴿Abiding therein forever, they will find no protector﴾ who guards them from it, ﴿nor any helper﴾ who repels it from them). ﴿They will find no protector﴾ who takes charge of them by obtaining what they seek, ﴿nor any helper﴾ who supports them by repelling what they dislike. They will find on the Day of Resurrection no one who takes charge of them and obtains what they want by protecting them from the Fire and bringing them to the Garden, nor anyone who supports them against this Fire, repels it from them, or brings them out of it after entering. This is because these disbelievers will not benefit from the intercession of intercessors. As for the sinful believers, they may find intercessors on that day who intercede for whoever deserved the Fire not to enter it, and for whoever has entered it to be brought out.
﴿The Day their faces are turned over in the Fire, they will say: "O would that we had obeyed Allah and obeyed the Messenger."﴾ [al-Ahzab 66]. ﴿The Day﴾ is an adverbial expression of time, and an adverbial expression with its preposition requires a governing element, called the anchor (al-muta'allaq). So what is its governing element? It may be that the governing element is His saying ﴿and prepared for them a blazing fire﴾, the verb ﴿prepared﴾; it may be ﴿abiding﴾; it may be ﴿will find﴾, so the three operators compete for it; and it may be that the governing element is omitted, i.e., "Remember the Day their faces are turned over." All of this is possible, and all of it is the case.
His saying ﴿their faces are turned over﴾ means they are turned from one side to another, as meat is turned over the fire to be cooked, Allah protect us.
In His saying ﴿The Day their faces are turned over﴾ and not ﴿The Day they turn over﴾: this is because this matter happens to them by way of compulsion, Allah protect us, and it is not by their choice: ﴿their faces are turned over in the Fire, they say﴾.
There is a point I forgot: His saying ﴿abiding therein forever﴾, how does He say ﴿therein﴾ while ﴿blazing﴾ is masculine? Because the meaning of ﴿sair﴾ (blazing fire) here is the blaze of the Fire, which is feminine.
He said: ﴿The Day their faces are turned over in the Fire, they say: "O would that we had obeyed Allah and obeyed the Messenger."﴾ His saying ﴿they say﴾ may be a circumstantial clause, which is the closer view, from the pronoun in ﴿their faces﴾, meaning: their faces are turned while they express this regret: ﴿they say: O would that we had﴾. It may also be a resumptive clause, Allah relating what they say.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verses 62–69 (part 2 of 4):

﴿They say, "Oh, would that we had obeyed God and obeyed the Messenger!"﴾ The author said: (The ﴿yā﴾ serves to draw attention and is not a vocative particle.) Why? Because the vocative particle ﴿yā﴾ is used only with one who can be called, either literally or figuratively, and ﴿layta﴾ cannot be addressed, since it is a particle. ﴿Layta﴾ expresses wishing (tamannī). The author says it is for attention (tanbīh). It has also been said that it is a vocative with an omitted addressee suited to the context, so that they say, "O our Lord, would that we had obeyed God," and the omitted addressee is: "O our Lord, would that we had obeyed God and obeyed the Messenger." On the first view, the attention is meant to increase the regret, as though they are alerting themselves to this wish they make. On the second view, the addressee is omitted in order to hasten to mention the wish without mentioning the one addressed. Whichever view is taken, it indicates the intensity of their remorse.

As for His words, ﴿Oh, would that we had obeyed God and obeyed the Messenger!﴾: is this wish difficult to fulfil, or is it impossible at that time? It is impossible at that time. This is a greater impossibility than the words of the poet:

*Ah, would that youth could return one day,*
*So I could tell it what old age has done.*

As for ﴿أَطَعْنَا﴾ (aṭaʿnā), we drop the alif. ﴿aṭaʿnā﴾ is originally written with an alif, so we say ﴿aṭaʿnā llāha wa-aṭaʿnā r-rasūlā﴾, and we do not say that one must indicate the alif so that the nūn is not confused (...). Praise be to God, this is an error. Rather, you say ﴿وَقَالَا الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ﴾ [an-Naml 15], and there is nothing wrong with it. The alif is dropped here because of the meeting of two unvocalised letters (iltiqāʾ as-sākinayn), and we do not say that dropping it would make the first-person pronoun resemble the feminine plural pronoun, because the context shows the meaning.

Student: (...)?
Shaykh: They are alerting the listener to the fact that they are wishing for this.
Student: And the second aspect?
Shaykh: The second aspect is that it is the vocative particle, and the addressee is omitted; the meaning is: "O our Lord, would that we…"
Student: Shaykh, ﴿قَالَا الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ﴾ [an-Naml 15] (...)?
Shaykh: Yes indeed, it is written but not pronounced. Even ﴿أَطَعْنَا اللَّهَ﴾ is now written but is not pronounced in speech.
Student: (...)?
Shaykh: Like ﴿دَعَوَا اللَّهَ﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 189]: the alif is dropped.

As for ﴿الرَّسُولَا﴾ (ar-rasūlā), it has an alif, and this alif is for extension (alif al-iṭlāq, the alif added at the end of a word for prolongation). We have already encountered a parallel to it in this surah. What is it? ﴿وَتَظُنُّونَ بِاللَّهِ الظُّنُونَا﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 10]. And later another word will come: ﴿فَأَضَلُّونَا السَّبِيلَا﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 67]. So these are three words containing an alif called the alif of extension, and three readings apply to them: a reading with the alif retained both in continuous recitation (waṣl) and at pause (waqf); a reading with it dropped both in waṣl and waqf; and a reading with it dropped in waṣl but retained in waqf.

Let us see now. ﴿يَا لَيْتَنَا أَطَعْنَا اللَّهَ وَأَطَعْنَا الرَّسُولَا (66) وَقَالُوا﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 66–67]: this is according to both readings. ﴿يَا لَيْتَنَا أَطَعْنَا اللَّهَ وَأَطَعْنَا الرَّسُولَ (66) وَقَالُوا﴾ is one reading. Is it clear? It is not entirely clear in reality; that is, it is permissible to recite it in all three ways, according to the principle of al-nashr (the principle that all permitted readings are valid). ﴿يَا لَيْتَنَا أَطَعْنَا اللَّهَ وَأَطَعْنَا الرَّسُولَا﴾ and ﴿يَا لَيْتَنَا أَطَعْنَا اللَّهَ وَأَطَعْنَا الرَّسُولَا (66) وَقَالُوا﴾ is one reading; that is, we retain the alif in both waṣl and waqf.

The second reading: ﴿يَا لَيْتَنَا أَطَعْنَا اللَّهَ وَأَطَعْنَا الرَّسُولَ (66) وَقَالُوا﴾ and ﴿يَا لَيْتَنَا أَطَعْنَا اللَّهَ وَأَطَعْنَا الرَّسُولْ﴾ ﴿وَقَالُوا﴾ is also the second reading: the alif is dropped in both waṣl and waqf.

The third reading: ﴿يَا لَيْتَنَا أَطَعْنَا اللَّهَ وَأَطَعْنَا الرَّسُولَ (66) وَقَالُوا﴾ and ﴿يَا لَيْتَنَا أَطَعْنَا اللَّهَ وَأَطَعْنَا الرَّسُولَا (66) وَقَالُوا﴾ is the one where you retain it at pause but not in continuous recitation.

As for His words, ﴿أَطَعْنَا اللَّهَ وَأَطَعْنَا الرَّسُولَا﴾, what is "the Messenger" here?

Student: The canonical seven readings.
Shaykh: The seven readings. "The Messenger" here is a generic noun (ism jins) that includes every messenger, since the people of the Fire are not restricted to the community of Muhammad ﷺ but include all nations. So do they mean by "the Messenger" one particular messenger or the category? The category. And by "God"? One (the single God).

﴿أَطَعْنَا اللَّهَ وَأَطَعْنَا الرَّسُولَا (66) وَقَالُوا رَبَّنَا إِنَّا أَطَعْنَا سَادَتَنَا﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 66–67]. (﴿وَقَالُوا﴾ means: the followers among them.) This is correct, as the author said: "the followers" (...) of the leaders. ﴿رَبَّنَا﴾ means "O our Lord," the vocative particle being omitted. (﴿إِنَّا أَطَعْنَا سَادَتَنَا﴾ and in another reading) meaning the canonical seven readings: (﴿سَادَاتَنَا﴾ is the plural of the plural.) "Sādah" is the plural of what? Of sayyid (lord). And "sādāt" is the plural of "sādah," so it is a plural of a plural. There are two readings: ﴿سَادَتَنَا﴾ and ﴿سَادَاتَنَا﴾. It is pluralised because there are many lords among the nations. A sayyid is one who has honour and standing among his people and is foremost among them. That is what a sayyid is.

As for His words, ﴿وَكُبَرَاءَنَا﴾ (and our great ones), these are those above the lords, such as the rulers and the like. People have lords who are obeyed, and above these they have great ones. So they say: ﴿إِنَّا أَطَعْنَا سَادَتَنَا وَكُبَرَاءَنَا﴾, both categories together, and by obeying them ﴿فَأَضَلُّونَا السَّبِيلَا﴾, meaning: because of our obedience to them they led us astray from the path. Here "ḍalāl" (going astray) means what? Losing the right course and the truth, or wandering; that is, we lost the way. "As-sabīl" refers to the path, which is the path of God, and the definite article here is for a known reference. Is it a reference to something previously mentioned (ʿahd dhikrī) or a mental reference (ʿahd dhihnī)? A mental reference: the known path that leads to God.

﴿رَبَّنَا آتِهِمْ ضِعْفَيْنِ مِنَ الْعَذَابِ﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 68]. The author said: (﴿السَّبِيلَا﴾ the path of guidance. ﴿رَبَّنَا آتِهِمْ ضِعْفَيْنِ مِنَ الْعَذَابِ﴾ meaning double our punishment.) Look, how great is God! In the world they honoured them, respected them, esteemed them, and preferred them over themselves; in the Hereafter, it is the reverse: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed, and they see the punishment, and their bonds are cut asunder﴾ [al-Baqarah 166], and ﴿Those who followed say, "If only we had another chance, we would disown them as they have disowned us"﴾ [al-Baqarah 167]. So the leaders disown.

These also revile and curse; they say: ﴿Our Lord, give them double punishment﴾. By this supplication they are not acting unjustly, because by "double" they mean that these great ones went astray and led others astray, so they bear two sins: the sin of going astray themselves, and the sin of leading others astray. This is why the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever establishes an evil practice in Islam, he will bear its burden and the burden of those who act upon it until the Day of Resurrection."[[Recorded by Muslim (1017/69) from the hadith of Jarir ibn 'Abdullah.]] And God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt 13]. So the supplication of these followers is a supplication of justice, not of injustice, because these leaders deserve punishment twice.

﴿رَبَّنَا آتِهِمْ ضِعْفَيْنِ مِنَ الْعَذَابِ وَالْعَنْهُمْ لَعْنًا كَبِيرًا﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 68]. He says: (﴿الْعَنْهُمْ﴾ means punish them.) Why did he interpret the cursing as punishment? Because they are in the Fire, and so they are expelled from God's mercy. But if the author had left it as it is, it would have been correct. ﴿الْعَنْهُمْ﴾ means: remove them far, a great removal, from Your mercy, so that You never show them mercy at any time. As for His words, ﴿كَبِيرًا﴾ (great), he says: (many in number. In a reading with the letter bāʾ, i.e. ﴿كَبِيرًا﴾ with the bāʾ, meaning great in magnitude.)

Student: (...).
Shaykh: Yes indeed, there are two readings: ﴿وَالْعَنْهُمْ لَعْنًا كَثِيرًا﴾ (a great number) which is considered in terms of quantity, and ﴿لَعْنًا كَبِيرًا﴾ which is considered in terms of quality, meaning a great curse.

If you say: how can there be two readings when the statement came from these people as one utterance? Either they said "kabīran" or they said "kathīran," and God, Mighty and Majestic, is relating what they said. So what is the answer?

Or did you not understand the question? The question is: God relates that these disbelievers say, ﴿لَعْنًا كَبِيرًا﴾, and according to the second reading, ﴿كَثِيرًا﴾. So how can He relate two statements from one speaker? Did they say "kabīran" or did they say "kathīran"?

Student: (...) Sometimes they say "kabīran" and sometimes "kathīran," or some of them say "kabīran" and some say "kathīran"?
Shaykh: Correct. The answer is one of two possibilities: either some of them say "kathīran" and others say "kabīran," or they sometimes say "kabīran" and sometimes "kathīran."

If you say: is it not possible that one of them combines both in one expression, meaning that he says: "wa-l-ʿanhum laʿnan kabīran kathīran" (curse them with a great, numerous curse)?
The answer is no, because God did not relate this. Rather, the expression is one: either "kabīran" or "kathīran." This is why we do not combine the two words, neither in this verse nor in the words of the Prophet ﷺ when he taught Abu Bakr: "O God, I have wronged myself with much wrong (ẓulman kathīran),"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (834) and Muslim (2705/48) from the hadith of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.]] and in another wording: "ẓulman kabīran."[[Recorded by Muslim (2705/48) from the hadith of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.]] We do not combine them. We do not say: "O God, I have wronged myself with much wrong, great wrong." Rather, we say one of the two wordings, because the Sunnah has not come with combining them. Likewise here in the Qur'an: it is not permissible for anyone to say, "wa-l-ʿanhum laʿnan kathīran kabīran." This is forbidden, because whoever says that has added to the Qur'an. So we say: either this or that.

Student: (...)?
Shaykh: It does not contradict it, because the apparent meaning is that the hadith may be understood in the same way as the chapter we stopped at before. And in order to complete this surah...

Student: (...).
Shaykh: It is said "ḍaʿf" and it is said "ḍaʿfayn," with the same meaning (...).

The author says: (﴿وَالْعَنْهُمْ لَعْنًا كَبِيرًا (68) يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لَا تَكُونُوا﴾ with your Prophet, ﴿كَالَّذِينَ آذَوْا مُوسَى﴾ by their saying, for example: "Nothing prevents him from bathing with us except that he has a hernia (ādar).")

﴿O you who believe, do not be like those who hurt Moses﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 69]. The discussion has been repeated many times on His words ﴿O you who believe﴾: it begins with the vocative and with the description of faith. ﴿Do not be like those who hurt Moses﴾: the kāf in ﴿كَالَّذِينَ﴾ is a noun meaning "like," so it is a predicate: ﴿do not be like those who hurt Moses﴾. But they hurt him without any harm; they did not actually harm him by it. This verse is connected to what came before, His words: ﴿Indeed, those who hurt God and His Messenger, God has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 57].

In His words ﴿Do not be like those who hurt Moses﴾ there is both a warning and a consolation. The warning is for whom? For the believers, because if they hurt their Prophet they deserve what those who hurt Moses deserved. And the consolation is for whom? For the Messenger ﷺ, that if he is harmed, those before him were harmed too. This is why it is established from him ﷺ that he said: "May God have mercy on my brother Moses; he was harmed with more than this and he was patient."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3150) and Muslim (1062/140) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]]

As for His words ﴿Do not be like those who hurt Moses﴾, it refers to Moses son of 'Imran, peace be upon him, the best of the prophets of the Children of Israel. And how did they hurt him? The author said: (by their saying, for example: "Nothing prevents him from bathing with us except that he has a hernia.") They hurt him with other things besides this speech, and they also hurt him in action. But the example the author mentioned is because he said, "for example": Moses, peace be upon him, despite his severity, was modest (ḥayiyyan). The Children of Israel used to bathe naked, but he bathed alone and did not bathe with them; he did not undress. So the Children of Israel said: "Why does this man set himself apart from us? He would not do this unless he had a defect—a leprosy or a hernia." A ādar is one with a large swelling of the testicles. So the reason would be that he bathed alone and not with us, or that he had some defect, leprosy or something else, and therefore did not bathe with people. So God, Mighty and Majestic, wanted to show the Children of Israel that this man was among the best of God's creation and the most free of defects. One day he bathed alone and placed his garment on a rock. When he came out to put it on, the rock fled with his garment. He began to follow it, saying: "My garment, O rock! My garment, O rock!" He spoke to it and addressed it, but the rock, commanded by God, the Mighty and Majestic, did not stop until it reached a group (malaʾ) of the Children of Israel, and Moses was walking behind it naked. When he reached the Children of Israel they saw the man, and the man was sound with nothing wrong with him at all: among the best of God's creation and the most free of defect. The rock stopped, and he took his garment and put it on, and he began to strike the rock with his staff until there was a mark from the striking of the staff.[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (278) and Muslim (339/75) from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah.]]

Why did he strike the rock? Because when it acted like a rational being by fleeing with the garment, it deserved the discipline due to a rational being; otherwise the rock would gain nothing from it. For this reason, now there is a kind of imitation of Moses among us: when a child stumbles over a stone we say, "Come, let us strike the stone," and if you strike the stone the child calms down and stops crying. But the two matters are very different; I am only saying there is some kind of origin here. In any case, Moses, peace be upon him, was shown by God, Mighty and Majestic, to the Children of Israel, proving that he was not as they had said, and that he was sound. The wisdom in this story will come, God willing, in the lessons.

He said: ﴿So God cleared him of what they said﴾. The author said: (by his placing his garment on a rock to bathe; the rock fled with him until it stopped among a group of the Children of Israel. Moses caught up with it, took his garment and covered himself with it, and they saw that he had no hernia (ādrah). He said: (it is a swelling of the testicle), and they saw that he was sound, peace be upon him.)

﴿So God cleared him of what they said﴾. By His words ﴿of what they said﴾, the Glorified and Exalted informs us that the harm God pointed to was speech. And His words ﴿of what they said﴾: (mā) is a relative pronoun, and the returning pronoun is omitted, the meaning being: "of what they said."

He said: ﴿And he was honourable (wajīhan) in the sight of God﴾. That is, one of rank (dhā jāh), and jāh means standing and high position. So Moses, peace be upon him, was honourable in God's sight; that is, of high standing and lofty position. Has God described any other prophet as wajīh (honourable)?

Student: Jesus.
Shaykh: Jesus. He said: ﴿honourable in this world and the Hereafter, and of those brought near﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 45], and ﴿He will speak to people in the cradle and in maturity﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 46]. Anyone else?

Student: Jesus.
Shaykh: We have mentioned Jesus. Is there anyone else?

Student: ﴿a leader and chaste﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 39].
Shaykh: ﴿a leader and chaste﴾ [Āl ʿImrān 39]. (Honourable) I cannot recall now, but I cannot deny it; there may be someone. But if Moses was honourable in God's sight and Jesus was too, then Muhammad, peace be upon him, is greater in standing than them, because he is the best of the messengers.

But does standing before God necessarily mean that a person may seek a means to God through the standing of the Prophet?

The answer is no, because the standing of the Prophet is a rank and special position that belongs to the Prophet; you do not benefit from his standing, because the mere standing of the Prophet with God does not benefit anyone. This is why the preponderant opinion among the scholars is that seeking a means (tawassul) through the standing of the Prophet ﷺ is forbidden.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verses 62–69 (part 3 of 4):

He said: (﴿And he was esteemed in the sight of Allah﴾: he was of high standing. Among the things by which our Prophet ﷺ was harmed: he distributed a share, and a man said, "This is a division by which the countenance of Allah was not sought."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3150) and Muslim (1062 / 140), from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.]]), and this is among the gravest forms of insult. But insulting the Prophet ﷺ is a right that belongs to him; if he pardons it and waives it, the right is his. No one accuses the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, of not seeking the countenance of Allah. No one says this, though some people may have said it out of jealousy. As some of the Ansar said when the Prophet ﷺ divided the spoils of Hunayn, they said: "The man has met his own people and wants to lavish wealth upon them, while we fought and did all of this, yet he has given us nothing." But what was said was said by young men among the Ansar, who had no standing compared to their elders. Nevertheless, the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, addressed them with that great sermon, as you know, in which he explained their merit and explained the wisdom behind giving these people over them: that he gives to these in order to win their hearts to Islam and strengthen their faith, or to restrain their evil. As for the Ansar, they had no need of that, because people go away with a sheep and a camel, while they go away with whom? With the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. How vast is the difference between this and that. He said to them: "If the people were to take a valley or a pass, and the Ansar took a valley or a pass, I would take the valley or pass of the Ansar."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4330) and Muslim (1061 / 139), from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Zayd ibn 'Asim.]] He also said to them: "The Ansar are the inner garment, and the people are the outer garment."[[This is a shortened form of the same hadith; see the reference above.]] He said to them: "Were it not for the migration, I would be a man of the Ansar." All of this persuaded them, did it not? It persuaded them, to the point that they wept until their beards were wet with tears, may Allah be pleased with them. This is because this reality is worth the whole world. As (...) said, "The one who goes away with a sheep and a camel, and the one who goes away with the Messenger of Allah: there is a great difference between them.")

So in this there is wisdom from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: Allah may decree for a person something he dislikes, so that afterward it becomes something he loves. Musa, peace be upon him, certainly disliked that the stone ran off with his garment, but there was in it a great wisdom: all the speech and accusations that the Children of Israel had made were removed.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, the connection. This will come to us, God willing, in the lessons drawn from the passage: it is a clarification that he, peace and blessings be upon him, although he is cleared of what they say and was harmed by it, has a high rank with Allah.

Then he said: ﴿The people ask you about the Hour﴾ [al-Ahzab 63].
* Among the lessons of this noble verse: people have continued to ask about the Hour.
* And from this lesson branches another: the matter of the Hour is great, because questioning is frequent only about great matters, not trivial ones.
* And among its lessons: the Prophet ﷺ does not know the unseen. Had he known the unseen, he would have known when the Hour will occur.
* And among its lessons: the knowledge of the Hour is with Allah alone, and no one knows it, due to His saying: ﴿Say: Its knowledge is only with Allah﴾, and this is a restriction.
* And among its lessons: the Hour is near, due to His saying: ﴿And what would make you know? Perhaps the Hour is near.﴾ What indicates its nearness is that the Prophet ﷺ was the last of the prophets, and it has been established from him ﷺ that he said: "I was sent, and the Hour is like these two,"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (6504) and Muslim (2951 / 133), from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]] and he pointed with his index finger and the one next to it. This means that we are closely joined, or that between me and the Hour there is no more than the distance between the middle finger and the index finger in nearness.
* And among its lessons: Allah addressed His Prophet with His saying: ﴿And what would make you know﴾, and this is evidence that the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is a human like other humans, addressed with what humans are addressed with. It should not be said: how does Allah address His Prophet and say ﴿what would make you know﴾? If you addressed a person and said, "What would make you know about these matters or this affair?", this would be counted as belittling, or disparagement. But Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, addresses His Prophet with what befits him.

Then he said: ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blazing Fire﴾ [al-Ahzab 64], to the end.
* Among the lessons of the verse: Allah, the Most High, has cursed the disbelievers, distanced them, and expelled them from His mercy.
* And among its lessons: a warning against disbelief, because it is a cause of the curse.
* And among its lessons: the affirmation of causes and means ('ilal wa asbab). From where is this derived? From His saying ﴿the disbelievers﴾, because "disbelievers" is a description to which the curse is attached. It links the curse to disbelief, and so in this there is affirmation of causes and means, and this is common.
* And among its lessons: a refutation of the Jahmiyyah (the followers of Jahm ibn Safwan) who say that Allah does things not for any wisdom but merely by will.
* And among its lessons: the affirmation of the existence of the Fire, due to His saying: ﴿and prepared for them a blazing Fire﴾.
* And among its lessons: the greatness of the Fire, because "sa'ir" (blazing fire) is said only of a great, kindled fire, and this is a matter established in several verses and hadiths.
* And among the lessons of the verse: the perpetuity of the disbelievers' abiding in the Fire, due to His saying: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾.
In it is a refutation of those who say the Fire will perish. Those who said the Fire will perish are a group from the early generations (salaf) and later scholars, but their view is weak. As for the everlastingness of the Fire, the salaf and the People of the Sunnah have agreed upon it, and none has opposed this except a group of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school), who deny the perpetuity of Allah's actions and say that an infinite succession in eternity is impossible, just as they hold that an infinite succession in the past is impossible.
* And among the lessons of the noble verse: those who are tormented in the Fire will not find anyone to take charge of them, to repel the punishment from them or to prevent it before it descends upon them, due to His saying: ﴿they will not find for themselves any protector or helper﴾. The "walī" (protector) is one who takes charge of them, protects them, and guards them from harm, and the "naṣīr" (helper) is one who repels the affliction from them after it has descended.

Then he said: ﴿The Day their faces will be turned over in the Fire﴾ [al-Ahzab 66], to the end.
* From this verse is derived the severity of the punishment of the disbelievers in the Fire, may Allah protect us. He mentioned the punishment in the manner in which it is a greater humiliation than punishment of the rest of the body, because the face feels pain more than other outward limbs, and because the face is the nobility and the outward appearance of a person. So when punishment falls upon it, the psychological pain becomes more intense, due to His saying: ﴿the Day their faces will be turned over in the Fire﴾.
* And among the lessons of the verse: this turning over occurs without their choice, due to His saying ﴿will be turned over﴾. They are turned over in it, may Allah protect us, as meat is turned over on the fire to be cooked.
* And among the lessons of the noble verse: the manifestation of regret on the part of those disbelievers at the time of their punishment, due to His saying: ﴿They will say, "Oh, would that we had obeyed Allah and obeyed the Messenger!"﴾ But this is a matter whose time has passed.
* And among the lessons of the noble verse: obedience to Allah and His Messenger is a cause of salvation from the Fire, because they wished for nothing except obedience to Allah and His Messenger, by which they would have been saved from this punishment.

Then Allah, the Most High, said: ﴿And they will say, "Our Lord, indeed we obeyed our leaders and our elders, and they led us astray from the way."﴾ [al-Ahzab 67].
* In this verse is evidence of their acknowledgment that they were imitators and not those who were followed, due to His saying: ﴿Our Lord, indeed we obeyed our leaders﴾.
* And among its lessons: blind imitation does not avail against punishment. That is, even if there were elders and leaders, and the truth was made clear to them, if they opposed it in order to conform to their leaders, this does not save them from punishment.
* And among its lessons: the prohibition of following a scholar when the textual evidence has become clear. From where is this derived? From the fact that Allah punished these people for imitating their elders and leaders in opposing the truth. So when the truth becomes clear to you, do not say, "Allah said" through a certain scholar, or "such and such an imam said." Otherwise you would be resembling whom? The people of the Fire who said: ﴿Indeed, we obeyed our leaders and our elders﴾.
* And among its lessons: it is permissible to attribute a thing to its cause, due to His saying: ﴿and they led us astray﴾, although the one who truly misguides and guides is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. But these elders became a cause of misguidance, so the misguidance was attributed to them.
* And among its lessons: a refutation of the Qadariyyah (those who deny divine predestination in their own way) in their saying: ﴿we obeyed﴾ and their saying: ﴿they led us astray from the way.﴾
* And among its lessons: their allegiance to these elders and leaders will turn into enmity on the Day of Resurrection, due to their saying: ﴿Our Lord, give them double the punishment and curse them with a great curse.﴾
* And among its lessons: a warning to those around rulers, whether they are ministers, managers, or someone higher than that, a warning to those around them against following them in disobedience to Allah. There will come a day when they will regret, disavow, and call down this kind of curse upon them.
* And among its lessons: the leaders and elders who misguide do not benefit their followers on the Day of Resurrection, due to His saying: ﴿they will not find for themselves any protector or helper,﴾ and because they called down curses upon them and said: ﴿Our Lord, give them double the punishment﴾. Had they been benefiting them, they would not have cursed them.
* And among the lessons of the noble verse: a warning against bad companions. What is its basis? His saying: ﴿and they led us astray﴾. Every person who you see will mislead you from the path of Allah, it is obligatory for you to keep away from him. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has said, reporting this state: ﴿And the day the wrongdoer will bite on his hands, saying, "Oh, I wish I had taken a way with the Messenger! Woe to me! Would that I had not taken so-and-so as a friend! He had led me away from the reminder after it had come to me"﴾ [al-Furqan 27–29]. This "so-and-so" is not one of the elders and leaders, meaning merely a certain person. And this is the key point. So His saying here, ﴿and they led us astray from the way﴾, means: after the reminder had come to them and the truth had become clear, they followed these people, and so this punishment befell them.
* And among the lessons of the noble verse: the Hereafter is not a place where obligation ends entirely, because Allah affirmed that these people call upon Allah, and supplication is a form of worship. We do not say that in the Hereafter there is no supplication, no prostration, and no work. There is, but it is not like the world. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says in Surah al-Qalam: ﴿The Day the shin will be uncovered and they will be called to prostration but they will not be able to﴾ [al-Qalam 42]. This is an obligation, ﴿their eyes humbled, humiliation covering them, though they used to be called to prostration while they were sound﴾ [al-Qalam 43].
* And among the lessons of the noble verse: the demonstration of the intense hatred of these followers toward those they followed, since they called for Allah to double the punishment upon them and to curse them as well, and not a small curse but a great and immense one: ﴿and curse them with a great curse﴾ [al-Ahzab 68].

And Allah, the Most High, said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not be like those who harmed Musa﴾ [al-Ahzab 69], to the end.
* From the noble verse is derived: the prohibition of harming the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, due to His saying: ﴿do not be like those who harmed Musa.﴾ The prohibition is understood as prohibition in the strict sense. It has already been mentioned that harming the Messenger is among the major sins, due to His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who harm Allah and His Messenger, Allah has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Ahzab 57].
* And among the lessons of the noble verse: Allah's care for His Messenger, in that He sets forth for him the examples of the messengers before him, for consolation and to make the matter easier for him, and that this is a matter that has happened before you. This is frequent in the Qur'an: ﴿And messengers were denied before you, but they were patient over what they were denied and harmed, until Our help came to them﴾ [al-An'am 34].
* And among its lessons: a warning to believers that they may suffer what befell those before them when they audaciously opposed the messengers of Allah, due to His saying: ﴿do not be like those who harmed Musa.﴾
* And among the lessons of the noble verse: Allah's care for His messengers, due to His saying: ﴿So Allah cleared him of what they said.﴾
* And among its lessons: clearing can be by speech and can be by action. It is by speech, like the saying of Allah, the Most High, to His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him: ﴿You are not, by the favor of your Lord, a madman﴾ [al-Qalam 2], negating the madness with which his enemies accused him. And ﴿So remind, for you are not, by the favor of your Lord, a soothsayer or a madman﴾ [al-Tur 29]. This clearing is by what? By speech or by action? By speech. Clearing by action is as happened to Musa, peace be upon him: Allah, the Most High, did not say to the Children of Israel that he was not a man with a defect, but He arranged for him this actual event which served as clearing from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, for His Messenger, by what? By action.
* And among the lessons of the noble verse: the virtue of Musa, in that Allah cleared him of what was criticized about him, on one level, and in that He said of him: ﴿And he was esteemed in the sight of Allah﴾.
* And among the lessons of the verse: an indication that what matters is a person's standing with Allah, not with creation, because He said: ﴿And he was esteemed in the sight of Allah﴾. He placed ﴿in the sight of﴾ before ﴿esteemed﴾, indicating that what matters is that you be esteemed in the sight of Allah.

By what does a person become esteemed in the sight of Allah? A person becomes esteemed in the sight of Allah, the Most High, through worship. The more a person worships Allah and obeys Him, the more esteemed he is in Allah's sight. The evidence for this is His saying, the Most High: ﴿Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ [al-Hujurat 13]. Whoever is more God-conscious is more noble in the sight of Allah and of higher rank.

* Student: (...) The Messenger ﷺ, is this by action or by speech?
* Shaykh: No, this is testimony by action. Allah did not send down a Qur'an saying that the Messenger is truthful, but Bayt al-Maqdis was raised before him so that he could witness it.

* Student: Regarding the recitation: ﴿And he was 'abd Allah (the servant of Allah) esteemed﴾?
* Shaykh: This is an irregular recitation (shadhdh).
* Student: And if someone argues with it to negate the "in the sight of," what is said to them?
* Shaykh: It is said: this is irregular, while that one is mutawatir (transmitted through continuous multiple chains). The Muslims received it from the Messenger until our day. As for that one, it is irregular.
* Student: And the discussion of "in the sight of" in this verse and nearness to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic?
* Shaykh: We refute them with the many verses and hadiths as well. This establishes nearness to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, but nearness does not necessarily entail incarnation (hulul). For example, when He says: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near﴾ [al-Baqarah 186], it does not follow that He is near to you in your place. Rather, He is near though He is above, because ﴿there is nothing like Him﴾.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: That is, applying the meaning of His saying: ﴿But perhaps you dislike a thing and it is good for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 216]. But this was not mentioned in the Qur'an, so we did not make it a separate lesson. Otherwise it is a great lesson: a person may dislike a thing and it is good for him.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: He did not put it first, because he said: "and in one reading." 
* Student: In the context?
* Shaykh: Yes, because he, may Allah have mercy on him, interpreted according to this reading, since the copy of the Qur'an he had was according to this reading.

* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No.

* Student: His saying, the Most High: ﴿And you will never find any change in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab 62] (...) that Allah, glorified and exalted, may change His practice regarding His creation?
* Shaykh: No, he says: ﴿you will never find﴾, and this is a negation.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Yes, because he did not say, for example, "and you will not find Allah changing," as in the other verse: ﴿There is no changer of His words﴾ [al-An'am 115].
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: Never, it is tied to its causes.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: No.
* Student: (...)?
* Shaykh: It never differs, it is tied to its causes. When the cause differs, the practice differs. But if the cause is one, it cannot differ.

**Student:** Why do we not say, regarding His saying ﴿And He has prepared for them a blaze﴾ (...), that its occurrence is certain?

**Shaykh:** This goes against the basic principle, and the existence of the Fire is already established. We do not resort to saying that He used the past tense for the future to indicate the certainty of its occurrence except in a matter that has clearly not yet happened, such as His saying: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [al-Nahl 1]. His saying ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾ means that it has not occurred yet.

**Student:** (...) the refutation of (...) ﴿And you will never find any change in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab 62] (...) relies on (...) the honours from Allah, glory be to Him (...)?

**Shaykh:** By Allah, I do not know. This appears to be a lame point. Look, if the lame man had an honour, we might accept it from you.

**Student:** (...)?

**Shaykh:** No, because *wijaha* (standing, rank, status) is a non-physical matter. So the nearness here is a nearness of rank. But physical nearness is like His saying (...): ﴿Those who are with your Lord do not disdain His worship, and they glorify Him, and to Him they prostrate﴾ [al-A'raf 206].

**Student:** (...)?

**Shaykh:** In this verse? No (...), because standing and rank are non-physical.

**Student:** (...)?

**Shaykh:** Yes, physical, yes. There is no doubt that those among the angels who are close to Allah, the bearers of the Throne, are nearer than others.

**Student:** (...)?

**Shaykh:** It is not (...). As long as it exists, it is not (...).

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verse 62–69 (part 1 of 4):

Then He said: ﴿The way of Allah concerning those who passed away before, and you will not find any change in the way of Allah.﴾ [al-Ahzab 62].
Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿The way of Allah concerning those who passed away before, and you will not find any change in the way of Allah.﴾ ﴿The way of Allah﴾: sunnah (way, custom, practice) means the path or manner. The sunnah of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is of two kinds: the cosmic sunnah (sunnah kawniyyah) and the legislative sunnah (sunnah shar'iyyah).
As for the legislative sunnah, it is according to the interests of the servants and differs with the differing of nations, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿For each of you We have made a law and a way﴾ [al-Ma'idah 48]. Although all these laws agree on the foundations of monotheism concerning the Essence of Allah, His Names and His Attributes, they are in agreement.
Likewise, in the general principles of the Shari'ah, which Allah indicated in His saying: ﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden indecencies, whether apparent or concealed, and sin, and oppression without right, and that you associate with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority, and that you say about Allah what you do not know﴾ [al-A'raf 33]. How many are these? ﴿The indecencies, whether apparent or concealed, and sin, and oppression without right, and associating with Allah that for which He has sent down no authority, and saying about Allah what you do not know﴾. These are the five foundations. The scholars have mentioned that all the laws agree upon them. But as for the laws whose interests differ with the difference of time, place and nations, their rulings must necessarily differ according to what wisdom requires, the wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.
As for the cosmic sunnah, it is what Allah, Blessed and Exalted, causes to occur by decree, of punishments and other things. This sunnah does not change or alter. Although Allah, Mighty and Majestic, may double the punishment for some people and not others, as we have already explained regarding the wives of the Prophet: ﴿Whoever of you commits a clear indecency, the punishment will be doubled for her, twofold﴾ [al-Ahzab 30]. Allah, Exalted, may also reward some doers of deeds more than others, as in this Ummah, which was given a double portion of reward over the nations before it, and as with the Companions of the Messenger, peace be upon him, about whom the Messenger ﷺ said: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, if one of you were to spend gold equal to Uhud, it would not reach the mudd of one of them nor half of it"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3673), and Muslim (2541 / 222) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.]].
But regarding punishments, Allah says: ﴿The way of Allah﴾. The author said: (That is, Allah has prescribed that). From this estimation, the author informed us that ﴿sunnah﴾ is in the accusative as a verbal noun whose verb is omitted; i.e., We have prescribed for them the way of Allah; i.e., We have prescribed for these hypocrites, those in whose hearts is a disease, and the rumour-mongers in Medina, the way of Allah concerning those before them, for whoever opposes the servants of Allah and His allies, Allah empowers over them.
(﴿The way of Allah concerning those who passed away before﴾ from the nations), ﴿passed away﴾ means departed. For this reason the author said: (from the earlier nations, concerning their hypocrites who spread rumours against the believers, ﴿and you will not find any change in the way of Allah﴾ from Him) — and not from others? Yes, and not from others: the cosmic sunnahs. Yes indeed.
As for the legislative, Allah erases what He wills and establishes, and it may be changed. But the cosmic sunnah of Allah, you will not find any change in it, neither from Him nor from others, in sending punishment upon those who deserve it. And although this punishment may differ, the opponents must necessarily face a punishment. And Allah knows best.
(...) Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿The people ask you about the Hour﴾ [al-Ahzab 63]. ﴿The people ask you﴾: the author said: (i.e., the people of Makkah). The correct view is that it is more general. In His saying ﴿asks you﴾ rather than ﴿asked you﴾ is evidence that this questioning continued to be directed at the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, people asking him about the Hour. Questioning about the Hour may be motivated by denying it and considering it far-fetched; and this comes from whom? If the motive is denial and considering it far-fetched, it comes from whom? From the disbelievers. At other times it is asked about in the form of a question: when will it be? while being certain of it; and this may come from whom? From the believers. At other times it is asked about in order to show people that its knowledge cannot be attained, as Jibril asked the Prophet ﷺ about the Hour, and said: "When is the Hour?"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50), and Muslim (9 / 5) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.]] He asked not out of denial or disbelief, nor seeking guidance as to when its time would be, but to inform that its time is known only to Allah.
But someone may say: the saying ﴿The people ask you﴾ does not include the question of Jibril, since Jibril is not one of the people? It is answered that when Jibril asked, he was in the form of a man.
(﴿The people ask you about the Hour﴾, when will it be?) Allah commanded His Prophet to answer with His saying: ﴿Say: Its knowledge is only with Allah﴾. ﴿Say﴾ in answer. This is an instruction from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, instructing His Messenger in the answer that he should say this. Allah instructed him so that it would be clear to people in general that His saying ﴿Its knowledge is only with Allah﴾ comes from Allah and not from his own accord, so that people might be convinced of it and be certain of it.
And His saying ﴿Its knowledge is only with Allah﴾: this sentence contains restriction (hasr). By what means?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, it is not fronting; the means is ﴿innama﴾ (only). ﴿Its knowledge is only with Allah﴾ means: no one knows it except Allah alone. This is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman 34]. So no one knows when the Hour will come except Allah, Mighty and Majestic. And everything said about its time by those before and after is nothing but baseless fabrication, which we know with certainty, because Allah said: ﴿Say: Its knowledge is only with Allah﴾. And who is the most knowledgeable of the messengers of Allah, among humans and angels? Muhammad ﷺ and Jibril, and both do not know. When Jibril asked the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "The one asked about it is no more knowledgeable than the one asking"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (50), and Muslim (9 / 5) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.]]. So if you, O questioner, are ignorant, then I am like you, more ignorant than you.
﴿Say: Its knowledge is only with Allah﴾. And this encompasses not only the general Hour, when people are raised from their graves to the Lord of the worlds, but also includes the specific hour, which is the death of each person, for whoever dies, his resurrection and his hour have come, since he has passed from the world to the abode of recompense. The saying of Allah, Exalted, indicates this: ﴿No soul knows in what land it will die﴾ [Luqman 34]. What is the point of evidence?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Yes, but what is the point of evidence from the verse you mentioned?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: What is the point of evidence that no one knows when he will die?
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No.
* Student: The point of evidence is (...) a certain land he has not gone to (...).
* The Shaykh: I say: the point of evidence is that if his knowledge of which land he will die in is negated, then in which time is more so; because a person has the ability to go to a land or not go, whereas time is not within his control. So if his knowledge of what is within his control, which is moving from one place to another, is negated, then the negation of his knowledge of what is not within his control is all the more so.
Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: (﴿And what will make you know﴾ informs you of it; i.e., you do not know it), ﴿And what will make you know﴾: ﴿what﴾ may be negative, meaning nothing informs you of it; and it may be interrogative, meaning what makes you know of it so that you are asked about it. Either way, Allah, Exalted, negates the knowledge of His Messenger ﷺ of it and says to him: ﴿What will make you know﴾.
And His saying: (﴿Perhaps the Hour is near﴾ it exists ﴿soon﴾) the author's or commentator's wording indicates that the saying ﴿Perhaps the Hour﴾ is a new independent clause, unconnected to the preceding verb, and that it is a new statement from Allah: that is, you do not know about it, but it is near: ﴿Perhaps the Hour will be soon﴾, and ﴿perhaps﴾ here indicates expectation, i.e., it is anticipated.
Some grammarians held that the saying ﴿Perhaps the Hour﴾ is the object of ﴿will make you know﴾, a second and third object, but it is suspended, suspended by what? By ﴿perhaps﴾, since ﴿perhaps﴾ is among the suspending words; that is: what will make you know about the expectation of its nearness; i.e., you do not know about its nearness either, and whoever does not know about its nearness does not know about its occurrence all the more.
In any case, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, negated that the Prophet ﷺ knew it or its nearness, and if the Prophet's ﷺ knowledge of that is negated, then the knowledge of others is all the more negated.
Furthermore, the question about the Hour is not of great value. The great value is what the Prophet ﷺ indicated, when a man asked him about the Hour and he said: "Look at what you have prepared for it"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3688), and Muslim (2639 / 163) from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik.]]. That is the value. As for when it will come or not, it is not of great value; the true value is that a person looks at what he has prepared for it.
Therefore Allah, Exalted, followed this with His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blazing fire﴾ [al-Ahzab 64], and so on; i.e., beware lest the Hour come upon you while you are among them.
﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers﴾..
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: No, the suspension occurs only after the operator.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Where is this?
* Student: (...) ﴿Do the people think they will be left﴾ [al-Ankabut 2].
* The Shaykh: No operator precedes it, so there is no suspension.
* Student: The interrogative hamzah?
* The Shaykh: The hamzah is for interrogation, but the sentence is initial, like if you say: Did Zayd stand? Did Amr sit? There is no suspension.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: Its object is "an" (that) and what follows it.
* Student: (...).
* The Shaykh: No, it is not suspended; this is a verbal "an" (masdariyyah), so the verbal noun takes the place of the two verbs; i.e., "Do the people think their leaving alone?"
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: It is for emphasis, and it may also be for causation, like: ﴿And follow him that you may be guided﴾ [al-A'raf 158] and similar. But it is not for expectation. Some said it is for expectation when considering the addressee rather than the speaker.
Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers and prepared for them a blazing fire﴾ [al-Ahzab 64]. ﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed﴾: la'n (cursing), the people of knowledge said, means expulsion and distance from the mercy of Allah. This sentence is emphasized by ﴿indeed﴾ (inna). And His saying ﴿the disbelievers﴾: disbelievers in whom? Disbelievers in Allah and in what must be believed in. And His saying ﴿has cursed the disbelievers﴾ means He has distanced them from mercy.
Then He said: ﴿and prepared for them a blazing fire﴾: meaning they are not merely distanced from mercy and spared from sin, but rather there is combined for them both distance from mercy and punishment. ﴿Prepared for them﴾ means He made ready for them. ﴿A blazing fire﴾: (a fierce fire they enter), a fire kindled for them, and Allah protect us, they are its fuel and the stones; a fire that rises over the hearts, reaching their hearts within their bodies, and Allah protect us. They will not remain in it for a day or two, or a year or two. He says: ﴿Abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Ahzab 65]. He said: (determining their eternal abiding). The author indicated that the state here is a determined state (hal muqaddarah), because eternal abiding is not the state of their disbelief but the state of their recompense on the Day of Resurrection, so this state is a determined state: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾. And ﴿abadan﴾ (forever) indicates the continuation of time into the future, and ﴿azalan﴾ (without beginning) indicates its continuation into the past. For this reason we say that Allah's knowledge is established for Allah without beginning and without end.
And His saying ﴿abiding therein forever﴾ is one of three verses in which Allah explicitly declared the eternity of the abiding of the people of the Fire. The second verse is in Surat an-Nisa: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and wronged, Allah would never forgive them, nor guide them to a path, except the path of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [an-Nisa 168-169]. The third verse is in Surat al-Jinn: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, then indeed for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Jinn 23]. In some of these verses, indeed in one of them, there is a clear refutation of the view that the Fire is not eternal. For this reason the creed of Ahl as-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah is that the Fire is eternal like the Garden. This does not contradict the mercy and wisdom of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, nor does it nullify His saying in the hadith qudsi: "Indeed My mercy precedes My wrath"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (7422), and Muslim (2751 / 15) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah.]]. This is because this punishment has been warned of to those who did what deserves it and upon whom the proof has been established, so they have no excuse. They are thus treated according to justice; their punishment is a justice from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, with no oppression in it. Whoever is warned of something and then, by his own choice, does what leads to it, is the one who has brought harm upon himself.
* Student: (...)?
* The Shaykh: He said: ﴿except what your Lord wills﴾ [Hud 107]; i.e., beyond that.
Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: (﴿Abiding therein forever, they will find no protector﴾ who guards them from it, ﴿nor any helper﴾ who repels it from them). ﴿They will find no protector﴾ who takes charge of them by obtaining what they seek, ﴿nor any helper﴾ who supports them by repelling what they dislike. They will find on the Day of Resurrection no one who takes charge of them and obtains what they want by protecting them from the Fire and bringing them to the Garden, nor anyone who supports them against this Fire, repels it from them, or brings them out of it after entering. This is because these disbelievers will not benefit from the intercession of intercessors. As for the sinful believers, they may find intercessors on that day who intercede for whoever deserved the Fire not to enter it, and for whoever has entered it to be brought out.
﴿The Day their faces are turned over in the Fire, they will say: "O would that we had obeyed Allah and obeyed the Messenger."﴾ [al-Ahzab 66]. ﴿The Day﴾ is an adverbial expression of time, and an adverbial expression with its preposition requires a governing element, called the anchor (al-muta'allaq). So what is its governing element? It may be that the governing element is His saying ﴿and prepared for them a blazing fire﴾, the verb ﴿prepared﴾; it may be ﴿abiding﴾; it may be ﴿will find﴾, so the three operators compete for it; and it may be that the governing element is omitted, i.e., "Remember the Day their faces are turned over." All of this is possible, and all of it is the case.
His saying ﴿their faces are turned over﴾ means they are turned from one side to another, as meat is turned over the fire to be cooked, Allah protect us.
In His saying ﴿The Day their faces are turned over﴾ and not ﴿The Day they turn over﴾: this is because this matter happens to them by way of compulsion, Allah protect us, and it is not by their choice: ﴿their faces are turned over in the Fire, they say﴾.
There is a point I forgot: His saying ﴿abiding therein forever﴾, how does He say ﴿therein﴾ while ﴿blazing﴾ is masculine? Because the meaning of ﴿sair﴾ (blazing fire) here is the blaze of the Fire, which is feminine.
He said: ﴿The Day their faces are turned over in the Fire, they say: "O would that we had obeyed Allah and obeyed the Messenger."﴾ His saying ﴿they say﴾ may be a circumstantial clause, which is the closer view, from the pronoun in ﴿their faces﴾, meaning: their faces are turned while they express this regret: ﴿they say: O would that we had﴾. It may also be a resumptive clause, Allah relating what they say.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 33, verses 62–69 (part 2 of 4):

﴿They say, "Oh, would that we had obeyed God and obeyed the Messenger!"﴾ The author said: (The ﴿yā﴾ serves to draw attention and is not a vocative particle.) Why? Because the vocative particle ﴿yā﴾ is used only with one who can be called, either literally or figuratively, and ﴿layta﴾ cannot be addressed, since it is a particle. ﴿Layta﴾ expresses wishing (tamannī). The author says it is for attention (tanbīh). It has also been said that it is a vocative with an omitted addressee suited to the context, so that they say, "O our Lord, would that we had obeyed God," and the omitted addressee is: "O our Lord, would that we had obeyed God and obeyed the Messenger." On the first view, the attention is meant to increase the regret, as though they are alerting themselves to this wish they make. On the second view, the addressee is omitted in order to hasten to mention the wish without mentioning the one addressed. Whichever view is taken, it indicates the intensity of their remorse.

As for His words, ﴿Oh, would that we had obeyed God and obeyed the Messenger!﴾: is this wish difficult to fulfil, or is it impossible at that time? It is impossible at that time. This is a greater impossibility than the words of the poet:

*Ah, would that youth could return one day,*
*So I could tell it what old age has done.*

As for ﴿أَطَعْنَا﴾ (aṭaʿnā), we drop the alif. ﴿aṭaʿnā﴾ is originally written with an alif, so we say ﴿aṭaʿnā llāha wa-aṭaʿnā r-rasūlā﴾, and we do not say that one must indicate the alif so that the nūn is not confused (...). Praise be to God, this is an error. Rather, you say ﴿وَقَالَا الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ﴾ [an-Naml 15], and there is nothing wrong with it. The alif is dropped here because of the meeting of two unvocalised letters (iltiqāʾ as-sākinayn), and we do not say that dropping it would make the first-person pronoun resemble the feminine plural pronoun, because the context shows the meaning.

Student: (...)?
Shaykh: They are alerting the listener to the fact that they are wishing for this.
Student: And the second aspect?
Shaykh: The second aspect is that it is the vocative particle, and the addressee is omitted; the meaning is: "O our Lord, would that we…"
Student: Shaykh, ﴿قَالَا الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ﴾ [an-Naml 15] (...)?
Shaykh: Yes indeed, it is written but not pronounced. Even ﴿أَطَعْنَا اللَّهَ﴾ is now written but is not pronounced in speech.
Student: (...)?
Shaykh: Like ﴿دَعَوَا اللَّهَ﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 189]: the alif is dropped.

As for ﴿الرَّسُولَا﴾ (ar-rasūlā), it has an alif, and this alif is for extension (alif al-iṭlāq, the alif added at the end of a word for prolongation). We have already encountered a parallel to it in this surah. What is it? ﴿وَتَظُنُّونَ بِاللَّهِ الظُّنُونَا﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 10]. And later another word will come: ﴿فَأَضَلُّونَا السَّبِيلَا﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 67]. So these are three words containing an alif called the alif of extension, and three readings apply to them: a reading with the alif retained both in continuous recitation (waṣl) and at pause (waqf); a reading with it dropped both in waṣl and waqf; and a reading with it dropped in waṣl but retained in waqf.

Let us see now. ﴿يَا لَيْتَنَا أَطَعْنَا اللَّهَ وَأَطَعْنَا الرَّسُولَا (66) وَقَالُوا﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 66–67]: this is according to both readings. ﴿يَا لَيْتَنَا أَطَعْنَا اللَّهَ وَأَطَعْنَا الرَّسُولَ (66) وَقَالُوا﴾ is one reading. Is it clear? It is not entirely clear in reality; that is, it is permissible to recite it in all three ways, according to the principle of al-nashr (the principle that all permitted readings are valid). ﴿يَا لَيْتَنَا أَطَعْنَا اللَّهَ وَأَطَعْنَا الرَّسُولَا﴾ and ﴿يَا لَيْتَنَا أَطَعْنَا اللَّهَ وَأَطَعْنَا الرَّسُولَا (66) وَقَالُوا﴾ is one reading; that is, we retain the alif in both waṣl and waqf.

The second reading: ﴿يَا لَيْتَنَا أَطَعْنَا اللَّهَ وَأَطَعْنَا الرَّسُولَ (66) وَقَالُوا﴾ and ﴿يَا لَيْتَنَا أَطَعْنَا اللَّهَ وَأَطَعْنَا الرَّسُولْ﴾ ﴿وَقَالُوا﴾ is also the second reading: the alif is dropped in both waṣl and waqf.

The third reading: ﴿يَا لَيْتَنَا أَطَعْنَا اللَّهَ وَأَطَعْنَا الرَّسُولَ (66) وَقَالُوا﴾ and ﴿يَا لَيْتَنَا أَطَعْنَا اللَّهَ وَأَطَعْنَا الرَّسُولَا (66) وَقَالُوا﴾ is the one where you retain it at pause but not in continuous recitation.

As for His words, ﴿أَطَعْنَا اللَّهَ وَأَطَعْنَا الرَّسُولَا﴾, what is "the Messenger" here?

Student: The canonical seven readings.
Shaykh: The seven readings. "The Messenger" here is a generic noun (ism jins) that includes every messenger, since the people of the Fire are not restricted to the community of Muhammad ﷺ but include all nations. So do they mean by "the Messenger" one particular messenger or the category? The category. And by "God"? One (the single God).

﴿أَطَعْنَا اللَّهَ وَأَطَعْنَا الرَّسُولَا (66) وَقَالُوا رَبَّنَا إِنَّا أَطَعْنَا سَادَتَنَا﴾ [al-Aḥzāb 66–67]. (﴿وَقَالُوا﴾ means: the followers among them.) This is correct, as the author said: "the followers" (...) of the leaders. ﴿رَبَّنَا﴾ means "O our Lord," the vocative particle being omitted. (﴿إِنَّا أَطَعْنَا سَادَتَنَا﴾ and in another reading) meaning the canonical seven readings: (﴿سَادَاتَنَا﴾ is the plural of the plural.) "Sādah" is the plural of what? Of sayyid (lord).
